paragraphs.text: This is, I think, the man who became bishop of Mopsuestia; but in the second place: “This Theodore [?] seems to be the one of Mopsuestia” (and indeed [?] the book, whose title is “Of Theodore of Antioch”; but he is the one of Mopsuestia, as [?] from certain letters [?] he wrote commentaries. Certainly in place of ἄλλην one should read [?] “Avoiding allegories as far as he can, and making his interpretation according to the historical sense; but he repeats himself very often, and seems somehow graceless and unpleasant.” Then codex [?]: “He is not very brilliant in his diction, but very dense in his thoughts and arguments, and excellently rich in scriptural [?]. He is [?] obscure, although he uses no outlandish vocabulary; but by mostly using long-drawn-out periods and parentheses piled one upon another, through which the sense of the matters under discussion is stretched out to great length; by abounding in oblique cases of nouns and in participial expressions; by often going back over the same things, and that without elegance; and by filling his recapitulations, more than his narratives, with circumstantial detail (which is altogether unmethodical) — by such things he casts no little gloom over his writings.” Further, regarding the avoidance of alleg[ory], it would require not [going] further than the obvious sense [?]

OF THEODORE OF ANTIOCH, ON THE PROPHET [?]. … of those who undertake to approach the prophetic utterances without examination, and also in preparation for what follows, let us begin the elucidation of the prophetic books, God granting it, making our start with Hosea, who happens to be the first in time of the other prophets. For since blessed David, as I said earlier, plainly went through in the Psalms all the changes that would come upon the people, silence held the intervening period, because he had sufficiently foretold everything. But when the time arrived at which the ten tribes began to suffer ill, as the Assyrians besieged them until Sennacherib removed them altogether from their own land and resettled them in foreign lands, [?] long before by blessed David [?] [Note: “from God.”]

[?] spoken, and that long ago, so that he might show the Israelites to be responsible for the hardships to come, since they had departed from the service and knowledge of God and devoted all their zeal to idols and demons; and so that he might make it clear that these things were not happening by some chance, but had been foretold long before and predetermined by God, who knew their wickedness and knew clearly in what way he ought to order their affairs, in preparation for the manifestation and coming of Christ the Lord. For, so that it might become clear to all that he exercises his care for the people for the sake of the one who was expected to appear from among them, he hands the ten tribes over to captivity by the Assyrians, but preserves in its place the tribe of Judah alone, from which the Lord Christ was to appear according to the flesh. This tribe, when it later went into captivity under Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Babylonians, because of their own transgressions, he caused to return against all expectation. A few, easily counted, from each of the other tribes returned as well, but the tribe of Judah alone returned entire, so that it might become clear that God could, had he wished, have brought back all the others just as he did this one; but he disregarded the others and placed all his care on this one, from which the Lord Christ was to be revealed, appearing for the common salvation of all. On this account the declarations of the prophets were necessary, showing that what had long ago been decreed by God and spoken through blessed David was now reaching its fulfillment, God ordering all their affairs in an ineffable way. This is just what blessed Hosea the prophet does, plainly declaring what was to happen to the people by the divine will on account of their impiety. He begins thus:

Verse 1. — “The word of the Lord that came to Hosea son of Beeri in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash, king of Israel.” This is a kind of comprehensive title of the book, showing both the prophet whose sayings these are and the time at which he spoke them. Everywhere Scripture calls “the word of the Lord” the divine activity exerted on any matter whatever, as in “By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm,” meaning that they came into being by the divine activity. Here it calls “divine activity” that by which the revelation of things to come was given to the prophet, from which he also had the power to speak and declare what was to come. For greater precision he also adds the name of his father. And he necessarily states the time at which, according to the revelation that came to him from God, he declared what was to come: he says it was the time when Uzziah reigned, and Jotham, and Ahaz, and Hezekiah. From this one may reasonably conclude that the prophet did not compose the book as a single continuous work, but that he received revelations about the future at different times and made his declaration of what was to come,

often being reminded about the same things through divine revelation, and indeed speaking them to the people to make known what was to come. In the same way blessed David evidently spoke a great many psalms on the same subject, each of which he composed according to the revelation and reminder that came to him by the working of the Spirit, and uttered it for the benefit of others; he himself often received revelations about the same things and spoke accordingly, as often as he was granted the same revelations. Having named the kings of Judah at the time when divine grace roused Hosea to prophesy, he names also the king in Israel, that is, the one then reigning over the ten tribes, Jeroboam, son of Joash and grandson of Jehoahaz, who was the son of Jehu. God had put Jehu forward through the prophet Elisha to punish Ahab and his whole house, and promised that his descendants would hold the throne down to the fourth generation. Of these Jeroboam was the third, son of Joash and grandson of Jehoahaz; the fourth was Zechariah son of Jeroboam, who reigned for [six?] months and died. With him the divine promise reached its end, and the kingship passed from the family of Jehu to Shallum, who was not of the same kin. Now Jeroboam had come to the throne of Israel while Uzziah was reigning over Jerusalem, and from that time the ten tribes began to fare badly, until the king of the Assyrians took them captive altogether and deported them. So it is reasonable that Hosea came forward to prophesy at this time, reminding them of the predictions of blessed David and recalling that what had been said about them long ago would soon come to pass. And after this he says: Verse 2. — “The beginning of the word of the Lord to Hosea.” Clearly it was from this point that God began his revelation to him. He commands him to take a harlot as his wife and to have children by her, and he adds the reason: “For the land will utterly play the harlot, turning away from the Lord.” Now that God makes the prophets do things that seem unfitting to most people — as when he commanded Isaiah to go about naked and barefoot in the sight of all, and all such things — has an obvious reason. Since most of us are accustomed to listen to words carelessly, but are stirred by the novelty of things done and seen, especially when they are out of keeping with the character of the one doing them, God, because of the Jews’ disobedience, reasonably has the prophets often do such things, so that the people, somehow turned around by the novelty of what is done, may learn the reason and be taught what is needful. So he commanded the prophet to take a harlot as his wife. For it was a novel thing for the prophet to choose such a woman to take in marriage, and yet this is what God ordered him to do — since the prophet was permitted by the law to take a wife in marriage, and in taking the harlot he would presumably persuade her to live chastely. For everyone was bound to be astonished that a man who took great care for what was

proper should pass over women who seemed in some measure respectable and choose to take a harlot in marriage. And the novelty of the event gave the prophet occasion to say to them what was fitting, and by the comparison to make it appear far greater that God should choose to stoop to caring for such ungrateful men — if indeed it was astonishing that even the prophet, devoted as he was to propriety, should enter into union with a harlot. “Since, then,” he says, “I care for the Israelites, who have always shown a harlot’s ways toward me and every day up to now intensify this disposition, though I chose them above all men to be my own — before long they will furnish exact proof of their disposition toward me in the punishment I bring upon them, when they are handed over to captivity and wholly estranged from this land, in which, while they dwelt there and were counted worthy of my care, I commanded them to abide by my laws, just as it is customary for women taken in marriage to abide by the laws of marriage. Yet through all this they have no proper perception of what is happening, neither of what they are doing nor of what they will justly suffer. Come then, prophet, by the novelty of what you do, expose the outrage they commit.” Verses 3–5. — The prophet obeys these instructions and takes a harlot in marriage; he gives both her name and her father’s, so that what is said might not seem a mere fiction but a true history of events. And a son is born to him by her, whom he was commanded to name Jezreel. That was the name of the place where Naboth suffered his lawless slaughter, and where Jezebel too was slaughtered, paying the penalty for her lawlessness against him, when Jehu, by divine command, destroyed her and the whole family of Ahab for this lawlessness. “For in a little while,” he says, “I will avenge the blood of Jezreel on the house of Jehu, and I will put an end to the kingdom of the house of Israel.” “For,” he says, “Jehu, whom I appointed to the kingship, destroyed the whole family of the house of Ahab for the impiety and lawlessness it dared to commit against Naboth in the place just mentioned; yet he was not brought to his senses by this, nor did he guard against lawlessness on the basis of what he had been empowered to do against others who had transgressed, but [?] all who reigned over Israel after him imitated the disposition of Ahab. So before long I will put an end to the whole kingship of Israel” — since it was no longer possible for those under captivity to have a king of their own. “And I will break the bow of Israel in the valley of Jezreel.” Here he calls their whole country by the name of a part, meaning: I will render all their power useless in their own land, making them subject to their enemies — by whom he means the Assyrians. Verses 6–10. — Then he says that a daughter was also born to him by the same woman, whom he commands to be called “Not Pitied,” so that by her very name she would serve as a reminder that the Israelites would obtain no mercy but would be handed over to total captivity — not by the power of their enemies, but

because God himself was plainly making war on them; for this is what “I will surely set myself against them” means. “And as greater proof,” he says, “that these things befall them by my will, I will present the case of Judah. I will have mercy on them when they are in danger of suffering the same fate at the hands of the Assyrians who took those others captive, and I will save them by my power — not by bow and sword and war, nor helped at all by any human alliance, but escaping so great a danger by my power alone.” And this indeed happened, when in the night an angel killed one hundred and eighty-five thousand of the Assyrians all at once, so that the rest turned to flight and those in Jerusalem received an undeniable deliverance. Again another son is born, whom, in confirmation of what had been said, he commands to be called “Not My People,” and he gives the reason: “For you are not my people, and I am not yours.” “For from now on you will be estranged from my care, and I will hand you over, as strangers, to the evils that press upon you.” Then he adds: “And the number of the children of Israel was like the sand of the sea, which cannot be measured or numbered.” For the wonder was all the greater, and gave clear proof of divine wrath, if he handed over to captivity all at once people who were so numerous, while they could gain no benefit from being so many. Then, as is customary with the prophets, and indeed with blessed David, to announce pleasant things in the midst of grievous ones, and to foretell the change for the better as a consolation for those in a worse condition, he says: “And it shall be that in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ they will be called sons of the living God.” So too blessed David, after speaking of the Assyrians, adds: “Who will give out of Zion the salvation of Israel? When the Lord turns back the captivity of his people, Jacob will rejoice and Israel will be glad,” showing that there will be a time when God will surely release them from captivity. For he says the same thing here too: where they were called “Not My People,” that is, cast away from my providence, there they will be called sons of the living God — meaning, they will once again be made my own. He rightly said “in the place,” since he was going to bring them back to the very place from which he had removed them. He then adds, to make what he said clearer: Verse 11. — “And the children of Judah and the children of Israel will be gathered together, and will appoint for themselves one head, and will go up out of the land.” He means that after the Babylonian captivity of the tribe of Judah there will be one common freedom for them all, since they will be under one rule, no longer divided as before; and being under one rule, the tribe of Judah would lead them all, and those who belonged to that tribe would be established in kingship and rule. Then he adds: “For great is the day of Jezreel.” For since he had said that they would pay the penalty for this,

what he means is this: that for those who had suffered ill on account of their former impiety, that day will be awe-inspiring and glorious, on which, beyond all human hope, they will obtain their return to their own land. And what is the proof?

Verses 1–2. — “Say to your brother, ‘My People,’ and to your sister, ‘Pitied.’” “Say” stands for “You will say,” meaning that their names will be changed. “For it will suit them,” he says, “to be called ‘People’ and ‘Pitied,’ since they will then have been made my own and will enjoy my kindness.” Then, taking the starting point for his discourse from the image already set forth, he says: “Plead, plead with your mother, for she is not my wife, and I am not her husband.” In the image set forth, it is quite clear that he calls the harlot the mother, and the children those naturally born of her. But here he calls the congregation of the Jews the mother — the one whom long ago, as though betrothing her and joining her to himself by surpassing care, he brought out of Egypt, and granting her freedom, led into the wilderness, so as to train her in godliness and bring her into a closer relationship with himself. As blessed David also says: “Remember your congregation, which you acquired from the beginning; you redeemed the rod of your inheritance.” Her children are the people formed from her in succession. For just as the people of that time are called the fathers of those who came after — “For your fathers,” he says, “ate the manna in the wilderness and died” — so too that congregation could justly be called mother, since the later body of the Jews came from it. Reproaching them, then, for the wickedness of their character, he rightly says: “You have been wicked from of old, and you plainly resemble your own mother.” Indeed, if anyone compares the people of that time with those of now, he will clearly find a close kinship between them. Those, after obtaining so many and such great benefits, dared to make a calf and say, “These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.” And you, like them, have abandoned the knowledge of me, who have always shown you such great care, and have turned to the worship of idols; so you might fittingly be compared to the harlot. For since you are so disposed, it is no longer fitting for you to be called mine, and I am shown by the facts themselves to be estranged from you. What then? Verses 3–5. — “And I will remove her harlotry from my presence, and her adultery from between her breasts.” “For I will put them far from myself through captivity and through their deportation far from these places, so that I may no longer see her carrying out her harlotry before me, nor the adultery that she practices with great licentiousness, offering herself wholly to idols.” This is what “from between her breasts” means, as in the case of

harlots who in their excessive licentiousness offer their own breasts to their lovers. Then, stating what follows next: “So that I may strip her as in the days of her birth.” “Removing all the adornment,” he says, “that I put on her through my care, I will put her in the condition she was in when she was first formed in Egypt, when she was in hardship, toil and bitter slavery.” For he calls that time her birth, since that time was the beginning of the formation of the Jewish congregation. “And I will make her like a wilderness, and set her like a waterless land” — that is, deprived of every good, just as a desert and waterless land is wholly without fruit. “And I will kill her with thirst” — deprived of all good things, and naturally longing for them, but obtaining none. “And I will not have mercy on her children, for they are children of harlotry; for their mother played the harlot; she who bore them brought them to shame.” “And when they are found in such great evils, I will not show the mercy that I showed then in Egypt; for these have played the harlot just like their own mother, and their mother, having shown such a disposition toward me from of old, has covered her offspring with shame, since they have imitated their mother’s wickedness.” “For she said, ‘I will go after my lovers, who give me my bread and my water, my clothing and my linen, my oil, and everything that is fitting for me.’” “For they have all given themselves over to the worship of demons, saying that they have from them all the good things they possess, which they plainly have from me, the maker of all things.” He called the demons her lovers to show both the zeal the demons have for the destruction of human beings and the mad disposition of these people toward them, by which they dared to honor them as gods and as the cause of all their blessings. Verses 6–8. — “Therefore, behold, I will hedge up her way with thorns, and I will wall up her paths, and she will not find her track.” “Accordingly I will surround them with evils from which there is no way out, to this end: that just as someone shut in, with the roads walled up and blocked by many sharp thorns, would find it impossible to get out, so they, held fast by the weight of wars and captivity and the hardships that follow from it, may find no escape from their evils.” “And she will pursue her lovers and will not overtake them; and she will seek them and will not find them.” “Then they will call to their aid the demons they used to serve, but they will gain nothing from them.” “And she will say, ‘I will go and return to my first husband, for it was better for me then than now.’” “Then they will recognize their own error, and that it was better for them to hold fast to my worship than to be entangled in the deception of the demons.” “And she did not know that it was I who gave her the grain and the wine and the oil, and multiplied silver and gold for her. But she [?] silver and

…and gold, which they made for Baal.” They will learn how severe was the ignorance they suffered from when they credited those idols with the good things they had. Yet I, the maker of all things, was the one who plainly and continually supplied these things to them. I gave them not only crops but also silver and gold, both at the exodus from Egypt and afterwards on many other occasions. From these they did not hesitate to make idols for themselves, and they thought their worship of them something grand because of how much precious material it used. Verses 9–12. “Therefore I will turn back and take away my grain in its season.” So I will bring great barrenness upon them at the very time when they most expect to enjoy the harvest. Then I will take away all their crops at once through the many things that usually ruin such crops: blight, for example, and hail, and the like, which often strike all at once and completely destroy the crops that have appeared. In this way, through the punishment brought upon them and the loss of what had been given, they will clearly come to know the one whom they did not recognize as the cause of their good things. “And I will take away my garments and my linen, so that they do not cover her shame.” I gave them many different things that adorned them and made them look finer than the rest of humankind in what they enjoyed. I will take these away and make them more despised than anyone. “And now I will uncover her uncleanness before her lovers, and no one shall rescue her from my hand.” So through my punishment the lawlessness they practised will become plainer to everyone: they turned away from me and devoted themselves to the worship of demons. Before the eyes of those demons they will receive the heaviest punishments from me, and the demons will be unable to give them even a single bit of help, since the power of the punishment I bring upon them is too great [?]. “And I will put an end to all her mirth, and all her feasts, and her new moons, and her Sabbaths, and all her festal assemblies.” They will no longer have any occasion for a festal assembly, or a feast, or any mirth, since they will be handed over to captivity and oppressed in all kinds of ways by the demands of their captors. “And I will destroy her vine and her fig trees, of which she said, ‘These are my wages, which my lovers have given me.’” I will take away all their crops, since they credited the demons with giving them. “And I will make them a testimony.” So their loss will be the strongest testimony to their earlier lawlessness, when they credited the demons with things that were mine to give and mine to take away. “And the wild beasts of the field, and the birds of the sky, and the creeping things of the earth shall devour them.” I will hand them over to everyone to be ruined, so that these people get no benefit from them. By “wild beasts of the field, birds of the sky, and creeping things of the earth” he meant to show how varied the enemies who would ravage them would be. The wild beast is ready to do harm through its savagery. The birds do harm because they easily swoop down on whatever they like. The creeping things do harm through the severity of their damage. Verses 13–14. “And I will punish her for the days…”

…of the Baals, on which she sacrificed to them, and put on her earrings and her necklaces, and went after her lovers, but forgot me, says the Lord.” They will suffer these things as punishment for devoting themselves to the idols. They offered sacrifices to them and held festal assemblies to honour them. They put on lavish adornment and held festivals for the service of demons, but they did not remember me at all. He says “Baals,” meaning the idols, naming the whole by a part. As usual, he calls the demons “lovers,” for it is clear that in the worship of idols it was demons whom they were worshipping. “Therefore I will lead her astray and make her like a wilderness.” I will hand her over to captivity, he says, so that she will be stripped of every good thing and wander along roads she did not know before but was now forced by misfortune to travel. Then he mixes the change for the better into the sentence of punishment, as the prophets usually do. In this too they imitate blessed David, who in the Psalms often spoke of misfortunes and promised release from them in the same breath. In the thirtieth Psalm, for example, he says: “Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am afflicted; my eyes are troubled with anger, my soul and my belly; for my life has failed in pain, and my years in groaning,” and other things like these. Then a little further on he says: “Blessed be the Lord, for he has shown his mercy wonderfully in a fortified city,” and other things like these. One could find many such passages in the Psalms. The prophets necessarily followed this example, and it gave their hearers great benefit: the words about misfortune made them afraid, while the promise of good things gave them hope. Verse 15. What, then, does he say? “And I will speak to her heart.” After this, he says, I will comfort her as she struggles with her troubles and has no consolation. “And I will give her her possessions from there.” I will pull her out of captivity and let her enjoy her former blessings again. “And the valley of Achor, to open her understanding.” So whatever they suffered in that place will in the end help them improve and correct their earlier offences. For the change for the better will naturally make them realise that they did not suffer these painful things because I neglected them. They suffered them because, having sinned, they needed to become aware of their own sins. By “the valley of Achor” he seems to mean the place where they suffered their worst defeat in the war, after which came captivity and the evils that followed. As usual, he names a part and probably means their whole country, where they endured a great many evils at the hands of their enemies before the enemies carried them off into captivity. “And she shall be humbled there as in the days of her infancy, and as in the days of her coming up out of the land of Egypt.”

He calls it arrogance to turn away from God and neglect him. So he calls it humility to recognise what is right and to fear him rightly as Master, Judge, and Lord of all. This, he says, is what she will gain in her time of misfortune. It will be like what happened in Egypt. There the people were crushed by the work of making bricks, and they recognised where they should look for release from it. They all cried out to God, and he granted the requests of those who cried out and gave them his help in a wonderful way. Now, he says, it will happen as it did then. They will be taught self-control by their misfortune and will recognise the cause of their good things. They will ask for help from that source, and they will receive it very easily. Verses 16–20. “And in that day, says the Lord, she will call me ‘My husband,’ and will no longer call me ‘Baalim’; and I will remove the names of the Baals from her mouth, and they shall no longer be remembered by their names.” Then, he says, they will recognise the one who truly cares for them. They will turn away from all the others and devote themselves to my worship. They will give up all worship of idols, so that they no longer remember them at all or take any account of them from then on. As for “She will no longer call me ‘Baalim,’” since it is God who says this, he means: They will no longer give my name to the Baals. They will be free of the deception those idols caused, and from then on they will have learned to look to me, the true God. “And in that day I will make a covenant for them with the beasts of the field, and with the birds of the sky, and with the creeping things of the earth.” Those who formerly plotted against them and were hostile to them, he says, I will lead to choose friendship with them. “And I will break bow and sword and war from the land.” I will put them beyond any experience of war. “And I will make them dwell in hope.” Through the good things that come to them, I will lead them to hope for even better things in the future. “And I will betroth you to myself forever; and I will betroth you to myself in righteousness and in judgment and in mercy and in compassion.” I will make you my own again. I will give you, he says, my close bond. I will uphold justice and punish those who wronged you during the time of captivity, judging everyone justly, and I will also govern your affairs with mercy. “And I will betroth you to myself in faithfulness, and you shall know the Lord.” I will receive you with the faith that befits God [?], since you will recognise me as your own Master. Verse 21. “And in that day, says the Lord, I will answer the heaven, and the heaven will answer the earth, and the earth will answer the grain and the wine and the oil, and they will answer Israel. And I will sow her for myself on the earth, and I will have mercy on her who had not received mercy. And I will say to Not-My-People, ‘You are my people,’ and he will say, ‘You are the Lord my God.’” Then you will also have a great

abundance of crops. At my will the air will give the earth its rain. He calls the air “heaven,” just as when he speaks of “the birds of heaven” he means the creatures that cut through the air. The earth, naturally, will be watered and will yield its crops in abundance, and from these Israel will gain an abundant enjoyment of the good things of the earth. I will also enable them to live again in their own land, which they had been deprived of before, so that while living there they may devote themselves to my worship. That is the meaning of “I will sow her for myself on the earth.” He takes this as a metaphor from those who sow and means: I will spread them out again over the whole of their own land. They will live in it securely and from then on hold fast to what concerns me. These things will happen because my care is changing your situation for the better. So she who had not received mercy receives mercy, and the one who was not a people before becomes a people. This will rightly happen to them, because they too will turn away from their former error and recognise what they ought to. They will declare in a clear voice that he alone is truly their Lord and God, the maker and master of all things, who long ago gave them his special care.

Chapter 3, verse 1. “And the Lord said to me, ‘Go again and love a woman who loves evil and is an adulteress, just as God loves the sons of Israel, while they look to foreign gods and love cakes made with raisins.’” As we have often said, it is clear from this passage too that the prophets' writings were not composed as a single book with one continuous arrangement. They were spoken separately, at the times when the prophets received their revelations. Following these divine revelations, the prophets were bound to speak to the people about them. He has already told of taking a wife as a picture of those things, spoken to rebuke the people. Here he rightly goes on to tell of another revelation, and he is bound to set it out because he received it from God. That is what “The Lord said to me” shows: he is saying that the revelation that came to him from God was the voice of God. So he says that God told him to take a woman who was an adulteress and who did all kinds of evil. This too was meant to picture the attitude God says he has been eager to keep towards the sons of Israel, even though they live in every kind of wickedness and openly show their own adultery. They have pursued various gods that the nations falsely believe in and have made a great point of offering them the worship customary among those nations. That is what he means by “cakes made with raisins.” He means loaves which they prepared in various ways, mixing in raisins and sweets according to some custom connected with these things, and offered to the idols. “They love cakes made with raisins” means that they take pleasure in doing these things to honour the idols. His earlier words were aimed mainly at rebuking the ten tribes, who had forsaken God and devoted themselves to idols. These words, however, are aimed at rebuking those who belonged to the kingdom

of Judah. They had the temple among them, and they even showed some zeal for the true God through festivals and sacrifices. Yet like an adulterous woman they combined the worship of idols with their outward display of devotion to the Divine.

Verses 2–5. Then he says: “So I hired her for myself for fifteen pieces of silver, a homer of barley, and a nebel of wine.” He gives these exact details to show what really happened. The illustration of “I hired” was also necessary, since God too bound the Jews to himself with great gifts and rewards. “And I said to her, ‘You shall stay with me for many days, and I with you; and you shall not play the harlot or belong to another man.’” In the same way God wanted the Jews to devote themselves to him for a long time, not a short one, and he promised them his care. So he wanted them not to turn towards idols but to remain loyal to him. Then he says: “For the sons of Israel shall remain for many days without king or ruler, without sacrifice or altar, without priesthood or revelations.” She did not keep her agreements but, with a harlot's mind, turned to others. So here he says: Since the Jews have done the same kind of thing to me, I will bring a fitting punishment upon them. I will hand them over to captivity for a long time and leave them stripped of everything they had in their own land. They will have no king or ruler of their own, because they will be placed under a foreign king whom they must serve as captives. They will lose their sacrifices, the use of the altar, and all priestly service, because as captives they will be far from the places where they were permitted to serve God as priests. They will also lose the revelations given through the prophets when they were at a loss, which they used to receive in many ways. “And afterwards the sons of Israel will return and seek the Lord their God, and David their king.” Then, he says, they will become aware of their own sufferings and change their minds, eagerly pursuing the knowledge and worship of God. And they will gladly accept as king a descendant of David. He says this will happen after the return, when they were all under one king, Zerubbabel, a descendant of David. They no longer followed the attitude that had led the ten tribes to break away from the kingdom of blessed David's successors and choose other kings. “And in the last days they shall be amazed at his good things.” Everyone will be astonished by the wonder of it all as they consider how many good things divine providence has allowed them to receive. In these words he has said what serves to rebuke the people of Judea as well. From here on he addresses everyone together, sometimes rebuking one group, sometimes the other, and sometimes all of them at once.

Chapter 4, verses 1–5. So he says: “Hear the word of the Lord, sons of Israel, for the Lord has a case against those who live in the land. There is no truth, no mercy, no knowledge of God in the land. Cursing and lying and murder and theft and adultery have spread over the land, and they mix blood with blood.” Because of this, he says, listen as God brings his case against you and shows you what kind of evils, and how great, you have repaid his care with. No one among you cares about truth, and you have no regard for kindness either, since you do not even care about the knowledge of God. Deceit and everything that deserves a curse—murder, theft, and adultery—are done freely throughout the whole land. You are so eager to murder one another that you are always mixing the blood of new victims with the blood of the old. “Therefore the land shall mourn and be diminished, together with all who live in it.” The whole land will mourn because of the terrible evils that come upon them. The enemies will kill them so mercilessly that the number of inhabitants will be reduced. That is what “the land will be diminished, together with those who live in it” means. “Together with the beasts of the field, and the creeping things of the earth, and the birds of the sky.” He speaks figuratively, as usual. He means that the powerful among them will perish along with everyone else. Like wild beasts they abuse the weaker. Like birds they swoop down all at once to snatch from the poor. They are no less eager than creeping things to harm their neighbours. “And the fish of the sea will fail.” In short, all those who fill the land like the fish of the sea will perish completely. To this he adds: “So that no one may either go to court or be rebuked.” Such desolation, he says, will cover everything that there will no longer be anyone to judge or anyone to correct the offences of others, since everyone will share the single misfortune of captivity. “But my people are like a priest who is spoken against.” They have fallen from all their former dignity and seem to deserve no regard at all, just as a priest who had been spoken against would be rejected and dishonoured by everyone. “And he will be weak for days.” For a very long time he will remain weak under the evils pressing upon him. “And the prophet with you will be weak by night.” Those who once used false predictions to deceive you will, most of them, also become weak. The misfortune that grips them will be like a night-time darkness wrapped around them, and they will see that their deceitful practice is useless to them. “I have made your mother like night,” so that she remains always in ignorance and error. Verses 6–8. “My people have become like one who has no knowledge.” You too, then, have followed her example and taken no account of knowing me. “Because you have rejected knowledge, I will also reject you from serving me as priest.” Just as you have thrown away the knowledge of me, so I too will…

…I will cast you out of my service, removing you far, through captivity, from the places where it was fitting for you to serve me as priests. This is what he means by "I will reject you from serving as priest to me." The priesthood is a benefit common to all; as blessed Paul says, this is why the priest must offer for the ignorances of the people just as for himself. So he rightly says that all are cast out of the priesthood when it has ceased. While it was carried on, its benefit was shared by all, and when it ceases, the loss is shared by all. "And you have forgotten the law of your God; I too will forget your children." I will hold of no account those who have set my ordinances aside. "According to their multitude, so they sinned against me." They became many, indeed countless, through my care, and they ought to have acknowledged me as the one who gave them this gift. Instead they showed lawlessness toward me in proportion to their own numbers, making it great and beyond measure. What then? "I will turn their glory into dishonor." I will bring them from their former blessings to the experience of worse things. "They will eat the sins of my people." That is to say: since my people have sinned against me in this way, they will reap fruit in proportion to what they have done, and will enjoy the very fruits they sowed. For "They will eat the sins of my people" stands for "Those of my people will enjoy the same sort of things as they sinned." Verses [?]–11. "And in their iniquities others will take their souls." For the sins they committed against me they will pay the penalty through others, that is, through the enemies who are about to attack them. "And it shall be: as the people, so also the priest." Captivity will bring them into such confusion and misfortune that there will be no difference at all between the one who serves as priest and the one under the priesthood. At that time none of the things proper to the divine priesthood will be done, and all alike will be surrounded by the misfortune of captivity. "And I will avenge their ways on them, and I will repay them for their schemes." For I will punish them in proportion to what they planned and set out to accomplish. "And they will eat and not be satisfied." Their experience of evils will never cease, for new ones will always be added to the first. He is speaking figuratively here, drawing on people who eat, are not satisfied, and eat again. He means that these too will experience evils: when the first have come, there will be others again, and there will be no end to what befalls them. For here too he said "they will eat," as above in "They will eat the sins of my people," meaning "they will experience." "They committed fornication and will not prosper." Since they have departed from me completely, nothing will turn out for them as it should. "For they have forsaken the Lord to give heed to fornication; and the heart of my people has taken in wine and strong drink." For they utterly neglected God and devoted great care and zeal to the idols, so that, drunk with evils, they no longer had any sense even of their own lawlessness.

Verses [?]. "They inquired by signs, and by their rods they gave him answer." He says they were doing what was customary among the pagans. Some consulted the demons, or the demons' priests, wanting to learn through signs something they needed. The priests, using certain rods as was their custom, gave answers to their questions, and did so deceitfully. "They were led astray by a spirit of fornication, and went whoring away from their God." Following a whorish mind, they turned [?] to error, departing completely from God. "On the tops of the mountains they sacrificed, and on the hills they offered sacrifice, under oak and poplar and shady tree, because shelter is good." They ran up to the mountains and the hills and performed sacrifices to the demons there. They picked out large and shady trees and carried out their deception there, thinking the great shade of the trees something grand and solemn, and so regarding them as well suited to impiety. "Therefore your daughters will commit fornication and your brides will commit adultery; and I will not punish your brides when they commit fornication, nor your brides when they commit adultery; for they themselves consorted with harlots and sacrificed with the initiated, and the people that understood was entangled with a harlot." You will pay penalties to match your own offenses when the enemies seize you and outrage your daughters and your brides. When this happens I will take no account of it, since you will justly suffer these things. You mixed yourselves up in whorish error and made [?] common cause with one another in forsaking me and attending to the idols. Many of you were initiated into the mysteries customary among the pagans and offered sacrifices for them, as if for some very great blessings. In short, the whole people, which ought above all to understand what is right and to know God its maker, chose fellowship with those who practiced this wicked and licentious fornication. They departed from God and devoted themselves to the service of demons. Verses 15–19. "But you, Israel, do not be ignorant; and Judah, do not go into Gilgal, and do not go up to the house of On, and do not swear by the living Lord." Do not all suffer from ignorance so badly that you go up to Gilgal to worship the idol set up there and yet pretend to honor the eternal God who truly is. You ought to know that these things cannot go together. There is a great difference between the eternal God and an idol made yesterday by human hands. Anyone who confesses the eternal God ought to keep away from everything that falsely bears this name, such as the idol On, whose house you enter to offer it worship that is not fitting for it. "For Israel has run wild like a heifer stung by a gadfly." For like a heifer driven to unruliness by the stirring of natural desire,

you have departed from my service and turned with a licentious mind to the worship of idols. "Now the Lord will pasture them like a lamb in a broad place." So I will scatter them, driving them here and there through the attack of the enemies, so that they will be no different from a lamb running about and wandering in a vast country in search of its mother. For by "pasture" he means "scatter," taking the image from those who hand something out lavishly and scatter it. "Ephraim is a partner of idols." They chose fellowship with the idols. Here, as in many other places, he names Israel by a part, Ephraim, taking the name from the strongest of the ten tribes, as in "The sons of Ephraim, bending and shooting with bows." "They set stumbling blocks for themselves." He devised for himself his own turnings toward the worse. How, and in what way? "He chose the Canaanites": he imitated their impiety. "Committing fornication, they went whoring." From then on they turned completely to the worse. "They loved dishonor because of its insolence." In great folly and in contempt of me they chose the worship of idols, which will bring them every kind of dishonor. "A whirlwind will whistle them away in its wings." A flying bird drives the air with its wings and is lifted aloft by its flight. In the same way these people, seized by my wrath and lifted up as it were, will be carried off into captivity with much outrage. "And they will be put to shame because of their altars." Then they will realize that their zeal for the altars of the idols was vain and harmful. Verses 1–5. "Hear these things, O priests, and attend, O house of Israel, and give ear, O house of the king." Clearly he is again beginning a new discourse here, arising from another revelation, addressed to the priests, to Israel and to all those of the royal house. "For the judgment is against you." For I have come to bring you under my judgment and to exact from you the penalty for what you have dared to do. "For you became a snare to the watchtower, and like a net spread out on Tabor, which the hunters fixed for the prey." You contrived plots of every kind [?] against my prophets, he says, like those who spread nets to catch their prey, eager to entangle them in various evils. By "watchtower" he means the company of the prophets, as in Ezekiel: "I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel." "But I am your instructor." Because you were vexed when they announced to you what was to come, and devised such schemes against them, I myself will bring the punishment. I will discipline you for your sins, and you will certainly undergo it [?], even against your will. "I have known Ephraim, and Israel is not far from me." For I know exactly what they are doing, since I am always

present with them. "For now Ephraim has gone whoring; Israel is defiled." So I know that they have departed from me entirely and been defiled by the worship of idols. "They did not set their minds to return to their God, for a spirit of fornication is in them, and they did not know the Lord." They did not change their minds and turn to me, since they had run aground completely on what is worse and were unwilling to take any account of me. "And the insolence of Israel will be humbled before his face." But for the drunken outrage and insolence they committed in departing from me and devoting themselves to idols, they will pay a fitting penalty. They will become spectators of their own humiliation, into which my punishment will bring them. "And Israel and Ephraim will grow weak in their iniquities, and Judah too will grow weak with them." All who offend together will also suffer punishment together for wronging the knowledge of me. So also blessed Paul speaks of "those who hold the truth in unrighteousness," meaning those who wrong the truth by turning toward the worse. Verses 6–9. "With sheep and calves they will go to seek the Lord, and they will not find him, for he has turned away from them, because they forsook the Lord." Even if they bring sacrifices, thinking they can appease God with them, they will gain nothing from it, because God has turned away from them completely. For they abandoned him and devoted themselves wholly to the idols. "For they have begotten foreign children for themselves." Against what had been commanded they mingled with the nations and had children from foreign unions. Blessed David too charges them with this when he says, "And they mingled among the nations." Here too, then, he shows how completely they mingled with foreigners, so that they even had children by them. "Now the blight will devour them and their portions." That is: like blight, I will hand over both them and all they possess to destruction. "Blow the trumpet on the hills; sound aloud on the heights; proclaim in the house of On." In all the places where you practiced your impiety, he says, leave off your usual pursuits and cry out instead, announcing the evils that will come upon you because of them. What are these? "Benjamin was astonished; Ephraim became a desolation in the days of reproof." By Benjamin he means the kingdom of Judah, and by Ephraim he means the ten tribes. He does not mean that the one was astonished and the other became a desolation. He is saying both things of both together: they will be astonished and will become a desolation. And "in the days of reproof" refers to the attack of the enemies that he will bring upon them, plainly exposing their lawless deeds. So they will be astonished, he says, and stunned at how suddenly their fortunes have changed, a change that will destroy them utterly. For I am bringing the enemies upon them and exposing the lawlessness committed [?]

among them. One will often find this way of dividing up something that applies jointly in blessed David too, as when he says, "By day I cried out, and by night before you." He does not mean that he cried out by day and spoke before God by night. He means "By day and by night I cried out before you"; so he divided up something that applies to both. So too here he says, "Benjamin was astonished, Ephraim became a desolation," meaning that both alike were astonished and became a desolation. "Among the tribes of Israel I have shown things that are faithful." By doing these things to them I will prove the truth and certainty of my threats, which they did not believe when they were spoken through the prophets. They will learn from experience that everything said was faithful and true. Verses 10–12. "The rulers of Judah became like those who move boundaries." Those who remove the markers that divide lands violate the rights of ownership. In the same way, he says, there is a great division between me and the idols, since the honor and name of God belong to me and not at all to them. Yet you, as far as it lay with you, dissolved rights that cannot be broken, rights marked off in many and various ways, by attaching to the idols the name and honor that belong to me. "Upon them I will pour out my onslaught like water." I will turn a fearful onslaught against those who dared such things, flooding them like water with a multitude of enemies. "Ephraim oppressed his adversary; he trampled judgment." They had no regard for justice. Each wronged the other as far as he was able, trampling on justice and taking no account of it. As the Lord says in the Gospels, "You have neglected love and judgment and mercy," meaning, you have no regard for love, justice and kindness. The Lord also evidently calls the person who is wronged an "adversary," as in "Make peace quickly with your adversary," where he urges wrongdoers to do all they can to reconcile those they have wronged. "For he began to go after vain things." They did these things once they chose to devote themselves to the worship of idols, and no longer took any account of my laws or of what is fitting. "And I will be like turmoil to Ephraim, and like a goad to the house of Judah." Through the enemies I will bring them into great turmoil, striking them with the pains that follow as with a heavy goad. It is clear that he does not mean the one for Ephraim and the other for Judah. He says he will bring both the turmoil and the goad on both together, as we showed above as well. Verses 13–15. "And Ephraim saw his sickness, and Judah his pain; and Ephraim went to the Assyrians and sent envoys to King Jareb; and he could not deliver you." Then indeed they will become aware of their own

evils, for that is what he calls sickness and pain. This will happen when Ephraim is carried off captive to the Assyrians and, sending envoys to the king of the Egyptians, gets no help at all from there. "And pain will not cease from you; for I am like a panther to Ephraim and like a lion to the house of Judah; and I will seize and go and take, and there will be none to rescue." You will remain in unending evils, since I will be to you like a panther and a lion. I will seize you and carry you off with great swiftness through the attack of the enemies, and no one will be able to free you from the evils pressing upon you. "I will go and return to my place, until they are destroyed." He added this too in keeping with the image he had used. It is characteristic of such beasts to seize swiftly whatever comes their way and carry it off to their own den, and there devour and consume what they have taken. To match "like a panther and a lion," then, he added this as well, meaning: having seized you through the enemies and made you captives, I will keep to myself. I will not turn to look at what is happening or give you any help, until you suffer complete destruction at the hands of those who hold you. "And they will return and seek my face." For then they too will change their minds and plead for my help.

Verses 1–3. "In their affliction they will rise early to seek me, saying: Let us go and return to the Lord our God, for he has struck us and he will heal us; he will strike and bind us up. He will make us whole after two days; on the third day we will rise up and live before him, and we shall know." Under the afflictions pressing upon them they will hurry to me with great eagerness. They will be fully confident that, having struck them, I will surely heal them as well, and will apply treatment suited to the wounds [?] they have suffered, restoring their condition completely with great speed and ease. This is what "He will make us whole after two days; on the third day we will rise up" means. He will heal us so quickly, they say, that in two or three days at the very most we will be restored again to our former prosperity. And "and we shall know" stands for "we shall enjoy better things," as in "You have made known to me the ways of life," which means "You have set me in life." "We shall press on to know the Lord." We will devote ourselves eagerly to knowing him. "We shall find him ready as the dawn." For we will receive his help like the dawn, as he changes our condition from darkness to light. "And he will come to us like the early rain upon the earth." He will provide good things in abundance, like the fruits the earth sends up when it receives suitable rain in every season. Verses 4–7. "What shall I do to you, Ephraim? What shall I do to you, Judah? Your mercy is like a morning cloud

and like the early dew that passes away." This too is the beginning of another discourse that the prophet delivered to the people, taking his starting point from the revelation he received. What, he says, was fitting for me to do for you, when you were so eager to break the law? I want to have mercy on you, but your actions do not allow it, since they inevitably draw punishment upon you. Even if I did intend to have mercy on you, that intention would have to remain unfulfilled in your case, made to vanish entirely by what you do, like a cloud or dew that appears briefly at dawn and is immediately dispersed. "Therefore I have mown down your prophets; I have slain them by the word of my mouth." And yet, he says, I became the cause of death even for my own prophets, whom I sent for your sake. I ordered them to remind you of what you ought to do, and they obeyed and came to you. But you had no respect either for what they said or for me who sent them, and you put them to death in various ways. So "I have mown down" and "I have slain them by the word of my mouth" stand for "By what I ordered them to do, I became the cause of this for them." He does not mean that he himself, by his own voice, did such things to the prophets. He means that, by ordering them to go to you, I all but did this myself. There is a similar passage in blessed David: "You have turned our paths aside from your way." It is not that God himself turned them aside; but because he allowed them to suffer such great evils, David ascribes the cause of what happened to him. "And my judgment will go forth like light." But I will not leave this lawlessness of yours unpunished; I will exact the penalty from you. Then the evils you are about to suffer will make it clearer than light to all that I brought such great evils upon you as judgment for your lawless treatment of the prophets. And to show that he does not do this without reason, he says: "For I desire mercy rather than sacrifice, and knowledge of God rather than whole burnt offerings." I sent the prophets because I valued doing you good, and leading you to know me, above sacrifices and whole burnt offerings. But since you repaid what I did by treating them so cruelly, you will pay a just penalty for your transgressions. For it is part of mercy to punish wrongdoers on behalf of those who suffer wrong. "But they are like a man who breaks a covenant; there they despised me." For you have remained in your own base condition [?]. You took no account of the agreement made between you and me long ago and despised me utterly, so that you even killed the prophets who reminded you of it. Verses 8–11. "Gilgal, a city that works vain things." The cause of these things for you is Gilgal, where

…shows their harmful and futile zeal for idols. This is also what he says further up: “Do not go into Gilgal, the city”; and “they work futile things,” he says, meaning the things done there. “Muddying water”: [?] muddying, by mixing in idols, the pure water of godliness that shone clear in the knowledge of me. “And your strength is like that of a pirate.” It shows all its own power in harming those who are deceived, just as pirates make a habit of working hard to harm others and of showing off their own power by destroying others. “Priests hid the way; they murdered Shechem, because they committed lawlessness.” He wants to show their wickedness by comparison. Your fathers, he says (he means the sons of Jacob, Levi and Simeon), when they saw that their sister had suffered the outrage of fornication, were so indignant at what had happened that they spoke secretly and deceitfully with the Shechemites, pretending friendship. This is the meaning of “They hid the way.” Then, when they saw their chance, they killed them all together for what had happened. “In the house of Israel I saw horrible things; there was the fornication of Ephraim.” That is what they did, he says. But now I have seen things full of horror in all Israel: the fornication of everyone, not of the body, but consisting in the corruption of the soul and in desertion from God. “Israel was defiled, and Judah abandoned his harvest.” All of them looked to one and the same transgression and were defiled by the worship of idols, and all of them made their own salvation incomplete and ruined. Think of a farmer who, when the seed has ripened and the crop calls for harvesting, now turns to idleness, loses what he has grown, and by his own idleness makes all his earlier labor worthless. In the same way, he says, you enjoyed so many and such great good things. You came out of Egypt, crossed the desert, received the law, took possession of the promised land, and acquired the form of worship that befits it. Yet when you should at last have been bringing fruit to God, you made everything done for you useless by your own wickedness. You neglected to give God the fruit owed for so many and such great benefits, and devoted yourselves entirely to turning aside to what is worse. Similar to this is the saying in Isaiah: “I waited for it to produce grapes, but it produced thorns.” “Begin to gather the vintage for yourself, when I bring back the captivity of my people, when I heal Israel.” So you will need yet another beginning, which I will provide out of my surpassing love for humankind, bringing you back from captivity beyond all human hope. Then indeed, if you are willing to look to what is better, you will need another beginning, so that, ashamed at least by the greatness of the gifts you receive then, you may turn yourselves from then on to caring for what is better. Then indeed, he says, you will be able to do this. For he says “Begin” in place of “You will be able to begin,” if you choose to look to what you ought. But now what?

Verses 1–4. “And the injustice of Ephraim will be uncovered, and the wickedness of Samaria, because they worked falsehood.” The lawlessness that you all practiced, and the fact that you turned away from me and looked to falsehood, will become plain to everyone through the punishment you will suffer [?] for such transgressions. How, and in what way? “And a thief will come in to him, a robber stripping people on his road, so that they may sing together, singing in their heart.” A thief or robber, meeting people on a road, might strip whoever he came across, or enter a house and take what is inside. In the same way, he says, the enemies will fall upon you and seize everything you have, both in the house and outside, carrying off some things and destroying others completely. So all of you, in the grip of the calamity, will sing songs full of lament together, grieving at heart over what is happening and wailing in words of mourning over the magnitude of the calamities that befall you. “Now their own counsels have surrounded them; they have come before my face.” Remembering all the things they carried out with great wickedness, I will surround them with the greatest evils, in proportion to what they plotted and did with great shamelessness before my eyes. “In their wickedness they gladdened kings, and in their lies rulers.” So that the hostile kings and rulers will take great pleasure as they overpower them and take them captive, because of the evils they committed, and because they abandoned the knowledge of me and pursued the false and deceitful worship of demons. “All of them committing adultery, like an oven burning for baking.” For with one accord they all turned away from the knowledge of me and took up an adulterous mind, so to speak, [?] turning aside to the service of demons. Like an oven heated for baking, they leaned with a kind of hot eagerness toward that licentiousness. “He will burn them up from the flame.” Indeed, they will be consumed by this very mind of theirs. “From the kneading of the dough until all of it is leavened, such are the days of your kings.” Just as dough, once taken and worked into flour, leavens and completes the whole, so from the time you set up this lawless kingship, having taken its beginning from Jeroboam, all of you alike have inclined to the same wicked mind. Verses 5–9. “Rulers began to be inflamed with wine.” Their rulers gave themselves over to drunkenness and wine-bibbing, and as a result of such drunkenness they vented their anger on everyone without restraint. “They stretched out their hand with pestilent men.” They looked to greed, choosing to make common cause with all those who were corrupt in their ways. “For their hearts were inflamed like an oven while they were overthrowing things all night long.” Their minds were inflamed like an oven by the drunkenness they kept up the whole night through. “Ephraim was filled with sleep.” So, as if from such drunkenness, like people held fast by heavy sleep, they took of what was proper no

account. “Morning came, and it was kindled like the light of fire; all were heated like a burning oven.” When day came on, they took up the same things again, kindled like fire, heated through like an oven, and roused to doing outrageous things. “And fire devoured their judges.” So they suffer a fitting punishment: like fire, all who were thought to rule among them are handed over to slaughter by the enemies. “All their kings have fallen.” They will all be handed over to destruction and slaughter. For what reason? “There was none among them who called upon me.” Because they were of one mind, all of them wishing to take no account of me at all. “Ephraim mingled himself among the peoples.” The blessed David also accuses them of this, saying, “And they mingled among the nations.” Mingling with foreigners had been absolutely forbidden them by the law, so he rightly reproaches them for it here as well. “Ephraim became a loaf baked in ashes, not turned over.” He has remained so unchanged in his ways, continuing in the same wickedness, just as such a loaf usually stays unmoved in the place where it has been set. “Foreigners devoured his strength.” So he suffers a punishment that matches his offense: having unlawfully mingled with foreigners, he will be utterly destroyed by those very people. “But he did not know it; gray hairs blossomed on him, and he did not know it.” Because he has persisted in ignorance of what is proper and has not chosen to look to what he ought even over a long time, he will suffer such things. Verses 10–12. “And the insolence of Israel will be humbled before his face, and they did not return to the Lord their God, nor did they seek him in all these things.” For the outrages they committed against the Deity, clinging so shamelessly and so unalterably to the service of demons and preferring zeal for them to zeal for the true Deity, they will see their own humiliation, which they suffer justly, since they were unwilling even to change and incline toward God. “And Ephraim was like a silly dove without understanding; they called on Egypt, and they went to the Assyrians.” Like the dove, which takes no account even of its own young: when they are taken from it, it usually nests in the same places again, having no foresight at all against the loss of its offspring;

Verses 13–16. Then he tells again what the cause of these things is: “Woe to them, because they leapt away from me! They are wretched, because they acted impiously toward me.” For they will suffer these things because of their transgression against me. “But I redeemed them, and they spoke lies against me.” From the beginning I did them good, but they showed me their ingratitude. I freed them from slavery under the Egyptians, but they uttered every kind of blasphemy against me. At one time they made a calf and said, “These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of Egypt”; at another, when he struck the rock and waters flowed and torrents overflowed, they said, “Can he also give bread, or prepare a table for his people?” “And their hearts did not cry out to me.” It did not enter their minds to turn to me with a sincere mind and wait for the gift that comes from me. “But they howled on their beds; for grain and wine they cut themselves.” On the contrary, when they had entered the land of promise and obtained the rest I gave them (this is what he calls their bed), they took no account of me but busied themselves with the worship of demons, howling and cutting themselves according to the custom of those people. They performed these rites because they credited the demons with supplying the good things I had given them. “They were disciplined by me.” For the transgressions they committed against me, they will receive from me fitting and ample discipline. And he teaches them that in doing such things they were transgressing: “And I strengthened their arms, and against me they devised evil.” That is, it was I who gave them all their strength against their enemies, but they pursued everything outrageous and full of impiety, acting impiously toward me. “They turned to nothing.” When they changed, I showed them through my wrath and my punishment to be nothing. “They became like a bow that is not strung.” They will be no different from a bow whose string is not drawn tight, which is useless to the warrior as long as it remains in that state. So they will be ineffective and weak against their enemies. This, then, is what “They were disciplined by me” means. It is as if he were saying: Since they did not acknowledge that they enjoyed what they received from me, [?] by their change for the worse I taught them what they ought, giving them clear proof of their transgression. “Their rulers will fall by the sword because of the undisciplined speech of their tongue.” These people, then, will be weakened, and their enemies will have such strength against them as to kill even their rulers along with the rest, because of the undisciplined things they said against me.

Verses 1–3. “This is their contempt in the land of Egypt, in their throat; like an untrodden land, like a trumpet, like an eagle upon the house of the Lord.” They will suffer [?] these things because they imitated the mind of their fathers, who in Egypt held in contempt the gifts given to

them by God. They will be like an untrodden land, handed over to complete desolation. They will be brought to this when the war trumpet sounds loudly against them and announces the coming attack of the enemies, which will fall on them with great swiftness, like an eagle swooping suddenly on its prey. This is how the enemies will come, destroying the people and burning the divine house. He added this to show the greatness of his wrath: he does not spare even his own house, but hands it over to the enemies to be destroyed along with everything else. Then he shows why these things will happen: “Because they transgressed my covenant and acted impiously against my law.” For I thought it absurd, when they had transgressed my covenant and acted with utter impiety against my law, to spare the house that they soiled and defiled by setting foot in it. “They will cry out to me: O God, we have known you.” Then, through what happens to them and the punishment brought upon them, they will acknowledge my power against their will. “For Israel turned away from good things; they pursued an enemy.” Those who were ungrateful for the good things I gave will rightly suffer such things, even though, whenever I gave them my help, they overcame their own enemies with great ease. Verses 4–6. “They made kings for themselves, and not through me; they ruled, and did not make it known to me.” They disregarded me so completely that they set aside the king I had given and set up a kingdom of their own, taking no account of me at all. This is the meaning of “They did not make it known.” “Their silver and their gold they made into idols for themselves, so that they might be destroyed.” They set aside both the kingdom that came from me and the worship prescribed by the law, and set up a kingdom of their own. (He means the kingdom that arose among the ten tribes, beginning with Jeroboam, who was also the first to make the heifers for them.) Acting in keeping with the absurdity of their choice of kingdom, they made many and various idols, some of gold and some of silver, from which they will gain nothing but their own destruction. And since he has reproached them for the novelty of their kingdom, from which the outrage of the heifers first arose, he fittingly adds: “Cast away your calf, Samaria; my anger is kindled against them.” Now turn away from the impiety of the heifers, for I am not angry at the lawlessness of what has happened in any casual way. “How long will they be unable to be cleansed in Israel? A craftsman made it, and it is not God.” Has not even this long time taught you what you ought? Have you not put away the filth of such great impiety? Instead you gape after idols made by human hands. How could they ever reasonably be thought gods, when their existence has such a cause? “For your calf, Samaria, was leading you astray.” And you have not been able to see that the making of the heifers caused you to stray from God, so that for this very reason you ought to hate them [?].

Verses 7–10. “For they are blasted by the wind, and their destruction will await them; a sheaf with no strength to make flour; and even if it does make some, foreigners will devour it.” They are no different from crops that a scorching wind has dried up and ruined, so that they are completely useless for feeding people. Decay and destruction overtake them, and they are useless to people, unable to yield flour fit for food; and if anything at all comes of them, it is thrown to irrational animals to eat as worthless. In the same way the worship of idols is harmful and gives no benefit whatever, so that if you have anything left over from elsewhere, that too will be the enemies’ gain because of the impiety that is in you. “Israel was swallowed up; now he has become among the nations like a useless vessel, because they went up to the Assyrians.” For these things you will suffer complete destruction. Captured by the Assyrians, you will be among foreigners like some utterly useless vessel, held to be of no account. “He blossomed on his own, against me [?].” Through my care they grew into a multitude, yet they would take no account of me, though I was the cause of so many good things for them; they did everything in self-will, as seemed good to themselves. This is the meaning of “on his own.” “Ephraim loved gifts.” Not even content with what they had, they looked to greed. “Therefore he will be handed over among the nations.” So it is fitting that, having come under their enemies, they will come to perceive both their impieties toward me and their wrongdoing. “Now I will receive them.” For I will wait for them in the land of the Assyrians, drawing them there through captivity, so that they may then become aware of their own impieties. How, and in what way? “And they will cease for a little while from anointing a king and rulers.” For they will stop setting up these lawless kingships and rulerships, disciplined by captivity and becoming aware of their own lawlessness. Verses 11–14. “Because Ephraim multiplied altars, they became sins for him.” They rightly suffer these things because they set up that impious kingdom. Since they found in it a way to devise the many-sided worship of idols, and raised up for themselves many and various altars, at which above all they offended, they will justly pay the penalty. “I will write down against him a multitude, and his ordinances.” This multitude of altars, and of the new laws they devised for the worship of idols, I will lay up against them as a just accusation in writing, so to speak, and bring out the sentence against them for such great transgressions. “The beloved altars were reckoned as foreign.” Indeed, the altars for which they showed great love and zeal will come under the power of the enemies. “For if they offer a sacrifice and eat meat, the Lord will not accept them.” Even if they try to propitiate the Deity with sacrifices, tasting the meat of the sacrifices as is customary, not even of these will there be any

account with God, nor will he grant them any release from their transgressions on this account. “Now he will remember their iniquities and avenge their sins.” Remembering their impieties, I will not be merciful to them, but will bring upon them punishments proportionate to their transgressions. “They turned back to Egypt, and [?] among the Assyrians they will eat unclean things.” In these dire straits they will ask Egypt for help, but they will reap no benefit at all from it; they will be led away captive to the Assyrians and will experience the miseries of captivity. “And Israel forgot the one who made him and built sacred precincts; and Judah multiplied walled cities. And I will send fire upon his cities, and it will devour their foundations.” They would take no account of the one who made them, but built sacred precincts for the worship of idols. Then on top of this they tried to fortify their cities with walls, as though they would find in this some release from their troubles. But these things will not help them at all, since through the enemies I will bring upon them a punishment so great and so fearful that, spreading over everything like fire, it will all but destroy all their cities from their foundations.

Verses [?]. “Do not rejoice, Israel, and do not be glad like the peoples, because you have played the harlot away from the Lord your God.” It is not fitting, then, for you to be glad and rejoice like the rest of humankind. They received no teaching capable of leading them to godliness, but you, after much instruction and knowledge of God, turned away through the depravity of your mind from the knowledge you had before and turned to the worship of idols. “You have loved gifts on every threshing floor of grain.” Indeed, you brought the firstfruits of everything to the demons, crediting them as the cause of what had been given. “And threshing floor and winepress did not know them.” You will therefore pay a fitting penalty: the loss of your crops. “They did not dwell in the land of the Lord.” For you will not remain in the land given to you. “They did not dwell” stands for “they will not dwell”; he uses the usual interchange [?] of tenses, as we have shown in many places in the blessed David as well. “Ephraim dwelt in Egypt, and among the Assyrians they will eat unclean things.” You will become fugitives in Egypt, and from there you will all be handed over against your will to captivity among the Assyrians. “They did not pour out wine to the Lord, and they did not please him.” They showed such zeal and eagerness in their offerings to the idols that they gave them firstfruits from every threshing floor. But to God, who [?] was the cause of their good things, they never once chose to bring even libations of wine, nor to do anything that could please God through the intention [?] of those who do it. For just as the blessed David says, “May my meditation [?] be pleasing to him,” meaning, may it seem sweet and agreeable to him, so here he says: “[?] did not please

…[pleased] him”, meaning that they never chose to do anything that was pleasing to him. Then, to show that he is reproaching their attitude and not saying that God takes delight in such things, he says: “Their sacrifices are like the bread of mourning to them; all who eat it will be defiled.” God is so far from needing sacrifices, or from measuring the honor due to him by them, that even if they were to offer sacrifices, he would not accept them. Suppose someone brings food to people in mourning: the sight of things that everyone else finds pleasant is painful to them, because it stings them with the memory of their grief, (p. 65) and they cannot bring themselves even to touch the food set before them; anyone in mourning who is forced to take food treats it as a kind of defilement or filth and will not touch it. In the same way God looks on the sacrifices they offer, if they should ever want to offer any. He gladly accepts sacrifices from those who offer them with a right disposition, but he finds even the sight of the offerings of the wicked painful, because it reminds him of the impiety they live in while they offer the sacrifice as a kind of pretense [?]. “For their bread is for their own souls; it will not enter the house of the Lord.” So every offering they make will be turned back on them, since it is in no way acceptable to God.
