This is what “it will not enter the house of the Lord” means: their offerings will not be acceptable to God, nor will he count them as presented to the Lord; he sends them away from a distance as offered with an impious disposition. When God speaks to Cain, who had made his offering wrongly, he says: “Its turning is toward you, and you shall rule over it”, meaning, “What you offered has been turned back to you; you can be its master yourself. I have accepted nothing at all.” In the same way he says here, “Their bread is for their own souls”, meaning, “What they offer will remain theirs, since God does not accept it.” He called the offerings “bread”, naming all the offerings by one part of them, (p. 66) since they also used to offer bread; as he said above: “They loved cakes with raisins.” Verses 5–7. “What will you do on the day of festal assembly, and on the day of the Lord’s feast?” Since you have behaved like this toward God, what escape from evils will you find on that day, when a festal assembly and a feast is held for God over your destruction, as though his enemies and foes were being justly slaughtered? “Therefore, behold, they will go out of the distress of Egypt, and Memphis will receive them, and Machmas will bury them; destruction will inherit their silver, and thorns will be in their tents.” After the great distress you will endure, you will flee to Egypt as if to safety, but the Assyrians will drag you away and lead you off into captivity among them. You will pass through the cities of Egypt, with one danger after another coming upon you. That is what “Memphis and Machmas” means. In other words: “You will pass through the cities of Egypt

while the Assyrians crush and destroy you. Everything you own will also perish, and your cities and lands will become so desolate (p. 67) that thorns will grow there, since no one will live there.” “The days of your vengeance have come; the days of your recompense have come.” You will suffer these things when the time draws near at which your impiety must be punished and you must be paid back fittingly for the impious things you did. “And Israel will sit like the prophet who is out of his mind, the man who carries a spirit.” You will be in such misery that you will be just like a false prophet who has fallen into a deep frenzy through the working of the evil spirit and does not even perceive what is in front of him. In the same way the sheer size of your troubles will drive you out of your mind. And why? “Because of the multitude of your iniquities your madness has multiplied.” For you lived in great iniquity and had given yourself up completely to a great madness for idols. Verses 8–10. “Ephraim is a watchman with God; the prophet is a crooked snare on all his ways.” You ought to have been a watchman of the good for others, and with God to teach everyone else what is right, since you had learned it from him. Instead you became the opposite, a road to evil for everyone, no different from a cruel snare that entangles those who fall into it in danger. That is how you became a law of impiety for all. (p. 68) “They fixed madness in the house of his God.” For you filled the whole land of promise with idolatry. He calls the land of promise the house of God because God dwells in it. “They were corrupted as in the days of the hill.” All of you went from better to worse, and your thinking was corrupted just like that of those who once committed impiety in the wilderness, who made a calf and said: “These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.” He calls that time “the days of the hill.” So you were corrupted in the same way as they were; that is, you caught the same disease they had. “He will remember their iniquities; he will punish their sins.” Accordingly, then, he will remember your impieties and exact from you penalties proportionate to your sins against him. “Like grapes in the wilderness I found Israel, and like an early fig (9) on a fig tree I saw their fathers.” I showed their fathers as much affection as someone would feel who saw grapes in the wilderness, finding them beyond all hope, or a fig on the tree that had appeared before its usual season. “But they went in to Baal-peor, and were estranged to shame, and became like the abominable.” They turned to the worship of the idol (p. 69) and chose to be estranged from me, proving themselves worthy of nothing but utter shame, because they abandoned God, the cause of so many good things for them, and went over to an idol from which they had received nothing good. That is also why they became abominable, falling into the hands of their own enemies. Having said this about them, he goes on: (9) The manuscript reads σκοπόν.

Verses 11–14. “Ephraim has flown away like a bird.” He wants to confirm the earlier statement, “They were corrupted as in the days of the hill.” For in the same way as their fathers, he says, these too, after all the care they received from me, flew away like a bird in their disposition. “Their glories are from births and birth pangs and conceptions.” And while committing such impiety, they think themselves blessed because they are so numerous. That is what “from births and birth pangs and conceptions” means, since what is born comes from conception, birth pangs and childbirth. “For even if they raise their children, they will be bereaved of them among men.” They do not reckon that even if their offspring reach full maturity, they will gain nothing more by it; for the slaughter of war will reduce them to childlessness. “For woe to them indeed, because I have abandoned them.” Once I have withdrawn my care from them, destruction and ruin await them. “My flesh is from them.” (p. 70) And yet my bond with them was once so close that I thought I was one of them, and I had the kind of feeling toward them that people naturally have toward those they regard as their own kin. “Ephraim, as I saw, has set out his children for prey; and Ephraim is to lead out his children to slaughter.” But although I once had such a bond with them, since they have turned entirely to evil, the opposite of what they once had will happen to them. They will be handed over like prey into the hands of their enemies, and all of them will be pierced, wounded and killed. “Give them, O Lord—what will you give them? Give them a childless womb and dry breasts.” This punishment they suffer is just and fitting: to be reduced to childlessness and to be unable to raise the children born to them, since for people such as these utter destruction [?]

Verses 15–17. Then, having told what God would justly bring upon them, he goes on to what follows: “All their evils are in Gilgal; for there I hated them because of the wickedness of their practices.” There they practiced every kind of impiety, and for this I justly hated them for doing such things. “I will drive them out of my house.” I will drive them out of the land of promise, he says. He calls the whole land his house because he chose to dwell in it. (p. 71) “I will no longer love them; all their rulers are rebellious.” My hatred toward them remains firm, since they have all turned to disobedience, and those who are supposed to rule among them lead the way in evil. “Ephraim is afflicted; his roots are dried up; he will no longer bear fruit.” Using a metaphor from trees, he said that they will perish utterly, like trees that wither completely once the root is destroyed and can no longer bear fruit. “For even if they bear children, I will kill the beloved offspring of their womb.” For I will wipe out all their offspring too, he says. “God will reject them, because they did not listen to him, and they will be wanderers among the nations.” For he will make them all strangers to his

care, since they were unwilling to listen to him and to turn to repentance. For this they will be seized and will become captives among foreigners, forced by their [?] want to wander about here and there.

Verses 1–2. “Israel is a vine with fine branches.” In its numbers Israel was just like a vine luxuriant with a great many large branches. “Its fruit is abundant.” And they grew in number day by day, (p. 72) as many children were born to them because of the prosperity they enjoyed. “In proportion to the abundance of his fruit, he multiplied altars.” But they repaid the great numbers that God’s blessing had given them with a great increase of impiety; in proportion to their own number they set up altars in honor of the idols. “In proportion to the good things of his land, he built pillars.” And while enjoying many good things from the land, they set up pillars for the worship of idols in return. “They divided their hearts.” And their madness for idols was so great that their minds were divided in their zeal for idols, some eager to worship these, others those. “Now they will be destroyed.” They will suffer a just destruction for this. “He himself will tear down their altars.” For God, whom they neglected, will himself overthrow everything they impiously set up for the worship of idols. “Their pillars will be in misery.” They too will be brought low when they are demolished. Verses 3–5. “For now they will say: We have no king, because we did not fear God; and what will the king do for us? Speaking words, pretexts, he will make a covenant.” For now they will realize their own folly in choosing a king against God’s will. (p. 73) Because they did not fear God, they set up an empty and lawless kingship in opposition to the line of David, which reigned by divine promise; so their kingdom has been taken from them and they have all been handed over to captivity. They gained nothing from the king. On the contrary, he used deceitful words and made a wicked covenant with them, so that they would desert God and worship the heifers he had made. “Judgment will spring up like couch grass on the dry land of a field.” For God will judge their lawless audacity and bring on them a punishment for it so severe that his judgment against them will flourish and appear very great and terrible, just as couch grass springing up all at once spreads widely over dry land. “The inhabitants of Samaria will dwell beside the calf of the house of On.” For when the disasters come, they will all attend on the heifers they worship, hoping to get some help from them. “For its people mourned over it.” But they will get no benefit from that. On the contrary, they will even mourn for the heifers themselves, (p. 74) seeing them terribly destroyed at the hands of the enemy.

“And as they provoked him, they will rejoice over his glory.” For the enemies will treat the idols with great contempt and will be filled with great pleasure to see them stripped of the glory they once falsely enjoyed among those eager to worship them. As blessed David says, “Let not my enemies rejoice over me,” meaning, “Let them not take pleasure in seeing what they wish come upon me”; so here “They will rejoice over his glory” means that they will take pleasure in seeing the idols stripped of their glory. “Because they have been removed from him.” For they see that all the glory the idols formerly and unjustly enjoyed has been taken from them. Verses 6–8. “And having bound it for the Assyrians, they carried it off as gifts to King Jareb.” For those who once seemed to worship them, seeing the Assyrians bearing down on them, will break up the heifers, since they were made of gold, and bind them together as if they were going to carry off ordinary gold. They will bring them as a gift to the king of the Egyptians, hoping to find some help there. The prophet clearly reproaches them for this in many places: that they waited in vain for help from the Egyptians. (p. 75) And what will happen? “In giving, Ephraim will receive shame.” Because of the giving and the bringing of the gift, Ephraim will be put to shame, having gained nothing and spent his effort in vain. “In his counsel Israel will be put to shame.” Naturally, he will be disappointed in his expectation. “Samaria has cast off her king like a twig on the surface of the water.” For they will gain nothing from that scheme and that venture. They will all be taken captive, and their king will be taken too. Captured by the Assyrians, he will be carried off like twigs swept along on water to a foreign land, taken wherever his captors please. “And the altars of On, the sins of Israel, will be removed.” The worship of idols, through which Israel sinned against God, will come to an end. “Thorns and thistles will grow up on their altars.” The desolation will be so great that, with no one setting foot there, thorns and thistles will grow where the altars stood. “And they will say to the mountains, Cover us, and to the hills, Fall on us.” In such a plight they will wish to suffer a swift destruction (p. 76) rather than endure their punishments one by one. Verses 9–11. “From the time of the hills Israel has sinned.” From then on they became eager to sin, abandoning God and busying themselves with the hills and the worship of idols. “There they stood.” But their lawlessness comes to an end through punishment. “It will not overtake them on the hill.” For captivity will take away their zeal for the hills, so that they are no longer found worshiping on the hills but are occupied with the miseries of captivity. “War has come upon the children of iniquity.” This will happen because of their wrongdoing and impiety, when the war of the

Assyrians is brought upon them. “I will discipline them according to my desire.” So I will bring upon them evils strong enough to discipline them, and through this discipline they will realize their own wickedness. “And peoples will be gathered against them when they are disciplined for their two iniquities.” For I will gather a great host of enemies against them, disciplining them because they both neglected me and devoted themselves to idols. “Ephraim is a heifer taught to love strife.” Like a heifer that kicks and wants to get the better of those taming it, he deserts God and will not submit to the yoke of servitude. “But I will come upon the beauty of her neck.” I will take away all her comeliness, of which she was so proud. (p. 77) “I will mount Ephraim.” I will mount him as one mounts a quarrelsome heifer, by my power. “I will pass over Judah in silence.” I will pass Judah by when he is beset by evils, giving him no help at all. It is like the words of blessed David, “Do not be silent toward me,” meaning, “Do not pass by my plight when I am beset by grievous troubles.” “Jacob will prevail against him.” I will display my strength to all Israel. For it is clear that the whole Jewish nation is called both Jacob and Israel, being named by both titles after their forefather, who was first called Jacob and after the vision was called Israel. So too in blessed David: “He chose David his servant and took him from the flocks of sheep; from following the ewes with young he took him, to shepherd Jacob his servant and Israel his inheritance.” There he clearly named the Jewish nation by both titles. Verses 12–15. “Sow for yourselves for righteousness, and reap for the fruit of life.” Do, then, the works of all righteousness; (p. 78) for from such seed one can reap the fruit of life. “Light for yourselves the light of knowledge.” While there is still time, seek the knowledge of the truth before the time of punishment comes, while you can still repent and be spared the experience of these evils. “Seek the Lord until the fruits of righteousness come to you.” Take every care over what pleases God, so that you may be granted to reap the fruit of righteousness. “Why have you passed over impiety in silence, and harvested its fruit, and eaten false fruit?” Stop doing what you did before, letting so great an impiety pass and keeping quiet while it went on, when you should have been indignant at it; for its fruit, which you gathered, was full of deceit and harm. “Because you trusted in your chariots (10), in the multitude of your forces, destruction will arise

among your people, and all your fortified places will be wiped out.” You thought your own power was enough for the war against your enemies, but everything turned out the opposite: destruction overtook the whole people, so that even the fortified cities were torn down. “As the ruler Salaman was wiped out from the house of Jeroboal in the days of war, (p. 79) when they dashed a mother to the ground upon her children, so I will do to you, house of Israel, because of your wickedness.” The kind of destruction those people suffered then, when war brought a most grievous destruction on them (sic) and parents were slain together with their children, is what you of Israel will now suffer as well, receiving punishment in proportion to your wickedness. He seems to be referring to some act of great cruelty that they committed at that time. Since they knew of it, he naturally mentioned it, as if to say: “What you did then out of extreme wickedness, you yourselves will now justly suffer.”

Verses 1–4. “At dawn they were cast off.” They will fall very quickly. “Like the dawn the king of Israel was cast off.” Like the dawn, which appears for a little while and then passes, their king will fall. (p. 80) “For Israel was a child, and I loved him, and out of Egypt I called them back; so they went away from my presence; they sacrificed to the Baals and burned incense to carved images.” He calls Israel a child with reference to the time in Egypt, when it began to take shape as a people and to receive God’s care. “For I,” he says, “from the very start, when they had only just begun to take shape, showed them great providence, even snatching them out of Egypt. But they displayed a wickedness as great as my love and care for them: they at once deserted me, turned to evil, and gave to the idols all the devotion that was due to me.” “And I bound Ephraim together.” Although they had been scattered throughout Egypt by their troubles, I gathered them into one by my care. “And I took him up on my arm.” And by my power I counted him worthy of my care. “And they did not know that I heal them.” They were not even willing to acknowledge me, who had freed them from such great evils. “In the ruin of men I drew them, with the bonds of my love.” Nor would they acknowledge that, when by the common lot of humans they were about to perish, I snatched them all away, binding them to me in an unspeakable way by my love. “And I will be like a man who strikes a man on his cheek.” In return for this folly I will bring upon them blows and punishments as heavy as it is to be struck with blows aimed at the face. “I will look upon him and prevail over him.” (p. 81) For I will turn my whole self to punishing him, so that by this at least he may come to know my strength. Verses 5–7. “Ephraim dwelt in Egypt, and Assur himself was his king.” They will flee to Egypt as fugitives, thinking they will escape the Assyrian attack; but they will gain nothing from it, since, as I have decided, they will overpower

…those will certainly be their [?]. And why will they suffer these things? “Because they would not turn back.” Since they have remained unyielding in their wickedness, unwilling to show even one change. “And he grew weak by the sword in his cities, and he ceased in his hands.” Therefore they will have no strength when they fight against their enemies, nor will they bring any safety to their own cities. All their weapons and all their preparation for war will prove feeble and useless, because I oppose them on account of their wickedness and bring the Assyrians upon them as punishment. “And they will eat of their own counsels.” They will reap the fruit of their own plans and suffer a fitting punishment. “And his people hanging [?] from their dwelling.” For they will not remain [?] in their own dwelling, nor is what seems secure [truly secure?]; this God will destroy in his wrath.

Verses 8–9. “What shall I do with you, Ephraim? Shall I shield you, Israel?” But what was it fitting for me to do concerning you, in the face of so many and such great evils? To help you, since you are caught up in the greatest evils? “What shall I do with you, Ephraim? I will make you like Admah and like Zeboiim.” But I find that you are not worthy to obtain that help. On the contrary, from what you have done I find that the punishment brought upon you would be just if you suffered the overthrow that once befell Sodom and Gomorrah and Admah and Zeboiim. “My heart has turned; in this my repentance was stirred up. I will not act according to the anger of my wrath; I will not abandon Ephraim to be blotted out.” But although I find you fully deserving of this punishment, I have changed my mind toward you. Somehow troubled by the sight of your misfortune, I am drawn to relent, so that I stop being angry any longer and cannot bear to abandon you as you are handed over to utter destruction. “For I am God, and not a man among you.” For I am God, who made all things and cares for all of them as his own works, and I am in no way like those who live among you and with you. “Holy, and I will not enter a city.” For I am set apart from all human affairs and above them. I do not live in cities after the manner of human beings, nor am I accustomed to spend my time there with you. Therefore I do not share the mind of you who have been eager to live with wickedness. On the contrary, although you are about to undergo a just punishment, I am moved by the abundance of my mercy to deliver from it those who suffer. Verses 10–12. “They will walk after the Lord.” The prophet has added this as a conclusion to the preceding words of God, saying something like this:

that from now on it is fitting to follow such a one, and to do everything according to the will of God, who is so gentle and kind toward you. “He will roar like a lion, and the children of the waters will be struck with amazement.” For if we show ourselves to be such, then like a lion that terrifies the cattle he will send forth his voice against all those who have come upon you like waters in their multitude, and he will throw them all into terror through fear of him. “And they will come like a bird from Egypt, and like a dove from the land of the Assyrians; and I will restore them to their houses, says the Lord.” For God promises that he will bring them back from every side, freeing them from the captivity that holds them, and that he will restore them all to their own homes like birds, both the captives among the Assyrians and the fugitives in Egypt. “Ephraim has surrounded me with falsehood, and the house of Israel and Judah with ungodliness; now God knows them, and they will be called a holy people of God.” For formerly, since they had all turned aside to falsehood and the worship of idols and were living in ungodliness, taking no account of me, he necessarily surrounded them with those evils. But when they repent and look to what is better, I will make them all my own (for this is what “He knew them” means); and from the events themselves they will be shown to be mine, since through my help they are counted worthy of so many and such great goods. Such, then, are the things I am ready to provide on my part. But what about them? Verses 1–4. “But Ephraim is an evil spirit.” That is, a wicked disposition; for in many places Scripture calls the disposition “spirit,” as in “They were led astray by a spirit of fornication,” and “Renew a right spirit within me”; and it is said of Caleb son of Jephunneh and Joshua son of Nun that “another spirit was in him.” “He pursued the scorching wind all day long.” For he continually did things that brought destruction upon them, like a scorching wind that ruins the crops. “They multiplied empty and vain things.” They set up a multitude of idols that were utterly useless and the causes of the greatest harm. “And he made a covenant with the Assyrians, and traded oil into Egypt.” Then, having fallen into evils because of these things, he hoped to obtain some good, sometimes through the Assyrians, sometimes through the Egyptians. With the one he wanted to make treaties of friendship, and from the other he asked for military alliance; but he gained no benefit from any of them. “And the Lord has a case against Judah, to punish Jacob.” For God himself comes, through the course of events, to enter into judgment with them and to avenge what they have wrongly done. Here too he calls the nation of the Jews “Jacob,” since it was called both Jacob and Israel after the name of their forefather, as we showed above. Hence he adds: “According to his ways

and according to his practices he will repay him.” That is, he will bring upon them a punishment proportionate to their offenses. Then he exposes their wickedness by comparing them with their forefather. “In the womb he took his brother by the heel.” For even before his birth he displayed in his posture the cunning with which he would later lay claim to the birthright. “And in his labors he prevailed with God.” Although he endured many toils and wanderings, he did not allow himself to abandon his loyalty to God. “And he prevailed with an angel, and was able.” Indeed, when he feared his brother’s plotting, he was granted a vision of an angel, and when he seemed to wrestle with him he proved strong. Such were his deeds; and what are those of his descendants? “They wept and entreated me.” They are all in tears and supplications, asking to be delivered from the evils in which they find themselves because of their own ungodliness. What ungodliness is this? “In the house of On they found me.” For they were occupied with the worship of idols, honoring with my name things that could have nothing to do with it, and honoring me, who was not present, as though I were present there. So “In the house of On they found me” means “as though they found me present there”: in this way they transferred to the idol the name and the honor of God, the one whom they ought to have honored as God. “And there it was spoken to them.” And there they received a just sentence for their acts of ungodliness. Verses 5–8. “But the Lord God Almighty will be his memorial.” But he will meet with such things as will make him recognize the true God, and he will always keep the greatest remembrance of the one who made them and has always been their benefactor. And now too, having disciplined them for their ungodliness, he will change them for the better by his own power. “And you, return to your God; keep mercy and judgment, and draw near to your God continually.” Show, then, a genuine turning to God, and cultivate kindness and justice. Always be eager to be with God, holding fast to his worship, which is rightly owed to him, and abstaining completely from zeal for idols. “Canaan: in his hand is a balance of injustice; he has loved to oppress.” Having called them to repentance through those words, here he again reproaches them for their wickedness. “For you have proved,” he says, “in no way better than the Canaanites, whom God drove out of the land because of their excessive ungodliness and wickedness, and in whose place he brought you in. So you too look to injustice, and with great diligence crush the weaker by the power you possess.” Verses 8–9. “And Ephraim said: Yet I have become rich; I have found relief for myself.” Then, gathering wealth through injustice, he delights in being rich, and he even considers the enjoyment of it sweet. “None of his labors will be found for him, because of the injustices he committed.” He ought to reckon that all these things that he gathered by unlawful toil

will all perish because of the injustice with which he gathered them, whenever God wishes to exact from them the penalty for the transgressions in which they constantly engaged. “But I am the Lord your God, who brought you up out of Egypt.” You ought to have abstained from all injustice against the poor, remembering that when you were in bitter slavery I brought you out of Egypt. “I will yet make you dwell in tents, as in the day of a feast.” Indeed I gave you a dwelling, that is, the enjoyment of the promised land, allowing you to celebrate as you enjoyed what had been given you. For he says “I will make you dwell” instead of “I made you dwell,” using a change of tense as is customary. That this is customary we also showed sufficiently in the Psalms, for example: “But I cried to God, and the Lord heard me”; to which he adds: “Evening and morning and noon I will tell and declare, and he will hear my voice.” Yet “he heard” does not fit with “he will hear”: for if it has already happened, why do you ask for it to happen? Rather, in the earlier phrase, “and the Lord heard me,” he says “heard” instead of “will hear.” In general this occurs frequently and abundantly in the Psalms, owing to the idiom of the Hebrew language; hence one would naturally find the very same thing in the prophets too, as when it says, “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter,” instead of saying,

Verses 10–11. “And I spoke to the prophets, and I multiplied visions, and by the hands of the prophets I was represented.” I then raised up prophets and granted visions to very many people of that time, appearing in many ways to the righteous of that age: I mean Moses and Joshua son of Nun and those of their time. And I chose to do all these things eagerly. Remembering these things, they ought to have been content with what was given them, and not to have taken away what belonged to others through injustice. “If Gilead is not, then they were false in Gilgal.” This is what he says: If anything had come to you from Gilead and Gilgal (that is, from the idols), what you are now doing would have some excuse. But if nothing came to you either from Gilead or from Gilgal, that is, if nothing came to you from the idols, how is it not obvious that you have devoted yourselves to falsehood? Now you have abandoned the truth, departing from your benefactor and turning to those who have done you no good at all; and then you offer sacrifices to them together with your rulers. For by “Gilead” and “Gilgal” he means the idols. Just as he says above, “Do not go into Gilgal,” meaning “Do not busy yourselves with the idols,” naming what was worshiped there after the place, so here too he mentions Gilead and Gilgal, where much idol worship took place. So by naming the places he signifies the worship of idols, saying this: Although you received so many things from me, and nothing from the demons and the idols, it is through deception and an inclination toward falsehood that you have departed from me and devote yourselves to their sacrifices. “And their altars

are like turtles on the dry ground of a field.” “For you will gain no benefit,” he says, “from your zeal for those things, since God will utterly destroy them all through your enemies.” For since the turtle normally lives in water, but perishes completely when caught on dry land, he wished to show the destruction of the altars by this illustration. Verses 12–14. And again, showing them to be ungodly by comparing them with their ancestors: “Jacob withdrew into the plain of Syria, and Israel served for a wife, and for a wife he kept watch.” For Jacob, because of his virtue and the blessing of the birthright, chose to become a fugitive from his family and to wander in Syria, and to endure servitude with Laban; and to come to marriage with a wife only through great hardship, so as not to take a Canaanite woman against his father’s wishes. He endured such hardship, guarding himself against taking a wife contrary to the customs of his ancestors and the will of God, which is exactly what his brother did when he took Canaanite women against the will of both God and his parents. “And by a prophet the Lord brought Israel up out of the land of Egypt, and by a prophet he was preserved.” And since, after all those things, Jacob went down into Egypt, God took such care of his descendants that through the ministry of the prophet Moses he brought them all up out of Egypt and guarded them by his own care in the wilderness until he brought them into the promised land. “Ephraim provoked me and angered me.” Though they were descended from such ancestors and had received so many good things from me for their sake, they roused me to the greatest anger, showing ingratitude to me who had done them so much good, and turning to the worship of idols, from which they have gained nothing. “And his blood will be poured out upon him.” Therefore the punishment for his transgressions will fall back upon him. “And the Lord will repay him his reproach, according to the word of Ephraim.” For the slander that he brought upon God through his ungodliness, God will exact a just penalty from him, proportionate to what he uttered against him.

Verses 1–3. “He too received ordinances in Israel, and he assigned them to Baal and died.” For having received from the law of Moses the ordinances that he ought to have kept, he transferred them all to Baal, diverting to those things the worship that belongs to me by law; and by this he brought death upon himself. “And now they have gone on sinning, and have made for themselves molten images from their gold and silver, in the likeness of idols, works of craftsmen completed for them.” They persisted in ungodliness, making idols, some of gold and some of silver, produced by human hands. Then they show such zeal for them that—what? “They themselves say: Sacrifice men, for the calves have run out.” So that after the many sacrifices they had offered by means of animals, not satisfied with the great number of those victims, they even extended their sacrificial undertakings to human beings.

As the blessed David also says: “And they sacrificed their sons and their daughters to demons.” “Therefore they will be like a morning cloud, and like early dew that passes away, and like a spider’s web blown away by a whirlwind from a threshing floor, and like vapor from locusts.” For just as a cloud or the morning dew dissolves and vanishes completely, and a spider’s web on a threshing floor is swept away by a gust of wind, and indeed a little vapor appears briefly from the flight of locusts, so you will all vanish at once under my wrath. Verses 4–6. “But I am the Lord your God, who makes firm the heaven and creates the earth, whose hands created all the host of heaven; and I did not show them to you so that you should go after them; and I brought you up out of Egypt; and you shall know no God but me, and there is no savior besides me.” Above all, I will justly bring upon you the punishment set forth, because you have turned to idols and departed from me. I am the maker of all things, both in heaven and on earth; and when I brought you out of Egypt through the multitude and greatness of those wonders, both freeing you from the slavery that held you and teaching you to know my power, I clearly charged you to give the name of God to nothing else, neither to anything on earth nor to the lights in heaven, but to confess and know me alone as God, who alone can save and deliver from the evils that press upon you, since I am Lord of all. I did this so that you would not think my laws mere words and phrases, but rightly grounded in truth and in deeds. “I shepherded you in the wilderness, in an uninhabited land, according to their pastures.” Having brought you out of Egypt, I led you through the wilderness by my own care, in an uninhabited land where wild beasts and serpents had their haunts, and I did not let you lack anything necessary. “And they were filled to satiety, and their hearts were exalted; for this reason they forgot me.” Then, having entered the promised land, having enjoyed so many good things beyond all human hope, and having been shown to be great before all people in the world through what I did for them, they no longer remembered me, who had given them such an abundance of good things. Verses 7–8. “And I will be to them like a panther and like a leopard on the road of the Assyrians.” Therefore, crushing and destroying them with great swiftness like a panther and a leopard, I will drive them all into captivity under the Assyrians. “I will meet them like a bear in distress.” And like a bear robbed of her young, which in her great distress over them mauls whoever she meets, I will bring about the slaughter of very many of them. “And I will tear open the enclosure of their heart.” And all their reasonings, which they kept shut up within themselves and by which they practiced ungodliness (15) The manuscript reads “he will bring.”

with great diligence, since these reasonings are superfluous and vain, I will expose through the punishment brought upon them. “And the cubs of the thicket will devour them there, and the wild beasts of the field will tear them apart.” For the enemies will consume them with slaughter of every kind, as though lions from a thicket, or other beasts like them, fell upon them all at once with their teeth and tore them all apart. “In your destruction, Israel, who will help you?” When you are being destroyed and are perishing under so many evils, what help could you find? Verses 10–11. “Where is this king of yours? Let him save you in all your cities; and let him judge for you, he of whom you said, Give me a king and a ruler. And I gave you a king in my anger.” For you will gain no benefit from a king’s care or from generalship either, since he too will be powerless to help while I oppose you. And yet you utterly set aside Samuel, who led you according to my will, a righteous man who administered both the priesthood and the leadership of the people with every virtue, and like the rest of the nations you said that you must have a king who would be able to fight your wars against foreigners. But the time has come when you will perceive your own folly. Those who appear to reign among you will be of no benefit to you, since all the cities among you will fall in a single destruction. Nor, then, will any of them judge on your behalf when you suffer an unjust attack from your enemies, and give you any help against them, as kings customarily do for their own people to help those who are wronged. For your present enemies are far more powerful than those who reign among you. And when you asked for the rule of a king, thinking it a good thing, I was angered at the wickedness of your intention, but I nevertheless allowed you to have the king, so that I would not seem to oppose you while you were doing what you thought best for yourselves. “And I held it in my wrath.” And being angry now too, both at that and at your later transgressions, I have withdrawn my alliance from you and have let you learn from events themselves how much better it would have been for you always to be led by those whom I appointed for your salvation than to entrust yourselves to royal power. Verses 12–14. “A conspiracy of injustice is Ephraim, in his hidden sin; birth pangs as of a woman in labor will come upon him.” And since you have been shown in everything (for, as is his custom, by “Ephraim” he means the whole people, naming the whole by a part) to put great concerted effort and diligence into acting ungodly and sinning against me in various ways, and sinning is for you a matter of inward meditation (for by “hidden sin” he means that the counsels of the soul are invisible to those outside), for these things, he says, you will fall into such punishments that, like a woman in labor giving birth, you will be seized by the pains of the evils that have come upon you. “Is this your wise son?” These are the works of your understanding, you who could not discern how great the difference is between pleasing me and being under my care, and

to incline toward the idols and to do what is contrary to what pleases me. "For now he will not hold out in the crushing of his children." So, having taken such counsel, you will not be able to bear your own destruction. Then, promising as usual a release from these evils, he adds: "I will rescue them from the hand of Hades, and redeem them from death." Yet after all this, once I have disciplined them with punishment, I will snatch all of you from what is very nearly death itself, beyond all human hope. "Where is your penalty, O death? Where is your sting, O Hades?" So that you will then be able to say these words, when you see punishment brought upon those who brought that manifold death upon you. He means the Assyrians. "Comfort is hidden from your eyes." For you will receive comfort amid such great evils. For the present it is still hidden from you, but then you will see it in the events themselves. Verse 15. "For he will divide between brothers." Some have understood it this way: of the Israelites he carried off the ten tribes into captivity but left the people of Judah. This did not happen as the Assyrian intended, since he wanted to treat Jerusalem and the people of Judah in the same way, but he was prevented by the power of God and by the angel's blow. So it was not he who made the division. Rather, the prophet wanted to describe how great the evils were in which those taken by the Assyrian would be tried, in order to show what God would grant them, since he meant afterward to punish those men. For the Assyrian took them captive and scattered them here and there, settling them in different places, so that they could neither give one another any help nor any longer take counsel together about escaping from there. Blessed David says the same: "He will gather together the dispersed of Israel," meaning that he will bring them back, scattered as they were here and there, beyond all hope. And elsewhere: "Let those redeemed by the Lord say so, whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy and gathered from the lands, from east and west and north and the sea," showing how widely they had been scattered. This is what he says here too: This man took you captive, led you away into a foreign land and scattered you into many different places, so that you could not draw any comfort from being gathered together in one place, and so that the evils might rather be intensified for you, divided as you were among different

Having said this to show both the power and the cruelty that the Assyrian used against them, he adds: "The Lord will bring a scorching wind from the desert upon him, and he will dry up his veins and make his springs desolate, and all his desirable vessels." For he will bring an enemy upon him. He means the king of the Babylonians, who will come upon him suddenly, like a scorching wind from some land lying far off, and will blot him out completely, turning his prosperity and the abundance of his goods into desolation. And all

his possessions, and everything he had prized so highly, he will blot out once and for all. For after "Where is your penalty, O death? Where is your sting, O Hades?" there follows "For he will divide between brothers" and what comes next. So the words "Comfort is hidden from your eyes" stand in parenthesis, showing that what is still hidden from them for the present will come to pass. Then, having spoken of their change for the better, he speaks again of the punishment that is about to overtake them now.

Verses 1–3. "Samaria will be destroyed, because she rose up against her God. They will fall by the sword, their infants will be dashed to the ground, and their pregnant women will be ripped open." Then, he says, he will grant those things beyond all hope to those who have become captives. But before that a most grievous destruction will overtake them now, because they chose what was contrary to God. For they will experience a most bitter war, so that the enemy will have no pity either on children still at the breast or on pregnant women. And since he has sufficiently chastened them by recalling the evils that would overtake them, he follows the promise he made earlier and, pointing to the release from their sufferings that would come to them, he adds: "Return, O Israel, to the Lord your God, for you have grown weak in your iniquities." But now turn to God and do what pleases him, considering how weak you have become because of your impiety. And since, beyond hope, you have received release from the evils that befell you, be eager from now on to attend to what is fitting. "Take words with you and return to the Lord your God. Say to him, 'You are able to take away all sin,' so that you may not receive iniquity and that you may receive good things." Use some such words with one another, by which you will turn to God wholly and entirely, and you will have an undoubting faith that God is fully able to take away all your sins, if he sees you repenting over the evils that befall you. Then, no longer inclining to impiety, you will have an abundant supply of good things from God. And all of you, urge one another to offer him unceasing hymns and thanksgivings for what you have received.

Verses 4–8. "Assyria will not save us; we will not mount on horses; never again will we say 'Our gods' to the works of our hands." For we will no longer need the Assyrian's help, since through God's care we have become stronger than he is. Nor will we take to horses and turn to flight, for God our helper is present. And from now on we will be far from that error of calling the things we make gods. "For in you he will show mercy to the orphan." Along with your gratitude toward God, take care also to show compassion toward the needy. "I will heal their dwellings; I will love them openly, for my anger has turned away from them." For if you do such things, he says, you will hear God

promising these things concerning you and carrying them out: that he will restore to you your former dwelling, with the same authority as before, and will show equal and like love toward all, since he has taken away all anger from you. "I will be like dew to Israel." I will nourish him with my care, just as dew is accustomed to nourish the crops. "He will blossom like a lily." He will be glorious in the sight of all. "And he will strike his roots like Lebanon." He will grow to a great multitude, like that mountain crowded with cedars. "His branches will spread out." Those who come from him will extend to the greatest prosperity. "And he will be like a fruitful olive tree, and his fragrance like frankincense." Through my care he will always flourish with fruit, and like frankincense he will be sweet to those who hear of his good fortune. "They will return and sit under his shelter, and they will live and be established with grain." Having returned, they will enjoy their own possessions and will continue to have an abundant supply of crops through my care. "And his memorial will blossom like a vine, like the wine of Lebanon." He will be as sweet and pleasing to those who see him as a vine in flower and the wine that is usually produced on Mount Lebanon. Verses 9–10. "What has Ephraim to do any longer with idols? I humbled him, and I will strengthen him." It is no longer fitting for you to have any fellowship with idols, since you will not need anything from them. For I, who surrounded you with humiliation for your zeal for them, raised you up again to your former prosperity once you repented. "Like a dense juniper—from me your fruit will be found." Since this tree is evergreen, he says that just as it always keeps its foliage, so these too will have a continual abundance of the good things they will enjoy through my care. In keeping with all this the prophet added: "Who is wise, and will understand these things? Or who is prudent, and will know them? For the ways of the Lord are straight, and the righteous will walk in them." Truly one would pronounce wise and prudent the person who knows what has been said and is zealous about it, for from this it will be possible for people, once separated from evil and zealously pursuing the good, to be set free from what is worse and to enjoy what is better. For everything God does is full of great rectitude: with it he brings punishment on those who sin, and he knows how to save those who repent. And one would pronounce righteous those who live by these things and know how to benefit from both, becoming more self-controlled under punishment and taking the enjoyment of the good things that come from repentance as an incentive to virtue. But one would pronounce wholly impious, and deserving every kind of evil, those who are capable of none of these things, because they are wasting away in their inclination toward the worse and for that reason cannot understand anything of what they ought to. Commentary on the Prophet Hosea.

COMMENTARY ON THE PROPHET JOEL. We now set out to begin our explanation of the blessed prophet Joel. The subject of his words is, broadly speaking, the same as that of all the prophets. They were eager to make known what would happen to the people, through the grace of the Holy Spirit given them for this purpose. As I said before, the first of them was blessed David, who long, long ago, and well before the events came to pass, told of everything that would happen to the people at various times. The other prophets did the same: they later repeated what he had said many years before, and did so almost at the very moment the events came to pass. In this way they reminded everyone of what had been foretold, and by speaking of things soon to happen they showed the truth of those predictions. Since the things that we said earlier were spoken by blessed David were various, and came to pass at different times, each of the prophets naturally appears to speak mostly of those things whose fulfillment was clearly near in his own day. But, led on by a certain sequence, they also added some of the things that would happen afterward, which of course had also been spoken by blessed David. Thus blessed Hosea speaks of what would later happen to the people at the hands of the Assyrians and the Babylonians, trying to chasten them by reminding them of these things. Joel also mentions the same things, since he lived at the same time as Hosea and was charged by spiritual revelation to speak of the same matters. But he adds as well what happened to them immediately after the return from Babylon, when a Scythian nation, led by Gog and his followers, came against them, intending to destroy them all utterly. Yet with God fighting on their side the Jews proved stronger than they were. Blessed David also spoke of these events in the Psalms.

Verses 1–3. "The word of the Lord that came to Joel the son of Bethuel." This too is a kind of superscription, like that of Hosea. It shows that, moved by God through a revelation that came to him, he says what follows for the benefit of the people. "Hear these things, you elders, and give ear, all you who inhabit the land, whether such things have happened in your days." Since they were rather indifferent to what was said, he tries to rouse them by fear of what he announces, so that the threat serves as the preface to his words. To you, then,

he says, who inhabit the land of promise, I address my word, and above all to the elders among you, who because of their many years ought to know somewhat more: do you know of anything like this happening either in your own time or in your fathers' time, such as God will now bring upon you? He has borne with you for a long time, but he bears with you no longer, since he sees that you gain nothing from his forbearance and, on the contrary, are going from bad to worse. "Tell your children about it, and let your children tell their children, and their children another generation." For the evils that are now coming upon you are so great that you must pass on the knowledge of them through your own descendants to those who come after, so that the strangeness of these events, when they hear of it, may chasten them too. Verses 4–5. "What the caterpillar left, the locust has eaten; what the locust left, the hopper has eaten; and what the hopper left, the blight has eaten." He means figuratively the evils that came upon them, and how each earlier evil was always made worse by those that followed. For there came, he says, Tiglath-pileser king of the Assyrians, who like a caterpillar ravaged no small part of your possessions. After him came Shalmaneser, who like a locust devoured still more of what was yours. After them came Sennacherib, who like a hopper brought total destruction on the ten tribes of Israel. And in addition to the rest, like a blight, came the Babylonian, who took the people of Judah as well and made the evil of captivity common to all. What then is the purpose of announcing these things? "Sober up, you drunkards, from your wine, and weep, all you who drink wine to drunkenness, for gladness and joy have been taken from your mouth." Put away the drunkenness that now holds you because of your inclination to the worse, so that you are unwilling even to see what you ought to do. Turn instead to tears and laments, in the hope that by repentance you may wash away your old drunkenness. For since what is going to happen will no longer [?] let you rejoice and be glad, it is better to turn to lament and tears in repentance, so that this may bring you some relief from the evils. Then, showing why these things are happening, he says: Verses 6–9. "For a nation has come up against my land, strong and without number; its teeth are a lion's teeth, and its molars a lion cub's." For many powerful enemies have come against my land, no different from lions, which slaughter and devour with their teeth and molars whatever animals fall in their way. So they destroy and subdue with their weapons. "It has made my vine a desolation, and my fig trees splinters." He has utterly destroyed and ruined all Israel, which I tended like a vine and made beautiful by my care, together with the fig trees in its midst, all of which he has shattered. By this he means to hint at those among them who were preeminent in wealth and power, since such trees seem to rise above the

vine plants. "He has searched it out thoroughly and cast it away; he has made its branches white." Going all around it, he uprooted it and led it away into captivity so completely that they were all no different from branches whitened and wholly withered once the vine has been torn out. "She will lament to me more than a bride girded with sackcloth for the husband of her youth." Then they will become aware of their own lawlessness, and they will turn to me with great laments, bewailing the evils that have befallen them, no less than a woman newly joined in marriage who then suddenly loses her husband, for the suddenness makes the grief of the loss heavier. "Sacrifice and libation have been cut off from the house of the Lord." Here he plainly indicates the evils that the Babylonians would bring upon them. For the liturgy performed in the temple of God ceased at the time when the Babylonian burned the house and took captive all who were in the city. Verses 10–13. "Mourn, you priests who minister at the altar, for the grain is ruined, the wine has dried up, the oil has dwindled, the farmers are put to shame. Lament, you estates, for the wheat and barley, for the harvest has perished from the field. The vine has dried up, and the fig trees have dwindled; pomegranate and palm and apple and all the trees of the field have dried up." Lament is fitting for those who serve as priests at the altar, because total barrenness has seized the plains from which they received the firstfruits and tithes that gave them an abundance of necessities. Lament is no less fitting for the land, which has been stripped of all its fruits, so that those who farm the land are put to shame, having labored in vain. And the same holds for all the estates in the country, since one can see nothing brought in as usual, neither of what grows from the ground nor of what is produced on trees. "For the sons of men have put joy to shame." That is, no one has any reason to rejoice; they would be ashamed not to mourn over evils so many and so great. By all this he shows that the land of the Israelites was seized by the most severe barrenness, so that the evil was twofold: enemies were treating them most cruelly, and the land refused to yield any of its fruits. What follows next? Verses 13–16. "Gird yourselves and beat your breasts, you priests; lament, you who minister at the altar; go in, sleep in sackcloth, you who minister to God, for sacrifice and libation have been withheld from the house of your God." Above all it befits you who have been appointed to the priesthood to put on sackcloth and not to take it off, whether you are sleeping or performing the divine liturgy, and to give yourselves to lament and mourning, because all the worship duly rendered to God has ceased. "Sanctify a fast." Since what is set apart and separated from the many is called holy, he says "Sanctify a fast" in the sense of: Devote yourselves to it; let go of everything and separate yourselves completely, set yourselves apart and dedicate yourselves to carrying it out. "Proclaim a service of worship." And

announce to everyone that they should let go of human affairs and devote themselves to the worship of God. "Gather the elders, all who dwell in the land, into the house of your God, and cry out earnestly to the Lord: Alas, alas, alas for the day! For the day of the Lord is near." And all of you in your land who, as is fitting, lead the rest, hurry to go together into the house of God while you are still free to enter, and cry out with many groans—for this is what he means by "Alas, alas, alas"—praying that you may not come to experience that day, which, according to God's threat, is not far off. "And it will come like misery upon misery." Pray that you may not fall into one evil after another. "For before your eyes the food has withered, and gladness and joy from the house of your God." Pray that you may not see those evils with your own eyes: that there will be a great and terrible failure of the crops, and that the worst of all will be added to it, that the house of God will be stripped of all the worship that is fitting and due to God, which could fill with the greatest gladness and joy those who look to what is right. Verses 17–20. "The heifers have leaped at their mangers." For, driven by the want that grips them, they will turn to leaping and agitation: by nature they seek food, but since there is nothing to feed them, they are moved to leap about in disorder. "The granaries have grown moldy from their plaster." Since it is customary to plaster grain storehouses for safekeeping, he says that, since there is nothing to put in them, the clay plastered on them will grow moldy, because nothing at all is being stored. "The storehouses have been ruined." Every place that usually receives any kind of produce will be useless, since there is nothing to put in it. "The winepresses have been torn down." These too will prove useless, since nothing is brought in. "For the grain has withered; what shall we lay up for ourselves?" By naming one part, the grain, he meant all the crops. He says this to confirm what was said before: since the crops have been completely taken away, every place that usually receives the crops will be useless, since there is nothing to store. "The herds of cattle have wept, because there was no pasture for them, and the flocks of sheep have perished." The animals have been deprived of their usual food in the countryside. "To you, O Lord, I will cry, for fire has consumed the fair places of the wilderness, and flame has set ablaze all the trees of the field." All of us together, in the evils that grip us, will ask you for release from such great evils, because the whole land, together with its trees, has been destroyed as if by fire. By "the fair places of the wilderness" he means the places in the mountains suitable for sowing, which are commonly called "plateaus." So he means that every place and every tree has been destroyed, as though burned up by fire. "And the beasts of the plain have looked up to you, because

the day that God has threatened against you. It is a day that can fill everyone with darkness and gloom, so that, with everything set as if in a cloud and mist, they cannot see. He does well to summon everyone to Mount Zion, where by Mosaic custom God was to be worshipped. In this way he might shame even those of the ten tribes who had abandoned the worship of God there and, on Jeroboam's advice, had devoted themselves to the heifers. He wanted them to give up that madness now at least, to look toward Mount Zion and the Lord of all who was to be worshipped there, and so to find release from the evils awaiting them. One can plainly see that this is what actually happened to those living around that place in the time of Sennacherib, when Hezekiah was king of Judea. "Like the dawn a great and strong people will spread over the mountains; there has been none like it from of old, and after it there will be none again, until the years of generations upon generations." At its proper time the dawn fills [?] the whole earth. In the same way, he means, a countless host of enemies will come and fill all the mountains. There has never been one like it before, and there will not easily be one again. "Before it is consuming fire, and behind it a blazing flame." Like fire, it will destroy everything all around by its onslaught [?]. "Like a garden of delight is the land before it, and behind it a plain of destruction." The places it has not yet invaded look no different from a paradise, with their many inhabitants and their beautiful buildings. But once it has arrived, one sees all that beauty destroyed at a stroke. "And there is no one who escapes from it." So it is hard for anyone to escape its assault. Verses 4–8. "Like the appearance of horses is their appearance, and like a horse, so they will charge; like the sound of chariots they will leap upon the mountaintops, and like the sound of a flame of fire devouring stubble, and like a great and strong people drawn up for battle." Here "like" is used for description, not for comparison, as in "How good is God to Israel," which means simply "good." For this [?]

is what he is saying here too. He means that one can see a great cavalry belonging to it. Those who ride the horses against their opponents are fearsome. It has a great many chariots that carry their attacks even to the highest places. They are just like fire spreading through stubble as they overrun every place they wish, for they are very many, exceedingly brave, and ready for war above all else. "Before its face peoples will be crushed; every face like the scorching of a pot." It is likely, then, that their onslaught will destroy very many, so that everyone who falls under it looks like a pot burnt by fire. He continues to describe it, so as to put greater fear into his hearers: "Like warriors they will run, and like men of war they will climb the walls." They rush into battle with great speed, and they will attack the walls of cities with great boldness, without fearing the harm that may come from there. "Each goes on his own way, and they will not turn aside from their paths, and no one will keep apart from his brother." They fight in formation. No one ever turns aside to the right or to the left. Each completes the course set and assigned to him, and they all charge into war in perfect harmony. "Weighed down with their weapons they will march, and with their missiles they will fall, and they will not be finished." A very strong proof that they are ready for war is that they are never separated from their arms. This is what he means: they do not lay down their arms even on the march, since they would rather bear the weight than be seen unarmed. Nor do they ever take off their arms when they stop to rest. "They will fall" stands for "they will recline and lie down." He means that they both march and rest with their arms. So he fittingly adds, "and they will not be finished," that is, they know no end of war, but are always in arms and at war. Verses 9–11. "They will seize the city and run upon its walls; they will climb onto the houses and come in through the windows like thieves." They subdue cities with great force and do not hesitate to run up onto the walls in their armour. Once inside, they overrun the whole city and enter every house through doors and windows, to carry off everything in it. That is what "like thieves" means: to carry off and steal everything. "Before its face the earth will be confounded and the heaven will be shaken; the sun and the moon will be darkened, and the stars will withdraw their light." The prophet seems to speak hyperbolically in most things, to astonish his hearers all the more, since whatever is said falls short of the deeds themselves. But here too he is clearly not saying that the elements are thrown into confusion and altered. People caught up in evils tend to have their perceptions changed by the pressure of their plight. So what he means is that everything is filled with confusion when it

advances upon the things of the earth. To those on earth who suffer such things from it, it seems that even the heaven is shaken and that the sun, moon and stars no longer shine, because the weight of their evils robs the sufferers of the sense of light. "And the Lord will utter his voice before his army, for his camp is very great; for strong are the works of his words; for great is the day of the Lord, great and very manifest, and who can stand it?" God himself will also speak over what is happening, since it is by his will that you will suffer these things because of your own wickedness. Then you will know that this whole battle array is his, since it moves by his will. You will also know how great is the power of his words. He spoke them long ago, when you did not believe what was said. Later he carried them out and showed that every word of his is a mighty deed. You will know, too, that the day of the evils coming upon you is so great and so manifest. That day will come by God's will, and no one will be able to endure the magnitude of the evils that happen then. Having described here how severe the enemies are, he adds: Verses 12–14. "And now the Lord your God says: Turn to me with all your heart, with fasting and weeping and mourning; rend your hearts and not your garments, and turn to the Lord your God, for he is merciful and compassionate, patient and abounding in mercy, and he relents over evils." Since this is how things stand, come, let us all change our thinking from worse to better. Let us all turn to God with our whole mind, with fasting and weeping and mourning. Let us not tear our garments, as you often do out of habit rather than from the heart. Let us open our hearts and bring them bare to God, so that you may put off your old wickedness and show plainly that you hold to his purpose. For it is quite likely that he, who loves humankind exceedingly and shows great forbearance toward sinners, will change his mind about the evils he planned to bring upon you. "Who knows whether he will turn and relent, and leave behind him a blessing, a sacrifice and drink offering to the Lord your God?" Not all of you, struck as you are by your own consciences, may see this clearly. But we ought to know very well that if we change and are willing to turn to him, he too will repent of what he decreed against us, and in the time to come he will grant us a supply of his good things. This is what he calls a blessing. Its first sign will be that we are again allowed to offer him sacrifices and drink offerings as was customary. For it is clear that God is said to bless when he does good by his gifts, and so he has called such a gift a blessing. Then he adds: Verses 15–18. "Blow the trumpet in Zion, sanctify a fast, proclaim a solemn service, gather (19) The codex has ὑπολήψεται in the first hand, but ὑπολείψεται in the second.

the people, sanctify an assembly, choose elders, gather infants at the breast; let the bridegroom come out of his chamber, and the bride out of her bridal room." Since God has so kind and loving a purpose, he says, this is what we must do. We must gather everyone to Mount Zion with trumpet signals, set apart and proclaim a fast for the worship of God, and gather all the people, so that once they are assembled they may set themselves to a change of heart. The old should be there, and the infants too, down to those still nursing. Even the newly married should withdraw from the joys of marriage to attend to repentance. In short, every age and every person, whatever their condition, should leave everything else and be present for the repentance. "Between the step and the altar the priests who minister to the Lord will weep and say: Spare your people, O Lord, and do not make your inheritance a reproach, for nations to rule over them, lest they say among the nations, Where is their God?" All who stand before the altar, who have been appointed to the work of the priesthood and assigned to the divine service, should beg God with tears for reconciliation. Then he may spare his own people and not hand them over entirely to the power of the nations. Nor will he leave them to be taunted among the nations that we boast in vain of our kinship with God. To this he adds: "And the Lord was jealous for his land and spared his people." He is not reporting something that has already happened but saying what will happen. He will be jealous for you and spare you, he says, if he sees you repenting and doing what has been set out. The tense has been changed in keeping with Hebrew idiom, so that he says "spared" instead of "will spare." We have shown this elsewhere from the Psalms as well. Clearly he is not speaking of things already done, since the evils came upon them after this announcement. Verses 19–20. "And the Lord answered and said to his people: Behold, I am sending you grain and wine and oil, and you will be filled with them, and I will no longer make you a reproach among the nations. I will drive the one from the north far from you and drive him into a waterless land; I will make his front vanish into the first sea and his rear into the last sea, and his rottenness will rise and his stench will rise." "The Lord answered and said" stands for "will answer and will say," since here too the tense has been changed. He means that he will certainly restore an abundance of crops to you when you repent and will rout your enemies. And God did this after the return. Likewise blessed David, foretelling the return of the people, first said: "Praise befits you, O God, in Zion, and to you a vow shall be paid in Jerusalem," and then, "Holy is your temple, wonderful in righteousness." He was showing that they would return to

their own land and would again offer God the customary worship in the temple. After this he adds: "You have visited the earth and drenched it; you have greatly enriched it," and so on, describing the abundance they would then enjoy. In the same way, here too he speaks of the restoration of plenty and says, "I will no longer leave you under the nations," for that is the meaning of "I will no longer make you a reproach among the nations." He also says: I will punish those who came against you and hand them over to desolation and utter destruction. First I will punish the Assyrians through the Babylonians. After that I will utterly destroy the Babylonians through the Persians. I will make their destruction so complete that, as with those who die and are utterly dead, their decay and stench will escape no one's notice. That is what he means by rottenness and stench, as of people already dead and lying as corpses. And "will rise" means, he says, that everyone will hear of it. What is the cause of all this? "Because his works have been magnified." For in punishing them God will show the greatness of his works. Then he adds accordingly: Verses 21–22. "Take courage, O land; rejoice and be glad, for the Lord has done great things. Take courage, beasts of the plain, for the plains of the wilderness have sprouted, for the tree has borne its fruit; the vine and the fig tree have given their strength." So the land will be glad at the greatness of what God has done, now that it has recovered the yield of its crops. The beasts of the plain too will enjoy abundant pasture. Above all, the trees will provide abundant fruit for those in need. "And you children of Zion, rejoice and be glad in the Lord your God, for he has given you food for righteousness, and he will rain on you the early and the late rain as before; the threshing floors will be filled with grain, and the vats will overflow with wine and oil." What he said earlier had been taken away, he now says is restored. All who gather on Mount Zion, he says, and offer the worship due to God would have good reason to be glad. They will enjoy an abundance of crops, which God has justly given them because they repented of their sins. He will also give them timely and sufficient rain, so that both the crops that grow from the ground and the fruit of the trees will come to them in great plenty. "And I will repay you for the years that the locust and the grasshopper and the blight and the caterpillar devoured, my great army that I sent against you. You will eat your fill and praise the name of the Lord your God, who has done wonders for you, and my people will never be put to shame. You will know that I am in the midst of Israel, and that I am the Lord your God and there is no other besides me, and my people will never again be put to shame." So whatever

the enemies consumed of your goods in all their various ways when they invaded, I will restore to you. For it is clear that this is what he calls locust, grasshopper, blight and caterpillar. Then you will have rich enjoyment of what is given and will offer God the hymns you owe him for the great and wonderful things he has done for you. You will no longer be ashamed that I left you without help when you fell into so many evils. Instead, you will learn exactly from the events themselves that I am among you, as the only master and guardian you have. Verses 28–32. "And afterward I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh. Your sons and your daughters will prophesy, your old men will dream dreams, and your young men will see visions. Even on my male and female servants in those days I will pour out my Spirit, and they will prophesy. I will show portents in the heaven and on the earth, blood and fire and vapour of smoke. The sun will be turned to darkness and the moon to blood before the great and manifest day of the Lord comes. And everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved, for on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be those who escape, as the Lord has said, and those who bring good news, whom the Lord has called." I will give all of you abundant care, he says, for that is what "I will pour out my Spirit" means. Those who lived under the Old Testament did not know the Holy Spirit as a single being, distinct in hypostasis from the others, who is of God and from God. They used "Holy Spirit," and every expression like it, for God's grace, care and goodwill. In the same way "soul" is used of God: "Your new moons and your sabbaths my soul hates." Here he means the disposition by which he hated the feasts. The same is true of "Your good Spirit will lead me on level ground," meaning: because you care for me, you will provide these things in your great goodness. So too with "Do not take your Holy Spirit from me," meaning: do not withdraw your care for me. There are many other such passages, but we will not lengthen this writing needlessly. He says something similar here too: I will then give you such abundant care that everyone will be granted visions and will be able to declare something about what is to come. Besides all this, I will work wonders in the heaven and on the earth: great slaughter of your enemies and punishment upon them, and [?] and vapour of smoke hinting at God's wrath. The sun too will be turned to darkness and the moon to blood, to the eyes of those who see them, because of the greatness of the evils that befall them. These things will happen before that day, which he will make manifest through the

punishment of the enemies. Through all this, those who call on the name of God will find salvation. They will also go up to Mount Zion and Jerusalem safe and sound, since God promised these things and granted that the good news be announced to all whom he has called to this return. This, then, is the plain sense of the passage. But blessed Peter used it, very fittingly, when he spoke to the Jews at the descent of the Holy Spirit. For the law had a shadow of all things to come, and the people were granted God's care because of their expectation of what would be revealed at the coming of Christ the Lord. Everything in their time was small and happened as if in a shadow, so that it was described in terms grander than the facts warranted. But the truth of these words proved to be fulfilled in Christ the Lord. Then everything was great and full of awe, truly new and wondrous, and far beyond what happened under the law. So the events of the Old Testament hold the place of a riddle, while the greatness of what took place in Christ the Lord is the truth. Thus blessed David says of the people, "His soul was not abandoned to Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption." This cannot be understood of what actually happened. He is speaking metaphorically, or rather hyperbolically, to say that they were rescued from the danger of corruption. But the real truth of these words is shown in Christ the Lord. His soul was not left in Hades but was restored to his body through the resurrection, and his body underwent no corruption at all. It did not merely remain in the form in which he died, but was changed into an immortal and incorruptible nature. So the former was a riddle and this the truth. That is why blessed Peter too used the saying. It had once been spoken metaphorically for a certain reason, but now it had been truly fulfilled in the events themselves. So people ought to believe what had now happened far more than they had once marvelled at that. Divine Scripture has many such passages, and the present one is clearly similar. The Lord God, speaking to the Jews through the prophet in the manner customary at that time, said that he would give them his care abundantly, along with the rest, in the sense we have explained. But all of it truly came to pass in Christ the Lord. The sun really was darkened, and the moon with it. Great portents took place in the heaven and many on the earth. The saving blood of Christ the Lord appeared. Fire appeared too, in the form of the Spirit who came, showing his power. A vapour of smoke went before it, as a sign of the punishment that would overtake those who had dared to crucify him. Then indeed all shared in the

…of the grace of the Holy Spirit, and were counted worthy of many different gifts. Some of them foretold the future; others worked a great many wonders, to confirm the greatness of what was taking place and to prove the glory that surrounds the Lord Christ. So what the prophet had spoken long ago, figuratively or by way of hyperbole, [?] the demonstration of the facts, with the words even falling short of the facts. The reason, then, both for this saying and for the others that the prophets spoke about other matters and that the blessed apostles took up and applied to the dispensation of the Lord Christ, may justly be supposed to be something like this (18). It was so that the history of the events of that time might be seen not to be invented, and so that the greatness of present things might be proved all the more by comparison with them.
