It was also so that it might be shown precisely, through all of them, that those things would bear some affinity to these, and yet that what came before falls as far short of what is present as a shadow must fall short of the body, even if it seems to have some connection with it (19). (p. 150) Now the prophet, having announced in what he said before the return from Babylon and the various good things that would come to them at that time, very consistently goes on to add what follows.

Verses 1–3. "For behold, in those days and at that time, when I turn back the captivity of Judah and Jerusalem, I will gather all the nations and bring them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat. There I will enter into judgment with them on behalf of my people and my inheritance Israel, who were scattered among the nations; and they divided up my land. They cast lots for my people, gave the boys to prostitutes, and sold the girls for wine and drank it." In these words he is speaking of what comes after the return. He indicates both the ascent of Gog and his followers, which they will make when they rush against Jerusalem with a great multitude, and the destruction they will suffer for this audacity. For when I bring you back to Jerusalem, he says, many nations will gather against you from many places. He says "I will gather all the nations" not because he leads them, but because he allows them to put their own purpose into action. And he punished those who had undertaken the ascent against the Israelites. They achieved nothing of what they [?] against the Jews, but by the decisive weight of God they suffered a fearful and extraordinary punishment. (p. 151) That is why he says that he himself gathers "all the nations." What he means is this: "I allowed them to follow their own wicked intent and rush against Jerusalem, so that by exacting justice from them right there I might give everyone a demonstration both of my care for the people and of my own (20) power." So, having said "I will gather all the nations," he went on: "And I will bring them down into [(15) The manuscript reads λειφθ. — Patrologia Graeca 66.]

the valley of Jehoshaphat." That is: "I will lead them there, to Jerusalem. There, as if convening a trial against them on behalf of my people, I will punish them justly for what they did against my people. They wanted to scatter them everywhere and to divide up the land, which belongs to me and in which my people lived by my will, and to divide the people themselves by lot. On top of all this, they dared to sell off their children, boys and girls alike, so that through them they might gratify their own lust with prostitutes and have drink in abundance." Having said this about Gog and his followers, he adds: Verses 4–8. "And what are you to me, Tyre and Sidon and all Galilee of the foreigners? Are you paying me back for something, or are you bearing a grudge against me? Swiftly and speedily I will return your recompense on your own heads. For you took the silver, and carried the choice and fine things into your temples. You sold the sons of Judah and the sons of Jerusalem to the sons of the Greeks, to drive them out of their own borders. (p. 152) Behold, I will rouse them from the place to which you sold them, and I will return your recompense on your own heads. I will sell your sons and your daughters into the hands of the sons of Judah, and they will sell them into captivity, to a nation far away; for the Lord has spoken." When the Tyrians and Sidonians and all the neighboring foreigners saw Gog and his followers advancing on Jerusalem, they thought they had a chance to wipe out the Israelites completely. They bore a grudge against them because the Israelites had often fought them and, with divine help, had overcome them. So he says this: "Why have you, nursing a grudge and finding an opportunity to do what you pleased, dared such things against those who belong to me? Know that I will swiftly bring on you the punishment for this intent, because you took everything they owned and carried it into your temples. You even sold their sons, hoping to drive them all out of their own borders. For this I will exact justice from you. (p. 153) I will free them from the constraint that holds them, and I will now make them stronger than their enemies, so that they repay you for what you dared against them. They will take your sons and daughters captive and sell them somewhere far away, from where you will never be able to recover them." He inserted this against the Tyrians and Sidonians and all the neighboring peoples because at that time they had tried to join Gog and his followers in destroying the Jews. Then he keeps to his own sequence and says: Verses 9–12. "Proclaim this among the nations: sanctify a war; rouse the warriors; draw near and go up, all you men of war. Beat your plowshares into swords and your sickles into spears; let the weak say, 'I am strong.' Gather together and come in,

all you nations round about, and assemble there; let the gentle man become a warrior." Above he said, "I will gather them," for the reason already given; in the same way here he speaks as if he himself were giving them orders. "All of you," he says, "who hold this intent against those who belong to me, gather with great zeal and join battle against them. (p. 154) Turn your farming tools into weapons, so that you have enough weapons for your whole multitude of attackers, and so that with greater numbers it may be easy for you to bring about the destruction of all the Israelites, as you have chosen to do." Then he states why he rouses them to war: "Let all the nations rouse themselves and go up into the valley of Jehoshaphat, for there I will sit to judge all the nations round about." That is: "For [?] you who wish to come together against those who live in Jerusalem, I allow you to do it, so that there I may exact justice from you for this audacity and this attempt, destroying all of you, gathered from everywhere, by various deaths." What then? Verse 13. "Send out the sickles, for the vintage has come; come in and tread, for the winepress is full; the vats overflow, for their evils have multiplied." So great will be their slaughter, and so complete the fall of them all as they take up arms against one another, that you who live in Judea will have no need to fight. Rather, you will think a vintage has arrived, when sickles are needed, and men to tread the winepress so that the wine may be pressed out and flow. "Something like this is happening now. (p. 155) Since the war is being won by my power and they all lie slaughtered, you must be there to see them cut down like clusters at the vintage, falling on one another in the slaughter, and to see the blood of the slain overflowing like a trodden winepress. In this way their evils will be multiplied, and so great will be their slaughter, not because you fight, but because they turn their own right hands against one another, as I see fit." Then he consistently goes on to what follows. Verses 14–17. "Sounds have resounded in the valley of judgment, for the day of the Lord is near in the valley of judgment." Fearful sounds will rise from the multitude of the slain in this valley, where "I will exact justice from them for their audacity against you." He called the valley of Jehoshaphat the valley of judgment because of the punishment that God was going to bring on them there. "The sun and the moon will be darkened, and the stars will withdraw their light." It follows that he said the slain will have no light. Then, to show how these things will come about, he adds: "And the Lord will cry out from Zion; he will cry out, and from Jerusalem he will utter his voice, and heaven and earth will be shaken. But the Lord will spare his people, and the Lord will strengthen the sons of Israel; and you will know that I am the Lord your God, who dwells in Zion, on my holy mountain." (p. 156) For God himself, he says, who decreed that the lawful worship be offered to him in Zion,

will utter a great voice against them. Heaven and earth will seem almost to be shaken by it, because of the astonishing nature of what is happening and of so great a slaughter carried out so astonishingly. God will bring this about, sparing his own people and making them strong against their adversaries, so that it may become clear to everyone that he is truly the God of all, and the Lord who is accustomed to be worshiped on Mount Zion. Verses 18–21. "And Jerusalem will be holy, and foreigners will no longer pass through her. And in that day the mountains will drip sweetness, and the hills will flow with milk, and all the channels of Judah will flow with water; and a spring will go out from the house of the Lord and water the brook of the rushes." Jerusalem will be shown to be holy by the facts themselves, since no foreigner will dare to set foot in her any longer. All the Jews living in the land of promise will have a great abundance of good things, so that the mountains and the hills will yield them many fruits of every kind. The springs too will yield their wealth of water as usual, (p. 157) [the gifts usually supplied from the divine temple (21)] and will pour out an abundant wealth of good things for those who come in there and are eager to fulfill their duties to God. This is what he calls the spring going out from the house of the Lord. It will be so great that its generosity reaches even those far away. Then he says, "And Egypt will be made desolate," and Idumea along with it, for what they did against you and for killing many of you unjustly. He adds: "But Judea" will be inhabited securely in its own prosperity, and Jerusalem by its own people. To this he adds: "And I will avenge their blood and will not leave it unpunished; and the Lord will dwell in Zion." It is as if he said: "I will surround with the most extreme punishments anyone who still attempts anything against them, and I will remain among them, showing myself from now on through my ineffable care, which I will go on providing for them abundantly for all time to come."

[?] OF THE PROPHET. It is clear that the blessed prophet Amos too, whom by God's grace we now set out to interpret, speaks throughout almost his whole prophecy (p. 158) about what would happen to the people. He tells of what the ten tribes would suffer first at the hands of the Assyrians, and of what was going to happen at the hands of the Babylonians to Jerusalem and the tribe of Judah, and also to the rest (22) of that kingdom. The prophets did not concern themselves with this without reason. God exercised all his care for the people with a view to the manifestation of the Lord Christ, which would take place at its proper time for the common salvation of all humankind. That is why he set them apart from the nations, marked them off by circumcision, arranged for them to have a land of their own, and commanded them through the ordinance of the law to perform his worship in a separate place, on Mount Zion. In this way, when the Lord Christ appeared, in keeping with the prophetic announcements and with the arrangement made from the beginning for the people with this end in view, he would make it clear to all people that God had not introduced the salvation of all people as a later novelty. Rather, God had predetermined it from the beginning and long ages before, as blessed Paul says. Holding this purpose in himself, he chose Abraham, established the race descended from him, and cared for it in the way we have described. So when the Lord Christ later appeared from them according to the flesh for the salvation of all people, (p. 159) it would be evident that he had come to fulfill the dispensation in accordance with what had been decreed from the beginning. For these reasons he also arranged for the whole people to be deported through the captivity, and then brought back those of them whom he wished. The tribe of Judah alone led them; it alone received the return as a whole, since from it the Lord Christ was to appear according to the flesh. From each of the other tribes only a few followed it and came back with it. Through the captivity that took place, and the return accomplished in this way, God's purpose in his care for the people would become clear: he was doing everything for the sake of the one who would appear from them for the salvation of all people. But those who had endured that captivity must not fall into complete despair and mingle with the nations, with no further room either for the return or for remaining separate from the other nations. [(22) For λοιπούς ('rest') it seems we should read περιοίκους ('neighbors').]

So he announced long beforehand through the prophets both that the captivity would happen and that the return would follow it, so that, sustained by these hopes, they might wait for the return even after the captivity had taken place. And the return did happen, in the way we have described and for the reason we have given. (p. 160) That is why these things had been spoken long, long ago by blessed David in many of the psalms. As the time of the events drew near, divine grace raised up the prophets. At one time they announced the imminent evils from the Assyrians; at another they showed what would come from the Babylonians after those. Besides all this they spoke of the return, and of whatever else that took place at that time it was fitting to [?]. Since the earlier events turned out in keeping with the predictions, their fulfillment guaranteed that what was foretold to come after them would also, in all likelihood, happen as predicted. Hence all of them speak of what was done both [?] and by the Babylonians. These invasions did happen separately, the Assyrians attacking first and the Babylonians later, with some time between the events. Yet it was a single, complete captivity, which began with the Assyrians and the ten tribes and was completed with the remaining tribes, those of the kingdom of Judah, at the Babylonian siege. This, then, is why the other prophets too announce these things and devoted their whole attention to them in their discourse, (p. 161) except that they added a few brief things not far removed from them. The present prophet did something similar. He clearly composed his whole prophecy about what would happen to Israel and Judah at the hands of the Assyrians and the Babylonians. But in the opening he also briefly mentioned what would happen at the same time to the neighbors who [?] had done the Israelites great harm. He did this to make clear that God had handed the people over to the calamities brought by the Assyrians and the Babylonians not out of harshness, neglect, or a change of mind, but because he wished to correct their impieties. At the same time he punished those neighbors who had sinned against them, and he would never have exacted justice from them on their account if he had not held the people in very high regard. By punishing those who had wronged them he showed his care for them; and in bringing evils upon the people themselves he made it clear that he did so not out of harshness, contempt, or hatred, but out of care, for their discipline, their correction, and their restoration to something better. This, then, is the subject of the book. (p. 162) So the prophet spoke of everything concerning the people, while briefly indicating what was going to happen at that time to the neighboring peoples, chiefly at the hands of the Babylonians, for the wrongs they had done against Israel, for the reason I have given. He delivers his prophecy not in Jerusalem but in places belonging to the nations near Israel, and at the shrine in Bethel, where to the idols [?] were offered

the sacrifices of the Israelites. If he had prophesied in Jerusalem, he would not have become known either to Israel or to the other nations he was going to speak about, since none of them would even agree to set foot in Jerusalem. By delivering his prophecy in the places mentioned, he was bound to be seen both by Israel and by the nations that lived nearby, who often mixed with one another through the worship of idols. In this way all those he spoke about would know what was said about them. Having received the prophecy before the events and then seen its fulfillment close at hand, they would have greater faith in the divine grace at work in the prophets. Some say that the prophets did not rebuke King Uzziah when he took on the works of the priesthood, and that for this reason they all stopped prophesying. (p. 163) This seems to me rather a fable. The book of Hosea reads: "The word of the Lord that came to Hosea son of Beeri in the days of Uzziah," and so on. In the prophet Isaiah it says: "The vision that Isaiah son of Amoz saw, which he saw concerning Judea and concerning Jerusalem in the reign of Uzziah," and so on. In the present prophet it says: "The words of Amos, which came to him in Kariatharim, from Tekoa, which he saw concerning Jerusalem in the days of Uzziah king of Judah." How then could prophecy have ceased in the days of Uzziah, as their account claims, when the titles of their own books show that Hosea, Isaiah, and Amos prophesied in the days of Uzziah? It is also clear that if the prophets had been commanded by spiritual revelation to rebuke Uzziah, they would never have put it off, since they obeyed divine revelations rather than showing deference to a king who was doing wrong. And if they had received no revelation to do so, no one could justly blame them for not undertaking something that divine revelation had not shown them. In everything they were accustomed to follow spiritual revelations, speaking or not speaking in accordance with them. They would never (p. 164) have chosen to speak or to keep silent about anything contrary to them [?]. I do not know how this story came to be current among many (25), but since it seems to me flatly contrary to what is written in the books, I thought it wrong to pass over it in silence. The whole book of the prophecy is occupied with Israel and Judah and with what befell both of them, first at the hands of the Assyrians and later at the hands of the Babylonians, while in the opening it briefly recalls the evils that would befall the neighboring peoples. We say that the reason for what concerns the people is the one we gave earlier: God bestowed all his care on the people for the sake of the one who was to be revealed [?] from them—

[?]… the Lord Christ according to the flesh, who would appear for the salvation of all. Before the rest, however, he has set out what would happen to the neighbouring peoples. This proves that God did not treat the affairs of his people carelessly either, since he exacts punishment from others even for their lawlessness against them. But now we must begin the book, which runs as follows:

Verses 1–2. “The words of Amos, which came to him in Kariathiarim from Tekoa, which he saw concerning Jerusalem in the days of Uzziah king of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash king of Israel, two years before the earthquake.” As we said with the other prophets, this serves as a kind of heading. It shows what the book is about, who spoke it, about whom, and when. It is not at all surprising that he said “words which he saw concerning Jerusalem,” even though he was also going to speak of what happened to Israel, that is, to the ten tribes, and no less of the neighbouring peoples. He regarded what concerned Jerusalem, that is, the people around it, as the most important matter of all. This people was the tribe of Judah, as we said earlier. Everything else is said and happens as a consequence, on its account. So he indicated the subject by naming the most important part of the prophecy. Then, beginning the prophecy, he says: “The Lord has spoken from Zion, and from Jerusalem he has uttered his voice; and the pastures of the shepherds mourned, and the summit of Carmel dried up.” He began his discourse from this point most admirably. He was speaking not in Jerusalem but in places that belonged to the nations and to the kingdom of Israel. So he rightly put first the words, “He has spoken from Zion, and from Jerusalem he has uttered his voice.” In this way his hearers would not attribute what was said to the demons worshipped in that region. Instead, all would know that he speaks these things by the will of God. Being Maker and Lord of all, God commanded that the worship due to him be carried out on Mount Zion according to the ordinance of the law. Now he gives the prophet these things to say, and in due time he will bring what is announced to pass. The words “The pastures of the shepherds mourned, and the summit of Carmel dried up” mean this: by his sentence all the neighbouring peoples, together with their leaders, will be turned to mourning. So too will the people of Israel along with them. He called them “the summit of Carmel” because they lived around that place and had used their eminence to no good purpose. Then, dividing his discourse part by part, he speaks about each of the neighbouring peoples. Verses 3–5. “And the Lord said: For three impieties of Damascus, and for four, I will not turn away from it, because they sawed the pregnant women of the Gileadites with iron saws. And I will send fire upon the house of Hazael, and it shall devour the foundations of the son of Hader; and I will shatter the bars of Damascus, and I will destroy the inhabitants from the plain

of On, and I will cut off a tribe from the men of Haran; and the people of Syria, called by that name, shall be taken captive, says the Lord.” He says “for three and four” in place of “for very many.” The number after one and two is called plural, so by “three” he means many, and by “four” he means many more. He wants to say that he overlooked many impieties of Damascus. But since they persist and stretch their impiety to the utmost, he can no longer help turning away from them and hating them. Then he passes over their other transgressions and names the one they committed against the Israelites. In this way he shows that, although they had committed many impieties, he will punish them above all for the wrongs done to those he had been eager to care for. So by “the Gileadites” he means the Israelites, naming a part for the whole, since Gilead was a part of Israel. He says: they carried their lawlessness against them so far that they cut their pregnant women in two with iron saws. (He seems to say this to show their savagery, since they did not spare even pregnant women. They cut them open, either literally with saws or with swords by the law of war. He said “with iron saws” to give greater emphasis to what happened.) For these things, he says, I will bring upon them those who will destroy them, so that even their palaces will be torn down. That is what “the foundations of the son of Hader” means. All the strength of their capital will also be taken away, which is what “I will shatter the bars of Damascus” indicates. Indeed, I will destroy all of them, even those of Haran who lived near them, who were suspected of giving them much help from their own forces. In short, I will hand over to total captivity everyone of that kingdom that bears the name Syria. Verses 6–8. “Thus says the Lord: For three impieties of Gaza and for four I will not turn away from them, because they took captive the captivity of Solomon, to shut them up in Idumea.” He says the same thing here too: they have committed many impieties and persist in their wicked purpose, so I will bear it no longer. I will punish them above all for this. Solomon had taken the Idumeans captive and placed them under the authority of the Israelites, and they stayed in that condition for a very long time. Then these people attacked, took that captive population away by the law of war, and forced them to go back to Idumea. Here too he names the offence they committed against the Israelites. What then? “And I will send fire upon the walls of Gaza, and it shall devour its foundations; and I will destroy the inhabitants of Ashdod, and a tribe shall be removed from Ashkelon; and I will bring my hand upon Ekron, and the remnant of the Philistines shall perish, says the Lord.” He says: I will bring the same punishment on these too. Here too he calls war “fire,” since it will consume them in the same way:

it will strip away the walls of the city, tear the whole city up from its foundations, and destroy its inhabitants along with those who live in Ashdod and Ashkelon. Nor will I spare those in Ekron. Gaza is mentioned because it was chief among the Philistine lordships, but he is saying that the punishment will come upon all the Philistines alike. That is why he adds: “And the remnant of the Philistines shall perish, says the Lord.” He means: in short, I will destroy all the Philistines, just as earlier he said that the whole people called by the name of Syria would be taken captive. Verses 9–10. “Thus says the Lord: For three impieties of Tyre and for four I will not turn away from it, because they shut up the captivity of Solomon in Idumea, and did not remember the covenant of brothers. And I will send fire upon the walls of Tyre, and it shall devour its foundations.” He says: I have borne with these people too for a long time, but since they stretch their impiety to the utmost, I will not tolerate it. Above all, they arranged for Solomon's captives to go into Idumea and shared in this lawlessness with the Philistines. They of all people ought to have refrained from such a thing, remembering the treaties of friendship that Solomon and their own king had made with each other. Yet they took no account of these and have now done such things. For this, by my will, the enemy will come, strip away their walls, and utterly destroy the [?]

Verses 11–12. “Thus says the Lord: For three impieties of Idumea and for four I will not turn away from it, because he pursued his brother with the sword, and ravaged the womb upon the earth, and seized his own horror as a testimony, and kept up his onslaught to victory.” He says: I have put up with these people for their very many impieties, but I will not tolerate them as they go on in impiety to the utmost. This is above all because they stirred up war against the Israelites. They were not even ashamed of their kinship with them, or of the fact that both peoples came from brothers, the one descended from Esau and the other from Jacob. That is what he means by “his brother.” “He ravaged the womb upon the earth” means that they slaughtered them all and struck them to the ground, which was an offence against the womb that bore them. He had called them brothers because they were born of brothers, so he called the killing of brothers a ravaging of the womb, as though in this way they had outraged their common mother. [?] They did things to them full of horror, in order to give onlookers greater proof of their own cruelty. They also attacked them with great and violent force, showing the same hatred toward them to the very end. That is what “kept to victory” means. And what follows for these things? “And I will send fire upon Teman, and it shall devour the foundations of its walls.”

Teman was the famous city of the Idumeans. So, he says, I will bring war upon them, and it will utterly destroy their greatest and most royal city, tearing it up from its foundations along with its walls. Verses 13–15. “Thus says the Lord: For three impieties of the sons of Ammon and for four I will not turn away from them, because they ripped open the pregnant women of the Gileadites, so as to widen their borders. And I will kindle fire upon the walls of Rabbah, and it shall devour its foundations with shouting in the day of war, and it shall be shaken in the day of its end; and Milcom shall go into captivity, their priests and their rulers together, says the Lord.” He says much the same about these people. He says he is especially angry with them because they ripped open the pregnant women of the Israelites, imitating the savagery of the Damascenes. By this lawlessness against pregnant women they hoped to destroy the whole nation and acquire its land, and so enlarge their own territory. So, he says, the enemy will come for these things. He will take away all the walls of Rabbah, which is their capital, tear the city up from its foundations, and stir up such a war against them that their wailing over what happens will be unbearable. The city itself will suffer total destruction, and their idol [?] with the rulers of the people.

Verses 1–3. “Thus says the Lord: For three impieties of Moab and for four I will not turn away from it, because they burned the bones of the king of Idumea to lime.” Clearly, throughout the rest of the passage he speaks of the transgressions the other nations contrived against Israel. Here too he has not changed the pattern of what came before by saying that he brings these things to avenge the king of Idumea, for he is seen to have threatened the Idumeans themselves with similar things above. The reason is this. The king of the Idumeans once wanted to make peace and friendship with the Israelites. The Moabites were enraged at this and, out of hatred for the Israelites, made war on Idumea. Having won, they offered the slaughter of the king of the Idumeans to their own idols as a kind of victory sacrifice, and even burned him whole as a burnt offering in the sacrifice. This is what “they burned the bones of the king of Idumea to lime” means. He is speaking of the offering and slaughter in which they reduced his bones to lime, as though making a whole burnt offering of him. So he says he is angry with the Moabites because, out of hatred for the Israelites, they showed such fury against the king of Idumea. And what follows for these things? “I will send fire upon Moab, and it shall devour the foundations of its cities; and Moab shall die in powerlessness, with a noise and with the sound of the trumpet; and I will destroy judges from

it, and I will kill all its rulers with it, says the Lord.” He says: the enemy will come and destroy all their cities. They will be brought down to utter weakness, unable to withstand the scale of the evils brought upon them, and will meet death amid a very great noise and the blare of war trumpets. In short, their destruction will be so great that not a single judge or ruler of theirs will be left, for all of them will have perished once and for all. Verses 4–5. Having told in this way what would happen to the neighbouring peoples for their lawlessness against the Israelites, the prophet now turns to what would happen to the people itself. He shows two things. The neighbours were to be punished for their wrongs against Israel, since in this way they were offending against God, to whom Israel belonged. And Israel will not escape punishment either, because they have been ungrateful to God. He mentions the tribe of Judah first, as most deserving of punishment, because although they lived beside the divine temple, they were as impious as anyone. He speaks as follows: “Thus says the Lord: For three impieties of the sons of Judah and for four I will not turn away from them.” He says that he hates these people too, who have often been impious, since they have persisted in their impiety. Then he also gives the cause of the punishment: “because they rejected the law of the Lord and did not keep his commandments; and their vain things which they made led them astray, the things their fathers followed after.” For these too, he says, refused to take any account of my laws and commandments, and devoted themselves to the worship of idols, following the ways of their fathers. What then? “I will send fire upon Judah, and it shall devour the foundations of Jerusalem.” He says: through enemies I will destroy everyone in that kingdom, and Jerusalem along with them. It is plain that he says this about the Babylonians, for they brought Jerusalem down and took the people of the tribe of Judah captive. Yet in what follows, when he announces the evils coming upon Israel, that is, the ten tribes, he naturally mentions the Assyrians, who took them captive and carried them off. So it is clear that he regards what the people suffered at the hands of the Assyrians and of the Babylonians as a single captivity. Different peoples took them, it is true: the Assyrians took the ten tribes, and the Babylonians took the tribe of Judah, and some time passed in between. But the captivity of the whole people was completed in this way, beginning with the ten tribes and ending with the tribe of Judah. That is why the prophets, when announcing what would happen to the people, sometimes mention the one and sometimes the other. Both belonged to the one people and are treated as one common captivity, even if it took place at different times. Verses 6–8. “Thus says the Lord: For three impieties of Israel and for four I will not turn away from him.” Having said that he justly turns away from them because of their intense impiety, he goes on to list their offences too, which were very many

indeed. “Because they sold the righteous for silver.” Here by “righteous” he means not someone righteous in virtue, but someone who had right on his side in a dispute. That is, they betrayed for money those whose cause was just. He sharpens the charge: “and the poor for sandals that tread on the dust of the earth.” He says: they carried their greed so far that they betrayed the rights of the poor for the cheapest gains. That is what “sandals that tread on the dust of the earth” shows. It was clear proof that they took no account of justice, since they did such things readily even for paltry gains. “And they struck the heads of the poor with their fists.” He is speaking of the same people: not only did they refuse to help them when they asked for justice, they even beat them without fear. So he adds: “And they turned aside the way of the lowly.” He says: even when these people had acted rightly, they turned the judgment the other way, disregarding them because they were lowly. “And son and father went in to the same girl, so as to profane the name of their God; and binding their garments with cords they made curtains beside the altar; and they drank wine got by extortion in the house of their God.” In their excessive licentiousness they took no account even of the laws of nature: father and son shamelessly lay with the same women. In this way they brought great blasphemy upon the God they claimed to call upon. They even made tents out of garments near the altar and, without respect for the nearness of the holy things, carried out their debauchery there. And with what they took from the poor, whom they wronged in many ways, they held a kind of drunken feast in the house of God. Verses 9–12. “Yet I removed the Amorite from before them, whose height was like the height of a cedar, and he was strong as an oak; and I removed his fruit from above and his roots from beneath. And I brought you up out of the land of Egypt, and led you about in the wilderness forty years, to inherit the land of the Amorites. And I took some of your sons to be prophets, and some of your young men for consecration.” He says: you did these things without remembering my benefits. You forgot that I utterly destroyed the Amorite, great and powerful as he was, leaving no trace of him on the earth. You forgot that I brought you out of Egypt when you were slaves, and that I fed you in many ways in the wilderness for forty years, so as to give you as a possession the land of the Amorites, which was in no way yours. On top of all this, I gave some of you the grace of prophecy for the common good. I also chose some among you to devote themselves to a more careful and better life, as an ornament to all the rest. These things were plain to everyone, so he also says: “Is it not so, sons of Israel? says the Lord.” He means: you cannot deny that these things are so.

Following on from what came before, he adds: “And you gave the consecrated wine to drink, and you commanded the prophets, saying, You shall not prophesy.” He says: you plainly persist in insulting my grace. You force those set apart for a stricter life to take wine and all the other things they were eager to abstain from because of their vow, and you openly prevent the prophets from doing their proper work. And what follows for these things? Verses 13–16. “Therefore, behold, I roll beneath you, as a wagon full of straw is rolled; and flight shall perish from the runner, and the strong shall not keep hold of his strength, and the warrior shall not save his life; and the archer shall not stand, and the swift of foot shall not escape; and the horseman shall not save his life; and the strong shall not find his heart among the mighty.” He says: I will bring such punishments on you that you will be like a wagon heavily loaded, which creaks loudly under the weight of its load as it is drawn along. Weighed down by your evils, you will wail and groan with great intensity. Even one trained to run will not be able to escape the evils. The strong will gain nothing from their abundant strength. One prepared for battle and war will find no safety in it. The trouble will be too much even for the skilled archer. Neither swiftness of foot nor skill in riding horses will bring anyone safety. And those who pride themselves greatly on their strength will not find a way to use what strength they have left. Having said these things to show how great the evils will be, he adds: “The naked shall flee in that day, says the Lord.” He means that the very poorest, so destitute and worthless as to count for nothing among the rest, would be the only one to find safety then, because the enemy would not bother to capture him, since he was worthless. Then he attaches to [?]

Verses 1–[?]. “Hear this word which the Lord has spoken against you, house of Israel, and against every tribe which I brought up out of Egypt, saying: You alone have I known out of all the tribes of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your sins.” He says: do not treat these things God has declared about you as unimportant. The one who freed all of you from slavery in Egypt, and at that time showed you exceptional care above all other people, is the same one who now declares these things about you. He threatens a just punishment because you have been so ungrateful to so great a benefactor. “Will two walk together at all unless they make themselves known to each other?” He adds this to confirm what has been said and to show that it was not said at random. He says something like this: is it possible, he asks, for two people travelling together on a long road to hide from each other the reason for their journey the whole way, and not to share

…themselves about this, and indeed to complete the journey by common agreement, (p. 161) then it is also possible that the enemy will not come against you by God's will. "Will a lion roar from his thicket when he has no prey? Will a young lion utter his voice at all unless he has seized something?" Is it possible, he says, for a lion to roar from its own den when it has no expectation of prey? Or, if it has seen something, not to seize it? For here again he calls the lion a "young lion," as when one says, "What is man, or the son of man?" If, then, he says, these things can happen, it is also possible that your enemy will make his attack on you without seizing all of you like prey. "Will a bird fall to the ground without a fowler? Will a snare be sprung on the earth without catching something?" For just as birds, he says, are regularly caught by fowlers, and snares spring only at the moment when they are about to catch something, so too it is inevitable that you will be left with this great weight of evils, as the enemy comes against you by divine will, seizes you, and indeed leads you away into captivity. "Will a trumpet sound in a city, and the people not be alarmed?" If it is possible that when a trumpet suddenly sounds in a city no one is alarmed at not knowing what is happening, then it will also be possible for you to hear the trumpet of war without disturbance and without harm. "Will there be evil in a city (p. 162) which the Lord has not done?" Just as it is impossible for these things not to happen in the way he has described, so it is impossible for evils to befall your city unless God brings them upon you. Verses 7–10. "For the Lord God will do nothing unless he reveals his instruction to his servants the prophets." So we too do not speak in vain, but only what God has given us to say. Before events take place he wishes what is to come to be made known through us, including what he is about to bring upon you for your correction, so that you may know the cause of the evils coming upon you: from whom they will come, and for what. "A lion will roar, and who will not be afraid? The Lord God has spoken, and who will not prophesy?" Just as, when a lion roars loudly, the beasts cannot help being seized with fear, so when God makes a declaration, we cannot help serving his will with awe. "Proclaim to the regions in Assyria and to the regions in the land of Egypt, and say: Gather on the mountains of Samaria, and see the many marvels in her midst and the oppression within her; and she did not know what will come upon her, says the Lord." As if he has confirmed that he declares what is to come to them by God's will, he says: All of you, Assyrians and Egyptians, come to Samaria and see how great a tyranny they have exercised over the weaker, (p. 163) without reckoning what they will suffer for it when God is angry with them. For you will know that he is bringing upon them a just punishment of this kind for what they do. For the Assyrians, having besieged them, dragged out from there those of them who had fled to Egypt

and punished them in Egypt itself, as he also says in Hosea: "They will go from the misery of Egypt, and Memphis will receive them, and Michmash will bury them." That is why he addresses those nations: they ought to learn the cause of Israel's punishment. "Those who store up injustice and misery in their lands." For they have practised a great and immeasurable injustice against the poor, surrounding them in various ways with [?]

Verses 11–12. "Therefore thus says the Lord God: Tyre, and the land around you, will be made desolate; and he will bring down your strength from you, and your lands will be plundered." For these things, he says, God is bringing the Assyrian upon you, who will make Tyre and all your surrounding land desolate, that is, all who live around you, so that no hope of safety is left even to you, besieged by so great an enemy. (p. 164) For after destroying everything belonging to your neighbours, he will make your whole land a plunder too, so that nothing will be left in you of what seems to be of any worth. Then, indicating the severity of the destruction they will suffer, he says: "Thus says the Lord: As when a shepherd snatches from the mouth of a lion two legs or the lobe of an ear, so will the sons of Israel who dwell in Samaria be snatched away, opposite the tribe of Damascus." For so great, he says, will your destruction be that, with very few saved, the situation will be just like that of a sheep caught by a lion and devoured to such an extent that the shepherd can barely retrieve a few small pieces of it that have fallen from the lion's mouth, and only those which the lion disdains as fleshless and unfit for food. That is what "two legs or the lobe of an ear" means. In the same way, a few insignificant people will be left in this war from among those who dwell in Samaria opposite the Damascenes, for they will see the Damascenes destroyed by the enemy just as they are. He mentioned Tyre earlier and now Damascus to show the magnitude of the evils: not even any of the neighbours can escape the Assyrian onslaught. (p. 165) What he says was quite appropriate, since he had announced the destruction of all those peoples at the beginning. Verses 13–15. "Priests, hear and bear witness to the house of Jacob, says the Lord God Almighty. For on the day when I punish Israel for his ungodliness, I will also take vengeance on the altar[?]

…will be completely wiped out from the [?] care of those who worship impiously. For indeed I will also tear down their houses from the foundations, he says. By the "house with colonnades" he means the winter house, (p. 166) since it is enclosed on every side against the onset of cold. He means to say: I will destroy all the houses everywhere, so that no part of either the summer houses or the winter houses is left among them; and I will utterly destroy the splendid ones among their houses, for that is what he means by "ivory houses," which will fall together with many others, since God pronounces a single sentence against them all. Chapter 4, verses 1–3. "Hear this word, you heifers of Bashan who are on the mountain of Samaria, who oppress the poor and trample the needy, and who say to their lords, 'Give us something to drink.'" Here he turns his speech to the women who, inclined to an idle and arrogant life, wronged the poor through the power they possessed. Making use of this power, and even ruling over their own husbands, they used them as agents for unseemly deeds. Something of the kind is seen in the case of Jezebel: Ahab respected Naboth's objection, since it was just, but she, acting in a foul, shameless and murderous way, did not even hesitate to kill Naboth in order to take from him the vineyard which he, with good reason, would not consent to give. He calls them heifers of Bashan because the heifers raised in that region were especially wild and untamed. (p. 167) Having spoken of their injustice to the poor, he added, "who say to their lords, 'Give us something to drink,'" meaning that they did not shrink from using even their own husbands, whom they ought to have respected as their heads in accordance with the order of nature, to serve their own licentiousness, and all but ordered them to do whatever would further it. What then? "The Lord swears by his holy ones that, behold, days are coming upon you, and they will take you with weapons, and those with you they will throw into cauldrons heated from below; and you will be carried out naked, woman and man facing one another, and you will be cast out onto the mountain of Armana, says the Lord." God has declared, he says, things that admit of no change, for this is what "swears" shows: a time will come when you will pay the penalty for these things. For enemies will come upon you who will take you captive and plunge you into incurable evils, so that, stripped all at once of all the good things you now have, both the women who do such things and the men who serve them in such things will be led away captive to the land of the Assyrians. For by "Armana" he means the mountain of the Armenians, (p. 168) which at that time was under the Assyrians.

Verses 4–5. "You went into Bethel and transgressed, and into Gilgal and multiplied your ungodliness; and you brought your sacrifices in the morning, and your tithes on the third day; and they read the law outside and called for confessions." Here he reproaches them for their zeal for idols; for this is what he means by "into Bethel and into Gilgal [?]"

…by this indicating, as is his habit, the worship of idols. You acted impiously with great eagerness, he says, and you offered your sacrifices with zeal. "On the third day" means either "every three days," to show that they offered sacrifices continually, or some ritual by which they performed sacrifices to the idols at that time. [?] You also offered your tithes, and you read some law of your own devising, making covenants with the idols on that basis. In short, all that you ought to perform for God in Jerusalem according to the divine law, you do in the places mentioned and for the idols, in imitation of what I have ordained. To this he aptly adds: "Proclaim that the sons of Israel loved these things, says the Lord God." Let their zeal for such things be made plain to all, so that it may also become clear why they are paying the penalty. (p. 169) For what follows? "And I will give you a crushing of teeth in all your cities, and a lack of bread in all your places; and you do not return to me, says the Lord." For I will crush you utterly, he says, and surround you with a lack of necessities, and not even when chastened by this will you turn to me. By "crushing of teeth" he means extreme crushing, as also in blessed David: "God will break their teeth in their mouth; the Lord has shattered the molars of the lions." He means an overwhelming crushing, one that will reach even the teeth and the molars. Verses 7–10. "And I withheld the rain from you three months before the harvest; and I will send rain on one city, but on another city I will not send rain; one plot will be rained on, and the plot on which I do not send rain will dry up; and two or three cities will gather into one city to drink water, and they will not be satisfied; and you did not return to me, says the Lord." I also took away your rain, so that you fell into the greatest barrenness. This is what "three months before the harvest" means, since a drought lasting from then to the end brings complete destruction of the crops, (p. 170) which can neither grow nor ripen; and it also keeps the earth from producing suitable pasture for the cattle. What follows he says from what usually happens: in severe droughts it often happens that a slight gathering of the air occurs and a meagre rain falls in certain scattered places, from which no benefit [?] (Note: the manuscript reads synathroisthēsetai.)

(Commentary on Amos, Chapter 4.) …two or three cities, often joining together, will go off to a place where they learn that water can somehow be found, yet even so not obtaining all they need, but enjoying only a little relief from there. But not even from these things, he says, will you become better. "I struck you with fever and with jaundice, and you multiplied your ungodliness." I surrounded you with various diseases, but you intensified your ungodliness. "Your gardens, which you multiplied, and your vineyards, your fig orchards and your olive groves, the caterpillar devoured; and even so you did not return to me, says the Lord." I destroyed all your crops with the caterpillar, yet even so you have remained the same. "I sent death among you on the road to Egypt, and I killed your young men with the sword, together with the capture of your horses; (p. 171) and I sent your camps up in fire in my wrath; and even so you did not return to me, says the Lord." And when you have fled to Egypt in hope of safety, there I will surround you with deaths and slaughters; and further, I will lead away into captivity those of you who are left, along with all that belongs to them [?], and consume your whole multitude as if with fire by the punishment I bring upon you through your enemies. Yet not even then will you repent. Verses 11–13. "I overthrew you as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and you became like a brand snatched from the fire; and even so you did not return to me, says the Lord." Finally I brought complete desolation upon you, as on Sodom and Gomorrah, so that, like a charred brand, you were scorched and engulfed by the evils brought upon you. But not even from these things have you been able to accept any correction. Having said all this, listing the things brought upon them by which they did not become better, he adds: "Therefore thus will I do to you, Israel; but because I will do this to you, prepare to call upon your God, Israel. For behold, I am he who makes the thunder firm and creates the wind, and announces to mankind his anointed; who makes the dawn and the mist, and treads upon the heights of the earth: the Lord God, (p. 172) the Almighty, is his name." But even if you have behaved toward me in this way, he says, I have nevertheless resolved, after you have experienced those evils, to change your situation for the better, if only, having become more sober through such great evils, you are willing to turn to me then. For I, who can compress the air, soft and loose, slack and altogether thin, so tightly that the crash of thunder produced from it is unbearable to those on earth, I myself will also bring about a great change in your affairs, revealing to you, beyond all hope, the greatest salvation. And I announce to you Cyrus, king of the Persians, who will be appointed by me for this purpose, so that, having conquered a great many nations, he may free you from the evils that hold you fast and order you to return to your own land. For I who make the dawn out of darkness, who let the mist form and dissolve it at the rising of the sun, and who am always on high and above the earth, I the same will dissolve your misfortunes like darkness

and make your delight in good things shine forth like the day. Removing every burden that weighs against you, I will show clearly, through my care for you, that I am above all things, (p. 173) since I am the Lord and Maker of all. Throughout, he has confirmed what he says about the present from the things God does universally. It is not surprising that he called Cyrus "anointed," since Scripture is accustomed to use this word not only for those who have been anointed but for all who have been chosen in any way, as in: "Do not touch my anointed ones, and do my prophets no harm." For there he calls Abraham and his household "anointed," not because they had been anointed, but only because they had been chosen.

Chapter 5, verses 1–2. "Hear this word, which I take up over you as a lament: The house of Israel has fallen; it will rise no more. The virgin of Israel has stumbled on her own land; there is no one to raise her up." Having announced in the preceding passage the release from evils, he again threatens punishment, as is his habit, using the threat to frighten and chasten them and the promise to call them to repentance. Your situation, he says, deserves a lament, for through your own transgressions you have fallen a very great fall, from which, given the magnitude of what has happened, one cannot even hope for release. "For thus says the Lord: The city from which a thousand went out will have a hundred left, and the city from which a hundred went out will have ten left in it, for the house of Israel." For the slaughter the enemy inflicts on you will be so great that barely a hundred out of a thousand, and barely ten out of a hundred, will be found in each (p. 174) city. "For thus says the Lord to the house of Israel: Seek me and you will live. Do not seek Bethel, do not go into Gilgal, and do not go up to the Well of the Oath; for Gilgal will surely be taken captive, and Bethel will be as if it did not exist." I advise you, then, to look to me and to turn away from Bethel and Gilgal and the Well of the Oath, where you now flock together to serve idols and demons in those places, knowing well that desolation will overtake all these places along with you. "Seek the Lord and you will live, lest the house of Joseph blaze up like fire and devour it, and there be no one to quench it for the house of Israel." Abandon these things and devote yourselves to God, so that the punishment that comes from God does not burn you all up like fire; for when God sends these things upon you, no one can be found who is able to defend you. Verses 7–9. "He who executes judgment on high, and has established righteousness on the earth." For you have no reason to disbelieve anything God threatens or promises you, since he is the one who executes judgment and righteousness on high and establishes them on earth. That is to say: he is the one who can judge on your behalf when you are wronged by your enemies, and punish

those who bring such great evils upon you, and display the righteousness and judgment (p. 175) which he exercises on behalf of you who are on earth, a judgment that is great and full of every wonder. And to confirm this he adds: "He who makes all things and transforms them." For he can easily both make all things out of nothing and change what has come into being into whatever he wishes. "Who turns the shadow of death into morning, and darkens day into night." He is able to turn dangers that bring death into bright and sweet gladness, and he can easily plunge into the darkness of misfortune those who seem to live in splendour. Here too he wants to show from what God does universally that he is able to change their affairs as he wishes, at one time bringing them from misfortune to prosperity, at another casting them from prosperity into misfortune. "He who summons the water of the sea and pours it out on the face of the earth: the Lord God, the Almighty, is his name." He who lifts the water of the sea through the clouds and pours it out over all the earth is able now too, in his wrath, to pour out upon you the army of the Assyrians, as vast as the sea; for he is Lord of all and able to do whatever he pleases. "Who deals out ruin upon strength, and brings misery upon the fortress." He who also dispels the affliction that oppresses, (p. 176) and makes strong even those who have been weakened by evils, suddenly fills with misery those who seem to have great power. He who by his will changed your fortunes from better to worse will, if he wills again, easily change them from worse to better. Verses 10–11. "They hated the one who reproves in the gates, and they abhorred a holy word." From here on he begins to recount their transgressions. They hated the prophets, who were commanded to reprove their transgressions in order to correct them, and they abhorred everything the prophets told them when they advised them to turn away from evil and choose what is better. He speaks of "the gates" for this reason: it was the custom in ancient times for the people of a city to hold their deliberations on the most pressing matters at the gates, to give their answers there to enemies who sent embassies to them on any matter, (p. 177) and also to hold the more important trials there, so that what was done might be visible to all who entered and left the city through the gate. That is why blessed David says, "They will not be put to shame when they speak with their enemies in the gates," since they gave their answers to outsiders there; and, "Those who sat in the gate talked idly against me," since they were accustomed to hold most of their gatherings there. In the same way, here he speaks of those who reprove in the gates, since the prophets were eager to proclaim to them there what was in accordance with God's will, where indeed what was said became plain to all

[…] not only to their own people but also to outsiders, whenever they came into the city. Then he lists in order those transgressions which he had also mentioned before: “Therefore, because you beat the poor with your fists and took choice gifts from him, you have built houses of hewn stone, but you shall not live in them; you have planted desirable vineyards, but you shall not drink their wine.” Since you inflicted evils on the poor and seized the best of what they had by plunder, and built handsome houses from what you gathered unjustly, and cultivated fields with great care, there is no way you will enjoy what you have thus gained through injustice. You will not remain in those houses, nor will you receive the fruits of such fields. Verses 12–15: “For I know your many ungodly deeds, and your sins are mighty: you trample on the just, you take bribes, and you turn aside the needy in the gates.” For the number and the size of your impieties and sins have not escaped me, nor that you [?] justice for money. Receiving this money from wrongdoers, you turned the judgments of the poor to the opposite of the truth. And here too he has added “in,” as we said earlier. “Therefore the one who understands will keep silent at that time, for it is an evil time.” So when the threatened punishment is brought upon you, all who are able to understand what is fitting will think it right to keep quiet, as though stunned by the size of the evils, recognizing the time at which it had long ago been announced that these things would happen. “Seek good and not evil, that you may live; and so the Lord God Almighty will be with you, just as you have said: ‘We have hated evil and loved good.’ And restore justice in the gates, so that the Lord God Almighty may have mercy on the remnant of Joseph.” But while there is still time for this, I counsel all of you to turn away from the worse and choose the better. In this way you will enjoy good things, as God gives you his own care because you chose the good and turned away from the worse. And if you change your old disposition and are willing to give just judgments in the gates as was customary, you will obtain the divine loving-kindness, which will save most of you. By “Joseph” here he means the ten tribes, naming them after the one that led them, I mean Ephraim, who was the son of Joseph. Verses 16–18: “Therefore thus says the Lord God Almighty: In all the squares there will be wailing, and in all the streets they will say in lament, ‘Woe, woe!’” Since you take no account of these things, both city and countryside will be full of laments and wailing because of the great slaughter the enemy will carry out. “The farmer will be called to mourning and wailing, and to those skilled in lamentation; and in all the streets there will be wailing, for I will pass through your midst, says the Lord.” Even the farmers will leave their work on the land and busy themselves with wailing and mourning and every kind of lament, [?] both the slaughter by the enemy and the barrenness of the land,

as they lament. And they will suffer these things because God comes into their midst through the enemy and surrounds them with so many and such great evils. “Woe to those who long for the day of the Lord! Why would you want this day of the Lord? It is darkness and not light.” Many had turned wholly to the worse and, as though the prophets were lying in what they foretold, dared to say: “Let the evils come that you speak of and announce, if there is really any truth in your words.” So he says this: “You are most pitiable,” he says, “for seeking that day. You do not believe it will come, but you will see it by experience, as it brings gloomy darkness on you through the multitude of its evils.” Then he confirms what he has said by an illustration. Verses 12[?]–23: “It is as if a man flees from a lion, and a bear meets him, and he rushes into the house and leans his hands on the wall, and a snake bites him. Is not the day of the Lord darkness and not light, gloom with no brightness in it?” For he wanted to show the harshness of that day by an illustration. It is as if someone, he says, heard on the road that a lion was attacking, and ran to the city; but in the city he fell in with a bear that was mauling everyone it met, and so he rushed into his own house, hoping to find some release from his troubles; then, as he put his hand on the wall of his house for some purpose, he was suddenly bitten by a snake. After such an experience of evils and such turmoil, and after falling victim to the inescapable bite of the snake, must not the day that seems bright to others be darkness to such a man, so that he cannot even make out what is before his own eyes? So too with you, he says. When you hear of the enemy attacking from every side, you will go into the city. But you will be thrown into confusion by the turmoil there, which is bound to arise when the enemy is upon it, and you will go into your own houses. Yet you will gain nothing more by this either, for the enemy will drag you out of the inner rooms of your houses into captivity. How could that time not be darkness to those who suffer such things? Then, to show their wickedness, he adds: “I have hated and rejected your feasts, and I will take no pleasure in the smell of your festal gatherings.” Because of the wickedness of your ways, I hate even the feasts which you think you celebrate in my honor, and I do not accept them. “For even if you bring me your whole burnt offerings and sacrifices, I will not accept them; and I will not look on your manifestations of salvation.” So even if you offer sacrifices or whole burnt offerings, hoping through them to receive salvation from my manifestation, I will not accept them, and I will pay no attention at all to what is done. What then? “Take away from me the noise of your songs; I will not listen to the psalm of your instruments.” Stop, then, singing your psalms to me, since I have no regard for this either.

Verses 24–27: “And judgment will roll down like water, and righteousness like an impassable torrent.” For as I look at your life, he says, and judge your affairs by it, I see that a most just punishment will be brought upon you. I will bring it upon all of you like a torrent, utterly impassable because of its size. “Did you offer me victims and sacrifices for forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel?” You ought to have known, above all from this, that I have no regard for sacrifices: for forty years in the wilderness I asked nothing of the kind from your fathers, but I myself continued to give them fitting care. “And you took up the tent of Moloch, and the star of your god Rephan, the images that you made for yourselves. And I will deport you beyond Damascus, says the Lord God; the Almighty is his name.” But because you do not want to reckon what is right, you expect to appease me with sacrifices, you men who take no account of me and are eager to devote yourselves to idols. By “Moloch” he means an idol worshiped among them; and he says “the tent of Moloch” to mean, “You tend the idol’s temple and devote yourselves to it.” And moreover you busy yourselves with the worship of a star, having given it the name of god (they say that the morning star is called this in the language of the Hebrews). And indeed you spend all your leisure on the images that you made with your own hands. Then, while devoting yourselves to idols and taking no account of my worship, you expect to appease me with sacrifices, from which you will get no benefit at all. For you will be led away as captives to places very far from the places around you. This is what he means by “Damascus”: by naming a part he refers to places very far away. The blessed Stephen, at any rate, in the Acts of the Holy Apostles, used this testimony against the Jews and said, “I will deport you beyond Babylon,” naming more clearly the places indicated here. And since they devoted themselves to these things, having turned away from God, he adds: Chapter [?]. Verses 1–2: “Woe to those who despise Zion, and to those who trust in the mountain of Samaria!” But you are the most pitiable of all, for you have struck out Mount Zion and the God worshiped there, and you devote yourselves to Samaria and the idols set up there. “They stripped the chiefs of the nations like a vintage, and they entered in for themselves, O house of Israel.” You have not considered how great are the things God provided for you, he who commanded that all worship be brought to him on Mount Zion; nor that he cut down and utterly removed very many nations and their rulers, and granted you entry into their territory and a dwelling there.

And showing how great the divine gift is, he says: “Cross over, all of you, and look: go to Calneh, and from there go through to Hamath the great, and from there go down to the land of the foreigners, the strongest of all these kingdoms, and see whether their borders are larger than your borders.” Go around, he says, the land of the foreigners and of all your neighbors; and when you have seen the greatest of their cities, compare the size and breadth of your own land with theirs, so that from the comparison you may learn how much more land he has given you to live in than all of them, so that you might dwell in it with plenty of room. Then he again reproaches them for their outrageous deeds. Verses 3–8: “You who are coming to an evil day, who draw near and lay hold of false sabbaths; who sleep on beds of ivory and live in luxury on their couches; who eat kids from the flocks and suckling calves from the midst of the herds; who clap along to the sound of the instruments—they thought these things lasting and not fleeting; who drink strained wine and anoint themselves with the finest ointments; and they were not grieved at the ruin of Joseph.” But you will come to experience that day, which brings upon you a vast swarm of evils. You pretend to observe the Sabbaths, not for the sake of piety but in order to abuse the day of rest for lawlessness. You display great wealth and debauchery, down to your beds and their coverings, out of what you have plundered from the poor. You slaughtered kids and oxen and every kind of animal, with songs to instruments and clapping of hands. You take your wine strained, so that you can drink more of it, and you anoint yourselves with choice ointments. And you pursued these things expecting that your enjoyment of them would last and never leave you, never considering what punishment you will endure for them. For here again, by “the ruin of Joseph,” he refers to all of them by naming a part, as if to say: “You give no thought to the ruin you will now endure for these things.” “Therefore they will now go into captivity, under the rule of potentates, and the neighing of horses will be removed from Ephraim. For the Lord has sworn by himself, saying—the Lord God of hosts—‘Because I abhor all the arrogance of Jacob, and I have hated his lands, I will also remove a city with all who live in it.’” Since you take no account of the threats, you will learn the truth of what is announced by experience itself. For you will all be led away captive by rulers invested with great power, so that your military equipment, along with your horses, will be utterly wiped out. For God abhors all your lawlessness, which you do not hesitate to commit to his insult, so that your cities and lands are full of this impiety; and so he will rightly destroy all your cities, together with their lands and their inhabitants. Then, to show how great the desolation will be, he says: Verses 9–10: “And it shall be that if ten men are left in one house, they will die; and those who remain will be

left behind, and their kinsmen will take them up and will struggle to carry their bones out of the house. And he will say to those in charge of the house, ‘Is there anyone still with you?’ And he will say, ‘No more.’ And he will say, ‘Hush!’ so as not to name the name of the Lord.” Because of the translation, a great deal of obscurity is bound up with this text. It resembles the passage in Genesis that speaks of the agreement Laban and Jacob made with each other, that of the lambs born to the sheep some should belong to one and some to the other. That too is obscure in its wording, but its sense becomes clear when it is explained. So we must also set out the sense of this passage, which is expressed obscurely in its wording. To show that the desolation that will overtake them will be extremely great, he wants to say this: Often, he says, out of a very large and populous household barely ten will be left, the rest having been killed in various ways in the war. This is like what he says above too: out of a hundred, ten will remain, and out of a thousand, a hundred. Then, he says, once these have died, [they will struggle] to carry out the bodies lying inside and give them burial. He says this because war brings slaughter of many kinds, and those killed in different ways lie in different parts of the house; and in such circumstances some parts of the house are also torn down and fall on the bodies. That is why he said “they will struggle,” showing that they are undertaking a forced and difficult task in wanting to give all the bodies burial. Then he says: worn out by the great number of dead they have carried out, they will talk with one another and argue over whether all the bodies have now been carried out or whether some still lie unburied. For by “those in charge of the house” he means the ten who are left out of all of them, as if to say that they will say these things to one another. When they have somehow managed to remove all the bodies and give them burial, they will know that there are no more dead; for they will see the silence that holds the house, because of the great number who perished and the emptiness of the dwelling, very few being left out of so large a household and so many inhabitants. Seized by a kind of silence at so many and such great evils, and all but struck dumb by the overwhelming evils that have come upon them, they will then reckon up the cause of so many and such great evils: because they neglected the worship of God, rejected the name of the Lord of all, and devoted themselves to idols, these evils have come upon them—captivity, the collapse of houses, a multitude slain, and homes left empty. So he adds, as if to confirm what he has said: Verses 11–13: “For behold, the Lord commands, and he will strike the great house with shatterings and the small house with cracks.” As if giving the reason why there will be so much toil in carrying out the bodies of the dead and giving them burial, he says: God has given the command, and therefore every house, great and small, he will hand over, one to partial damage

(for this is what “cracks” means), and the other to total damage (for this is what “shatterings” indicates). He does not mean that the great house will receive shatterings and the small house cracks, each in turn, but that neither great house nor small will escape punishment. But it will come differently: some will suffer damage in part, and others will be brought down entirely, as tends to happen in war and in a long siege. And showing that what he has said cannot be disputed, he adds: “Will horses run on rocks?” No one would drive horses over rocks, but only where the ground helps the horses run; and these things would not have befallen you either, had you not yourselves given cause for suffering them. “Will they keep quiet among the mares?” Nor would horses that find themselves among mares keep quiet, when there are mares present able to receive their advances. So neither is it possible for the enemy to keep quiet toward you, since by your lawlessness you have given them occasion to do such things to you. “For you have turned justice into wrath, and the fruit of righteousness into bitterness.” For now, he says, because of what you have done, you will suffer such things, since you have stirred God to anger, so that he judges your affairs; and since he knows that you will undergo a just punishment, he brings upon you such bitterness of evils. And again he mentions the things they were wrongly doing, for which the evils foretold will come upon them: “Those who rejoice over no good word, who say, ‘Have we not gained horns by our own strength?’” For you are unwilling to heed the counsels of the prophets, who remind you when you sin and lead you back to what is right. Instead, reckoning that by your own power you have always prevailed over all your enemies, you think nothing of the gravity of the threats, as though you were able to withstand the enemy now too. What then? Verse 14: “For behold, I am raising up against you, O house of Israel, says the Lord God of hosts, a nation; and they will press you hard so that you cannot enter Hamath, and as far as the torrent of the west.” Because of this attitude of yours, he says, the Lord of all powers everywhere will raise up enemies against you, who will bring upon you the most terrible experience of evils, so that from Hamath (he means a place lying on the borders of their territory) to the end of your borders the evil will engulf everyone. In Kings, at any rate, it says concerning Jeroboam son of Joash, in whose time this very prophet lived: “He restored the border of Israel from the entrance of Hamath to the sea in the west.” So it is clear that the places indicated by these names were the limits of Israelite territory. For he means: The evil will begin there and come upon all of you, so that, since none will be able to escape the hands of the enemy, you will perceive from the events themselves that neither before did you prevail at all against your enemies

without the support of divine power; and now you have come to the very experience of evils, since you have fallen outside his help. To these words he adds a revelation which the prophet saw, to confirm what he has said.

Verses 1–3: “Thus the Lord showed me: and behold, a brood of locusts coming at dawn; and behold, one locust larva, Gog the king. And it will be that if it finishes devouring the grass of the land—and I said, ‘Lord, Lord, be merciful! Who will raise up Jacob? For he is very few. Relent, O Lord, over this.’ ‘And this shall not be,’ says the Lord.” He says that he saw a multitude of locusts and larvae, of which the one signified the Assyrian and the other the Babylonian, since they would come and destroy everything like the locust and the larva. “But when I saw,” he says, “the [?], which was enough to destroy all the produce springing from the earth, I fell down,” he says, “and asked that pardon be granted for our offenses, seeing the multitude of those who would perish and the fewness of those left behind, and considering that even the survivors had no hope of salvation unless God, becoming merciful toward our sins, changed matters for the better.” But God did not accept this petition, he says, since he considered the multitude of their sins too great to be atoned for. One should not be surprised that he said “Gog the king.” For many of the Scythian nations also joined in the war, first with the Assyrians and afterward with the Babylonians. Gog was king over these, and he mentioned him not as the one leading the war at that time, but as an ally of those who led it. For it is well known that first the Assyrian ruled many nations, and after him the Babylonian; and it was not unlikely that all these nations, with their own satraps or kingdoms, were present and took part in the war. Then he relates another revelation: Verses 4–9: “Thus the Lord God showed me: and behold, the Lord called for judgment by fire, and it devoured the great deep, and it devoured the portion. And I said, ‘Lord, cease, I pray! Who will raise up Jacob? For he is very few. Relent, O Lord, over this.’ ‘And this shall not happen,’ says the Lord God.” For I saw God again, he says, calling for the judgment by which he is accustomed to judge all people, ordering their affairs with exactness and close scrutiny. He called for it by fire, since he considered their deeds deserving of such a punishment. At that, he says, when I saw the multitude of the Israelites, which was like a deep, being consumed, I cried out again that their evil might be lessened somewhat; but God declared that this would come to pass. He also relates a third revelation: “Thus the Lord showed me: and behold, a man standing on a wall of adamant, and in his hand was adamant. And the Lord said to me, ‘What do you see, Amos?’ And I said, ‘Adamant.’”

"And the Lord said to me: Behold, I am setting adamant in the midst of my people Israel; I will no longer pass him by. The altars of laughter shall be destroyed, and the rites of Israel shall be laid waste, and I will rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword." For he showed me, he says, someone standing on a wall of adamant and holding adamant in his hand.
