These were signs that the sentence God had issued against the Israelites was firm and could not be undone, since adamant surpasses everything else in hardness. So with all firmness, he says, I will bring evils on the people, no longer bearing to overlook their transgressions. All the altars at which they took their pleasure in the worship of idols will be destroyed. In short, he says, everything they now perform in the worship of demons will be handed over to desolation. And I will destroy in war all the power of Jeroboam, who now reigns over you. Here he seems to use "the house of Jeroboam" for the whole kingdom, signifying the entire nation by its ruler, since it is clear that the Assyrian invasion against Israel took place in the times after Jeroboam. Verses 10–13. — The prophet had announced that such things would come upon the nation of Israel for their various impieties and transgressions. Amaziah, who served as priest in Bethel and led the whole people in this great impiety, saw that if the prophet kept saying these things, most people would grow more negligent in the worship of the idol, gripped in advance by fear of what the prophet announced. So he tried to provoke King Jeroboam himself against the prophet, claiming that he was saying a great many things against the king and his whole kingdom, and that the threats he uttered were so great that no one could even bear to hear them. For he was announcing, Amaziah said, the death of the king and the captivity of the whole people. The part about the king was plainly false, since the prophet had said nothing of the kind. Yet Amaziah wove it in with the sentence against the people, in order to provoke the king all the more. But Amaziah did not find the king persuaded, for the king was afraid to do the prophet any harm. He knew what had happened with Elijah and Elisha, who had prophesied and lived before him. Above all, he knew that his own forefather Jehu had come to the throne by the decision of Elisha, to punish the lawlessness of Jezebel and Ahab, and that the kingdom had come down to him too through the promises God had made to Jehu. So Amaziah himself, in his own insolence, says to Amos: "Seer, go, withdraw into the land of Judah, and live there, and there you shall prophesy; but at Bethel you shall prophesy no more, for it is the king's sanctuary and a royal house." He said "seer" ironically. For since they used to call the

prophets this, as men who by divine power saw certain extraordinary visions through revelation (as it also says in Kingdoms that the people formerly called the prophet "the seer"), he said "seer" ironically, in the sense of "you who announce these things." Go away from here, then, to the land of Judah, where you will be free to say these things. Keep away from the places here, since everything here belongs to the kingdom of Israel. It is not lawful for you, a man of the tribe of Judah, to be here and say whatever you please, and so throw our kingdom into turmoil. Verses 14–17. — To this the prophet, by divine revelation, gave this answer: "I was not a prophet, nor a prophet's son." For I neither learned this as a craft nor received it from my father as an inheritance, since it is the work of divine grace and is given to whomever God wishes. "But I was a goatherd and a scraper of sycamore figs." He means that he was occupied with tending goats and also, as occasion allowed, with farming the land. He says "sycamores" for "figs," as blessed David also says: "He killed their vine with hail and their sycamores with frost." For it is clear that he meant that fig trees, not sycamores, perished along with the vines. By "scraping" he means hoeing around them and tending them. By naming the sycamores as a part for the whole, he meant to say: I was always devoted to herding goats and farming. But the Lord, he says, took me from the sheep (which makes it clear that he said "goatherd" as one who tended goats and sheep together) and commanded me to prophesy and to announce to everyone what he would bring upon the people. These were not things for me to know, but for God alone, who teaches them, to prove the truth of what was said. Now hear what concerns you. You order me to stop prophesying here, so that I will not gather crowds to hear such teachings. But know that everything I have said will happen. The enemies will come, and besides the many other evils they will do, they will abuse your wife in the middle of the city, outraging her shamefully. Your children will all be slaughtered along with many others, and the land that is yours will be parceled out by measure to others who are going to possess this place. "And you shall die in an unclean land." You yourself will die among foreign and lawless men (this is what "unclean" means), to whom you will be carried off captive along with everyone else. Having said this, he goes on to the revelation that was shown to him after these things.

Verses 1–3. — "For the Lord showed me," he says, "and behold, a fowler's basket. And the Lord said to me: What do you see, Amos? And I said: A fowler's basket." The vision showed that, like a bird caught by the fowler's skill, all Israel would be seized by the enemy and carried off captive, and no one would be able to take them away from those who held them. Just as a sparrow caught in birdlime can no longer get free, so the power of the invaders, being stronger than any birdlime,

will hold them fast and carry them off into captivity. He goes on: "And the Lord said to me: The end has come upon my people Israel; I will no longer pass him by; and the panelled ceilings of the temple shall wail." For he told the meaning of what had been shown. The time has come, then, he says, when all of them will be handed over to punishment, and with them the impiety will cease, along with all their devotion to impiety and lawlessness. For I will no longer bear to overlook their evils and leave such things unpunished. The evil will reach even the temple, since it too will be given over to fire along with the destruction of everyone. And it is clear, as I have often said, that when he announces the evils, even if he is speaking about Israel, he also joins to it what would happen to the tribe of Judah under the Babylonians, when Jerusalem was taken and the temple was burned. "In that day, says the Lord, many will be the fallen; in every place I will cast silence." Then, he says, there will be much death everywhere, and countless will be the slaughters of those who fall, some killed and others taken captive. And because of the utter desolation, silence will hold everything. Then he again reminds them of the transgressions they committed. Verses 4–14. — "Hear these things, you who crush the poor in the morning and oppress the needy from the land, who say: When will the month pass, so that we may sell? And when will the Sabbaths come, so that we may open our storehouses, to make the measure small and the weight large, and to make an unjust balance, to buy the poor for silver and the lowly for sandals, and we will make a profit from every sale?" These things, he says, are said above all [?] ... not so that you might keep festival to God on those days, but so that you might make your trade more abundant, exploiting the occasion of the festival, and gather unjust treasures for yourselves. You make measures and weights both small and large, so that you can use each for your own peddling, and gather silver by wronging the poor. You do not refrain even from the meanest gains, which is what "for sandals" means, and in every transaction you look for what profit will come to you, which is what "we will make a profit from every sale" means. Against this arrogance of yours (he calls arrogance the injustice they did to the poor without reckoning on God's judgment), God issued a firm and irrevocable sentence. That is what "the Lord swears" shows: that he will not consign what they did to oblivion altogether. Rather, all but shaking the whole earth, he will surround them with such evils through the invasion of the enemy that everyone will be gripped by mourning at the greatness of the calamity that has come upon them. For like the river of Egypt, which floods and then

recedes again, the enemy will come upon you, destroying all of you, and will take captives and carry them off to his own country. Then, he says, the sun at the height of midday will seem to have vanished for those in distress, and darkness will seem to hold everyone on earth, because of the greatness of the evils. You will abandon your lawless feasts and give yourselves to mourning. Instead of your old songs you will raise loud lamentation. Instead of soft clothing you will put on sackcloth, mourning the evils that are upon you. You will neglect your old adornment of the head and think that shaving off your hair befits such great evils. In short, all of you will go on, under the pain that grips you, as if mourning a beloved only son, lamenting the greatness of the evils that surround you. The prophet then shows that what would come after this would be heavier still: "For days will come," he says, "in which you will not only fall into want of food and drink, but will endure the heaviest want of all: you will not be granted a single divine word, such as used to come through the prophets to comfort those in hardship." He is saying what was also said by the blessed prophet Hosea: "The sons of Israel shall sit without a king, without a ruler, without sacrifice, without an altar, without priesthood, without manifestations." By this he means that after the captivity in Babylon all these things were taken from them. The prophet now shows the very same thing: You will be handed over to evils. Then you will look for the prophets you now neglect, longing to learn whether your situation will take any turn for the better. "For the waters will be shaken from sea to sea, and from the north to the east they will run about seeking the word of the Lord, and they will not find it." He means that the whole countless multitude of Israel will be thrown into turmoil everywhere in all sorts of ways, looking for some prophet to appear and announce to them by God's will what is to come. But this they will not obtain then. Next, he says, everything that now seems most beautiful to you and worth striving for will be utterly destroyed. The girls whom you now guard as virgins with great care will perish, and so will the young men most admired for their youth. And why will you suffer these things? "Those who swear by the propitiation of Samaria and say, 'As the god of Dan lives,' and 'As your god lives, Beersheba'—they shall fall and never rise again." Because they abandoned God, the Lord of all, and were eager to serve the idols in Samaria and called them gods, for this they will fall a fall that can never be repaired. Then he tells of another revelation:

Verses 1–3. — "I saw the Lord standing on the altar, and he said: Strike the mercy seat, and the gateways shall be shaken; and cut into the heads of them all, and the rest of them I will kill with the sword. No one of them who flees shall escape, and no one of them who seeks

safety shall be saved." For I saw, he says, the Lord standing before the altar, clearly the one in Jerusalem, and telling me to strike the mercy seat, meaning the altar. He calls it the "mercy seat" because sacrifices were offered on it for propitiation. And the command to the prophet to strike it is a sign that it would be struck and suffer. So he adds: "And the gateways shall be shaken," meaning, by naming a part, that the whole temple would be shaken by this blow, since the whole house necessarily shared in the damage to the altar. And put certain marks, he says, on the heads of them all, as a token that all of them are from now on marked out to be handed over to destruction, with no one escaping that danger. For just as in Egypt he gave the sign of blood on the doorposts to distinguish those who would perish from those who would be saved, so here, in the divine revelation, he commands him to put a sign on the heads of them all, as proof that all have been handed over to death. To confirm this he adds: Even if they go down to Hades, I will drag them up from there; even if they go up to heaven, I will bring them down from there; even if they hide in the recesses of Carmel (meaning the mountains, naming the whole by a part), I will track them all down and hand them over to captivity; even if they go off to the depth of the sea, I will destroy them by the beasts there. And after the multitude of evils that all of them will suffer when they are carried off into captivity, they will perish there by my command, as they deserve. To this he adds: Verses 4–6. — "And I will fix my eyes on them for evil and not for good." That is, I will keep watching over them, not to give them any good, but to put them through every kind of evil, since by their own deeds they have shown themselves deserving of such things. For there is, he says, a God, the maker and Lord of all, who is able to shake the whole earth by a mere touch. This very thing he will also do to your land, [?] shaking all of it and reducing it to great desolation, so that all who live in it are gripped by mourning. [?] Like the river of Egypt, the enemy will come upon them and destroy [?] many, and will sweep away the rest and carry them off into captivity. Then, to confirm what he has said: "He who builds his ascent into heaven and founds his promise upon the earth." This one, he says, who is always shown to be in heaven, where he dwells and abides forever, beyond all toil, confirms everything whatsoever he has promised to do on earth. He is the one who takes the water of the sea and pours it out [?] over the whole earth; and he is doing the same now, bringing upon your land the Assyrian, who is like the sea in his multitude. For these are the works of God, the Lord and maker of all. Then, wishing to expose their ingratitude by pointing to God's goodwill toward them, he adds:

Verse 7. — "Are you not to me like the sons of the Ethiopians, sons of Israel? says the Lord." Did I make you like Ethiopians in my eyes, to whom I have clearly given nothing special? "Did I not bring Israel up out of the land of Egypt?" For I have never been seen to do anything of the kind for the Ethiopians, as I did for you when I took you out of Egypt, freed you from that bitter slavery, and made you masters of a land so great and so fine, which did not belong to you. "And the foreigners from Cappadocia, and the Syrians from Bothros?" Some have said that "from Bothros" means from Carrhae, as the place is now called, which was once Harran. But I will set aside this needless precision, since it contributes nothing to the sense, whatever the place meant here may be, and I will explain what is meant in the present passage. He is not saying, "I brought up the foreigners from Cappadocia and the Syrians from Bothros." He wants to show the opposite: that he provided nothing for others like what he provided for these people, so that they, more than anyone, ought to keep up their gratitude toward him. And it is clear that if he had brought up others as he did these, he would surely have mentioned some providential care for them, and the purpose of that providence would be well known to all. For he did not simply bring Israel up out of Egypt; he led them with great care in order to make them fit for Christ the Master, the salvation of all, to appear from among them. What, then, does he mean? There have been very many migrations from place to place. Something of the kind happened with Terah, the father of blessed Abraham, who left the land of the Chaldeans, came to Harran, and died there; from there Abraham then moved to Palestine. And it is well known that blessed Jacob, with all his household, moved to Egypt. Much the same, we may suppose, happened with others too. Some set out from Cappadocia, moved into the territory of the foreigners, mingled with them and became part of them. Others again moved from Bothros to the Syrians, settled among them and intermarried with them. So God, wishing to say that he had given such gifts to no one as he had to them, said, "I did not rank you with the Ethiopians," meaning all the nations by naming a part. And he said that he had never been seen to grant anyone the same favors. For I brought you alone up out of Egypt, he says, with many wonders and many marvelous deeds, and brought you into a land so great and so fine, and made you its masters, though it in no way belonged to you. Nor did you come into it the way the foreigners from Cappadocia mingled with others, or those from Bothros with the Syrians.

Those people underwent certain migrations that had nothing marvelous about them and showed no special care of mine for them; besides, they live as resident aliens among the people they are with. But as for you, it is clear with how many wonders I brought you out, how I led you through the desert, how I brought you into the promised land, how great a land I made you masters of, after destroying everyone who lived in it before you, and how much care I went on giving you, more than to all other people. For all this you owed me great reverence, yet you have plainly shown no regard at all for what I have done for you. What then? Verses 8–10. — "Behold, the eyes of the Lord God are on the sinful kingdom, and I will remove it from the face of the earth; except that I will not utterly remove the house of Jacob, says the Lord." For this ingratitude, then, I will remove you from the land and carry this wicked kingdom off into captivity. Yet I will not allow you to be completely destroyed, remembering the goodwill with which I gave you so much care. "For behold, I give the command, and I will winnow the house of Israel among all the nations, as grain is winnowed in the winnowing fan, and no fragment shall fall to the ground." For like those who winnow a threshing floor and separate the wheat from the chaff, I will hand you over to the nations in captivity, but I will not destroy you completely; I will preserve those whom I judge worthy to obtain this salvation. "All the sinners of my people shall die by the sword, who say: Evils will not draw near or come upon us." For I will destroy in war those who lean toward what is worse and do not believe that anything grievous will come upon them as the prophets have announced. Having thus announced in all these ways the evils that would come upon the people—what was to befall the ten tribes at the hands of the Assyrians, and later the rest at the hands of the Babylonians—he also announces their change for the better after that, and says: Verses 11–12. — "In that day I will raise up the tent of David that has fallen, and rebuild it as in the days of old, so that the rest of mankind may seek me, and all the nations on whom my name has been called, says the Lord who does all these things." But after they have experienced these sorrows, I will change everything for the better and raise up the fallen kingdom of David, and once again give the whole people a leader from it. So not only those who were left, but also many of their enemies, stirred by amazement at what had happened, will confess God, the maker and Lord of all. For God, who will also bring these things to fulfillment, declares them. Here, then, he is speaking of the return from Babylon: when they returned to their own land, they would all have Zerubbabel, a descendant of David, as their ruler. Blessed James, however, in the Acts

…of the holy apostles evidently used this saying with reference to Christ the Lord, since it found its true fulfilment at the time when the fallen kingdom of David really did rise again. It cast off all decay and was established in perfection. It was then that the kingdom of David's line received its confirmation, "like the days of old," since it now stood firm for ever, and also because the knowledge of God came to the rest of humanity and to all the nations. The truth of the saying was seen in the events themselves. So the prophet spoke these words to indicate, for the time being, what would happen at the return from exile. But because the truth, certainty and permanence of what was said were shown and established in Christ the Lord, blessed James had good reason to use the saying. Then, describing in general the good things that would then be theirs, the prophet says, like the other prophets, that they would have an abundance of fruits in every way. The vintage would follow straight on the harvest gathered from the threshing floor, and their fruits would be given to them ripe. The mountains and hills would all but pour out plenty for them and bring forth a great many good things. "And I will end the captivity of my people," he says. Having gained their freedom and being back in their own land, they would rebuild their houses as they had been of old, work the land and gather its fruit. "And I will establish them securely in their own land": this is the meaning of "I will plant them in their land." I will no longer let them be outside their own country, which I made theirs in the beginning. For "They shall never again be uprooted from their land, which I gave them" means that they will no longer be outside [?] it, held by captivity as if under a kind of covering, so that they cannot even see their own land. These things, he says, are the decree and the work of God, the maker of all things.

[?] OF THE PROPHET. From of old the Idumeans were hostile toward the Israelites. They set great store by their destruction and rejoiced at the calamities that befell them, so much so that they even cooperated

in everything with their attackers whenever, by God's permission, the Israelites came to experience misfortune. The Israelites traced their descent from Jacob and the Idumeans from Esau, and these two were brothers, sons of Isaac. By divine judgement the rights of the firstborn passed to Jacob, so Esau hated him and wanted to kill him when he found the chance. Their mother arranged for Jacob to go away to Haran, so that with Jacob far away Esau's anger might die down. And indeed Jacob, granted God's providence, escaped harm from his brother entirely. Yet the enmity passed on to their descendants. The Idumeans, descended from Esau, remained hostile toward the Israelites descended from Jacob, as I have already said. They showed their enmity against them in various ways, and they displayed the same attitude no less at the time when the Assyrians attacked the Israelites, and later the Babylonians attacked Jerusalem and the tribe of Judah. They even cooperated with the Babylonians in a great many ways to destroy the Jews. That is why blessed David, prophesying about Babylon, says: "By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down and wept," and so on. With these words he showed the evils that befell them in that captivity. And since he was also going to announce their change for the better, he adds: "Remember, O Lord, against the sons of Edom the day of Jerusalem, how they said, 'Strip it, strip it, down to its foundations!'" It is clear that by "the sons of Edom" he means the Idumeans, who are called by both these names. One can learn this in many places in divine Scripture, and not least from the history of the Kingdoms. Amaziah struck Edom in war and then sent to the king of Israel, challenging him to battle. The king answered him insolently, and among other things said: "You have indeed struck Idumea, and your proud heart has lifted you up." Here he calls "Idumeans" the people who had been called Edom earlier. So the psalmist says: Remember the Idumeans and what they did to us. They made the time of our calamity an excuse for their own wickedness, so that they helped those who attacked us, hoping somehow to tear the whole city up from its foundations and leave not even a trace of it. And he adds: "Wretched daughter of Babylon, blessed is he who will repay you with the recompense you have paid us." He shows that God would punish the Idumeans as well for that attitude at the time when he would tear down the dominion of the Babylonians. He would hand over their royal city, together with its king and [?] its inhabitants, to the Persians, so that they would suffer at their hands the very things they had already done to Jerusalem. And he would free the Israelites from the captivity that held them and bring them back again to their own land.

God had often spoken through the prophets about the evils that would overtake the Israelites, first at the hands of the Assyrians and after that at the hands of the Babylonians, and he had said that all Israel would be led away captive in this way. As I have said, in those times the Idumeans gave the enemy every help they could, thinking they had found the right moment to wipe out completely everyone descended from the Israelite stock. In doing so they were plainly fighting against God, who had judged Jacob worthy of the blessing of the firstborn and had always shown great and exceptional care for all his descendants. The Israelites would naturally be disheartened by this. They were descended from the man who received the blessing of the firstborn by God's decree, yet they were suffering such things from the descendants of a forefather who had been cast out of the divine blessing. For this reason God necessarily moved the blessed prophet Obadiah to announce, throughout his prophecy, the punishment that would overtake the Idumeans. It would come when God decided to change the fortunes of the Israelites for the better: he would bring them back from captivity and restore them to their own land, so that they could rebuild Jerusalem and set up the temple in it. That was the place above all where they were meant to gather again and offer God the worship that the law required. At the time, the announcement of these things gave the wronged no small comfort. And after what was announced had come to pass, they were all the more convinced that God had willed these things when they were foretold long before, and that he had later brought them about in fact. Both of these things proved God's care for them. So it is clear that he made this announcement too out of forethought for the people, whose salvation, as I have often said, God took great care to secure.

Verse 1. "The vision of Obadiah." In meaning this does not differ at all from "The word of the Lord." By "the word of the Lord" he means the working of God by which the prophets, through the grace of the Spirit, received revelations of things to come. And by "vision" he means this same divine revelation, by which they were given knowledge of hidden things. The prophets received certain visions in their own souls, in a way that cannot be described, through the Spirit's working. They also heard the teaching about what was said [?] as if from someone speaking, by the working that the Holy Spirit produced in them. That is why he calls it both "vision" and "word of the Lord." And it is reasonable that he also calls it "hearing," since they received knowledge of the Spirit's teaching as if by a kind of hearing. This is why the blessed prophet Isaiah says: "Lord, who has believed what we heard?" That is: who has believed the knowledge of the things shown to us and of what we were taught by God? And blessed Paul very fittingly added, by divine inspiration: "So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God." He shows that it is impossible for such

hearing to come to the prophets in any other way than by the working of the Holy Spirit. Blessed David also says: "I will incline my ear to a parable; I will set out my riddle on the harp." That is: having lent my ear and received knowledge from God, I will pass on to people the teaching about what is fitting. So here too, after saying "The vision of Obadiah," which was a kind of heading for the book like the others, indicating whose words these were and how he had received the power to speak them, he begins the words of the prophecy: "Thus says the Lord God to Idumea." He shows whom the prophecy concerns. "I have heard a report from the Lord." What will happen to Idumea, he says, is hidden for now and will happen only after a long time, but I have received the teaching about it from God. Then what is the report? "And he has sent out an encircling force among the nations." By "encircling" he means something that surrounds a thing all around, such as a wall or the like. This is the sense of "Who will lead me into the city of encircling?", which means "into a walled city," that is, a city surrounded all around by a wall. So, he says, this is the report I heard: God sent out his command to the nations like a kind of encircling force, gathering them all from round about against Idumea. "Arise, and let us rise up against her for battle." The word "saying" is understood here by ellipsis, so that the sense is: "And he sent out an encircling force among the nations, saying: Arise, and let us rise up against her for battle." It is as though God himself were saying and commanding this, gathering the nations against her from every side, and even about to lead them as their general in the wars against Idumea. Blessed David says something similar: "Who will lead me into the city of encircling, and who will guide me as far as Idumea? Is it not you, O God, who rejected us?" That is: God will lead the wars against Idumea for me. This idiom can be found in blessed David too, where "saying" (in the singular or the plural) or some such word is implied by ellipsis. One example is: "Why did the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain? The kings of the earth and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Anointed: Let us break their bonds and cast their yoke from us." Here too "saying" is understood by ellipsis, to show the intention with which they carried out that lawless act. Another example is: "To the Lord I cried in my distress, and he heard me: Lord, deliver my soul from unjust lips and from a deceitful tongue." Here too "saying" is implied by ellipsis, so that the sense is: "To the Lord I cried in my distress, saying: Lord, deliver my soul from unjust lips and from a deceitful tongue." The words "and he heard me" are inserted in the middle to anticipate the outcome of the whole. So

here too he says that God gathered the nations, rousing them to war against Idumea by his command, as if by a kind of voice. Then, having announced the war, he turns to Idumea itself. Verses 2–4. "Behold, I have made you least among the nations; you are utterly despised." He says: I will bring great slaughter upon you through your enemies and reduce your nation to a few, so that you will be fewer than all and held in great contempt, besieged by many and surrounded by countless evils. Then what is the cause? "The pride of your heart has lifted you up, you who dwell in the clefts of the rocks and set your dwelling on high, who say in your heart: Who will bring me down to the ground?" Since the Idumeans lived in mountainous country, what he means is this: you became proud beyond measure, living in crevices of the rocks, yet thinking you had made your home great and mighty. You even thought there would never be anyone able to throw you out of your present prosperity. For this you will suffer what has been foretold, so that you may realize how vainly you thought yourself something when God's will was set against you. "Though you soar aloft like an eagle, and though you set your nest among the stars, from there I will bring you down, says the Lord." So even if you rise to the heights like an eagle, which by nature flies far above the mountains, and in your surpassing eminence set yourself among the stars, you will be no match for my power when I choose to drag you down. Verses 5–7. "If thieves came to you, if robbers by night, where would you have been cast out? Would they not have stolen only what they wanted? And if grape-gatherers came to you, would they not have left gleanings? How Esau has been searched out, and his hidden treasures seized!" If thieves, who usually rob secretly at night, had broken into your house, they might have taken a few things and left. But you would not have been driven from your house, since people who take whatever they come across by robbery could not deprive you of your home. And people who go into a vineyard for the vintage would certainly leave some fruit on the vines. But what is about to happen to you now will be nothing like that. Enemies will come who will overpower you so completely that they will search out everything you have and leave you nothing untouched, not even what you have hidden. Everything will be in their power, and they will go off taking whatever they please. Then, to prove how severe the evil will be: "All the men of your covenant have driven you to your borders; they have risen against you and prevailed over you." For even those who had treaties of friendship and alliance with you before will see how great your calamity is and go over to the side of your enemies. Together with the enemy you will be driven out of all your territory, as they push you into captivity to please your foes. They will rise against you and prevail, working together with your enemies. And he says the same thing again in another way: "Your allies who ate with you have laid an ambush under

you; there is no understanding in him." Those who embraced you as friends and shared salt with you will themselves lay ambushes for you and lead you to destruction, since in your excessive folly you cannot even tell true friends from enemies. Verses 8–11. "On that day, says the Lord, I will destroy the wise from Idumea and understanding from Mount Esau. Your warriors from Teman will be terrified, so that everyone will be cut off from Mount Esau because of the slaughter and the wickedness done to your brother Jacob. Shame will cover you, and you will be cut off for ever." All among you who boast of being wise and powerful in war will perish. Those who pride themselves on their battles in Teman, which appears to be the greatest of your cities, will be overcome by fear of the evils that come upon them and reduced to terror and cowardice. So great will be the destruction of your people, because you yourselves handed over to lawless slaughter your own brothers, who are descended from Jacob, the brother of your ancestor. For this you will be covered with shame and suffer utter destruction. "From the day you stood aloof, on the day when foreigners carried off his army captive and strangers entered his gates and cast lots for Jerusalem, you too were like one of them." The sentence for the evils that will come upon you was passed on you from the time you dared to do such things against your own brothers. When strangers were taking them captive, you stood aloof; that is, you took your place on the enemy's side. Foreigners entered their other cities and Jerusalem as well, and divided everything in them by lot, and you took part with those who dared such things. Verses 12–14. "Do not gaze on your brother's day, the day of strangers. Do not rejoice over the sons of Judah on the day of their destruction. Do not speak boastfully on the day of their distress. Do not enter the gates of peoples on the day of their troubles. Do not you too gaze on their gathering on the day of their ruin, nor join in attacking their army on the day of their destruction. Do not stand at their escape routes to wipe out those of them who survive, nor shut in those of them who flee on the day of distress." He says "do not gaze" instead of "so that you may not gloat"; that is, he says, so that you may not do these things. Following on from what he said before, he means: for these things you will pay the penalty and suffer the punishment announced. You rejoiced at your brother's calamities at the time when they were being destroyed by strangers. When they were in distress, you uttered such words as one would who was delighted at their destruction; this is what "speak boastfully" means. When they were in distress, you yourself entered the city with the others to do them every harm you could. And if any of them could somehow escape, hoping to save themselves that way,

you were eager to destroy them too, seizing those of them who fled and handing them over to punishment. This is what "Do not stand at their escape routes to wipe out those of them who survive, nor shut in those of them who flee on the day of distress" means. Throughout he wants to say: you were glad at the destruction of the Israelites, who are your brothers. You even helped the enemy against them, you delighted in their misfortunes, and you yourself, as far as you were able, heaped all kinds of evils upon them. For these things you will suffer the punishment that is coming. Hence he adds: Verses 15–17. "For the day of the Lord is near upon all the nations. As you have done, so it will be done to you; your recompense will return upon your own head." The time has come when he will punish all who have done anything at all against them. Above all he will bring heavy punishment upon you, bringing on you a calamity to match what you did against them. "For as you drank on my holy mountain, so all the nations will drink wine; they will drink and be bound [?], and they will be as though they had never been." You yourself have received punishment for what you dared to do on my mountain to those who live on it. And those who shared your attitude and your deeds will naturally share your punishment. They will be overtaken by utter destruction, so that they will be no different from things that have never existed at all. "You drank" and "they will drink" indicate the punishment that will be brought on them and on the others, as in the verse: "A cup is in the hand of the Lord, of unmixed wine, full of spiced wine; he has tipped it from one to the other, but its dregs have not been emptied; all the sinners of the earth will drink." And "on my holy mountain" means: for what you dared to do against my mountain and those who live on it, you have received punishment. And those who shared your attitude and your deeds will naturally share your punishment, overtaken by utter destruction. "But on Mount Zion there will be salvation, and it will be holy, and the house of Jacob will possess those who possessed them." This, then, is what will happen to you and to those who shared your attitude. But those who were attacked before will be saved on Mount Zion and freed from every distress, so that the mountain will truly be seen to be holy through the help given to them. For the descendants of Jacob, whom you and the others attacked from there, will hold in subjection all who formerly overpowered them. Verses 18–21. "And the house of Jacob will be a fire, and the house of Joseph a flame, and the house of Esau stubble; they will be set ablaze among them and devour them." The Israelites will prevail over all the Idumeans in this way: like fire consuming stubble, they will wipe them all out by force of arms. "And there will be no one left to carry fire for the house of Esau, for the Lord has spoken." Since he said that Israel would be fire to Esau, as if all…

…them, since they were going to destroy them in war. For this reason, he says, there will be no fire-bearer left to the house of Esau; that is, there will be no one among them able to do the Israelites any harm. They will suffer no ordinary things at the Israelites' hands, but they will be utterly unable to defend themselves or to do anything to injure them. All this will certainly come about, since it is God who has declared that it will happen. And since he said earlier that the house of Jacob will take possession of those who took possession of them, he wants to say this more fully. So he says that the Israelites in the Negev will take possession of the places belonging to Esau, and those in the Shephelah the places of the Philistines; and they will also recover their own land, as is natural: the men of Ephraim the plain of Samaria, and Benjamin the land of Gilead. Their return to their own land will begin from the country of Zarephath and end at Ephratha. He means that they will hold all the places of the Canaanites in between, which they had held before, (p. 227) and so too they will all receive back all their own cities in the Negev. To put it briefly: those who belong to Mount Zion and perform there the worship due to God will themselves obtain complete deliverance, and will bring a very great punishment on the descendants of Esau in return for what they suffered at their hands. To all this he added the words with which he concluded the prophecy: "And the kingdom shall be the Lord's." He means that through everything—both the good the Israelites enjoy and the penalty paid by those who have acted lawlessly against them—God will be shown to be the true King, the Lord and Maker of all things, who does with authority whatever he wills, both with his own people and with those who are reckoned strangers.

COMMENTARY ON JONAH THE PROPHET. God, the Lord and Maker of all things, being one and the same God of both the Old and the New Testament, ordered the affairs of both with a single purpose in view. He had long ago resolved within himself to reveal the state of things to come, (p. 228) whose beginning he displayed in the dispensation of Christ the Lord. But he thought it necessary for us first to live in this state—the present one, I mean—and afterward to pass over into that one through the resurrection from the dead, so that by comparison we might better recognize the greatness of the good things that would be revealed. Then, so that this might be made clear, and so that it might not be thought that he had devised and decided something new about us only later, he had already, through many other means, planted among human beings the expectation of the coming of Christ the Lord, so that all the Jews looked for it

long beforehand. Not least he brought this about through what concerned Abraham and David, to whom he made promises: to the one, that all the nations would be blessed in his seed; to the other, that he would grant everlasting kingship to his descendants. On the surface these promises pointed to the people in whom they were to be fulfilled, but the real truth of the matter was shown to reach its fulfilment in the dispensation of Christ the Lord. In him the nations were truly blessed, and the kingdom became everlasting and unshakable for the seed. This is why God's care for the people was so great, (p. 229) since all of them, kept safe in the promises mentioned, were awaiting the expected coming of Christ the Lord. For this reason he arranged a great many things in the Old Testament in such a way that the events brought the greatest benefit to the people of that time, while also carrying some indication of the things that would be revealed later, and at the same time showing how very great was the superiority of the later things over the earlier. In this way the old things turned out to be a kind of type of the later ones: they bore some likeness to them and were also useful in their own times, yet the facts themselves showed how far inferior they were. God brought Israel out of Egypt and freed them from all that bitter slavery. He brought great death upon the firstborn, and by this he kept the Israelites' firstborn entirely safe. He marked them off by a sign so that they would suffer nothing like the Egyptians; this sign was the smearing of blood on the doorposts. When these things happened, they brought great benefit to the Israelites, who enjoyed them. But they also foreshadowed, as in types, that Christ the Lord would likewise set us free—not from slavery in Egypt, but from death and sin. (p. 230) This he granted us by the anointing of his own blood. For he poured it out for all and underwent death on our behalf; he brought about the resurrection of the dead and granted to all of us, freed from all slavery here, to await immortality [?]—teaching us, as it were, in certain types [?]. The blessed Paul makes this clear when he says: "All these things happened to them as types, and they were written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the ages have

come." In the same way, through the ordinance of the law, he arranged that those who used the sacrifices and the blood of irrational animals should be benefited by them, (p. 231) so that by comparison we might believe all the more firmly that we shall obtain the greatest good things in the blood of Christ the Lord. Hence the blessed Paul says: "For if the blood of bulls and goats, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled on those who are defiled, sanctify for the purification of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purify our conscience from dead works?" From the difference between Christ the Lord and irrational animals he has sufficiently assured us that we ought to trust in these things far more than the people of that time trusted in those. Again, in the wilderness, when the Israelites were perishing for their disobedience from the bites of snakes, God commanded the blessed Moses to make a bronze serpent, so that those who were bitten might look at it and easily be released from the harm of what had bitten them. God could have prevented their being bitten at all, or found some other cure for the bite; but he chose that they should be released from the harm of the biting creatures through an image of those very creatures. This was so that we should not be too astonished if God, undoing death by the death of Christ the Lord, (p. 232) grants us immortal life through the resurrection. Hence the Lord too says: "And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life." He shows that just as the likeness of the biting creatures then healed the harm of the bite, in the same way now death, which spreads over all human beings, having come upon Christ the Lord, will grant not to him alone but to all human beings [release from] death [?].

So it was too with what happened to the blessed prophet Jonah. When the Jews were disobedient and unwilling to accept the prophecies, God arranged for him to go over to the nations. Then, after keeping him alive in the sea monster for three days and nights in a marvelous way, he brought him to the city that was full of countless evils, and arranged that by preaching repentance he should become the cause of salvation for everyone there. This was so that by comparison we should not disbelieve that Christ the Lord too, kept free from corruption for the same length of time and risen from the dead into immortal life, grants to all the nations alike the salvation that comes from repentance—and this while the Jews disbelieve. Hence the Lord says at one point: "For just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the sea monster, (p. 233) so must the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth"; and at another: "The men of Nineveh will rise up and condemn this generation, because they heard the preaching of Jonah; and behold, something greater than Jonah is here."

He makes it clear that there is some resemblance between the events, but that the difference between these and those is great; and that these people will remain unbelieving just like the Jews of that time, while the nations will receive the salvation that comes from the preaching. It was clearly for these purposes that the blessed Jonah was put forward. For the prophet would not otherwise have been so disobedient to God as to refuse to do any of what he was told—and that when he was being sent for the salvation of so many people. Nor, if he was disobedient, was it absolutely necessary for him to experience the dangers of the sea, so as to be thrown to a sea monster, be kept alive inside it in a marvelous way, and undergo his still more marvelous return from there. God could have roused the hesitant and disobedient prophet to his duty by other means, as we know he did with Moses when he hesitated over the service of his mission, and with Jeremiah, who likewise shrank from the greatness of his service. (p. 234) But God chose to lead the blessed Jonah, quite openly, through such novel and astonishing events, because he intended to make him a type of what would concern Christ the Lord. For this reason, having been carried through such incredible novelty, he would be worthy of belief as he displayed the type of so great a reality.

This, then, one might call the principal reason for the astonishing things that happened to the blessed Jonah. But there is also a secondary reason, which takes its starting point from the type. The prophets could not help being deeply despondent. They were continually sent by God to the people; they announced to them what was to come and threatened the punishments that would be brought upon them; and they did everything that might contribute to their correction with great zeal. Yet they achieved nothing, because the wickedness of the Israelites worked against the care God was showing them through the prophets. As a result they naturally thought their own labor was in vain, and they came to despair completely of human affairs. For the nations had turned once and for all to what was worse, while those who were thought to have been chosen for the knowledge of God (p. 235) were in no way behind them in impiety and depravity of conduct. Wishing to console them in this state, God—who takes great care of all human beings but shows special concern for his own—often revealed to them the change in human affairs that would come about with the manifestation of Christ the Lord, when all people would by divine grace turn from the worse to the better. Last of all he performed this marvelous work in the case of the prophet Jonah, for the instruction and consolation of all the prophets. Through it he persuaded them by deeds that what was said about Christ the Lord would come true, and that all human beings would then by divine grace pass over to

[?] what is right. Now, the Jews were stubbornly persisting in their choice of the worse, because God allowed it so, to expose human will and weakness. But at the coming of Christ the Lord, when God chose to display his own grace, all human beings who had always inclined to impiety would turn toward the better. As the blessed Paul says: "Scripture has shut up all things under sin, so that we might be justified by faith." (p. 236) He shows that we were taught by people's earlier inclination toward the worse, so that we might learn that we need divine grace to discern the better and prefer it above all. God gave the prophets sufficient proof of this through the present events, thinking that it should be shown above all in the case of Jonah, who provided in himself a type of what would happen concerning Christ the Lord. For he sends him to the city of Nineveh, which was great and very populous and was the royal city of the Assyrians. Everyone there was given over to impiety and clung to a depraved life, living in luxury, indulgence, licentiousness and every kind of lawlessness. He commands him to announce the destruction of the city unless they turned to what was right. Then he brought it about that all of them, on hearing all at once the voice of the prophet—a man they did not know, whom they had not seen appear with miracles that might have struck them with amazement—should change their former mind and look to the better on the strength of the threat alone, even though they were gentiles and had never shown any sign of having heard teaching that led to godliness. In this way he would show by the present events (p. 237) that at the coming of Christ the Lord he would likewise, by his own grace, make all the nations turn to the better, even if the Jews chose to disobey the teaching of true religion. Hence the blessed prophet perceived from the present events that the Jews would be shown to deserve the utmost punishment, having accepted no correction from so much teaching, if the Ninevites, who lived and moved in impiety, were seen to change for the better all at once from a mere announcement. He perceived too that, since these things happened as a demonstration of what would happen concerning Christ the Lord, the same thing would happen far more fully when the nations, called by divine grace, turned to true religion, while the Jews remained disobedient and did not receive Christ the Lord, whose announcement and teaching they had among themselves, handed down from of old. And he perceived that as a result the people living everywhere on earth would be declared heirs of the kingdom of heaven, while the Jews would be shut out of this gift because of their own disobedience and impiety, even though they seemed to have been raised in such teaching of the better. So he was inevitably despondent, seeing the matter as deserving of grief from every side, and naturally sharing the Jews' pain, (p. 238) since they were such people and were about to

suffer so much. He lamented that even now, by comparison with the Ninevites, they would be shown to deserve punishment, and that after this they would suffer complete rejection by comparison with the nations all over the earth who would come to the teaching of true religion. For if the blessed Paul laments their rejection and said he would gladly suffer the utmost punishment if only they would look to what is right and not render vain the great care God had shown them—"I speak the truth in Christ, I am not lying, my conscience bearing me witness in the Holy Spirit, that I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart. For I could wish that I myself were accursed from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites; to them belong the adoption, the glory, the covenant, the giving of the law, the worship and the promises; theirs are the fathers, and from them, according to the flesh, is Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen"—how is it not obvious that the prophets too, being of the same mind, lamented and mourned over these things, whether because of what was happening then or because of what was announced for the future? It was for this reason that the prophet chose to flee, thinking he could avoid the announcement to the Ninevites and prevent what would follow from it, (p. 239) by which the wickedness of the Jews would be clearly exposed. What followed proves what has been said. For the Ninevites, who had accepted the change for the better so readily, marched against the Israelites not long afterward, took the rest of them captive, and were very eager to sack Jerusalem as well. For this they received the severest punishment from God, which the prophet Nahum announced and left recorded in his books. So the prophecy of Jonah, and what happened to the Ninevites at that time, is an indication of the divine grace by which they all so easily accepted the change for the better; while Nahum's prophecy reveals the depravity of those same people, which led them to attempt such great evils and to receive the punishment they deserved for them all. These things one may rightly learn from everything that happened earlier to the blessed Jonah and was said later in the New Testament, as we showed above. But what happened at that time and is set out in the writing of the book—which also gave the greatest benefit and use to the people of that time—we shall learn from the details themselves, which we shall now take up and interpret, with God's help.
Verses 1–2. (p. 240) "And the word of the Lord came to Jonah son of Amittai, saying: Arise and go to Nineveh, the great city, and

preach in it, for the cry of its wickedness has come up to me." Jonah the prophet received a divine revelation, he says, to go to the city of Nineveh and preach in it, since its people were committing great transgressions, so great that their magnitude was enough to move God. Since the city was very large, crowded with people, and at that time the most famous of all the cities of Assyria, it must have been known by report to those in Judea. That is why God sends him as to a familiar city, since he knew it not by sight but only by report. Here he says only, "Preach in it." But it is clear that he was sent for this purpose: to threaten the city with overthrow, and to admonish all its inhabitants to turn to repentance, so that in this way they might escape the city's overthrow. For divine Scripture is accustomed to abbreviate a great deal when readers are able to infer what follows. Just because he said here, "Preach in it," God did not send the prophet having said only this and without teaching him what he was to preach. (p. 241) Nor, when it says, "Yet three days, and Nineveh will be overthrown," was the prophet ordered to say only that; rather, he was to make them better by announcing the overthrow, so that they would take hope that if they repented they would escape what was threatened. Indeed, it would have been pointless to threaten the overthrow if it had to happen in any case, since nothing would be gained from the threat. So either they would change and escape the punishment, or, if they did not change, it would be shown that the punishment was justly brought upon them by God because of their own wickedness. Verse 3. Knowing this, the prophet, he says, fled to Tarshish from the face of the Lord. He would not have done this if he had known that the overthrow would certainly take place and that he had been sent only to announce that so great an evil would come, with nothing better at all coming of it. Some have said that Tarshish means Tarsus, because the names sound alike, but they were mistaken, it seems. For Tarsus is not a coastal city, whereas divine Scripture usually uses this name to denote coastal cities, as in the blessed David: "With a violent wind you will shatter the ships of Tarshish." This can be said of a coastal city with ships moored beside it, (p. 242) but it in no way fits a city as far inland as Tarsus clearly is from the sea. Others have said it is Rhodes. But I think all this precision is superfluous for the matter at hand, since the prophet's story stands just as firm whatever city one takes it to be. What should rather be noted is that he did not say, "He fled from God," but "from the face of the Lord." For it was not God that the prophet [?]

…he supposed, since he held Him to be Lord and Maker of all things and believed Him to be present everywhere. But because God had commanded that all worship be offered to Him on Mount Zion, He had given the Jews the impression that He dwelt there and made His own manifestation there. For this reason both the city of Jerusalem and the whole land of promise were called God's dwelling, as though God dwelt in all of it and watched over all of it. That is why Scripture says the prophet fled from the presence of the Lord: it means that he left the land in which God made His own manifestation and went away to some other, distant land. For this is what the prophet was doing. As long as he stayed in that land, God would certainly appear to him and press him to do what He wished. But if he went far away, he would be free of that pressure, since the Deity would not consent to appear in other places. In the same way the Jews in captivity considered sacrifices and all the worship offered to God to be pointless, since He did not appear in those places and would not consent to accept what was done there in His honour. The prophet was plainly reluctant about the task. He perceived that God was certainly sending him with some good hopes in view. God would not have sent him for destruction alone unless He also wished to bring about some good from it. And the prophet thought it utterly absurd that, appearing for the first time to people who had never known him, he should at once gain the reputation of a liar and a deceiver. He himself is seen to make this clear later in his own words. Verses 4–6. — So the prophet went down to Joppa for this reason. Finding there a ship bound for Tarshish, he paid the fare for his folly, went aboard with the others and sailed for Tarshish. He expected to escape the divine pressure there, since God did not appear to him in foreign places to urge him to go and do the task set before him. But when he was out sailing on the sea, God showed him, as it were, that the flight he had undertaken was pointless and vain. He stirred up a violent wind and raised such a surge on the sea that the ship was in danger of breaking apart, unable to bear the force of the waves. Fear then seized those on board, as was natural. Each of them called aloud to the god he believed in and was accustomed to worship, and begged to be delivered from the present danger. As the surge grew worse, they also threw the ship's contents into the sea, as people caught in a storm usually do, hoping that the lightened ship might somehow escape the danger. To this he adds: "But Jonah had gone down into the hold of the ship, and was sleeping there and snoring." This does not mean that he went down into the ship and fell asleep after those things had happened. It would be ridiculous for him to give himself up to sleep amid such turmoil, with everyone in danger for their lives. Rather,

he did this as soon as he boarded the ship. But Scripture first narrated the events of the storm and only afterwards added what the prophet had done at that time. It then tells how the shipmaster went and saw the prophet sleeping amid such turmoil and roused him. He marvelled that, with so great an evil happening, the prophet had no awareness of the evils gripping them, but was sleeping and snoring without a care. And he urged him to get up and call on his own god, in case they might at least be saved by him. Verses 7–9. — The prophet did none of this, for he thought it dangerous to offer prayers to the very one from whom he had fled. Meanwhile the evil of the storm grew worse. So they then tried to discover by lot who was the cause of the present evil. This showed that the storm was not general over the whole sea, but that all the turmoil was stirred up around that one ship. Reasoning from this to the cause, those on board wished to find out by lot who was responsible for their troubles. Perhaps the Lord God Himself had put this thought into their minds, so that the rest might follow in due order. They cast the lots, and blessed Jonah was shown to be the cause of what had happened. The sailors were astonished that he should have done something capable of producing so great an evil. Rebuking him severely, and practically taking on the manner of a court, as though speaking to a man already condemned by the lot, they demanded to know what he had done, what his occupation was, where he came from and where he was going, from what country he had set out, and to what nation of men he belonged. He answered them plainly: "I am a servant of the Lord, and I worship the Lord, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land." Since they were devoted to idols, he made known what was distinctive about his own religion by saying that he was a servant of God, that is, one whose whole concern was to attend to God's service. He did not say "servant" in the general sense, in which the sailors too were necessarily servants of God, having been made by Him. Then, stating also what was distinctive about the God he worshipped, he says: "I worship the Maker of the universe, who is the Maker of heaven and sea and all things." Verses 10–13. — When the men heard this they were afraid, thinking that the Maker of all had been stirred to anger against them. So they asked the prophet, "What is this that you have done?" They had learned that he had fled from God to avoid God's prompting, and that he had then fallen into the present evil along with them, so that he might learn that God is present everywhere and works His will everywhere alike, and that it is impossible to flee from such a one. So they then say to the prophet himself: "What shall we do to you, so that the sea will calm down for us?" From what had been said they had learned about him: that he was a servant and prophet of God. They had also learned that the

events agreed with what he said. So they wanted to learn from him what they ought to do to be rid of the present evil. And he adds that "the sea went on, and raised the surge still higher," showing that the storm kept growing worse, so that those on the ship would not treat what was happening lightly. Then he says: "And Jonah said to them: Take me up and throw me into the sea, and the sea will calm down for you; for I know that it is because of me that this great surge has come upon you." "I am the cause of these evils for you," he says, "and I advise you to throw me into the sea. Then I will pay the penalty for the sins I committed against God, and you will be released from the evils that grip you." But they thought it dangerous simply to cast into the sea so great a man, one who belonged to God. So they strove to get back to land if they could, and in that way put the prophet off the ship. When they were unable to do this, because the sea was making the storm worse against them, they made their defence to God for what they were about to do, and only then threw the prophet into the sea.

Verses 14–16. — For he says this: "And they cried out to the Lord and said: By no means, O Lord, let us not perish for the life of this man, and do not lay innocent blood upon us; for you, O Lord, have done as you wished." They mean: "Do not bring punishment on us as though we were casting a righteous man into the sea for no reason. For our part, we cared above all that the man be saved. But this did not happen, since apparently it did not please you, for the surge grew worse and would not let us do what might save the man." Having made their defence to God in these words, they threw Jonah into the sea, and at once the surge ceased. The men were then seized with great fear as they saw the power of the Lord of all, who had stirred up the sea as He wished and, when He wished, at once and immediately brought it all to calm. Then he adds: "And they sacrificed to the Lord and vowed vows." He does not mean that they sacrificed to the Lord on the spot, for they would not have performed sacrifices on the ship. He means rather that they abandoned the idols completely and dedicated themselves to the worship of God. They promised to hold fast to His service from then on and to offer Him the appropriate sacrifices. This is what "they vowed vows" means.

Verses 1–7. — Jonah, then, was carried a long way on the sea. And God commanded a great sea creature to swallow Jonah as he was being carried on the sea. The prophet spent three days and nights in its belly, wholly unharmed. He himself marvelled that he was kept safe inside the creature and wholly unharmed, as if he were in a little house in great safety. So he turned to prayer, which he sent up to God from the creature's belly. The words of the prayer are as follows: "I cried out to

the Lord my God, and He heard me; out of the belly of Hades you heard my cry, my voice." That is: "I was in the heaviest affliction, and through despair at my evils I had come into Hades itself. I cried out to you, and my requests did not fail." "You cast me into the depths of the heart of the sea, and rivers surrounded me; all your billows and your waves passed over me." That is: "When I fled from your service, you made me fall into the sea and endure a great surge. The sea was so violently stirred up by it that the waters of the waves poured over me like rivers." "And I said: I have been driven away from your sight; shall I ever again look upon your holy temple?" That is: "In my helplessness amid these evils I thought I had been cast out of your providence. I no longer had any hope of being in your holy temple and offering you the worship due to you, since I was far from it and hemmed in by the heaviest evils." "Water was poured around me up to my soul." That is: "The turmoil of the waters that poured around me reached my very soul." "The deepest abyss surrounded me." That is: "In the end I was swallowed up by the abyss itself." "My head sank into the clefts of the mountains." That is: "I seemed to myself no different from someone caught in the deepest clefts of the mountains, who then, when the mountains close together, finds no hope of escape." "I went down into a land whose bars are everlasting restraints." That is: "Then the creature received me from there, and I seemed to be living in a land from which it was quite impossible for a captive to escape. Inside it I was kept unharmed by divine providence, yet I could find no way out of it." Verses 8–11. — "And let my life come up from corruption to you, O Lord my God." That is: "It belongs to your power alone to deliver my life from the corruption that awaited it there." "When my soul was failing within me, I remembered the Lord." That is: "When I was close to giving up my soul in my helplessness, I asked for your help." "And may my prayer come to you, into your holy temple." That is: "Receive my prayer yourself while you abide in your own temple. The distance between the places does not prevent you from helping me." "Those who observe vain things and lies have forsaken their mercy." That is: "Those who follow the sailor's trade, although they are devoted to idols and taken up with that deception, wished to show me some mercy. But they were overcome by the evils and gave up that intention, seeing that they could not live unless they were rid of my presence." "But I will sacrifice to you with a voice of praise and thanksgiving; what I have vowed I will pay to you for salvation to the Lord." That is: "I have been preserved on every side by your grace alone and have received deliverance from death. So I will render you hymns and thanksgivings for having been saved by your providence." These, then, are the words of the prophet's prayer. And by the divine Spirit the creature vomited Jonah out onto dry land, as God saw fit for this to happen. It is the height of folly, when so many things

happened to him so extraordinarily, and above all his preservation inside the creature, to pry into how the prophet got out of the creature, and to try to grasp by human reasoning and explain in our own words how it happened.

Verses 1–4. — Now that the prophet is on dry land, God orders him once again to go to Nineveh and proclaim what He had told him before. This shows especially clearly that God did not simply tell him to proclaim, "Yet three days, and Nineveh will be overthrown," even though divine Scripture seems to put it that briefly. God also told him to make clear that He was threatening that these things would happen unless they repented and turned away from evil. That is why He says: "Proclaim in it according to the former proclamation which I spoke to you." By this He points him to the whole teaching that He had earlier commanded him to deliver to the Ninevites. The prophet, now chastened by experience, hastened to carry out God's commands. Scripture says that "the city was very great to God," meaning that it had grown to greatness by divine providence. This would teach us to think that nothing in this life can attain distinction unless God bestows His own care on it. "And it was," he says, "about a three days' journey." He does not mean that its length was that great, but that it would take that many days for someone who wished to go all the way around it and see clearly what it was like. So he adds: "And Jonah began to enter the city about a day's journey." This means that the prophet entered the city, began from one part of it and went around it, and spent about one day preaching and saying, "Yet three days, and Nineveh will be overthrown," along with everything else he was to say to those present in each part of the city for the instruction of his hearers, accordingly

Verses 5–9. — To this he adds: "And the men of Nineveh believed God." This shows that after the prophet began preaching in one part of the city, the message spread to everyone very quickly. All of them accepted what was said without doubting, and in great fear they obeyed it. The words "The men of Nineveh believed God" also show that this was not the only thing he said: "Yet three days, and Nineveh will be overthrown." From those words alone they could not have believed God. A foreigner, wholly unknown to them, would have been threatening destruction while adding nothing else and not even telling his hearers who had sent him. It is clear, rather, that he also spoke of God, the Lord of all, and said that he had been sent by Him. And he proclaimed the destruction in order to call them to repentance. Because they accepted this teaching, they were rightly said to believe God, whose sentence and teaching

they accepted. In accordance with the prophet's word they turned toward what was better, and so displayed a great and earnest repentance. As he says, they proclaimed a fast throughout the city. All of them, small and great, put on sackcloth, took on the appearance of mourners, and begged God to be merciful to them. When the word reached even the king, he too evidently did not neglect the matter. He cared little for his royal dignity. He left his throne and threw off his royal robe, and putting on sackcloth himself, he remained sitting in ashes. Next the king and his officials issued decrees that not only the people but also the animals kept for their service should go without any food or drink. Nor did they stop their repentance there. They also turned away from the evils they had long been practising and separated themselves from all injustice toward others. And they earnestly hoped that God too would change His mind about what He had pronounced against them and revoke the sentence He had issued altogether. "For who knows," they say, "whether God will repent and relent, and turn from His fierce anger, so that we do not perish?" They could not have said this unless they had been taught it by the prophet's words. The prophet says that this is what in fact happened. When God saw that they had turned away from what was evil and inclined toward what was better, He too revoked the sentence He had pronounced against them.

Verses 1–4. — "At this," he says, "Jonah was greatly grieved and confounded." This was natural. He was troubled because he was about to gain the reputation of a deceiver and liar among them, since he had threatened that the overthrow would come within three days, and nothing had happened. Then, looking to God, he said: "Were not these my words while I was still in my own land? That is why I made haste to flee to Tarshish, for I knew that you are merciful and compassionate, slow to anger and abounding in mercy, and that you relent from bringing evils." He showed clearly that this had also been the cause of his [?] for him: he knew that God, being a lover of humankind, would surely change His own sentence if He saw them change their ways. And he knew that as a result he would end up with the reputation of a liar and deceiver among them. So he adds: "And now, Sovereign Lord, take my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live." He means: "For this reason I judge death preferable to living among people with such a reputation." God, who is loving toward those who repent and exceedingly gentle toward His own, rebukes the prophet in a way meant to shame him, and says: "Are you so very grieved?" That is: "You seem to be disheartened that so many have been saved. You ought to have weighed the salvation of all against your own reputation, and thought it better that you yourself be regarded in this way than that so many should perish." Verses 5–8. — The prophet, having gone out of the

…the city, he sat down opposite it. He made himself a booth and stayed under it until he could see what more might happen to the city after all. Weighing the size of the threat, he supposed that something or other would still happen after this. Then God commanded a gourd to spring up all at once and fill with shade the whole booth in which the prophet was, so that its leaves were thick enough to give him the shelter of a house, and its fruit, hanging in clusters on every side, gave him a great deal of comfort. This pleased the prophet, who was naturally delighted by the wonder of the sight and by how useful the thing was. But when he had taken great pleasure in it and thought he had enough comfort from it, again all at once, at God's command, a worm appeared in the plant and devoured it all [?] and dried it up completely. When he says "a worm at dawn," he means that at dawn, at God's command, a worm suddenly sprang up on the plant and dried the whole of it up, so that when the sun rose its scorching rays fell on him with full force. So he says, "God commanded a scorching, burning wind, and it beat on Jonah's head, and he grew faint and gave up on his life." This shows that even the heat did not come in the usual way. By God's command he sent the blaze on him at its heaviest, so that the prophet would feel what had happened more keenly and be pained all the more, since the heat brought him close to giving up his life. That is what "and he gave up on his life" means. He said to God, "It is better for me to die than to live." He meant something like this: "I thought the plant was some comfort in the troubles that beset me. Then all at once it was gone, and through my own wretched assumption I have gained besides the severity of the heat and the danger that now afflicts me. How then is death not better than life, if I must wrestle with so many evils?" Verses 9–11. So God says to him, "Are you deeply grieved over the gourd?" Jonah answered that he was grieved to death. God had shown him the plant as something lovely and had made his grief at its loss all the greater, so that by comparison he might expose more strongly how wicked his grief at the city's salvation had been. So God continues: "So you were this pained over the gourd, though you put no labor into its growth? It came into being all at once in a night, and all at once in a night it perished. How then is it not more fitting for me to spare Nineveh, the city so very great that a hundred and twenty thousand people live in it who do not know their right hand from their left?" He means infants. Those who "do not know right or left" are those who, being infants, cannot yet tell things apart with any precision, and who have never been in sin, since their age does not allow it. He says this to show how large the city's population was. Where the infants were so many, how many must the grown men have been? But God, passing over all the rest,

mentioned the number of the infants. They plainly did not deserve to suffer any evil, since they had not yet sinned at all. "Surely," he says, "you would not claim that so many infants who had done no sin ought to perish. So even if the adults were not to be spared, the infants at least ought to have been remembered, and the city should have suffered no harm." And he added "and many cattle," since these too were harmless and ought rightly to be preserved for the people of the city who were saved.

COMMENTARY ON THE PROPHET MICAH. Verses 1–2. The blessed Micah plainly prophesies things like those of Hosea, Amos and the others who prophesied the same things. Moved by the grace of the Spirit, he too sets out to foretell what would befall the people at the hands of the Assyrians and the Babylonians.
