From the very opening he addresses all Israel together: I mean both the ten tribes, which were headed by Samaria, and the two, which were led by Jerusalem. He also clearly prophesied at the same time as those prophets, that is, in the days of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, kings of Judah. For it was in these days, he says, that "the word of the Lord came to Micah of Moresheth," that is, he received a divine working. For what purpose? "Concerning what he saw about Samaria and about Jerusalem." He means the whole people of Israel: both the kingdom of the ten tribes and that of the two, which was led by the tribe of Judah, with David's descendants ruling it in keeping with the promise made to him. Having received a revelation about these peoples and what would befall them by a divine working, Micah says what he was taught to say in the divine revelation, beginning like this: "Hear words, all you peoples." Consistently with this, "all you peoples" means all Israel, belonging to both kingdoms. That is why he went on: "And let the earth and all who are in it pay attention." That is, the whole land of Israel, or rather the people who live in it, which was given to them long ago through God's promise to the fathers. "And the Lord God will be among you as a witness." "God speaks to you through us," he says, "bearing solemn witness about what is to come, since

he has often told you what you ought to do, and saw that you did not change for the better even once. So it will be plain that he did everything for your benefit, while you refused to become any better and only drew evils down on yourselves." "The Lord from his holy house." This addition is necessary. He is addressing everyone together, and the ten tribes were much given to worshipping idols. They even built houses for them and tried to worship demons as gods through the idols. So he rightly added "the Lord from his holy house," to show that he speaks to all of them together, sent to say these things by the God who has his own house in Jerusalem, a house he made holy by his own working. Then he adds: Verses 3–5. "For behold, the Lord is coming out of his place. He will come down and tread on the heights of the earth, and the mountains will be shaken beneath him, and the valleys will melt like wax before fire and like water rushing down a slope." "God," he says, "will go out from the mountain that he declared the place of his own dwelling and take control of the whole land of Israel" (meaning the land his word is addressed to). He will throw its mighty men into turmoil, whom he calls mountains because they stand above others, and all the rest as well, since he calls the lowlier people valleys. He will consume them like wax that has touched fire. Clearly he does not mean that the mountains are shaken and the valleys melt as two separate things. Following the Hebrew idiom, which we have often pointed out, he expresses one common fact by dividing it: the divine wrath will come upon all, both the mighty and the rest of the populace, shaking them and destroying them like wax that has touched fire. It will drag them down to punishment like violent, torrential water rushing from a height to lower ground. The cause of these things is this: "All this is because of the ungodliness of Jacob and because of the sin of the house of Israel." Then he continues: "What is the ungodliness of Jacob? Is it not Samaria? And what is the sin of the house of Judah? Is it not Jerusalem?" The ungodliness of the ten tribes is plain, since they gathered in Samaria to worship idols, and it was there that most of the temples built for that purpose stood. The lawlessness of Judah is no less plain: though they had Jerusalem among them, they were not even ashamed enough before the temple to keep away from idol worship. Then he lists the punishments: Verses 6–9. "And I will make Samaria a watchman's hut in a field, a place for planting a vineyard. I will drag her stones down into a chasm and lay bare her foundations." "I will reduce Samaria to utter desolation, so that it is farmed like open country and huts are set up on it to guard the crops. I will wipe out her buildings completely and tear them up from their foundations." Of course, what follows will come of this too: "And they will smash all her carved images." Then they will see their own vain labors destroyed, as they watch the enemy demolish the idols they made. "And they will burn all her wages with fire." They will destroy with fire all the ornaments that adorned the idols

and the temples, which they paid to the demons as a kind of wage. "And I will bring all her idols to destruction, for she gathered them from a harlot's wages, and from a harlot's wages she has amassed them." "They took on a harlot's mind," he means. "They left me and turned to the idols. They collected what were, in effect, the wages of their fornication and offered them for the worship of idols. I will destroy all of this together." "Because of this she will beat her breast and lament; she will go barefoot and naked." She will be lamenting and beating her breast, handed over to the harshest captivity. That is what "naked and barefoot" means: she will be led away captive like this, stripped of all her finery. "She will make lamentation like serpents, and mourning like daughters of sirens, for her blow has prevailed. It has come as far as Judah and reached the gate of my people, as far as Jerusalem." He says "like serpents and sirens" in line with the myths some people tell. He means that what many tell of in myths they will undergo in actual fact, because I will bring a heavy blow on them. It will begin from Samaria and pass on to Judah, reaching Jerusalem too, since the Babylonians later captured that city as well. Verses 10–13. "You in Gath, do not boast; and you in Akim, do not rebuild from a house in mockery." He turns his discourse to the neighboring nations. Blessed Amos also spoke about them, saying that they too would suffer the same as the Israelites at the hands of the Assyrians. "You in those cities, then," he says, "do not be arrogant when you see the misfortunes of these people; [?] in mockery. It is fitting for you to sprinkle dust on yourselves instead, since you will become a laughingstock to others." How, and in what way? "While she dwells in comfort, I will destroy her cities." "However secure you think you are, living comfortably in your own cities, you will see every one of them destroyed." "She who lives in Aenan did not come out to mourn the house next to her." "They too," he says, "saw their neighbors the Israelites falling into such evils, yet would not come out of their homes to share their mourning. Instead, they kept on rejoicing at their misfortunes." What then? "You will receive a painful blow from yourselves." "Since you did not share in the pain of others' evils, you yourselves will receive a painful blow and pay the penalty for the wicked attitude that made you rejoice at others' evils." "Who has begun to do good to her who lives in pain?" Those who live in pain cannot share in any good at all, because the evils brought on them are so great. Then, to prove what he has said: "For evils have come down from the Lord upon the gates of Jerusalem, the noise of chariots and horsemen." "God's wrath on all of them," he says, "will be so great that not even Jerusalem will be spared then, when it is surrounded by chariots, horses and the whole enemy force." Verses 13–15. Then he turns his discourse to Lachish, a city of the kingdom of Judah full of many transgressions, and says: "You who live in Lachish, she is the beginning of sin for the daughter

of Zion, for in you were found the ungodly deeds of Israel." "You too, then," he says, "must know the evils that will befall you, since you led Jerusalem into evil and were no different from Samaria in your ungodly disposition." He calls Jerusalem the daughter of Zion. "Therefore you will give those who are sent away as far as the inheritance of Gath, vain houses; the houses of vain things became empty for the kings of Israel." "For these things, then, you too will undergo the same captivity." He says "you will give those who are sent away" instead of "you will send people from among yourself into captivity." She will suffer the same as those who live in Gath, and all the houses she built for ungodliness will be destroyed, just as the idol-houses in Samaria were destroyed. "Until I bring your heirs." "You will suffer these things when I bring the enemies, who will inherit your good things." "You who live in Lachish, the inheritance will come as far as Adullam, the glory of the daughter of Zion." They will take possession of Lachish and extend their own inheritance as far as Adullam. In other words, they will hold the whole land of promise. Besides this, Jerusalem too will be taken, which is thought glorious because of the temple in it. Some have said that the prophet says these things to Lachish because it killed King Amaziah, since this was the first time that people in Judah dared to kill their own king, although it had often happened before in the kingdom of the ten tribes. But one can see on every count that this claim is a myth and a fabrication, invented by people who did not understand the prophet's words. Amaziah was not the first king from the tribe of Judah to be killed by conspiracy. His father Joash had been killed in this way before him, as the history in Kings shows when it says: "The servants of Joash rose up and made a conspiracy, joined together against him and struck him down." Later, when his son Amaziah came to the throne, he seized these men to avenge his father's murder. The history also says about him: "And when the kingdom was firmly in Amaziah's hand, he struck down his servants who had struck down his father." Nor, it seems, were the people of Lachish the ones who killed Amaziah, for the text says: "And a conspiracy was formed against Amaziah in Jerusalem, and he fled to Lachish, and they put him to death there. They carried him on horses, and he was buried in Jerusalem." This clearly shows that it was men in Jerusalem who rose up against him, and when he fled to Lachish they sent men there and killed him. That account, then, is plainly a fabrication. Rather, the prophet speaks to Lachish and, taking it as one part of the kingdom of Judah, foretells what will befall the whole kingdom, just as he spoke about the things concerning Samaria. He had seen visions concerning both and was speaking about both, as the opening clearly showed. Consistently with this, the prophet says to her: Verse 16. "Shave yourself and cut off your hair for your

delicate children; widen your baldness like an eagle, for they have been taken from you into captivity." "It is fitting for you," he says, "to mourn the captivity of your people. Before, they lived in great luxury in their own homes, but now they will experience the evils of captivity." He says "Widen your baldness like an eagle" because this bird is said to shed all its feathers at a certain season. Then, as is his custom, he also states the cause of the evils.

Verses 1–3. "They were devising troubles and working evils on their beds, and at daybreak they carried them out." This means: they kept turning such thoughts over in their minds, and from these thoughts they bred these troubles for themselves. On their beds they sketched out their wicked deeds, and when day came they carried their wicked plans through to the end. "Because they did not lift their hands to God. They coveted fields, plundered orphans, oppressed households, and plundered a man and his house, a man and his inheritance." They refused to look to God or to pay any attention to the laws he had given. Instead they busied themselves with desire for other people's property, plundered the possessions of the poor and those who had no protector, and abused their power for wicked ends. "Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I am devising evils against this tribe, from which you will not lift your necks, and you will not walk upright, suddenly, for it is an evil time." "For these plans and deeds of yours I will bring on you a punishment so heavy that you will not even be able to lift your heads. You will stay bent double and looking at the ground under the weight of the evils pressing on you."

Verses 4–5. "On that day a parable will be taken up against you, and a lament will be sung in mourning by those who say: We are utterly wretched; the portion of my people has been measured out with a line, and there was no one to stop him from turning away; your fields have been divided up." Then a painful lament will indeed be fitting for you, which is what "in mourning" means. You will lament your own wretchedness as you see your own portion, that is, the land that belongs to you, occupied and divided up by strangers, with no one able to stop it. You will see your fields, which you seized out of greed, taken from you and handed out to others. Then he continues: "Therefore you will have no one to cast a line by lot." He commonly uses "line" for measuring out land, taking the word from those who use cords for measuring, as when it says, "The lines have fallen for me in the best places," meaning, "The finest part of the land has been measured out and allotted to me." So here he means this: "You will see others taking what is yours and measuring it out, while none of it at all is yours. Among you there will be no one measuring or casting a lot, since

everything of yours will be taken away and will belong to others. Though you had many possessions, you will be masters of none of them. You will see them come under the ownership of others, and others dividing up what is yours as they please." Verses 6–7. "Do not weep tears in the assembly of the Lord, and let them not weep over these things; for he will not drive away reproaches, saying: The house of Jacob has provoked the Spirit of the Lord." "When you gather, then, do not shed tears that are not tears of repentance. You grieve at how great the evils that have befallen you are, and in a way you bring an accusation against God, saying: 'We are not the only ones who have provoked God, nor are we the only ones who have done wicked things. Why, then, do others do whatever they please to us while we alone suffer?' You will gain nothing from these words," he says. "This accusation will not let you escape the evils, nor will you stop being reproached for the evils that have befallen you. So do not do these things." What then? "If these are his practices, are not his words good with him, and have they not walked uprightly?" "Look rather at this: God, who brings these things on you, has left nothing undone that was needed. He spoke fitting words to you, taught you many times what you must do, and wanted to turn you from wrongdoing by announcing the coming punishment. But you refused to heed what was said, and so you have clearly shown how right and just God's words are. At first they sought to improve you by their warning. But since you were not persuaded, they had no choice but to prove their truth to you, because you did not repent." Verses 8–10. Then, extending the accusation: "And before, my people rose up in enmity against his peace." "From of old you chose a hostile, warlike attitude toward me. You refused to obey what was said, and so you were making war on your own peace more than on anyone else's. At any rate, the present war is the profit you have gained from your disobedience." "They stripped off his skin, to take away hope, a crushing of war." "You took from the poor everything they had and cut off all their good hope. For this you have stirred up against yourselves the crushing blow of the present war." How, and in what way? "Therefore the leaders of my people will be cast out of their luxurious houses; because of their evil practices they have been driven out." All those who seem to rule among the people because of their power will be driven out of the houses where they lived in luxury, because of their injustice toward the poor, from whom they amassed great wealth. They will pay the penalty for their wicked conduct by losing ownership of the things they wrongly acquired. What then? "Draw near to the everlasting mountains. Arise and go, for this is not your rest, because of uncleanness. You have been utterly destroyed; you have been pursued when no one was pursuing." "So you have no pretext left even for fighting the enemy, since God has handed you over because of your own wickedness. Go away, then,

…to the territory of the enemy, which God long ago prepared for you, so that you may live there as captives. For you to find rest here is impossible. You were steeped in great uncleanness, both in your impiety and in the wickedness of your deeds, and for this you have been handed over to destruction at the hands of the enemy. You are being driven into it not by men leading you away, but by God, who has decreed this punishment for you. Verses 11–13. Then he states the cause of the ruin that came upon them for what they had done: "He has set up a lying spirit." What caused everything for you, he says, was your trust in the deceit of the false prophets. "It has dripped for you into wine and strong drink." From that source this punishment has dripped upon you, and under it you are no different from a drunkard, driven this way and that by one evil after another. We have shown elsewhere too that he speaks of wine in connection with punishment. "And it shall be from the drop of this people: Jacob shall surely be gathered together with all." From this deceit of the false prophets, which took hold among you to your harm, you have all been gathered into the present punishment, and there is no way for you to escape it. "I will surely receive the remnant of Israel; I will make their return one and the same." So I will wait for all of you, both those captured earlier by the Assyrians and those captured later, to be handed over to this great punishment. In it you will all alike be taken from your own places and be led away into captivity. "Like sheep in affliction, like flocks in the midst of [?] … their fold; they will leap away from men." Such fear will fall upon you at the enemy's attack that you will be no different from sheep that are asleep when a wolf suddenly comes upon them: they are thrown into confusion and terror, forced to struggle for their very lives. "Go up through the breach before them; they broke through and passed through a gate and went out by it; and their king went out before them." The Babylonians besieged Jerusalem for a long time and took the city with siege engines. They breached the wall, and having secured their way into the city in this way, they led everyone out through the gate into captivity, together with the king. This is what he means: Go up, he says, and see your wall cut through. By breaking through it the enemy has made empty the security you supposed it gave you. After killing those who fell, they took all the people in the city captive and went out through the gate [?] which you did not wish to bring up [?], with the one who seemed to lead them going before. And how will they be able to do this? Since God, in their campaigns against you, [?]…

Chapter 3, verses 1–[?]. "And he will say: Hear now, you rulers of Jacob and remnant of the house of Israel. Is it not for you to know judgment?" For he will side with your enemies, he says, bringing these charges against you and saying to all of you, both those who rule

among you and the rest: You above all ought to discern what is right, turning away from the worse and choosing the better. All of you have been taught this by me, through the ordinances of the law and through everything else I have often done to this end, and it was for this purpose too that the rulers came into this authority. "But you hate what is good and seek what is evil, tearing their skin off them and their flesh from their bones." You do the opposite of what you were taught: you turn away from what is good and do what is worse, and you treat the poor and the lowly with every kind of injustice, taking from them by various means everything they have. What then? "Just as they devoured the flesh of my people, and stripped their skin from [?] …" … and handing them over completely to the evils that grip them, since they have done such outrageous things, so full of injustice (p. 277) … he knows [?] about you. Having stated both what they were doing and what they will suffer for it, because they trusted the words of the false prophets, he turns his speech once more to the false prophets themselves and says: Verses 5–7. "Thus says the Lord concerning the prophets who lead my people astray, who bite with their teeth and proclaim peace to them; and it was not given into their mouth." God says this, he explains, about the false prophets. In various ways they led the people away from what was right by their deceptions, and all but devoured them themselves by what they said and did, urging them on to the very things for which they were to receive so great a punishment. They kept promising them peace, and assuring them that they would suffer no harm for their sins, according to the words of the prophets. But they did not announce this peace according to my mind; I had not taught them to speak of it. And what did they achieve by this? "They raised war against them." While promising peace, they stirred up war against them, and marked it out to fall upon them. "Therefore you will have night instead of a vision, and darkness instead of divination; the sun will set upon the prophets, and the day will grow dark over them. Those who see dreams will be put to shame, and the diviners will be laughed to scorn, and all of them will speak against them, because there will be no one to listen to them." Because of these things they pretended to see and to divine, deceiving the people, they themselves and all who believed them will be wrapped in darkness. Darkened by the magnitude of their evils, they will feel as though not even the sun shines for them. For those

who pretend to see and speak such things will be covered with shame when events turn out contrary to what they claimed. Everyone will laugh them to scorn, and no one will be willing even to listen to what they say, because people have learned by experience how many evils their deceit has brought upon them. Verses 8–11. "But truly I have been filled with strength by the Spirit of the Lord, and with judgment and might, to declare to Jacob his impieties and to Israel his sins." I, however, have left all that deceit behind and have been filled with the Holy Spirit. I know how to discern what is right, and I am moved with great strength and boldness to rebuke the people for their sins and impieties. I know that this will do them more good and bring them to their senses, since they can be led to what is right both by remembering their sins and by being warned of what is to come. "Hear these things, you leaders of the house of Jacob, and remnant of the house of Israel." For this reason, he says, I address my words to the leaders and to all the rest alike, reproaching you for what you have done. And what is that? "You who abhor judgment and pervert everything that is upright." You refuse to judge carefully between good and evil and choose the better, and you slander even what others say and do rightly, so that you disobey the words of us prophets as well. "You who build Zion with blood and Jerusalem with injustice." You have filled the whole city with murder and injustice. "Her leaders judged for bribes, her priests gave answers for hire, and her prophets divined for silver. Yet they leaned on the Lord, saying: Is not the Lord among us? No evil will come upon us." The rulers, caring nothing for justice, sold justice for money in their judgments. Those appointed to the priesthood tried to gather money unjustly under the pretext of their priestly office, as if it were a kind of wage. The false prophets too, delighting in money, gave their oracles to please those who paid them. And while doing such evils they pretended to entrust themselves to God, (p. 280) claiming that they had God among them, and that people deemed worthy of such things could not possibly suffer the evils we announced according to God's mind. What then? Verse 12. "Therefore, because of you, Zion will be plowed like a field, Jerusalem will become like a watchman's hut in an orchard, and the mountain of the house like a wooded grove." Since you disobey our words, spoken according to God's mind, and heed the false prophets instead, and all of you commit such impieties and transgressions every day, you will therefore learn the truth of our words. Such desolation will then overtake Mount Zion and the city on it that the mountain will be farmed like a field, and the city will be no different from a shelter put up for guarding fruit, its buildings thrown down on every side. In short, the whole mountain on which the house of God stands will be no different from an overgrown place, with so many plants springing up there out of the desolation. But up to PATROL. GR. LXVI.

this point he has spoken of the calamities that were to be brought upon them. Next he tells what will happen to them after the capture of the city, and how great a change for the better they will experience. As we have often shown, this is customary with the other prophets (p. 281) and with blessed David: after the experience of hardship they announce pleasant things, and then speak again of painful ones. In this way, by keeping both continually in their memory, they instruct the people, bringing them to their senses by the memory of painful things, and urging them by the announcement of better things to hold fast to their hope in God. So he says:

Verses 1–3. "And in the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord will be manifest, established on the tops of the mountains, and it will be lifted up above the hills. Peoples will hasten to it, and many nations will come and say: Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, and to the house of the God of Jacob; and they will show us his way, and we will walk in his paths. For out of Zion the law will go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem. He will judge between many peoples, and rebuke strong nations far away." After they have experienced the evils they will go through, taken captive first by the Assyrians and later by the Babylonians, so great a change will come over this place that the mountain on which God is believed to dwell will become conspicuous to all. It will be shown to stand above all the mountains, far surpassing every mountain and every hill, because of the glory that comes to it from God's care. Many will gather from many places, foreigners among them, hurrying to reach this mountain of God, (p. 282) on which God is glorified as dwelling. There they will be taught how they ought to conduct themselves and how to live rightly, so that the law in force here becomes law for those elsewhere too, and all will feel that they hear a divine voice telling them they should live by the laws of Jerusalem. And they will rightly think so, seeing the power of God that he will display when he brings many of those who mistreated us under his judgment, and rebukes even those who seem very strong, even if they seem to be far away, for the wrongs they have done us, and indeed brings upon them a punishment worthy of their insolence. I am amazed at those who have said that the prophet spoke these words about what would happen to the Israelites when they were to return from Babylon, but who also said that the words contain a type of what concerns Christ the Lord. In saying that the people's return from Babylon is signified here, I commend them for speaking very well. But how they were led to say that the passage contains a type of what concerns Christ the Lord, I do not know. It is clear that every type bears some likeness to that of which it is called a type. But the words "out of Zion the law will go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem" (p. 283) are far removed from the ordinance of Christ, who clearly said to the Samaritan woman: "Believe me, woman, the hour is coming when

you will worship the Father neither in Jerusalem nor on this mountain." And he gave the reason: "God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth." He clearly declared that all strictness about place would be completely done away with, and that there would be no reason to worship in Jerusalem rather than anywhere else. For all, having been taught that the divine is incorporeal, would worship him in that frame of mind, and wherever they did so, they would be doing nothing different. With regard to the return from Babylon, it may fittingly be said, "Out of Zion the law will go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem," since the Israelites were then restored to the place of Zion, so that they could perform there the worship prescribed by the ordinances of the law, which they could not perform while they were elsewhere. That is why, while in Babylon, they said: "How shall we sing the Lord's song in a foreign land?" But how could this [?] fit what concerns Christ the Lord, whose ordinance wills that divine worship be performed alike everywhere, (p. 284) so that those who perform it well are distinguished from those who perform it worse by their manner and not by their place? Verses 4–5. The prophet, however, adds the following to his prediction of what has been set out above: "They will beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into sickles, and they will never again learn war." He shows that all war will cease and peace will prevail everywhere, so that they will turn even their weapons of war into farming tools, since weapons will hardly be needed now that war has ceased, while farming, as in time of peace, must prevail. Then he says: "And each will rest under his vine, and each under his fig tree, and there will be no one to make them afraid." He means that all will enjoy the fruit of their own labor, since in peace there will no longer be anyone able to frighten and disturb them and drive them from their own places. And since what he was saying was extraordinary, he rightly added: "For the mouth of the Lord Almighty has spoken these things." That is to say, God has declared that these things will happen, and they will certainly happen. "For all the peoples will walk each in his own way, (p. 285) but we will walk in the name of the Lord our God for ever and beyond." Living as they will in peace, all will then go about the work proper to them, some turning to farming, others to the sea, others to whatever craft each happens to practice. But all of us will have one work in common: to live according to God's will from then on for all time to come. And to confirm this he says again: Verses 6–8. "In those days, says the Lord, I will gather her that is crushed, and I will receive her that was driven out, and those whom I drove away. I will make her that is crushed a remnant, and her that was driven out a strong nation; and the Lord will reign over them on Mount Zion from now on and for ever."

Then, he says, those who have been crushed by the greatest evils, and have fallen away both from my providence and from their own land, I will bring back again to the places that are theirs. And those who were crushed before I will so guard by my providence that the whole Israelite race will grow again from them; this is what he means by "remnant." And those who have now been driven from their own places because of their weakness I will make stronger than many. God will remain on Mount Zion, (p. 286) displaying his might through his care for those who live there and through the punishment he will bring on those who choose to make war on them. For "and for ever" clearly means throughout a long time. It is plain that they did undergo a certain change again under the Maccabees, but a very great and wholly irreparable one when, having dared to act against Christ the Lord, they suffered complete captivity at the hands of the Romans, banished from their own land and placed in long servitude. Up to this point he speaks of the people's return from Babylon and of the good things that would be theirs at that time. From here on he again turns to painful things, describing the calamities that would come upon them. So he directs his words to Jerusalem itself and says: "And you, tower of the flock, parched daughter of Zion." It is clear that he calls Jerusalem the daughter of Zion, since both the prophets and blessed David constantly call her so, as when he says: "That I may proclaim all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion." So there can be no doubt that the prophet here addresses his words not to Zedekiah, as some have supposed, I do not know how, but to Jerusalem. (p. 287) Having first called her daughter of Zion, as is customary, he fittingly names her tower of the flock, since she stood out above all the Israelites, and all of them hurried to her, both because of the worship offered to God there and because of the help they hoped to receive from there, since God was supposed to dwell there. He calls her parched as a reproach, because she is in the grip of impiety as if of a drought, and leads the whole flock in what is worse when she ought to lead them in what is better. "To you it will come, and the former dominion will enter, a kingdom from Babylon, to the daughter of Jerusalem." Because of the wrongs committed in you, a very great and exceedingly powerful king, the king of Babylon, will come against you, and he will treat you just as a powerful king who has attacked you might be expected to do.

Overpowered by these things, you are no different from a woman in the pains of childbirth. You would never have experienced this if you had been eager to follow my statutes. (p. 288) But since you did not: "Be in labor, be brave, and draw near, daughter of Zion, like a woman giving birth." Endure the pains that are upon you, and hold out under them like a woman in childbirth, as you approach the pangs of delivery. "For now you will go out from the city, and camp in the open field, and come as far as Babylon." Your affairs have come to an end: you will be taken from the city into captivity. Led away to whatever places chance brings, you will live cast out, as a captive being led along naturally would, until you reach Babylon itself, where you must live with your calamity. Then, having described the punishment, he speaks again of the deliverance: "From there he will rescue you, and from there the Lord your God will redeem you from the hand of your enemies." But when you arrive as a captive in those places, where not a single hope of release appears to you, you will receive unexpected help from God, which by his own power will free you from captivity and from the rule of those who hold you. Verses 11–13. "And now many nations will gather against you, and peoples saying: We will rejoice, and our eyes will look upon Zion." (p. 289) Then many savage Scythian nations (he means the forces of Gog), unable to bear your prosperity and your return, will come against you, fully expecting to inflict on you with ease whatever evils they please. "But they did not know the thought of the Lord, nor did they understand his counsel, that he has gathered them like sheaves on the threshing floor." They made their attack trusting in their own numbers and strength, not knowing the mind of our God. He allowed them to set out on this war, as they wished, so that he might display his care for you and demonstrate his power against them, handing them all over to be slaughtered by your hands, like sheaves that are reaped and laid on the threshing floor. And confident that this will certainly happen, he says to the Israelites: "Arise and thresh them, daughter of Zion." Now that the power of God has put them into your hands, he says, crush them all and consume them with slaughter of every kind, as on a threshing floor. "For I will make your horns iron, and I will make your hooves bronze." I have given you strength no less than horns of iron, enough to beat back your enemies, and to trample them more fiercely than anyone with hooves of bronze could trample. (p. 290) "And you will melt down nations among them and grind many peoples to powder; and you will dedicate their multitude to the Lord, and their strength to the Lord of all the earth." By this help supplied to you by God you will utterly destroy them all, many as they are, and you will count the destruction of their whole multitude [?] …

Verses 1–2. “Now the daughter shall be hemmed in with a fence; he has laid siege against you; with a rod they shall strike the tribes of Israel on the cheek.” They will suffer such things, he says, because they came against you trusting in their own numbers and power. They hemmed you in and surrounded you with their multitude as if with a fence, so that by besieging you they might utterly destroy you all, and they all but brought the blows of their power down on your very cheeks. Then he speaks also of the one who leads in the war, to show that these things will happen because the one who rules them was brought to this by the will of God. “And you, Bethlehem, house of Ephrathah, are not the least to be among the thousands of Judah; from you shall come forth for me one to be ruler in Israel; and his goings forth are from the beginning, from the days of eternity.” For the one from Bethlehem who now reigns over you will be fully equal to the war against your adversaries, many and powerful as they are, through my favor and power, even if you seem few in number compared with the enemy. (p. 291) For it has come about that his appointment was ordained from of old, ever since God promised David that he would preserve the kingdom for his descendants in succession. Since this man too has been raised to the kingdom by virtue of that promise, he will be equal to the magnitude of the present evils. He means Zerubbabel. For he was the one who then reigned over the Israelites, descended from David, when the return from Babylon took place and Gog and his forces tried to attack those in Jerusalem. It is clear, of course, that even though these things were said of Zerubbabel, as one descended from David's line, in keeping with the sequence of what comes before, the true fulfillment of what was said came to pass in Christ the Lord. For the whole promise made to David that his descendants would reign seems at first sight to refer to the kings of Israel who came from him in succession, but in truth it points to Christ the Lord according to the flesh, who was born of David's line (p. 292) and holds a true and unshakable kingdom over all things. One could learn this more clearly from the eighty-eighth psalm, where it indicates that the promises of the kingdom belong to those who would be his descendants in succession. Of them it says: “If his sons forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments, and profane my ordinances and do not keep my commandments, I will punish their transgressions with a rod and their iniquities with scourges; but my mercy I will not scatter from them.” It is quite plain that these words would fit those who were to descend from David one after another and to reign

over Israel, whom he promises to discipline when they sin but not to drive out of the kingdom entirely. As the psalm goes on, however, it points to Christ the Lord according to the flesh, in whom God showed the true fulfillment of his own promises. For the words “I will establish his seed for ever and ever, and his throne as the days of heaven,” and “his seed remains forever, and his throne is like the sun before me, and like the moon established forever,” plainly cannot apply to any of the successors. (p. 293) They clearly show the kingdom of Christ the Lord, perpetual and unshakable, enduring forever with great power and great splendor. In the same way one could see that the present testimony also fits Christ the Lord, in the true and indisputable reality of the events, according to the saying in the Gospels; [?] spoken of the kings of Israel from David because of the divine promise. Hence the prophet has now quite reasonably taken it as referring to Zerubbabel. Since he was speaking of what followed the return from Babylon, the assault of Gog and his forces, and the punishment God brought on them, it followed that he should also mention the one who, by divine promise, had then been entrusted with rule over them from David's line. He wanted to show that what was achieved for the nation through Zerubbabel drew its strength from the promise God had already made to David. Hence he said, “His goings forth are from the beginning, from the days of eternity,” meaning that on the basis of what God had said and promised long before, he advanced this man to rule and made him able to do such things. Then he adds: Verses 3–4. “Therefore he will give them up until the time of her who is in labor; she shall give birth.” Divine Scripture often calls it being in labor and giving birth (p. 294) when divine help appears unexpectedly in the midst of dangers. So it says, “Because of fear of you, Lord, we conceived and were in labor and brought forth the spirit of your salvation, which you have wrought upon the earth,” meaning: Because we feared you, we conceived in these things your ineffable grace, and from it, through many pangs amid the greatness of our evils, an unexpected salvation was born to us. Here too, then, it is as though Jerusalem had conceived by divine grace and brought forth this gift, through which the people were saved and the enemy met utter destruction. He says that he will hand the adversaries over to destruction, because God's gift was born to Jerusalem through the many pangs she endured in the enemy's assault. “And the rest of his brothers shall return to the sons of Israel.” For then all who had returned from captivity will hold Zerubbabel as their common king. The ten tribes will no longer be ruled separately, with only the tribe of Judah, together with Benjamin, having the kings from David as before. From then on all will hold Zerubbabel as their one king. So also the blessed Hosea says: “And the sons of Judah and the sons of Israel shall be

gathered together, (p. 295) and they shall appoint for themselves one head.” And the blessed David says: “Behold, what is so good or so pleasant as for brothers to dwell together?” By this he signifies the concord they would have at the time of the return, which they kept from then on, being under one king. In the same way the prophet says here, “And the rest of the brothers,” meaning that all, even those outside the tribe of Judah, will be gathered together with the rest of the sons of Israel and will hold one and the same king. “And the Lord shall stand and see, and shall shepherd his flock in strength; and they shall abide in the glory of the name of the Lord their God; for now he shall be magnified to the ends of the earth.” It will be God, he says, who through the one then reigning shepherds them all with his own care. He will also make them glorious because they bear his name, and he will continue to be praised with great wonder throughout the whole earth for the many great things he has done for those who bear his name, I mean the sons of Israel. Now he is bringing them back from captivity beyond all hope. After that he will win for them, few as they are, that victory in which, through these weak and few men, he will by his own power utterly rout a countless multitude of strong men (p. 296) trained in the experience of war. Having thus spoken of what would come to them after the return from Babylon, which was certainly to fall to them while Zerubbabel reigned over them from David according to God's promise, the prophet wished to show that God is mindful of his own promises and gives great strength to those appointed according to his good pleasure [?]. He did this by using the events of Zerubbabel's time as proof. But these things seemed likely to happen long afterward—I mean the return from Babylon and what happened to Gog and his forces after that return. So he mentions things close at hand that would soon be fulfilled, I mean what befell the Assyrians in the time of Hezekiah, so that from things near and soon to happen he might make credible those that would come after a long time. For it is clear, as the book shows, that the prophet foretold these things in the days of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah. So the prediction of what happened in Hezekiah's time was not made from afar. He announced it then, and all of it was promptly fulfilled, so that those who had received the word of prophecy before the events (p. 297) saw its fulfillment close at hand. In this way he would show the kinship between the events of Hezekiah's time, which were near, and those of Zerubbabel's, which would come long afterward. Through both he would also make clear how great was the strength of the divine promise. Israel benefited from it not only when it was under Zerubbabel's leadership, but also earlier, when Hezekiah reigned over them; for he too, according to the divine promise, (41) MS: δεδειγ.

had come to the throne. So great an army came against Jerusalem and could accomplish nothing, because divine favor was with the one who held the kingship of Israel according to God's promise. Yet these same men had conquered the kingdom of the ten tribes with great ease. After their victory over it they attacked Jerusalem and received the severest punishment from the angel's blow. For in that account too God is seen saying, “I will defend this city for my own sake and for the sake of David my servant.” He shows that, remembering the promises made to David, he would himself bring about the present deliverance as well, working together with the one who then held Israel's kingship, I mean Hezekiah. Verses 5–6. Having spoken, then, of the events of Zerubbabel's time, which, as I said, were far off, he necessarily mentions what happened with the Assyrian under Hezekiah, because the events are related, in order to support his subject. He says: (p. 298) “And this shall be the peace: when the Assyrian comes against your land, and when he goes up into your country.” What God did then through Zerubbabel, he says, ending so great a war and giving strong peace to his own people, he will also do at that other time, which is soon to come, when the Assyrian comes against Jerusalem. For then he will unexpectedly rout so great a multitude and give his own people unexpected peace, while Hezekiah reigns from David's line according to the divine promise. Then he tells what will happen: “And seven shepherds shall be raised up against him, and eight bites of men; and they shall shepherd Assur with the sword, and the land of Nimrod in its trench.” Some have understood “seven shepherds and eight bites of men” rather fancifully. They count seven prophets as the seven shepherds, and say that the eight bites are Hezekiah together with those who served him in the kingdom. Yet they could not even say who the eight are, and they supported their own view by mere assertion. If one wanted to speak of those who served the kingdom, there could be many more than eight. (p. 299) What led those who understood it this way into error was their failure to look to the idiom of divine Scripture. They were thus forced to make up old wives' tales in order to seem to be saying something. It is an idiom of divine Scripture sometimes to call the perfect number seven, and to take whatever goes beyond it as signifying excess. God made heaven and earth in six days and rested on the seventh (which is also why the Jews keep the sabbath as a day of rest), and the whole count of days regularly cycles through these seven, all beginning from the first, ending at the seventh, and after the seventh running back again to the first. For this reason divine Scripture uses seven for what is perfect and complete, and eight, as I said, for excess. Thus God says: “Sevenfold vengeance he shall

release,” meaning that whoever kills Cain for his incurable offenses will be found to be releasing him from a very great and complete punishment that lay upon him. The saying in Ecclesiastes is of the same kind: “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight,” meaning: Give generously to those in need, and do not refuse even to go to excess in this. Hence the blessed Peter said, “How often, if my brother sins against me, shall I forgive him? Up to seven times?” He named the perfect number as though it were enough. The Lord, wishing to exceed it by a great abundance, replied: (p. 300) “I do not say to you up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven.” He says something of the same kind here too. When the Assyrian came with his army, God surrounded him with a great and very heavy punishment through the ministry of the angel. Many were slain, and the rest turned to flight. Becoming easy prey for the people of the various places, they suffered a great many things in many places and at many hands, since people attacked them with great ease as fugitives and killed any who fell into their hands. Finally their king went back to his own country in great disgrace and was killed by his own sons. So the punishment God brought upon them appears most severe, not only through those struck down by the angel around Jerusalem, but also through the rest, who fled from there in great fear and were killed in various ways. Of them the blessed David also says, “For you will make them turn their back; among your remnants you will prepare their face.” He shows by this that all will be turned to flight, and that God will stir up his wrath against those who are left as well. (p. 301) This, then, is what he means here when he says that seven shepherds will be raised up: he wants to show the severity of the divine punishment, which God brought upon them, perfect and complete, through the angel's blow. And he speaks of “eight bites of men” to express the excess of evils that would overtake them after their flight from there. In various places men, including those living in their own land, destroyed both the fugitives and those who thought they had found refuge in their own places. Among them it happened that the king too was killed by his own sons. He rightly called these “bites of men,” to set them apart from the punishment that came through the angel. Then he adds: “And they shall shepherd Assur with the sword, and the land of Nimrod in its trench,” meaning: The Assyrian will be consumed by the sword and will see his own land laid waste. This he did indeed suffer later at the hands of the Babylonians. He calls it the land of Nimrod because Nimrod had lived in those places and held the kingdom there. He was regarded as great by the people of that time and prided himself on his power. For so the book of Genesis says: “He was a giant hunter before the Lord; therefore they will say, Like Nimrod, a giant hunter before the Lord. And the beginning of his kingdom was Babylon.” Since, then,

the Assyrians prided themselves on him, thinking themselves great in power because they were descended from such a man, the prophet wished to say something like this: the whole land of those who seemed so brave will be destroyed by enemies in its own places, and because of the divine wrath they will gain nothing from the strength in which they took such pride. In keeping with what he has said, the prophet goes on: “And he shall deliver you from Assur, when he comes against your land and when he sets foot within your borders.” Verses 7–9. Then, having brought the Israelites the good news that they will suffer no harm from the Assyrian, he adds: “And the remnant of Jacob shall be among the nations, in the midst of many peoples, like dew falling from the Lord, and like lambs on the grass, so that no one may gather or withstand among the sons of men.” For when these things have happened, those of Israel who were left in Judea, or in Jerusalem, will appear worthy of respect to all outsiders and of great regard, no less than dew is longed for by farmers when it falls in its season. (p. 303) They will be just like sheep grazing on grass, as they go after all the spoils of those who perished or fled. As a result, fear arose among all people of ever attempting war against them. “And the remnant of Jacob shall be among the nations, in the midst of many peoples, like a lion among the beasts of the forest, and like a young lion among flocks of sheep: as when it passes through and scatters and seizes, and there is none to rescue. Your hand shall be lifted up over those who afflict you, and all your enemies shall be utterly destroyed.” You will be just like a lion, he says, that terrifies the beasts. From then on you will be just as terrifying to all foreigners, because of the blow that fell on the Assyrians on your behalf. A lion (by “young lion” he again means the same thing, calling the lion's offspring by that name) falls suddenly on a flock of sheep and seizes as many as it likes by its strength. In the same way you will be thought stronger than your enemies from then on, since such destruction was brought on those who tried to attack you. Verses 10–15. Having said that these things would come to the Israelites through the blow on the Assyrians, the prophet next speaks more fully of the punishment of the Assyrians themselves. At that time, he says, he will destroy all your horses and chariots, (p. 304) meaning: He will make all your military equipment useless. He will destroy all your cities, even those that seem strong and fortified with great security. Along with them he will destroy everything you pursued through demonic worship. For he speaks of “your sorceries,” meaning the incantations and auguries and all such things as were customary among them. You will no longer have those who pronounce oracles, who practiced divination and gave oracles, since he will also hand over all your idols and pillars to utter destruction. So even if you wished, you could not do as you did before and worship the works of your hands. (42) MS: μετιείς.

The groves in which you perform your rites will also be cut down, and I will destroy all your cities. In short, in wrath and anger I will bring on you the greatest and heaviest punishment and destruction, because you were unwilling to keep away from my land and hoped, against my will, to hand it too over to desolation. Having finished describing the punishment that would be brought on the Assyrians for daring to attack Jerusalem, (p. 305) he turns his words to the people, judging that now was an especially fitting time to rebuke their ingratitude. And the prophet sets up a kind of court and speaks as follows: Chapter 6. Verses 1–5. “Arise, plead your case before the mountains, and let the hills hear your voice. Hear, you hills, the case of the Lord, and you valleys, foundations of the earth; for the Lord has a case against his people, and he will argue it out with Israel.” Since God has done such things for them, he says, and they nonetheless persist in their ingratitude, for which they also endure the captivity in Babylon, I would gladly hold a trial between God and them. I will take as judges the mountains, the hills and the valleys. Earlier they received that countless multitude of Assyrians that came against Jerusalem and spread out over all the places round about, which naturally filled those in the city with the greatest fear. Then suddenly they held within them, lying dead, the bodies of so many who shortly before had been so proud. These will be trustworthy judges in this trial, since they also witnessed what happened. Then, having as it were set up a court and made the Israelites' ingratitude plain before judges who were also witnesses of the events, he goes further and brings in God speaking to them: (p. 306) “My people, what have I done to you, or how have I troubled you?” What happened with the Assyrian is plain, he says, and so is the great proof you received of my care for you. But I give you leave to say whether you have ever been grieved by me in anything, small or great; whether I have done anything to harm you; whether I have grieved you at all; whether I have seemed burdensome to you in anything. Then, as though they had no reply even to this, he says, “Answer me,” meaning: Speak, if you have anything to say; I will accept it if you speak truly. Then, as though they had fallen completely silent because of their conscience, having nothing in what God had said to refute as false, he adds: “For I brought you up out of the land of Egypt and redeemed you from the house of slavery; and I sent before you Moses and Aaron and Miriam.” Or perhaps you hold this against me, that beyond all hope I freed you from so bitter a slavery, using Moses, Aaron and Miriam as ministers and leaders of this gift? “My people, remember what Balak king of Moab plotted against you, and what Balaam son of Beor answered him, from the reeds to

…Gilgal, so that the righteousness of the Lord may be known.” But remember also what happened with Balak, king of the Moabites. He sent and summoned Balaam against you. At first Balaam would not even come, because of my command. When he did come later, he did not curse at all, but blessed you [?], just as I willed. So it is clear to you from everything that I have always set justice in motion on your behalf against those who tried to wrong you, and have punished them all without sparing them.

Verses 6–8. — Since what had been said allowed no reply, the prophet takes the part of an advocate for the people and speaks in their person as follows: “With what shall I reach the Lord? Shall I lay hold of my God most high?” He speaks as though the people were saying: “Since I am convicted on every count of having been ungrateful for many benefits, what should I do so that now at least I may lay hold of God, from whom I separated myself by my own ways? And how shall I show that I hold fast to what pleases him?” “Shall I reach him with whole burnt offerings, with year-old calves? Will the Lord accept thousands of rams, or tens of thousands of fat goats? Shall I give my firstborn for my ungodliness, the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul?” He speaks as though they were at a loss over what they ought to do to make amends for such great ingratitude: “Shall I then appease him if I offer whole burnt offerings of year-old calves, or offer him thousands and tens of thousands of rams and sheep, or offer him the firstborn of my offspring, so as to remove the sin from my [?] soul?”

In answer to this perplexity of the people the prophet says: “You have been told, O man, what is good, and what the Lord requires of you: only to do justice, to love mercy, and to be ready to walk after the Lord your God.” Set aside burnt offerings, he says, and the multitude of sacrifices and the offering of firstborn. If you care to appease the Deity, do the things that God commanded you long ago through Moses. And what are these? That you exercise right judgment and discernment in all things, by which you ought to choose the better over the worse; that you go on showing all the kindness and compassion you can to your neighbours; and that you be ready to pursue in every way what pleases God. In short, he means the saying, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your mind, and with all your soul, and you shall love your neighbour as yourself,” which was spoken long ago through Moses. Pursue these, he says, for they are more precious to God than sacrifices.

Verses 9–12. — “The voice of the Lord will be proclaimed to the city, and he will save those who fear his name.” For if you do these things, he says, the city will appear as a kind of voice of God. It will do what pleases him and display the divine law in action, so that those who live in it [?] will be thought worthy of divine care in every danger and will suffer nothing painful. Then the prophet again turns his words to them by way of exhortation: “Hear, O tribe! Who will adorn a city? Will fire, or the house of the lawless man who stores up lawless treasures

together with insolent injustice?” Fire cannot adorn a city; on the contrary, it destroys it. Nor will a lawless man, who works lawlessness with great diligence and lives with much insolence and much injustice, gain anything but punishment. People like that, living in a city, will destroy it no less than fire. “Will he be justified with deceitful weights in a bag? With them they filled their wealth with ungodliness, and those who live in it spoke lies, and their tongue was exalted in their mouth.” Justice cannot appear in an uneven and unequal balance, and weights that are falsified and bent cannot become acceptable. In the same way, those who increase their own wealth by lawless deeds will not be able to enjoy what they have. All such people living in a city, who live with falsehood and keep an arrogant mind, so that they take no account of God's punishment for these things, will of necessity fall under divine punishment.

Verses 13–16. — “And I will begin to strike you; I will destroy you in their sins.” Since you do such things, I will strike you with my punishment and destroy you all in proportion to your sins. “You will eat and not be satisfied.” You will share in what you have for a little while, but you will not enjoy it to the end, because the punishment will take it from you. “And it will grow dark within you; you will turn aside and will not be saved.” The punishment from me will surround you like darkness, and though you want to escape the experience of these evils, you will be quite unable to. “And whoever is saved will be handed over to the sword.” Even if you seem for a short while to escape somehow, the punishment by the enemies will certainly overtake you. “You will sow olives but not anoint yourself with oil; you will make wine but not drink wine.” Once you have fallen in the slaughter of war, you will naturally not enjoy the fruits of your own labours, since the enemies will naturally destroy them all; this is what he means throughout. “And the statutes of my people will be destroyed, and all the works of the house of Ahab, and you walked in their counsels, so that I might hand you over to destruction and those who live in it to hissing, and they will bear the reproaches of my people.” Then all the statutes you kept for the worship of idols, imitating Ahab and the kings like him, which were brought in among you, will be destroyed along with you. So all outsiders who see your ruin will hiss in amazement at your great change for the worse, and will reproach you for what you have suffered because of your own lawlessness. Having stated in these words the threat of the punishment that will be brought upon them, he next, as usual, again gives the causes of what is about to come upon them, and he gives his account in the form of a lament. The form of lamentation suited the prophet very well, since he grieved over what they were suffering and made their offences his own. What, then, does he say?

(12) The manuscript reads φάγεσε.

…straw at harvest, and like a gleaning at the vintage when there is no cluster; my soul longed to eat the first-ripe fruit.” Lamentation comes over me as I see how far the people have sunk, so that no fruit of righteousness appears among them. I am led to feel about them something like what a farmer would feel at harvest time when the crops have perished entirely. He is forced to gather some worthless straw instead of sheaves, or what usually drops from the sheaves in seasons of good crops. Or at vintage time he finds no clusters, but gathers a few small gleanings. So now too, after all the care and attention God has given them, the time rightly calls for the fruits of piety and virtue, yet I find the good entirely lacking in all of them. One cannot see even a firstfruit appearing among them, and I have the greatest longing to see some such thing. We are accustomed to take firstfruits from crops that have come to full maturity, and these are also the “firstborn.” That is why blessed David says: “And he struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt, the firstfruits of all their labour in the tents of Ham.” So he means that because their barrenness was so extreme, he was seized by a longing to find something among them that could take the place of a firstfruit.

Verses 2–4. — Continuing his lament: “Alas, my soul! The devout have perished from the earth, and there is no one among men who does right. All go to law over blood; each crushes his neighbour with oppression. They make their hands ready for evil. The ruler asks, and the judge has spoken peaceable words; it is his soul's desire.” How is it not worth lamenting that there is no fear of God among them anywhere? That is why one cannot find anyone willing to care for what is right. All their charges concern murders, for they do not stop at small offences but stretch out their hands even to murder. Each of them tries, as far as he has the power, to load the poor man near him with pains and hardships, and they are ready to work evil. Besides this, the one appointed to rule neglects his duty and seeks money, and with it he sets aside the injustices of wrongdoers. The one who has received authority to judge abandons the task of deciding what is just and uses flattering words, so as to secure unjust gains for himself, and toward these he has bent all the thinking of his soul. “And I will take away their good things, like a moth that eats and walks along a rod, in the days of your watching.” For this I will reduce you to complete want of good things. Like a moth, I will destroy through the enemies whatever is good in you. A moth that has got into a rod of wood makes its way along it, eats it all and consumes it bit by bit; in the same way I will take away all your good things little by little. This will happen at the time when, having surveyed the

magnitude of your sins, I will bring punishment in proportion to what has been done. “Woe, woe! Your punishments have come; now there will be their weeping.” The day has come for you to pay the penalty for your offences. It is right for you to weep over them now, as you see from the evils brought upon you how much harm you did yourself by your [inclination] toward the worse [?]

Verses 5–7. — He shows the magnitude of the evils that will come upon them: “Do not trust in friends, and do not put your hope in leaders. Guard yourself against the woman who lies beside you, and do not confide anything to her. For a son dishonours his father, a daughter rises up against her mother, a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; a man's enemies are all the men of his own household.” At that time, he says, no one will have any help from anyone: no friend from a friend, no subject from [?] … waiting for salvation from him, who will also hear me and give me help.

Verses 8–11. — “Do not gloat over me, my enemy, because I have fallen; I will rise. Even if I walk in darkness, the Lord will give me light.” At that time I will be able to say to my neighbours, and above all to the Idumaeans: “It is useless for you to rejoice over my fall, for I will rise from my fall with God's help. So even if I have walked in the midst of evils as though in darkness, God's help will be brighter than light to me.” “I will bear the wrath of the Lord, because I sinned against him, until he justifies my cause and executes judgment for me. He will bring me out into the light, and I will see his righteousness.” As one who has sinned, I have experienced his wrath and the hardships that came from it. But he will grant me a change for the better. He himself will judge on my behalf concerning what I suffered from all who were unjustly hostile to me, and will give me justice in the judgment. He will set me in the splendour of my own good things, so that God's purpose becomes plain and beyond doubt to me: caring for justice, he freed me from the evils around me and justly punished those who had wronged me without cause. This is what “I will see his righteousness” means. And: “My enemy will see, and shame will cover her who says to me, ‘Where is the Lord your God?’” She will be put to shame

for what she reproached me with, as though I were getting no help from God, when she sees the ineffable care he has for me. “My eyes will look upon her.” Not only will I myself be freed from evils, but I will also see the punishments of those who were hostile to me. “Now she will be trampled down like mud in the streets. It is a day for plastering brick; that day is your wiping out.” You will be trampled by the enemies like mud that is trodden in the streets by crowds of travellers and kneaded in various ways for making bricks. Those who do this kind of work usually [?] it further, so that once it has been smoothed it may be better suited to the use at hand. Such, he says, will be your [?] at that time. That is, you will be wiped out in this way by the enemies who attack you, trampling and crushing you in various ways with great [?].

Verses 12–13. — “That day will thrust aside your statutes.” You will endure complete desolation, he says, for that is what the removal of the statutes indicates. While any state and government stands, its statutes must prevail, and those [?] are accustomed to use them. But when desolation and captivity overtake it, the order of its laws must vanish. Then he adds: “And your cities will come to siege and to division by the Assyrians.” He [?] shows the cause of the removal of the statutes: the Assyrians will tear down the cities and divide them up as they please. “And your fortified cities will be for division, from Tyre to the river of Syria, from sea to sea, and from mountain to mountain.” He means that the Assyrians will gain control of all these cities. The prophet Amos also shows this [?] when he speaks of the evils the neighbouring peoples suffer from the Assyrians. “A day of water and tumult [?]; and the land will become a ruin together with those who live in it, because of the fruits of their deeds.” A multitude of enemies will come upon you, flooding over everyone like water. You will be filled with great turmoil as a result, and everything you have will be destroyed along with you, since you will undergo this as a just punishment for your deeds. Having told in these words of the punishment of those who had caused [them] grief, he turns next [?]…

Verses 14–17. — “Shepherd your people with your rod, the sheep of your inheritance, who dwell alone in a forest.” But you, he says, freed from tumult and turmoil and living in peace, [?] … yourself. For God has counted you his own possession, [?] from the enemies, and has granted that you, set apart from all, may graze in safety like sheep in your own [lands]. “They will graze in the midst of Carmel [?] of old; and as in the days of your departure from Egypt I will show them wonders [?].” They will

THEODORE OF MOPSUESTIA

recover, he says, their own places, just as earlier, when they came out of Egypt, they took possession of them with great might. What I do for them now will be no less wonderful than what happened then. “Nations will see and be ashamed of all their strength.” What happens for them will be enough to cover with great shame even those who had earlier resolved to make war on them, when they see that through God's care these people have gained such power. “They will lay their hands on their mouths,” in amazement at the greatness of what happens. “Their ears will be deafened”: they will not be able even to bear hearing how great these events are. “They will lick dust like a snake crawling on the ground.” Unable to do anything more against what happens for you, they will fall to the ground like snakes, writhing [?] upon it. “They will be held fast in their confinement.” They will suffer no ordinary distress, as the enemies shut them in for slaughter. “They will be astounded at the Lord our God, and they will be afraid of you.” Overcome with amazement at the greatness of what God has done, they will from then on regard you too as fearsome, since you have been thought worthy of such great providence from God.

Verses 18–20. — Then, after announcing the good things that will be theirs, he offers the following to God as a thanksgiving on behalf of all: “Who is a God like you, who takes away iniquities and passes over ungodliness for the remnant of his inheritance?” Now, if ever before, the events themselves have shown you to be a great God, surpassing all in power and in love for humankind. You forgive sins, overlook ungodliness, and show your generosity to the remnant of your own people. “He did not keep his wrath as a witness, because he delights in mercy.” He did not bear to hold on for long to the wrath he justly had against us, though he would have been just in using it. He had often warned us about what we would suffer if we sinned, and we paid no attention at all to the correction his threats offered. Yet he overcame everything by his own mercy, which it is always his way to set above all else. “He will turn and have compassion on us; he will sink our sins, and all our sins will be cast into the depths of the sea.” He who sent us away into captivity again showed his own mercy and brought us back. He wiped out our sins completely and, as it were, hurled them down into some [depth?], from which they can no longer rise again and prevail against us. And he gives the cause of all this: “You will give your truth to Jacob and mercy to Abraham, as you swore to our fathers in the days of old.” You have done all these things, he says, because you remembered your own promises, which you made to our fathers in times long past with steadfast generosity. You made those promises to them then, and now you are bringing them to fulfilment for us, their descendants.

[?] OF THE PROPHET. Nineveh was a great city, teeming with people, as the divine Scripture teaches. It was the most famous of all the cities of Assyria; the palace was there, and the king of the Assyrians spent most of his time there. Now these people, I mean the inhabitants of Nineveh, were seized with such fear at a mere threat from an unknown man that they changed for the better with great speed. That happened because God wished to give a demonstration of his grace, as we have already explained more clearly on the prophecy of blessed Jonah. But when God allowed them to show their own choice, they displayed such wickedness of mind, such cruelty and depravity of character, that they marched against the whole people of the ten tribes and took them captive. They sacked their cities and plundered all their possessions, and they advanced even as far as Jerusalem, which they were eager to capture, showing no reverence for the temple or for the worship of God performed there.

Something happened here like what once took place in Egypt. Pharaoh, who reigned there, and all the Egyptians held Jacob and Joseph and all their kin in high regard, as long as God disposed them to keep that attitude. But when the people had grown into a multitude and the time of the exodus was pressing, God allowed Pharaoh and the Egyptians to show their own wickedness toward them, so that they made every effort to destroy them all completely. Using this occasion, God brought them out of Egypt. Blessed David says as much: “The king sent and released him; the ruler of peoples set him free. He made him lord of his house and ruler of all his possessions, to instruct all his princes as he pleased and to teach his elders wisdom.” Here he [describes?] the honour and esteem that Pharaoh showed Joseph, and then he adds: “And Israel came into Egypt, and Jacob sojourned in the land of Ham. And he made his people very numerous and made them stronger than their enemies.” Having spoken of Jacob's entry and of how greatly the whole people had grown in number, he adds: “He turned their heart to hate his people, to deal craftily with

…against his servants." Clearly, when God permitted it, the Egyptians together with their king were all changed, so that they came to hate the Israelites and wished to destroy them altogether. After this the blessed David goes on to the events of the Exodus. In the same way here too: God first displayed his own grace by bringing about a sudden change for the better in the king of the Assyrians and in all the people of Nineveh. But not long afterward he permitted them to reveal their own wickedness, and allowed them to do such things to the Israelites that they ravaged the ten tribes and marched against Jerusalem, setting out in great madness, as though they were all but going to make war on God himself. But God at once brought a most grievous blow upon them through the angel, and, putting the rest to flight, surrounded them with evils of every kind. Finally Sennacherib, then king of the Assyrians, having returned to his own country in great disgrace, was slaughtered by his own sons. Later still God destroyed their kingdom entirely, arranging for Nineveh to be besieged by the Babylonians, so that that most populous, illustrious and royal city was taken captive and reduced to utter desolation. For just as in the earlier events, which the blessed prophet Jonah narrates, God displayed his own grace by changing them all suddenly for the better, so here, once they had displayed their own wickedness, he surrounded them with a very great and fearful punishment. Through both he instructs all people, so that they may know the greatness of his grace whenever he wishes to show his generosity toward human beings, and the fear of his punishment whenever he judges deserving of it those whose mind is incorrigible in sinning. Those earlier events, then, the prophet Jonah makes known; these, Nahum, who speaks of the punishment that was to be brought on them in various ways for the arrogance they showed against the Israelites, against Jerusalem, and against the God of all who was worshipped in it. By these things it became clear to everyone that God would not have allowed the Israelites to suffer those things at their hands, had they not made themselves deserving of such suffering through their impious deeds. And since the Israelites suffered what those people brought upon them and endured that captivity, paying the penalty for their own impiety, God accordingly turns his wrath on those who had done such things, punishing them for what, out of depravity of mind, they had done and dared against God and against those who belonged to him. For he allowed the Israelites to suffer, as deserving such things for their impiety and their sins; but those who had done such things to them out of their own depravity he subjected to the punishment they had made inevitable, exacting a penalty from them

for the madness and depravity of mind by which they chose to run aground on such impiety as even to take up war against God, as far as it lay with them. For just as Obadiah speaks of the punishment of the Edomites, which they were to undergo later, after the people's return from Babylon, for the wrongs they had committed against Jerusalem and against those who lived in it at that time, and makes clear by his announcement that what befell them then would happen by God's purpose, so the blessed Nahum in this book speaks of the punishment brought by God upon the Assyrians, which they did in fact later undergo at the hands of the Babylonians.
