He too makes clear that it was by God's purpose that the Israelites were permitted to suffer these things for their own impiety, and that the Assyrians would in due time pay a penalty for their madness in proportion to their offenses. Such, then, is the subject of the book; now we must attend to the details.

Verse 1. "The oracle (lēmma) concerning Nineveh; the book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite." This is the usual heading of the prophetic books, but the meaning of lēmma needs to be explained. There was one Holy Spirit, who granted his own grace to those found worthy of such things, as the blessed Paul says: "Having the same Spirit of faith, according to what is written, 'I believed, and so I spoke,' we too believe, and so we speak." He shows that both those of old and those who serve the mystery of the New Covenant shared in the same grace of the Holy Spirit, but that its operations were carried out differently according to the pressing need. "For there are varieties of gifts," he says, "but the same Spirit": the things given are different, but the Spirit who supplies them all is one. Then, after listing the gifts, "To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit," and so on, he adds: "All these are worked by one and the same Spirit, who distributes to each individually as he wills." He shows that everything was worked by the one Holy Spirit, but that the operations within them were manifold and suited to the need, and through these they received the revelation of what was necessary. All of them, it seems, received knowledge of the more hidden things in ecstasy, since only by being in their thoughts somewhere far removed from their present condition could they give their attention to the contemplation of these things alone. For if we cannot receive precise instruction from our teachers unless we tear ourselves away from everything and attend with great care to what is said, how could they possibly have received such fearful and ineffable visions, unless their reasoning had first been taken out of present things at the time of the vision? So Scripture says that the blessed Peter, being in ecstasy, saw the sheet coming down from heaven, since the grace of the Spirit first drew his mind away from present things

[?] and then prepared him to give his attention to the vision of what was shown. Just as, when we are outside our present condition in sleep, we receive the sight of what is revealed, so somehow they, being placed by the grace of the Holy Spirit in a transported state of mind, would receive the vision of what was shown. But when they were in such a state, the grace of the Holy Spirit sometimes gave them such teaching that they seemed to hear someone speaking and to be instructed, and so received knowledge of what was necessary; as the blessed Peter, at the sheet, seemed to hear a voice saying to him, "Rise, Peter, kill and eat." Hence the prophet Isaiah too says, "Lord, who has believed our report (akoē)?", calling the revelation given him from God a "hearing," since he seemed to hear someone speaking. And sometimes they saw a vision and at the same time heard what was spoken; as when the blessed Peter both saw the sheet and received the teaching of what was said to him; and indeed the blessed Isaiah, when he says he saw God and the seraphim, also heard the voices addressed to him. For this reason Scripture sometimes says, "The word of the Lord which came to" this or that prophet, calling "word" the operation by which he seemed to be taught by a voice what was needed; and sometimes, "The vision which" this or that prophet "saw," giving this name to the revelation by which, seeming to see something, he was taught what was fitting. [?] means the same thing, even if it says, "The hand of the Lord came upon me"; for here too it calls the operation of the Holy Spirit "the hand of the Lord," by which, as though laying hold of the prophet's mind, it gave it teaching about what was necessary. This too is what lēmma means. For when God wished to show the prophets something full of astonishment, he brought about a sudden transport of their mind, so that, together with being in such a state, they might receive knowledge of what was to come with greater fear. So he calls it lēmma, a "seizing," because the grace of the Spirit, as it were suddenly taking hold of the prophet's mind, transported it to the revelation of what was being shown. He says the same here too: "The lēmma concerning Nineveh; the book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite"; meaning that the prophet's mind, suddenly seized by the grace of the Spirit, was transported to the vision of those things through which he learned what would befall Nineveh, and then passed on to his hearers the teaching drawn from what had been shown him. That is why he said both "lēmma" and "vision": by the one to indicate the manner of the Holy Spirit's operation, and by "vision" the contemplation of what was shown him. He begins: Verses 2–3. "God is jealous, and the Lord avenges; the Lord avenges with fury; the Lord takes vengeance on

his adversaries, and he himself destroys his enemies." He calls God's wrath "jealousy": the wrath he conceives against the impious when he is provoked by deeds that are utterly outrageous. So Scripture says, "The Lord saw and was jealous, and was provoked to anger because of his sons and daughters." Here too, then, he was about to speak of the wrath God had stirred up against the Ninevites, that is, against the Assyrians (for by the royal city he means the whole nation), because, having practised the greatest impiety and lawlessness, they had inflicted so many great evils on many others, and above all on the Israelites, and, by coming against Jerusalem, had all but taken up war against God himself. So he rightly began with the words "God is jealous," meaning that God knows how to be exceedingly angered at impieties, that he avenges with great wrath the impieties people commit, and that he punishes and utterly destroys all who adopt a hostile and opposing mind toward him. Then, since now these things, he says, although God had shown them great love for humankind when, persuaded by the preaching of the blessed Jonah, they looked to repentance [?]: "The Lord is long-suffering, and great is his strength, and the Lord will by no means acquit the guilty." "For just as he knows how to bear patiently and overlook a multitude of sins and impieties when he sees people inclined to repentance," he says, "so he shows that his power is equal to the task by the greatness of the punishment when he sees them sinning without repentance and pressing on to the height of impiety. These he does not release from the charges, nor from the punishment for their sins, since they are condemned by their own deeds." Verses 4–5. And what is the proof of these things? "His way is in destruction and in earthquake." He calls God's action his "way"; and he often says the same of human beings too, as in "The Lord knows the ways of the blameless." Here, then, he means this: Now he has resolved to do this, and this is the purpose of his onrush against you, to shake everything you have and to bring utter destruction upon you. "And clouds are the dust of his feet." Consistently with having said "way," he added, "Clouds are the dust of his feet." Since anyone who moves with great force naturally stirs up dust as he walks, the clouds, he says, are the dust of his feet; meaning, as he rushes against you he whirls the whole air up against you. "Threatening the sea and drying it up, and making all the rivers desolate." He is able by his voice alone to dry up the sea, and the rivers with it; this shows that it costs him no effort to destroy your whole community and your great multitude whenever he wishes. Then he gives proof of what happens: "Bashan and Carmel have dwindled, and all the blossoms of Lebanon have failed; the mountains quaked at him, and the hills were shaken, and the whole earth drew back before his face, and

all who dwell in it." For whatever the Israelites suffered at your hands, he says, happened according to his purpose. Having condemned them for their impiety, he let them suffer what you wished to bring upon them, so that not even those things were the work of your power, but of the divine purpose. That is why Bashan and Carmel and the glories of Lebanon came to ruin, and the mountains and hills were all but shaken together; and, in short, he removed that whole land, together with its inhabitants, from his sight, hating them for their impiety. Verses 6–10. "Who will stand before his wrath? And who will withstand him in the anger of his fury? His fury melts rulers, and the rocks were shattered by him." You have proof from those events, then, that no one can resist the divine wrath, since it is well able to shatter and utterly destroy both those who hold great dominions and those established in the greatest strength. And saying things like those before: "The Lord is good to those who wait for him in the day of affliction, and he knows those who revere him." For he is, he says, exceedingly loving toward humankind and knows very well how to do good to those who look to him and fear his threat. "And with an overwhelming flood he will make an end; darkness will pursue those who rise up and his enemies." But whenever he turns to wrath, having found some who deserve it, he brings on a kind of flood by his onrush, through which he brings about the utter destruction of the wicked; and all who rise against him and dare to want anything contrary to him he surrounds with darkness and great perplexity through the magnitude of the evils brought upon them. "What do you devise against the Lord?" Do you, then, have such a notion [?] about him? Do you think you can fight against such a one? It was from this notion that you earlier came against Jerusalem and launched such blasphemous words against God. "He himself will make an end; he will not take vengeance twice at the same time in affliction." For once he has resolved to make your destruction complete, he carries out what he has decided against you so suddenly that he will not need to bring a second blow, but your destruction will come upon you all at once from the first blow. "For they will be laid waste to their foundation": so that everything you have is reduced to utter desolation. "And like bindweed entwined they will be devoured, and like stubble full of dryness." Like that plant which twines around hedges and is then eaten up by every beast that comes upon it, you will all be consumed by your enemies; and like dry stubble in a fire you will be destroyed by those who attack you, being in no way able to withstand their assault. Verses 11–15. "From you will come forth a scheme against the Lord, one plotting evil things against him." So you dared to devise such things against God, and indeed to carry them out, by coming against the city that has the divine temple? Did you think it easy to destroy it, as though it received no help at all from God

[?] "of many waters." Hear, then, what God, the Lord of all the nations on earth, now declares concerning that one [?]; for this is what "of many waters" means. "And so they will be divided." For just as someone might with great ease separate water from water collected in some place, he says, so God will separate you from all the nations by handing you over to destruction. "Your report will no longer be heard": so that there will no longer be even a voice [?] of you, since you will have perished completely. "And now he will break his rod from off you, and burst your bonds." For he will break all your scepters and the kingdom you thought you possessed; and he will utterly sever all the dominion you held over your subjects, encompassing them with your authority as though with bonds, since, with the destruction you undergo, all your kingdom, your might and the authority you held over others will be wiped out. "And the Lord will give command concerning you." For God has commanded these things to happen to you. "No more of your name will be sown." Since those under a kingdom usually refer everything to their kings and are called by their name, as being under their authority, your name, he says, will no longer appear anywhere, since you will perish utterly. "From the house of your god I will destroy the carved images, and I will make the molten images your grave, for you have been dishonored." For I will destroy along with you the idols too, to which you gave great honor, so that, perishing and vanishing with you and all but buried with you in your disgrace, they will be a kind of grave for you. "For behold, on the mountains the feet of one who brings good news and proclaims peace." Then indeed, he says, there will be many running over the mountains of Jerusalem and announcing to all the good news of your destruction and of the peace that will thereafter be theirs. "Keep your feasts, Judah, pay your vows to God; for they will no longer pass through you to bring you to ruin." From now on be glad, and fulfil the fitting feasts and vows to God with all zeal [?], since they will not come again to destroy anything of yours, for they have perished [?]. Therefore he adds: "It is finished, it is taken away." For the one who dared these things, he says, has been wiped out.

Verses 1–[?]. "He has come up, breathing into his face, delivering from affliction." For a divine wrath, as with a kind of breath [?], has utterly quenched [?] the one who was blazing against you, so that from now on you need fear no affliction. Having said this as though to Judah, who ought to hold feasts over the destruction of the one who had dared such things against them, he now turns his words to the Ninevites. "Watch the road." Look, he says, at those who are about to come against you. "Strengthen your loins." Gird yourself up against so great an assault, if you can. "Be very strong in might." Now show that great power of yours. "For the Lord has turned back the insolence of Jacob, as the insolence of Israel." But it is not possible for you to escape the evils coming

upon you, since God has turned upon your own head what you did to Israel. "For the shakers have shaken them out, and destroyed their branches, the weapons of his power from among men." For so great will be the power of your enemies against you that, like those who shake out a garment, you will be shaken out of your own dignity and will lose everything you were so proud of, as though it surrounded you and was busy in your service. In short, they will destroy all your military skill and all your power from among all people. Then he also sets out their former power, which they used for wrong ends, as something that will be of no help to them at the present time. "Mighty men sporting in fire." You were the ones, he says, who in your excessive strength did not shrink from daring even fire. "The reins of their chariots on the day of his preparation, and the horsemen will be thrown into confusion in the roads." You who prided yourselves greatly on horses and chariots — all these will now prove useless to you. For at the time when God has prepared your punishment, confusion will seize both the chariots and the horsemen, and they will be unable to accomplish anything for fear of the enemy. "The chariots will be thrown into confusion, they will be tangled together in the squares." For all will rush to flee, he says, so that in the perplexity that grips them they will become entangled with one another and destroy themselves before the enemy even attacks. "Their appearance is like torches of fire, and like lightning flashing about." He says this ironically, in mockery: and yet, he says, you were thought to be no different from lightning and fire, flashing with your weapons and attacking your opponents with great violence. Verses 5–6. "And the nobles will remember, and will flee by day, and will hold fast in their perplexity, and will hurry to the walls, and will prepare their defenses." All that preparation and power of yours will be useless. Abandoning the fight, you will turn your thoughts to flight; yet you will not even make use of that course, because of the overwhelming fear of the enemy pressing upon you. Instead you will then run up onto the walls, abandoning the war in deep despair and hoping to find safety in them, and you will be wholly taken up with the usual watches on the walls. And what is greater still: "The gates of the cities were opened, and the palace fell, and the foundation was laid bare; and she went up, and her maidservants were led away, like doves moaning in" (46) The manuscript reads anabēsē.

NAHUM, CHAPTER II. … [?] “she shall go up.” He said “she was going up,” changing the tense as he usually does. She will go up, he says, led as a captive from now on to the king of her enemies. And all your subject cities and lands (he called them “maidservants”) will bid a long farewell to the kingdom you once had and will all be led into captivity with you. Like doves, they will groan inwardly and lament both their own misfortunes and yours. Verses 8–9. Next he speaks of their former prosperity, and he divides his discourse between these themes. At times he tells what evils she will suffer. At times he sets out the power they once had, so that this too may make her suffering seem greater, since she is to fall from such a state into such a state. “And Nineveh: her waters are like a pool of water; and they fled and did not stand, and there was no one to look back.” In the past she was just like a very great pool, overflowing with water on every side and feeding many fish within it. In the same way she was filled with a great multitude of her own people, and she held many captives taken in her wars. But now they have come to such misery that they cannot stand against the enemy even for a moment and can only think of flight. And no one was found to look upon such great evils or to bring them any relief. “They plundered the silver, they plundered the gold.” From then on the enemies took everything they had as plunder. “And there was no end to her adornment.” They stripped them of the countless wealth with which they had once been adorned. “She is weighed down beyond all her desirable vessels.” The enemies made their greatest efforts to take from them whatever seemed precious and whatever they had acquired with great desire. For “weighed down” is like the phrase in Kingdoms, “The battle was heavy upon Saul,” which means that the enemies pressed hardest at that point. So here too he says “weighed down” to mean that the enemies were most eager for those things. Verses 10–11. “Shaking and shaking out, casting out, and breaking of heart, and loosening of knees, and pains in every loin, and their faces like the scorching of a pot.” He means that the enemies will surround them with evils of every kind, shaking them and casting them out. The reasoning of their minds will be utterly quenched. They will be so undone by fear that they can hardly even stand, and all of them will share the same pains. In short, they will be so helpless amid their evils that they will be no different from a pot burnt by fire. Then he again reminds them of their former power: “Where is the dwelling of the lions, and the pasture that belonged to the cubs?” But their [?] and all their pasture are gone. By “cubs” he means the same thing, that is, the lions. He means this: In the past you who live in Nineveh were feared by everyone else, as lions are, and you took spoils from your wars on every side and gathered them to yourselves. Now

Nineveh, your dwelling, is gone, and with it everything you had gathered to yourselves before. “Where did the lion go, that he might enter?” This is said with great mockery. They were always at war, always attacking someone as if on a hunt. So he says, “Where has your ruler gone now? To what hunt has he gone?” He means that the king has stopped making war and has laid aside his former authority and power. Verses [12?]–13. So he adds: “There were the lions’ cubs, and no one to frighten them. The lion seized enough for his cubs and strangled prey for his lionesses, and he filled his den with prey and his dwelling with plunder.” In the past you attacked everyone like lions, and no fear held you back from doing such things. You took other people’s goods as plunder and gathered great wealth for yourselves, enough for your children to enjoy as well. You killed and strangled others, collecting your plunder like prey for your own young, and you increased your own wealth through robbery and lawlessness. What then? “Behold, I am against you, says the Lord Almighty. I will burn up your multitude in smoke, and the sword will devour your lions. I will destroy your prey from the earth, and your deeds will no longer be heard.” For all these things, God has now pronounced sentence against you. Your multitude will be consumed by fire and the greatest distress. The enemies will kill those among you who seem powerful. All that you wickedly gathered will vanish. Your whole power will be broken, and nothing more will be heard about you, as of one who had once achieved something [?] and then perished once and for all.

Verses 1–3. Having spoken of the punishment, he now reproaches their wickedness again: “O city of blood, wholly false, full of injustice.” You will suffer these things, he says, because you devoted all your leisure to murder. With lies and deceit you tried to [?] many people into irreparable harm. Rabshakeh did something like this at Jerusalem when he tried to lure the people out with promises of good things. “Prey shall not be groped for.” This means: You will no longer have a chance to hunt, and though you search hard you will not be able to accomplish anything like that. He uses a metaphor taken from people who carefully grope about in search of something. Why? “The sound of whips, and the sound of the rumbling of wheels, and of a galloping horse, and of a bounding chariot, of a charging horseman, and of a flashing sword and gleaming weapons, and a multitude of wounded, and a heavy fall.” These things, he says, will come upon you in place of what you had: whips, the clatter of wheels, galloping horses, the great din of chariots, horsemen in pursuit, and swords along with other weapons, terrible even to look at because of their brightness. Many will be wounded by them, and those slain will die in great numbers. “And there was no [end?] for her nations.” The evils will not stop for her subjects either. Each evil will always be followed by another. “And they will grow weak in

their bodies from the multitude of fornication.” Since many will be killed, he says, their number will be reduced to very few. This is what “they will grow weak in their bodies” means: few bodies will be left. Then he gives the cause: “from the multitude of fornication.” They will suffer these things, he says, because they turned so very far away from God. And it is fitting to do this to those who seem [?]

Verses [4?]–7. Then he adds a reproach: “A harlot, beautiful and charming, a leader in sorceries.” You, he says, are the one who turned away from what was right. You seemed handsome to yourself because of your great power, and charming because of those who were eager to court you on account of that power. You even led others into all the practices of impiety. “She who sells nations by her harlotry, and tribes by her sorceries.” You used your power over whole nations and entire tribes to draw them with you into the same impiety and the same eagerness for such things. “Behold, I am against you, says the Lord God Almighty. I will uncover your hinder parts over your face. I will show the nations your shame and the kingdoms your disgrace. I will cast abomination upon you, according to your uncleannesses, and I will make you an example.” So I will bring upon you, says God, a punishment that matches such outrages. I will clothe you in every kind of shame. It is as when someone about to torture a person strips off the garment and pulls it all up over the face: the sight of the nakedness is shameful, the expectation of the torture is bitter, and with the face wrapped in the garment the victim cannot even see what lies ahead. In the same way, he says, I will strip away all your adornment and bring you to the utmost disgrace through the punishment the enemies will inflict [?]. Your shame and disgrace will become plain to everyone everywhere, and you will seem abominable to all even by report alone, because you have been brought down to such worthlessness. You will be trampled by all and shown to be an example of utter disgrace through the extremity of your evils. “And everyone who sees you will go down from you and say, ‘Wretched Nineveh! Who will groan over her? Where shall I seek comfort for her?’” Those who see these things, and who know well the prosperity you once had, will give up their former opinion of you and turn their hatred into pity. This is what “will go down from you” means. They will pity you for the evils that have seized you, reasoning that no one can lament worthily the disaster that has come upon you, and that no comfort or remedy can be found for such great evils. Verse 8. “Tune the string, make ready, portion of Ammon, you who dwell among rivers, with water all around her. The sea is her dominion, and water her walls.” Some [?] have said that Ammon here means the city now called Alexandria in Egypt. Yet it is clear that some four hundred years after this prophecy, Alexander, king of Macedonia, came on the scene [?]. Among many other conquests he took Egypt, and he named Alexandria

after himself. Perhaps someone might say that even before this there was a city there called Ammon, and that the prophet is now speaking about it. But, as I have often said, I consider precision about such matters superfluous whenever it contributes nothing to explaining the meaning of the passage. Such precision is an empty display, meant to make people seem able to identify places whose names are rather obscure. Even more fanciful is their claim that the prophet speaks of the destruction of Alexandria to show that it would be nothing surprising if something similar happened to Nineveh. The prophet is not trying to console Nineveh with his words, and recalling the misfortunes of others would be a consolation, since it comforts the one who suffers. We always comfort mourners by reminding them of similar cases, so that they may not be too disheartened by thinking that what has happened to them is something new. On the contrary, throughout the book the prophet clearly joins Nineveh's former prosperity to his announcement of the evils that will come upon her, because that prosperity would make the evil befalling her seem all the greater. But let this be said in passing. The meaning of the words is this: The Assyrian advanced as far as Egypt and inflicted very many evils on the people there too. He even brought the gravest misfortunes upon the Israelites who had fled and were living there, as the prophet Hosea shows: “Therefore, behold, they will go out from the misery of Egypt; Memphis will receive them, and Machmas will bury them.” He clearly means what the Israelites who had fled to Egypt were to suffer from the Assyrians when they entered Egypt. Earlier, after speaking of the evils that would overtake the Assyrians, he turned his discourse to Judah and told him to keep festival, since he would now be at peace because the enemy who had come against her had been destroyed. In the same way, here he turns his discourse to Ammon, a city of Egypt, and says: Take up the lyre, and with great delight prepare to sing on it of his destruction and of your peace. You were surrounded by water on every side and fortified by sea and rivers, but none of this helped you when the Assyrian came. Now, however, you need no longer fear his wickedness. Then he adds: Verses 9–12. “Ethiopia was her strength, and Egypt, and there is no end to your flight. Put and the Libyans became her helpers. Yet she will go into exile as a captive, and her infants they will dash [?] at the head of her streets.” For these too, he says, the Ethiopians and Libyans and all whom I have mentioned, made an alliance with you and promised to help you in every need. Yet you gained nothing from them either. You were busy with flight and were led away captive by the hands of the enemies. They did not spare even your infants, but slaughtered them in many ways and threw their bodies along every road. It is clear that by Ethiopians he does not mean those who were settled far away,

but those who happened to border on the Egyptians. “And they will cast lots for all her glorious ones, and all her great men will be bound in manacles.” The enemies took all your precious things and divided them by lot, and they put manacles on those among you who were thought very powerful and dragged them off into captivity. “And you will be drunk.” Since he usually uses wine to stand for punishment, he means: you will endure the heaviest punishment, so that you will be tossed here and there by your evils like a drunkard. “And you will be disregarded.” No one will take any account of your affairs. “And you will seek for yourself a respite from your enemies.” You will long for some relief from the evils that the enemies are to bring upon you at that time. “All your [fortresses?] are like you.” Everything you once had for your own security will be destroyed just as you will be. “And they have watchmen; if they are shaken, they will fall into the mouth of the eater.” You will try to keep watch through many people for what is coming, as soon as you hear that the enemies are approaching. But they will be of no use to you. They will abandon their orders and fall into the hands of the enemies. Verses 13–[15?]. “Behold, your people within you are like women. The gates of your land will be thrown wide open to your enemies, and fire will devour your bars.” All your subjects throughout the city, he says, will wail and tremble like women when they see the gates opened by the enemies and the city in their hands, with all the security she once seemed to have consumed in a moment, as if by fire. “Draw [water] for yourself for the siege, and strengthen [?] your fortifications.” Many people make very large trenches in front of their walls and fill them with water, so that the enemy cannot easily cross to the walls. This is what he means here: Draw on the help that water gives, surround your wall with it, and take great care of everything that seems to have been prepared for your security, in case you may get some benefit from it. He says this ironically, mocking them, since nothing could help anyone at that time. So he adds: “Go into the clay and be trodden among the straw. Get the better of the brick. There fire will devour you, and the sword will destroy you. It will devour you like a locust, and you will be weighed down like a grasshopper. You multiplied your trade beyond the stars of heaven.” But at that time you will have no means of saving yourself. On the contrary, the magnitude of your evils will make you like someone who has fallen into clay, like the straw used in brickmaking, trodden down and kneaded together with the clay, and you yourself will be wailing amid all your evils. The [enemy?] will consume you like fire, and you will be destroyed by slaughter of every kind. The multitude of enemies will come against you like grasshoppers and locusts, [devouring?] you and making you suffer a heavy share of evils. And all the wealth you collected, as if you were competing with the stars of heaven, will be of no use to you.

[?] “The grasshopper rushed upon them and flew away.” Verses 16–17[?]. “The grasshopper rushed upon them and flew away. Your mixed multitude leapt away like a wingless locust, like a locust perched on a hedge on a day of frost. The sun rose, and it sprang away, and its place was not known.” All your subjects, he says, whom you gathered from many places to increase your power, as you thought (this is what he means by “mixed multitude”), have flown away from you entirely like a grasshopper. They have leapt away like a wingless locust. They have behaved like a locust perched on a hedge in a frost. Because of the cold it stays motionless in its place, but when the sun appears and melts the frost it suddenly regains its power of flight and flies off, leaving no trace of where it was before. In the same way, he says, these people were formerly subject to you through fear. But when disaster overtakes you, they will all gladly part from you, as though they had gained some kind of freedom. Then the prophet laments over all of them: “Woe to them [?]. Your shepherds have slumbered; the Assyrian king has put your mighty men to sleep.” All of you, he says, deserve to be lamented. Your leaders have been struck down by punishment and have fallen, as if overcome by sleep. Blessed David says something similar: “Those who rode on horses slumbered.” And your king, handed over to destruction, has destroyed along with himself all who formerly held power under him. “Your people have fled to the mountains, and there was no one to receive them.” From then on all of them could only think of flight, since no one was able to help them in their present evils. “There is no healing for your crushing.” Every remedy and every restoration for your evils has been taken away. “Your wound has festered.” Your evil [has grown so great?] that it remains incurable. “All who hear the news about you will clap their hands over you, for upon whom has your wickedness not come continually?” Those everywhere who hear the news of your evils will [rejoice?], showing their delight at your destruction by clapping their hands. For since you waged war against everyone alike, and [?] all [?] your own [?], it will come about that all share a common delight in your [ruin?].

[?] after he had received that terrible blow through the angel and, as one would expect, had returned home in great disgrace, the blessed Habakkuk [?] delivered this prophecy concerning Judea. He divides his discourse into two parts. The first is an accusation against those who held power and sat in judgment among the people, who [afflicted] the poor with many and various miseries. He says that it is chiefly for these things that the evils from the Babylonians will be brought upon them. The second is an accusation against the Babylonians themselves, because they conquered Jerusalem but did not use their power as they should, and instead showed boundless cruelty toward the people. For this he says that they too will be punished. Because of this division, his prophecy seems to resemble the ninth psalm. In the Greek version that psalm counts as one, but in the Hebrew language it is two, and each has its own subject. The first begins, “I will give thanks to you, Lord, with my whole heart; I will tell of all your wonders,” and ends, “Appoint, Lord, a lawgiver over them; let the nations know that they are but men.” The second begins, “Why, Lord, do you stand far off? Do you look away in times of need, in affliction?” and ends, “Your ear has attended to the readiness of their heart, to give judgment for the orphan and the lowly, so that man on earth may no longer boast.” In the first of these the psalmist accuses foreigners, I mean the neighboring peoples, for treating them with great cruelty, and he says that God brought punishment upon them for it. In the second he accuses those among the people who used their wealth and power for injustice, harm and abuse against the poor, and he says that they too will not escape punishment. The blessed prophet Habakkuk now does something similar. He divides his discourse between two groups. The first consists of those among them who used the power they held to wrong the poor. He accuses these first, and then speaks of the punishment that will be brought upon them for it. The second consists of the Babylonians, who also inflicted a great many evils on the people, and he announces the punishment that will later be brought upon them. Since this is the subject of the prophet's words, we must now examine them one by one. The book opens with the usual heading: “The oracle which Habakkuk the prophet saw.” He begins:

Verse 2. “How long, Lord, shall I cry out, and you will not listen? I will cry to you when I am wronged, and you will not save?” The prophet does not say this to bring an accusation against God. It was their custom, when people were perplexed or felt a just indignation against wrongdoers, to describe the outrageousness of what was being done in the form of a complaint. So he speaks in that way here, just as blessed David also says, “Why, Lord…”

"…have you stood far off? Do you overlook us in times of need, in afflictions? While the ungodly man is arrogant, the poor man is set ablaze," and so on. He does not say this to blame God. He says it in indignation at those who do such things, and in a way perplexed as to why they are not swiftly punished. So also elsewhere: "Why, O God, have you cast us off for ever? Why has your anger blazed against the sheep of your pasture?" Here too he speaks out of perplexity at the magnitude of what had befallen the people, and one could find many such passages. In the same way the blessed Jeremiah also says: "Why does the way of the ungodly prosper? All who deal treacherously have thrived." He too does not speak to blame God. He is indignant at what they were doing, because they were not paying the penalty. For all the prophets alike were persuaded of what the blessed David says: "Lord, your mercy is in the heavens, your truth reaches to the clouds; your righteousness is like the mountains of God, your judgments are a great deep." He said this in amazement at God's love for humanity, which is beyond measure, and at his care for justice, which is great. But he says that God's testing and judgment are beyond our reach: by them he does not bring swift punishment on offenders but often postpones it, even though many people are suffering harm. In the same way the prophet speaks here too. He is indignant at the injustice of those who held power among the people and heaped much and manifold abuse on the poor. He knows full well that what was being done deserved punishment, but he is disheartened that, while God postpones the punishment, great injustice is being done to the poor. So, as one who had often asked God to bring punishment on those who were acting so wickedly, and had gained nothing more, he says: "How long, O Lord, shall I cry out, and you will not hear? Shall I shout to you when I am wronged, and you will not save?" He takes on the person of the wronged and says this: "How long, tried by many miseries, shall I cry out asking for your help and not obtain it?" Verses 3–5. "Why have you shown me toils and troubles, to look upon misery and ungodliness?" That is: "Every day I see nothing else but the toil and ruin that those in power, with ungodly intent, try to bring on the poor." "Judgment has been set before me, and the judge takes bribes; therefore the law is scattered, and judgment is not carried through to the end." That is: "I complain, then, of what I have often seen. When a case is brought, justice is utterly disregarded. The judge looks to outward standing and decides the case in that man's favor, adding to the harm done to the one who was wronged. As a result, the exactness of your laws is neglected and no one has any regard for them. No case comes to a good end; each one ends in plain injustice." "For the ungodly oppresses the righteous." That is: "Those who live in ungodliness and take no account of your ordinances use their power to inflict every kind of abuse

on the poor." Here he calls the wronged poor man "righteous," since he will obtain a just vindication. "Therefore judgment will go forth perverted." As a result, one would see nothing done even by the judge that is not perverted, since he too neglects justice and inclines wholly toward the powerful. Having denounced the outrageousness of what was being done, he next announces the punishment. It is as if, after his plea to God, he has learned it by divine revelation and rightly makes it known to all. "Look, you despisers, and observe, and marvel, and see wonders, and vanish; for I am working a work in your days that you will not believe if anyone tells it." That is: you will not be allowed to go on for ever doing such things and despising the divine judgment. You will see a marvelous punishment brought upon you, enough to destroy you utterly, since God will bring such things upon you. This is what he means by "I am working a work": something that would be beyond belief from a mere report, before it is experienced. What does he mean by it? Verses 6–8. "For I am raising up the Chaldeans, the bitter and swift nation, which marches over the breadth of the earth to take possession of dwellings not its own." That is: because of your great lawlessness I will bring the Babylonians upon you. They are a most savage nation that accomplishes what it wants with great speed. By the power it has, it will overrun almost the whole earth, so as to acquire possessions that in no way belong to it. "It is terrible and notable": full of great fear, and conspicuous to all because it can do great things. "Its judgment will come from itself, and its taking will go forth from itself." It needs no one else's alliance but accomplishes everything by its own power, so that it both judges and subdues whomever it wishes, and at once inflicts on them whatever punishment it wants. "And its horses will leap beyond leopards, and they will be keener than the wolves of Arabia; its horsemen will ride out and rush from afar, and they will fly like an eagle eager to eat." It has cavalry ready for war, swifter than leopards and the wolves of Arabia. Its riders are so eager for war that they boldly ride against a land lying far away, and to those living far from them they all but seem to fly down upon them, like an eagle ready for the hunt. Verses 9–14. "Destruction will come upon the ungodly, who stand against them face to face." These will utterly destroy all those among the people who show ungodliness toward the poor, and who will not dare even for a moment to look them in the face or resist them. "And he will gather captives like sand; he will make sport among kings, and princes will be his playthings; he will mock every stronghold, and throw up a mound and take it." He will take many captives, as countless as the sand. He will increase his own pleasure by overthrowing many kingdoms, whose

destruction he will accomplish not with great toil but easily, as if at play. With great ease he will master even very strongly fortified cities and forts, throwing up mounds with great facility and pulling down every wall, or whatever else seems securely fortified. "Then he will change his spirit, and pass through, and make atonement." That is: God will see that the punishment inflicted is very great, since it is inflicted by such men and with such a disposition, and he will change his anger against us. As if coming into our midst with his care, he will grant pardon for our past offenses and lift the punishment laid upon us because of them. "Is this not the strength of my God? Are you not from the beginning, O Lord my God, my Holy One? And we shall not die." That is: this is the work of your power, which you have shown toward us from of old, because you are holy and above all that exists. Through it we also expect to live, once the punishment has been lifted from us. "O Lord, you have appointed it for judgment, and he has formed me to reprove his discipline." That is: from the beginning you yourself formed me for the judgment of sinners, so that by reproving them I might discipline them and take away their license to do wrong. Then he turns his speech to God himself: "Your eye is too pure to look on evil, and you cannot look upon toils." That is: you have great care for justice, so you cannot bear even to look at those who do evil and cause others toil and ruin. "Why do you look upon the despisers? Will you keep silent while the ungodly swallows up the righteous? Will you make men like the fish of the sea, and like creeping things that have no leader?" That is: you will not bear to watch those who, in contempt of your punishment, do such things, nor let such great injustice pass, so that the righteous are all but swallowed up by the ungodly. We shall seem no different from fish and creeping things that have no leader, unless you make yourself manifest by your punishment, presiding over us and examining human affairs with exactness. Verses 15–17. Having said all this about the Babylonians, who treated the people with great mercilessness, he next describes the Babylonian's power as well, as he uses countless evils against as many as he wishes [?]. (68) Coislin manuscript: "gatherings."

[?] He means, then, that the Babylonian imagines he can do everything as he pleases, almost as God can. And he gives the reason: "For by them he has made his portion fat, and his food choice." He credits the greatness of his successes to his own strength, and through them he has come to increase his own wealth. This is what "he has made his portion fat" means. And from this, he says, he enjoys everything that is prized and choice, which is what "and his food choice" means. "Therefore he will cast his net, and will not spare to kill nations continually." Emboldened by what he has often achieved, he goes on using his own power, wages ceaseless wars and mercilessly slaughters many of those who fall into his hands. Having described what the Babylonian does, and having stressed at every point his lawlessness toward the people, he next adds:

Verses 1–4. "I will stand upon my watch, and mount upon a rock." This is a metaphor from those who, in war and siege, share among themselves the guarding of the wall. "I will stand," he says, "at my watch," meaning: "I will not leave the post that belongs to me but will hold to it, for I consider that if I do this I will be in the greatest safety." And he makes his meaning clearer: "And I will keep watch to see what he will say in me, and what I shall answer to my reproof." He means: "Our task is to look toward God and receive what comes from him and is shown by him, for from this I will have the greatest safety. So I will keep watching for whatever God may declare about what is happening, so that once I have learned it, I in turn may answer and pass on to the people what is shown, to reprove them." Earlier he spoke of the offenses of those among the people, and then, as one who had learned it by divine revelation, he told of the punishment that would be brought on them through the Babylonians. In the same way here, having spoken of the Babylonian's lawless deeds, he says he is waiting to learn from God what he will declare about these too, and next he adds the revelation he received about them. So he says: "And the Lord answered me and said: Write the vision clearly on a tablet, so that the one who reads it may run." He has said he was waiting to learn what God would declare about these things, and now he says that God himself gave him this answer. As in a divine vision, God commanded him to write what was shown on a tablet, so that what was said and written might be clear and plain for all to read. He means the things that will befall the Babylonians, as he goes on to say. Then he adds: "For the vision is yet for a long time, and it will rise up at the end, and not in vain." What has been shown will not come to pass at once but after some time, which is still far off. Yet it will certainly happen and reach its fulfillment, since it was not shown in vain but as something that will surely come about. "If it delays, wait for it, for the one who is coming will come and will not tarry." So even if what has been announced should seem to be delayed, you must by all means wait for it in the meantime. For what has been announced as going to happen and to come

will certainly come and happen; it will not be put off for ever. "If he draws back, my soul takes no pleasure in him; but the righteous shall live by my faith." So if anyone hesitates to believe in what is to come and doubts whether it will surely happen, such a person is very hateful to me. For I define as righteous the one who believes what has been promised and reaps the benefit of it. Verses 5–6. Having said this about the revelation and urged them to believe what was being shown, he next sets out the content of the vision: "But the conceited and scornful man, the braggart, will accomplish nothing." Know well, then, he says, that this enemy of yours (he means the Babylonian) will not carry the affairs of his dominion through to the end. He indulges in boundless conceit, despises the divine forbearance and boasts in the misfortunes of others, but under the divine threat he will undergo a terrible reversal. "He who has made his soul as wide as Hades, and like death is never satisfied; he will gather to himself all the nations and take in to himself all the peoples." He stretched himself out against all like [?Hades] and destroyed them all. Like death, he never had his fill of those he destroyed. He subdued very many and brought peoples from every side under his own power. But through the divine wrath he will undergo a terrible reversal. "Will not all these take up a parable against him, and a riddle to tell about him? And they will say: Woe to him who multiplies for himself what is not his own (how long?), and who makes his yoke heavy and hard." That is: everyone everywhere will be amazed at his reversal, and they will all say, as in a parable: "Most pitiable of all is the man who seized what belonged to others and increased his own wealth, and who weighed heavily on his subjects through his excessive cruelty." That is what "making his yoke heavy and hard" means. He will not be able to do such things for ever, and that is what "how long?" means. It is placed in the middle, and it applies to the whole. He means that the man will not stay like this for ever, since his fortunes will be reversed by what God brings upon him.

Verses 7–10. Then he says how, and in what manner: "For suddenly those who bite him will rise up, and those who plot against you will awake, and you will be plunder for them." Enemies will appear beyond all expectation (he means the Persians). With their attacks, as if with bites, they will tear your power and authority apart. They will work with great diligence to harm you and will make everything you have their plunder. "Because you have plundered many nations, all the remaining peoples will plunder you, because of the blood of men and the ungodly deeds against the land and the city and all who dwell in it." Just as he attacked and took away what belonged to others, in the same way

what you have will be taken away by those left alive to punish you. This is because you killed very many of those who belonged to God and acted impiously against the divine land, the city and all who live in it; he means Jerusalem and everything in it. Then, as if trampling on him now that he has justly suffered such things, he lists the lawless deeds for which he received this punishment: "O you who covet evil gain for your house, to set your nest on high, to be delivered from the hand of evils! You have devised shame for your house; you have finished off many peoples, and your soul has sinned." It was you, he says, who indulged in boundless greed, to increase your own wealth from the misfortunes of others and to make your kingdom stand lofty. You did these things, but you could not see how you might find any deliverance from the evils that would come upon you. Instead, by wronging many and acting lawlessly against everyone without fear, you gathered for your own house not wealth, as you thought, but shame, as the outcome has shown. For everything you have plainly done, you have paid this penalty. Verse 11. "For a stone will cry out from the wall, and a beetle from the wood will speak these things." Because of the magnitude of the evils, and from the buildings you wickedly raised, voices, as it were, rise up and accuse you of greed. The stones all but cry out against you in this way, and with them the worms that commonly nest in the joints between stones and bricks and are often found inside timbers too. Here by "beetle" he means the creatures found both in wood and in walls, which usually nest among the bricks. It is as if someone [?] were calling small creatures and worms by this name, so that all such things are called by this common term. There are also certain creatures, found mostly underground amid the damp, which people call kantharides. Some have said that the Syriac version reads "peg." But it would be foolish to abandon the Hebrew wording in which the prophet spoke, which the Seventy men, who were approved and had an exact knowledge of that language, made clear to us in their translation. It would be foolish to attend instead to a Syrian who translated the Hebrew into Syriac and then, as often [?], wanted to make his own blunder a rule for the wording. It seems to me that he did not understand what the text says, and so for the beetle, which very commonly nests in walls, he put "peg," so that the saying might seem to make some sense. Yet a peg speaking from the wood makes no sense at all. It might come from a wall, but not from wood, for wood is not made up of pegs the way a wall is made up of stones.

Verses 12–15. Since the prophet has said that the accusation against him comes from the walls, or from the creatures that live in them, he fittingly adds: "Woe to him who builds a city with blood and establishes a city by injustice! Are these things not from the Lord Almighty? Peoples enough have perished in fire, and many nations have lost heart. For the earth will be filled

with the knowledge of the glory of the Lord, as abundant water covers the seas." That is: would one not lament you, who build cities out of murder and injustice? You did not see what God would bring upon you for this. As if with fire, you consumed many, countless people by your cruelty, and you brought many to the very end of their lives through incurable calamities. For this you will now suffer these things, so that all people on earth may recognize the greatness of the divine dispensation that does such things. So it is with you, who were able to do and did so much, as God brings upon you a terrible punishment, one that fits the great number of your sins. And again, reproachfully: "O you who give your neighbor a muddy overturning to drink, and make him drunk, so that he may look upon their caves!" I have often said that he speaks of wine and drinking it to refer to calamity. You, then, he says, were the one who offered all people a muddy drink, fully able to make the drinker drunk and overturn him; in other words, you brought the heaviest punishment upon all. And you did this, he says, out of desire for what belonged to others, searching out other people's treasures and wanting to make them your own. Verses 16–18. "Drink your fill of dishonor instead of glory, you too; heart, be shaken and tremble." What you have done to others, then, you would justly suffer. Filled with dishonor in place of all that glory, reeling and falling as if from drunkenness, you would remain [?] under the excess of the punishment. "The cup of the Lord's right hand has come round to you, and dishonor has been gathered upon your glory." God has brought his own cup upon you, meaning the punishment that comes from his own sentence. As a result your glory has now been turned into the deepest dishonor, gathered upon you from every side. "For the ungodliness of Lebanon will cover you, and the misery of wild beasts will terrify you, because of the blood of men and the ungodly deeds against the land and all who dwell in it." As you acted impiously against the people, you will now justly pay the penalty. Your enemies will attack you like wild beasts, and you will be reduced to great fear and misery. This is because you killed people in Jerusalem and acted impiously against the divine land and the city, refusing to spare even one of its inhabitants. And since in these words he has reproached him for his offense against the people, the city and the temple, he goes on to add: "What does a carved image profit, that they have carved it? They have fashioned it as a molten image, a false fantasy, because the maker trusts in his own handiwork, to make dumb idols." You neglected, he says, [?] and offended against what belonged to him, and you [?] that you would be helped by idols. What had been made by human hands you hastened to worship in a deceptive fantasy, thinking you would gain some benefit from lifeless [?] idols fashioned by human hand. Verses 19–20. Then he goes on to add: "Woe to him who says to the wood, Wake up, arise! and to the stone, Be lifted up! And it is a fantasy." That is

…a plate of gold and silver, and there is no breath at all in it. But the Lord is in his holy temple; let all the earth be reverent before him.” How then could you not be the most pitiable of men, talking to wood as though it were awake and seeking help from the idol as though from on high? The idol only impresses the one who looks at it, because it is made of costly material, but it is empty of all living power. It would have been far better for you to despise these things and take no account of them, and to consider instead the greatness of God. He has the dwelling place of the heavens as his awesome and ineffable temple, yet he has also acquired a temple on earth because of human need. It was fitting that not only you but all people on earth should look to him and hold the thought of him in their minds with great fear. With these words, then, blessed Habakkuk concluded the prophecy we have discussed above. (p. 572) He had rebuked those among the people who oppressed the poor and had told of the punishment that would be brought on them through the Babylonian invasion. After that he spoke of the Babylonians themselves and of the cruelty they showed toward the others and toward Jerusalem and its inhabitants, and of how they too paid the penalty for their own lawlessness,

THE PRAYER OF HABAKKUK. Verses 1–2. From this point he turns his discourse to prayer. In the form of a prayer he makes known the good things that would come from God for the people. He begins thus: “Lord, I have heard the report of you, and I was afraid.” By “report” he means the revelation that came to him from God, just as blessed Isaiah says, “Who has believed our report?” and blessed David, “I will incline my ear to a parable.” We have mentioned these passages above as well. Here too, then, he means this: “I have received your revelation, through which you made known how you would punish through the Babylonians those of the people who transgress, and how in turn you would bring on the Babylonians a punishment in proportion to their offenses. So I was, naturally, filled entirely with fear.” (p. 573) “Lord, I have considered your works, and I was astonished.” “For I reflected on all the varied things you do with regard to human beings: you show due forbearance, and you punish for fitting reasons those who sin beyond correction. And I was struck with amazement at the wonder of what your wisdom arranges in such an ineffable way.” “In the midst of two living creatures you will be made known.” “For see, now too, as in two living creatures, namely those of the people who offend and, after them, the Babylonians, you have made known your power, your wisdom and your care for justice by what you have done to each.” “When the years draw near you will be recognized; when the time is present you will be displayed.” “For now you have made these things known to us through revelation. But when the time arrives at which they must reach their end as seems good to you, you will give a greater and clearer display of your own power and

wisdom through the deeds themselves.” “When my soul is troubled, in wrath you will remember mercy.” “Then the abundance of your loving-kindness will also appear toward the people of Judea. When they are troubled in soul and beside themselves because of your wrath and of the punishment brought on them for their offenses, you will remember your own loving-kindness. You will deliver them from their evils and bring them back to their own land, beyond all human hope.” Verses 3–5. “God will come from Teman, the Holy One from a shaded mountain.” (p. 574) By Teman he means the chief city of Idumea, and by the shaded mountain he means the mountain of Jerusalem, as one that has been granted divine shelter on every side. “Then, therefore, you will appear coming from Teman of Idumea, whose people you will punish for their offense against us, and from the holy mount Zion, which you will make glorious in the eyes of all through our return.” “His excellence covered the heavens, and the earth is full of his praise.” By the greatness of the things he does he will fill both heaven and earth, so that from then on all will turn to hymns, marveling at the wisdom and the greatness of what he does. Here too he expresses the whole by dividing it into parts, which, as we have already shown in many cases, is a characteristic of divine Scripture. He says that both the heavens and the earth have been covered with God's excellence in order to say “the universe,” and he says that his praise must be filled up by everyone because of what has happened. “And his brightness will be like light.” By his own appearing, he says, he will fill all things with light. “Horns are in his hands.” (p. 575) He will show that he is fully able to defend his own and to subdue those who try to be hostile to them. He speaks this way by a metaphor taken from animals that fight with their horns. “And he established a mighty love of his strength.” He will do these things because he shows the greatest love toward us. “Before his face goes a word.” That is, he declares what will happen before the events take place. He always did this through the prophets, and he has done it no less now through me. “And it will go forth for instruction at his feet.” The deed follows as well, so that people are instructed in what is right by both: by the foretelling of what will happen and by its later coming to pass. Verses 6–12. “He stood, and the earth was shaken.” Merely by appearing he shakes the earth. Compare “God stood in the assembly of gods,” which means that he was seen in their midst. “He looked, and nations melted; the mountains were shattered by force, the everlasting hills melted, his everlasting ways.” Merely by looking he destroys whole nations and shatters mountains and hills that seemed to have stood firm for a long time in their own strength. For it has been his work from of old to do such things, and through such works to display the course of his own dispensation. “Instead of troubles I saw the dwellings of the Ethiopians; the tents of the land of Midian will be terrified.” “For long ago too, when we were slaves in Egypt and you willed to deliver us from slavery under the Egyptians, I saw

the dwellings of the Ethiopians and the Midianites deserted, and the dwellings of all who at that time chose to be hostile to us.” “Were you angry with the rivers, Lord, or was your wrath against the rivers, (p. 576) or your onrush against the sea?” “It is your custom to show your anger against rivers and sea.” For “not with the rivers” stands for: “Have you not always, when you willed it, shown your anger and your wrath against rivers and sea?” He goes on, at any rate: “For you will mount your horses, and your riding is salvation.” “For whenever you will,” he says, “you give commands to the invisible ministering powers, as if mounting horses. They punish all the adversaries at once, and from this salvation comes to your own people.” “You will draw your bow taut against the scepters, says the Lord.” “With continual punishments you shoot down those who seem to be established in kingship and power.” “The earth will be split by rivers.” So that the drying up of the rivers, which happens all at once because of your wrath, tears the earth apart. For this is what usually happens to the earth when the waters diminish, through the drought that follows afterward. “Peoples will see you and be in anguish.” Very many will be in pain, unable even to bear the sight of you. (p. 577) “Scattering the waters on their course.” “For when you will, you make every channel of water vanish.” “The abyss uttered its voice, the height of its apparition.” Then indeed the abyss too will let out a kind of voice in proportion to its own greatness, shaken by your nod. “The sun was lifted up, and the moon [?] will stand in its order.” Since he speaks elsewhere of the sun setting for those in distress, here he means this: “For those whom you establish in prosperity, the sun and the moon will appear bright, as is their own nature.” “Your darts will go into the light.” “You will bring blows on the adversaries openly and with great splendor.” “Into the brightness of the lightning of your weapons.” “Your weapons will flash like lightning.” By this he means: “your strength against the enemies.” “In your threat you will diminish the earth, and in wrath you will bring down nations.” “When you are angry you utterly destroy the whole earth, together with its inhabitants, by a mere sentence.” Verses 13–16. “You went out for the salvation of your people, to save your anointed ones.” “For you do everything for the salvation of your own people, whom you have chosen.” Here he calls the chosen “anointed,” not those who have actually been anointed. So blessed David, speaking of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, says, “Do not touch my anointed ones, and do my prophets no harm.” He calls them anointed not because they had been anointed but because they had been chosen. (p. 578) “You cast death on the heads of the lawless.” “For this reason you will surround the adversaries with death.” “You raised bonds up to the neck, to the end.” “And you will make them defeated and bound.” “In amazement you cut through the heads of the mighty.” “Those who formerly held power you cut down so

violently by your wrath that it became a wonder to all.” “They will be shaken in it.” That is, shaken by punishment. “They will open their bridles like a poor man eating in secret.” They will not dare to open their mouths and speak boldly. Instead, like a poor man who has stolen something and eats it secretly so as not to be caught, they will speak with great fear. “And you set your horses on the sea, troubling many waters.” “You let the invisible powers loose on the multitude of the enemies, and they caused them the greatest confusion.” “I kept watch, and my heart was terrified at the sound of the prayer of my lips; trembling entered my bones, and my frame was shaken beneath me.” “So often, in the face of the evils being done, I chose to keep quiet and turned to prayer. And when I received from this a revelation about what was to come, my mind was gripped with fear and trembling seized me through and through.” (p. 579) “I will rest in the day of affliction, to go up to the people of my sojourning.” “For I marveled when I learned of a thing beyond belief that your power would bring about: that after so great an affliction and so many evils, in which I was tested through the captivity, I will be at rest and set free from the terrors. And indeed I will go up to the place of our sojourning together with my own people.” Verses 17–19. “For the fig tree will not bear fruit, and there will be no produce on the vines; the yield of the olive will fail, and the fields will produce no food; the sheep have failed for lack of food, and there are no oxen at the mangers.” “For I saw,” he says, “that the wrath against the adversaries was also fearsome. Because of it they were not only afflicted by the evils that came from their enemies, but they were also gripped by total barrenness and could gather no fruit, either from crops or from trees. And on top of this they will lose all their livestock through lack of pasture and fodder.” “But I will exult in the Lord; I will rejoice in God my Savior.” “Such will be their lot, but for us, by your help, there will be gladness and salvation.” In saying “But I,” he speaks in his own person about the people as a whole, which the prophets often do. (p. 580) Blessed David too is clearly seen to make petitions in his own person, as when he says, “In you, Lord, I have hoped; let me never be put to shame,” and, “Lord, hear my prayer, and let my cry come to you.” He says these things on behalf of the whole community of those in captivity, so that each of them might fittingly use these words. In the same way the prophet now says these things as if on behalf of the community, since he is speaking of what will come to the community. “The Lord God is my strength. He will make my feet like a deer's, and he sets me on the heights, so that I may conquer in his song.” “For he is the one who grants me strength in all things. He will bring us out of captivity with great speed, like deer

making a swift departure from there. And he will make us higher than all, so that from then on nothing else befits us but to be occupied with the songs and hymns owed to God, because he has given us victory over our enemies beyond all human hope.”

COMMENTARY ON THE PROPHET ZEPHANIAH. Blessed Zephaniah delivered this prophecy not long after blessed Habakkuk. He prophesies these things in the reign of Josiah king of Judah, as the book shows. A short time after Josiah, (p. 581) the Babylonians came against Jerusalem. They inflicted a great many sufferings on the tribe of Judah, killing many and carrying off very many as captives, and they sacked Jerusalem itself. They burned the divine temple with fire, together with all the finest buildings of the city. They also tore down its wall completely, so that the inhabitants could have no security at all, even if any of them wanted it. This, then, is the customary preface to the book.

Verses 1–3. “The word of the Lord that came to Zephaniah son of Cushi, son of Gedaliah, son of Amariah, son of Hezekiah, in the days of Josiah son of Amon, king of Judah.” In these words he has shown who the prophet is, from whom he is descended, and at what time he delivers his prophecy. He begins his prediction of what was to come in this way: “Let all things utterly fail from the face of the earth, says the Lord.” The ten tribes had been taken captive entirely, and the Assyrians who had conquered them also came against Jerusalem, intending to take it as well. But when they received that terrible blow through the angel, the rest, as many as had escaped the angel's punishment, fled in great fear, and from then on Jerusalem enjoyed deep peace. Yet the tribe of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem were not brought to their senses by the greatness of the Assyrians' punishment, nor frightened by the captivity of the ten tribes. These too persisted [?] in lawlessness and impiety no less than the others. So he necessarily began by saying that the rest of the people too must perish: they would be removed from the land of promise and carried off into captivity, since they too had persisted and were seen to be no less impious than the others. (p. 582) And he rightly makes the announcement in the form of a decree, as if to show that they had made themselves deserving of these things

by what they did. This is why God was led to pronounce such things about them. Then, after saying in general, “Let all things fail,” he goes on to the particulars: “Let man fail, and let the beasts fail, the birds of the sky and the fish of the sea. The ungodly will grow weak, and I will remove the lawless from the face of the earth, says the Lord.” He added the birds and the fish to the people and the beasts by way of hyperbole. Or else he speaks figuratively, as he usually does, so that by the birds he means those who are lifted above the rest by their power, and by the fish he means those among the common people who creep along in great lowliness. And he adds the cause: “The ungodly will grow weak, and I will remove the lawless from the face of the earth, says the Lord.” (p. 583) For those who live in ungodliness and lawlessness will come to utter weakness when they fall into the hands of the enemy. The rest will be taken captive and removed from the land that they received from me and held while committing great lawlessness. Verses 4–6. Then he makes clearer whom he is speaking about: “And I will stretch out my hand against Judah and against all who live in Jerusalem.” Having said that he will bring the punishment on both the tribe and the city, he necessarily also states the causes of so great a punishment: “And I will remove from this place the names of the Baals, and the names of the sacred things together with the priests, and those who worship the host of heaven on the housetops, and those who swear by the Lord and those who swear by Malcam, and those who turn aside from the Lord, and those who do not seek the Lord, and those who do not hold fast to the Lord.” “For I will remove them completely from this place, some by slaughter and others by captivity. Together with them I will wipe out all the idols and their worship, along with those who appear to serve as their priests, and in addition all those who have been eager to worship the lights of heaven on the housetops. These especially will receive a just punishment. They live around my temple yet are not ashamed to busy themselves with the worship of idols. (p. 584) At times they make a show of caring for my worship, when they see fit to swear by me, and at other times they swear by the idols.” By Malcam he means the idol, so that, as he usually does, he refers to all the idols by naming one. Now, I know that I have passed over many fables told by those who gape after the Syrians, so as not to seem to fill divine Scripture with nonsense. But I thought this was the right moment to mention the matter, to refute either what they say improperly here or the other things they say, which I passed over for the reason I have given. They claim that by Malcam he means “the king” here. Since the king is called Malcam in the language of the Syrians and the Hebrews, they say, the translators made a mistake and put Malcam, which is the idol, instead of “the king.” Before anything else they ought to have noticed this: the words of divine Scripture were spoken in the Hebrew language. They were translated into the language of the Syrians by someone or other, for to this day no one knows who he was. But they were rendered into the language of the Greeks by seventy elders of the people, who were experts

in their own language and also experts in the divine Scriptures. They had been approved by the priest and by all the people of Israel (p. 585) as the most qualified of all for the translation. The blessed apostles too clearly accepted their translation and edition. To those from the nations who came to believe, who had previously paid no attention at all to the things of the Old Testament, the apostles handed down the divine Scriptures in the Greek language according to the translation of the Seventy. And all of us from the nations who have believed in Christ the Master have received them from the apostles and now have them, reading them in the churches and keeping them at home. How then is it not senseless to think that the Seventy erred over a word? There were so many of them, they were men of such quality, and they had been so thoroughly approved. Before any translation they certainly knew what stood in divine Scripture, and whether it says “king” or “idol.” Is one obscure person, who, as they say, rendered the Hebrew into the Syriac tongue, to be thought more trustworthy than all of them? Besides, this too is clear: in these words God, through the prophet, accuses them because of their worship of idols. Since they did such things while living near the divine temple, he reproaches them for appearing to worship the God of the temple, that is, the Lord of all, while not refraining from the worship of idols. Blessed Amos the prophet also mentions this idol (p. 586) as one worshiped by the Ammonites. He says, “And Malcam will go into captivity, his priests and their rulers together, says the Lord.” In saying this he states what the prophets are often seen to say: that the punishment brought in wrath on foreign nations extended even to their idols and to those who served them as priests. It is clear that the Israelites took all their idol worship from the demons worshiped among the Greeks, as blessed David says: “They mingled among the nations and learned their works, and served their carved images.” He shows that they embraced the idolatry of those nations. So it appears that in the same way they also practiced the worship of the idol called Malcam. Verses 6–7 [?]. The prophet, however, continues what he has said as follows: “And those who turn aside from the Lord, and those who do not seek the Lord, and those who do not hold fast to the Lord.” He means: “By these things they show that they are completely estranged from my goodwill and unwilling to take any account of me or of what pleases me. For clearly, if they had truly held fast to the knowledge of me, they would never have turned their attention to idols.” Having stated the just causes of the punishment, he continues: “Be reverent before the Lord God, (p. 587) for the day of the Lord is near. For the Lord has prepared his sacrifice; he has consecrated his invited guests

[?] “But since you have been careless toward God, now at least, under sheer compulsion, you will fear the Lord of all, when he brings upon you a punishment worthy of your offenses. That time is not far off; it is very near indeed, the time when he will hand you over as a sacrifice to the enemies, whom he has set apart by his own command and called for this purpose.” This is the meaning of “He has sanctified his guests”: he has set apart those called to this sacrifice. By them he means the enemies, who will slaughter you. “And on the day of the Lord's sacrifice I will take vengeance on the rulers and on the house of the king, and on all who are clothed in foreign garments. And on that day I will openly take vengeance on all at the gateways, on those who fill the house of their God with ungodliness and deceit.” At that time I will punish those who appear to rule among you, and I will wipe out the king's house entirely, since the man who then appears to reign over you is about to be led away into captivity. And I will punish, once and for all, everyone who has given himself over [?] so completely to imitating the Greeks that they even covet the use of clothing that the law forbids but that suits the gentiles. “I will punish them all,” he says, “in full view before the doors of the temple. They acted impiously against it. They entered it as if to worship me, but dared to come in with hypocrisy and deceit, since they were unwilling to take any account of piety and devoted themselves eagerly to idols.” Verses 10–11. “And on that day, says the Lord, there will be the sound of a cry from the gate of those who pierce, and wailing from the second quarter, and a great crushing from the hills.” Then a fearful sound will arise. It will begin from the gate, as the enemies enter and carry out great slaughter.
