That sound will be followed by the unbearable wailing of those who are being crushed and are perishing in various ways from house to house. It will also come from those who run to higher places in the hope of escape (this is what “hills” means). Not only will they gain nothing there; they will even receive the utmost punishment. Accordingly he adds: “Lament, you who inhabit the city that has been cut down.” “Here,” he says, “it is right for all who live in Jerusalem to lament.” The enemies will cut the city down in various ways through its inhabitants, cutting through its buildings and slaughtering the people who live in it. “For all the people have become like Canaan; all who were exalted by silver have been utterly destroyed.” Since they imitated the ways of the Canaanites, they received a punishment like theirs and perished utterly, just as the Canaanites perished when God handed the land over to the Israelites. Along with the rest, those who are proud of their wealth and think much of themselves will also be wiped out. They will gain nothing from their prosperity. On the contrary, once stripped of their possessions, they will be like the utterly destitute. (51) Manuscript: ἐκδίκησιν.

Verses 12–16. “And on that day I will search Jerusalem with a lamp.” People who look for things in the innermost parts, things wrapped in darkness, are accustomed to use a lamp so that they can search out hidden things more carefully. So he means that everything in Jerusalem will be searched out with great care, so that nothing inside escapes the enemies. To this [variant: “to which”] he fittingly added, “All who were exalted by silver have been utterly destroyed,” to show that all the possessions of the wealthy will be taken away in this way, since no one will be able to escape the enemies' search. “And I will take vengeance on the men who are contemptuous of their charges, who say in their hearts, ‘The Lord will not do good, nor will he do harm.’” “I will punish those,” he says, “who utterly despised my commands and my worship.” By these they could have been guarded and kept safe from every harm. Yet they were convinced that no evil could be brought upon them, even though they broke the law so badly. The words “The Lord will not do good” are to be read with an expressive intonation, in the sense of “He will do good.” “And their strength will become plunder, and their houses a desolation. They will build houses and not live in them, and they will plant vineyards and not drink their wine, for the great day of the Lord is near, near and very swift.” All their strength will be stripped away by the enemies, and all their houses will be destroyed. They will not enjoy the houses they built with great care, nor will they gather the fruit of their own farming. For the day of God is at hand and very near, the day on which everything God has pronounced against them will come to pass. “The sound of the day of the Lord is appointed bitter and harsh.” The time of the divine sentence has been announced, and it is full of great bitterness and harshness. “A mighty day of wrath.” The anger of that day is exceedingly strong. “That day is a day of affliction and distress, a day of untimely death and destruction, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and mist, a day of trumpet and outcry against the fortified cities and against the lofty corners.” Verses 17–18. At that time there will be great distress and affliction, and untimely deaths of those slaughtered in infancy. There will also be a great destruction of people, so that everyone seems wrapped in darkness and gloom, or in cloud and mist. The trumpet of war, and the shout of the enemies with it, will sound very loudly and announce the demolition of the strong cities and the greatest houses. “And I will afflict the people, and they will walk like the blind, because they have sinned against the Lord. And I will pour out their blood like dust, and their flesh like dung.” Their affliction will be so extreme that they will be no different from the blind, unable to see even what lies before their feet. To put it briefly, they will suffer everything, since they were exceedingly impious toward God. For this, blood will be shed as in a great slaughter. And since those who are killed will remain unburied, the flesh of the dead will be strewn like dung over every [?] LXVI.

place. “Their silver and their gold will not be able to deliver them on the day of the Lord's wrath, and in the fire of his jealousy the whole earth will be consumed. For he will bring an end, and a swift one, upon all who live on the earth.” The wealth they gathered unjustly will be of no benefit to them, since at that time all these things will count for less than the divine wrath. Like fire, that wrath will consume the whole earth and destroy all who live in it with great speed. Then, after announcing these evils, the prophet gives them hope, as he usually does, and adds:

Verses 1–3. “Gather together and be bound together, you undisciplined nation, before you become like a flower that passes away in a day, before the wrath of the Lord's anger comes upon you.” “All of you who until now have not received instruction in what is fitting, come together now at least and offer your common prayers to God. Otherwise, like a flower that suddenly withers, you will suffer total destruction when the divine wrath is brought upon you in full.” “Seek the Lord, all you humble of the earth.” “And you who, beyond all who live on the earth, have been humbled by the calamities brought upon you, take care to be pious and ask for God's mercy.” “Do justice and seek righteousness.” “Now become upright judges of what is fitting. Tell the better from the worse, and take care to do what is just.” “Seek meekness and give answer for these things, so that you may be sheltered on the day of the Lord's wrath.” “Choose gentleness and forbearance. In return for this, God would give proof of his care for you by punishing foreigners for the injustice they did you.” Verses 4–6. “For Gaza will be plundered, and Ashkelon will become a desolation, and Ashdod will be cast out at noon, and Ekron will be uprooted.” All the foreign tribes will receive no ordinary punishment for what they have done against you. He applies “at noon” to all of them alike, in the sense of “openly,” so that what happens escapes no one's notice. What he says about each of the cities, whether Gaza or Ashkelon or the others, he means for all of them alike. He has distributed it among them in his speech, as he usually does. He means that all the cities of the foreign tribes will be plundered and destroyed, and that they will be cast down from their prosperity and utterly destroyed. “Woe to you who inhabit the measured strip of the sea, sojourners among the Cretans! The word of the Lord is against you, Canaan, land of the foreign tribes. I will destroy you so that no one lives there, and Crete will become a pasture for flocks and a fold for sheep.” Since these cities happened to lie on the coast, he has called them “the measured strip of the sea,”

as blessed David says: “To you I will give the land of Canaan, the measured portion of your inheritance.” That is: “I will set apart the land of the Canaanites as your possession.” The image comes from those who measure and mark out land with a measuring line. So here too he says “the measured strip of the sea” for those who inhabit the coastal region. He says “sojourners among the Cretans” because some Cretans had come there to trade, as one does to coastal cities, and chose to live among them. In the same way he says in Amos, “I will cut off a tribe from the men of Charran,” speaking of people from there who were living in Damascus. So here too he speaks of “sojourners among the Cretans,” meaning the Cretans who live among them. What he means is this: “Most wretched of all are all of you who inhabit the coastal region, together with the Cretans living among you. For God has pronounced against all of you foreign tribes who inhabit Canaan that he will destroy you utterly. And the land where the Cretans live among you he will make so desolate that it becomes a pasture for flocks and a dwelling for sheep.” Verse 7. “And the measured strip of the sea will belong to the remnant of the house of Judah. They will pasture on them. In the houses of Ashkelon they will lodge at evening, before the face of the sons of Judah, because the Lord their God has visited them and turned back their captivity.” “Those of the tribe of Judah who are saved,” he says, “will occupy the whole coastal region and possess all of it as their own land.” The people of Ashkelon will then live in their own homes in great fear, suspicious of the strength of the sons of Judah. By this one city he means all the cities of the foreign tribes, since he usually names the whole by a part. This is what “they will lodge at evening” means. Since he took “at noon” to mean “openly,” he took “at evening” to mean fear. People in hiding avoid the daytime and usually slip away toward evening in the hope of escaping notice. “These things will happen,” he says, “when God visits the tribe of Judah, frees them from captivity and brings them back home with his help.” Verses 8–10. Then he moves his discourse from the foreign tribes to others: “I have heard the reproaches of Moab and the blows of the sons of Ammon, with which they reproached my people and boasted against their borders. Therefore, as I live, says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, Moab will be like Sodom, and the sons of Ammon like Gomorrah.” “I saw what the Moabites and Ammonites did to my people. They reproached them, saying they gained nothing from worshiping me, and they did them every harm in their power. They even laid hands on my borders with extreme arrogance, as if those borders were now bound to belong to them. For this they will share the desolation of Sodom and Gomorrah.” “And Damascus will be left like a heap on a threshing floor and destroyed forever. And the [?] Amos 1:5.

remnant of my people will plunder them, and the remnant of my nation will inherit them.” “And Damascus too,” he says, “will vanish, as a heap crushed on a threshing floor vanishes. It will be brought down from the greatest bulk and great arrogance to the deepest humiliation. Then those of my people who are left and are granted their return will plunder them all and take their possessions for their own.” “This will be theirs in return for their insolence, because they reproached the people of the Lord Almighty and boasted against them.” “They will suffer these things,” he says, “for what they dared against God. They insulted and reproached my people and exulted over them because of me, as if they were in the depths of calamity.” Verses 11–12. “The Lord will appear against them, and he will utterly destroy all the gods of the nations of the earth. And they will worship him, each from his own place, all the islands of the nations.” So God will make his vengeance plain for all to see. He will destroy all the foreigners together with the gods they worship. And all people everywhere else, whether in cities or on islands, will be struck with great amazement at what God does. They will offer him common worship, each in his own place, confessing the surpassing greatness of his power. “And you, Ethiopians, are slain by my sword.” “You too will be punished with the sword, through my people, for the wrongs you did them.” Here too by “Ethiopians” he means those who live near Egypt. He says these things in the manner of the blessed prophet Amos. When Amos spoke of what would happen to Israel and to Jerusalem, he also mentioned what the foreigners would suffer: I mean the Damascenes and Tyrians, the Idumaeans and Ammonites, and all the others he names. In the same way blessed Zephaniah, when he speaks here of what would happen to Jerusalem at the hands of the Babylonians, also mentions what was going to happen to the foreigners at that time. Therefore, after what has been said, he turns his discourse to the Assyrians and to Nineveh. For at that time the Babylonians overthrew the empire of the Assyrians. They sacked its royal city, I mean Nineveh, and left it utterly desolate. So he adds: Verses 13–15. “And he will stretch out his hand against [?] (55) Manuscript: ξίφη [“swords”].

and wild beasts to live there, along with all the other animals that usually make their lairs in the most desolate places. It will pay this just penalty for thinking itself so far above all other cities, as if it surpassed them all like a cedar compared with other plants. “This is the contemptuous city that dwells in hope, that says in her heart, ‘I am, and there is no other after me.’” Clearly, by the city he means the attitude of its inhabitants, since he does not say these things about lifeless stones. “This,” he says, “is the contemptuous one.” That is, she disparages everything, considers everyone else nothing compared with herself, and supposes herself sufficient for everything. This is what “dwelling in hope” means: she is confident that she will never suffer any harm from anyone else. “She is disposed,” he says, “as if she alone existed, as if the other cities were not even worth counting as existing beside her.” Having said this as a reproach, and having reproached her for her contempt toward all, he very aptly adds: “How has she become a desolation, a pasture for wild beasts? Everyone who passes by her will hiss and shake his hands.” “What a change you have undergone! How did you fall into desolation and become a pasture for wild beasts? Everyone who passes by hisses at you and shakes his hands, marveling at so great a change. And what do they say [?]

Verses 1–2. “O illustrious and redeemed city, the dove! She did not heed the voice, nor did she accept instruction. She did not trust in the Lord, and she did not draw near to her God.” “This,” he says, “is what they will say: How great her renown was, and how she was kept apart from all evils!” That is what “redeemed” means. How great her beauty was! This is what he means by “dove,” since this creature seems somehow delightful among birds and walks proudly. So blessed David also says: “If you lie down among the allotments, there are the wings of a dove covered with silver, and her back with the pale sheen of gold.” Through the comparison with the dove he says that the Israelites, once they received the promised land, would appear more delightful than all others. So here too he meant “beautiful” or “charming,” just as blessed Nahum says when he reproaches her: “A fair and graceful harlot.” “Though she was such a city,” he says, “she did not listen to the voice of the prophet sent to her to the end, nor did she fully accept his teaching. She seemed to change for a little while, but then ran back to her own wickedness. She took no account of the God who had sent the prophet, nor did she think fit to devote herself to him afterwards, even though she had experienced such things.” On the contrary, she abandoned him completely and set herself in war against him: after the destruction of the ten tribes she attacked Jerusalem, where God's temple stood. Here again the marvelous mythmakers of the Syrians [?] Nah. 3:[?].

say that in the Syrian language the dove is called *yona*. On their view, the prophet means to call it the city of Jonah the prophet, because Jonah preached there, while the translator made a mistake and called it a dove. We have already shown at sufficient length that the Seventy were not mistaken, and that the one who translated Scripture into the Syrian language could much more fairly be thought to have made this mistake. But how did these marvelous mythmakers fail to see that he is reproaching the city when he says, “O illustrious and redeemed city, the dove”? What follows is of the same kind, like Nahum's words, “A fair and graceful harlot.” Here too, in the same way, he reproaches her for the beauty she used to pride herself on. He would never have called it the city of Jonah the prophet as a reproach, on the grounds that it had been saved through him. But these people, not having understood what was said, turned to Syriac and old wives' [?]

Verses [?]. The prophet fittingly goes on to add what follows, speaking of her former prosperity both ironically and reproachfully: “Her rulers within her are like roaring lions.” That is, so powerful and so bold toward everyone. “Her judges are like the wolves of Arabia; they left nothing until morning.” That is, they were quick to bring matters to an end, so as to settle everything the same day and leave nothing unfinished for the next. “Her prophets are spirit-bearing men, contemptuous.” “And those within her,” he says, “who claimed to prophesy uttered whatever they pleased with great arrogance.” “Her priests profane the holy things and act impiously against the law.” “And those among them who appeared to act as priests acted impiously against my law and against the temple, stirring up those who obeyed them to do the same

saying: “I have pulled down the proud in destruction; their corners have vanished. I will lay waste their roads altogether, so that no one travels on them. Their cities have failed, because there is no one there, no one living in them.” “I have handed them over to destruction because of their arrogance. I will destroy all their cities and bring everything they have to such desolation that their roads will no longer be visible, since no one will travel on them. To this desolation I will also hand over all their cities, so that no one is found living in them.” But having made clear in these

[?]… and the desolation of Nineveh and the overthrow of the Assyrian empire, he turns his discourse to the people of Judea and says: Verses 7–8. “I said: Nevertheless, fear me and receive instruction, and you will not be utterly destroyed from her eyes for all the things I have avenged upon her.” I had already testified to you beforehand through the prophets that you should hold me in fear, since I can easily punish you if you stumble, and that you should receive the teaching offered to you. And I promised that if you did these things I would not make you vanish, removed from my sight, out of the places where you were appointed to attend to my worship, nor would I go on to inflict on you the things I have now brought upon you in vengeance for the sins you have so often committed. “Get ready, rise early; all their gleaning has been ruined.” But since you neglected your duty then and have suffered such things, now at least prepare yourselves to do your duty and hold fast with all care and zeal to what I have ordained. For you have proof of my care for you in the fact that all the power of your enemies has been taken away entirely. “Therefore wait for me, says the Lord, for the day of my rising up as a witness.” So keep looking to me, and await the help from me that I will give you in due time, raising you up as though from the dead, freeing you from captivity, and bringing you all back to your own land. These are the things I promised long ago through the prophets, and promise you now, that I will give you, so that you may have the [?] of these events as a testimony to the truth of what I foretold.

Verses 8–9. “For my judgment is for the gatherings of nations, to receive kings, to pour out upon them all the wrath of my anger; for in the fire of my jealousy the whole earth will be consumed.” For then above all I will make plain the judgment that I will carry out on your behalf, bringing to punishment the nations gathered from every side. I will receive many kings and satraps advancing on Jerusalem with their own armies, that is, I will allow them to come, so as to make my care for you plain by the events themselves, and to pour out great wrath upon them and stir it all up against them. For I will consume them all as if by fire, seized by a kind of jealousy, because they dared so much against my own people. He says this with regard to Gog and his followers, who attacked them after the return, countless as they were, and whom he destroyed one and all. “For then I will turn upon the peoples a tongue for their generations, so that all may call on the name of the Lord, to serve him under one yoke.” So a common wonder will seize all people everywhere at the novelty of these events. Those who live in different places and belong to different nations will, as though using a single tongue, confess with one voice the God of the Israelites as God, and, as though all placed under one yoke, they will count servitude under him most blessed,

[?] on account of the things that you yourselves are to receive from me. “From the ends of the rivers of Ethiopia I will receive those who supplicate me; together with the dispersed they will bring me sacrifices.” So they will come from the regions of Ethiopia, hastening to my service, and together with you, who are now dispersed in captivity but by then will have returned, they will offer sacrifices to me in common. Verses 11–15. “On that day you will not be put to shame for all your practices by which you acted impiously against me, for then I will take away from you the contemptuous deeds of your insolence, and you will no longer go on boasting on my holy mountain.” At that time you will endure none of the things for which, suffering now on account of your impieties, you have been clothed with the deepest shame. For all that you have done in contempt of what is mine, when through your worship of idols you became the cause of every kind of insult to me, I will remove from all of you, and with it I will take away the punishments brought upon you for these things. So you will no longer live with such arrogance on the mountain set apart for my worship, neglecting what is mine and offering all your worship to idols. “And I will leave in you a meek and humble people.” For I will bring you back from captivity disciplined, so that you will live in meekness and humility and treat what is mine with reverence. Hence he adds: “And the remnant of Israel will revere the name of the Lord, and they will do no injustice and speak no vain things, and no deceitful tongue will be found in their mouth; for they will graze, and there will be no one to frighten them.” For you who have returned from captivity will go on holding my name in fear, abstaining from all injustice and keeping clean of the abominations you once pursued. And then you will guard against pretending with a deceitful mind to worship me while devoting yourselves to idols. As a result you will also be able to graze in full security and enjoy what is your own, and live in complete rest, since no one will be able to disturb you or remove you from your own places. Having promised that these things would come to them as a result of the return, he then adds: “Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; proclaim it, daughter of Jerusalem; be glad and delight with all your heart, daughter of Jerusalem. The Lord has taken away your iniquities; the Lord has redeemed you from the hand of your enemies. The Lord reigns in your midst; you will see evil no more.” From now on, O Jerusalem, live in every kind of pleasure, spending your days in perfect gladness and delight. For God, having taken away all your transgressions, has necessarily also removed you from the dominion of the enemies under whom you had fallen as you paid the penalty of punishment. And from now on the Lord will be in you, showing his own kingship through his care for you, so that no evil will be able to come near you any more. Verses 16–20. “At that time the Lord will say to Jerusalem: Take courage, Zion, let your hands not grow slack. The Lord your God is in you; the Mighty One will save you. He will bring gladness upon you and renew you in his love, and he will rejoice over you with delight as on a feast day, and he will gather those who are

broken.” Then God will free Jerusalem from all faintness, himself preserving her by his own power, and, establishing her in great gladness, he will renew his love for you. For the sake of your salvation he will do and display things like those he once displayed when he brought you out of Egypt with many signs and wonders. So now too he will free you, who have been broken by captivity, from the evils that hold you, and give you back your own land again. “Woe! Who has taken up a reproach against her? Behold, I am acting in you for my own sake, says the Lord.” But most pitiable are those who have sinned against her, for upon them God will display his own power on your behalf, so that you will be renowned among all people for what has happened for your sake. “At that time I will save her who has been oppressed, and I will receive her who has been driven out.” For I will punish those people, but I will preserve those who have been crushed under such great evils, and I will bring back again to their own land those who were driven out of it. “And I will make them a boast and renowned in all the earth,” so that, because of what I do for them, they will be marveled at and praised among people. “And they will be put to shame at that time, when I do good to you, and at the time when I receive you.” For your enemies will be clothed with every kind of shame when I do the finest things for you and bring you back to your own land. “For I will make you renowned and a boast among all the remaining peoples of the earth, when I turn back your captivity before your eyes, says the Lord.” For I will do such great and so many things concerning you and on your behalf against your enemies that all people everywhere will remember you and marvel, with words of praise, at the way in which I freed you from such a captivity and brought you back to your own land.

[?] OF THE PROPHET. The blessed prophets Hosea, Joel, Amos and Micah addressed their discourse to the whole Israelite people in common: to those of the ten tribes over whom Samaria ruled, and also to those of the tribe of Judah who lived in Jerusalem, to both alike. They reproved them for the impieties and

transgressions that they committed in various ways, and added the evils that would befall them for these things if they went on sinning without repentance: those that befell the ten tribes first at the hands of the Assyrians, and those that later came upon the tribe of Judah at the hands of the Babylonians. To these predictions they also joined the change of their fortunes for the better, namely that, released from captivity, they would go back again to their own land. The blessed Obadiah spoke of the punishment that would be brought upon the Idumeans at the time of the return. The blessed Jonah threatened the Ninevites with destruction unless they turned from their wickedness. The blessed Nahum clearly announced the siege of Nineveh and the overthrow of the whole Assyrian kingdom, which they were plainly going to suffer at the hands of the Babylonians. The blessed prophets Habakkuk and Zephaniah, when the ten tribes had already been ravaged by the Assyrians and had undergone complete captivity and removal from their own places, reprove only those of the tribe of Judah and those living in Jerusalem for their impieties and transgressions. They foretell the punishment that God would bring upon them for these things through the Babylonians, not as something that would come after a long time, but as though all the evils announced were about to come upon them at once, immediately; and the prophet Zephaniah indicates that the fulfillment of what was to come would be nearer still. But the blessed prophet Haggai, whose explanation we now propose, by God's grace, to undertake, does not prophesy merely after the captivity that the Babylonians brought upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem had already taken place. Rather, when the Israelites had already been freed from captivity and had returned again to their own land, beyond all human hope, by divine grace, he addresses his words to them. He reproves those who had returned and were living in their own land, having so unexpectedly received such great grace, for their sloth concerning the building of the temple. It is clear that God did not have great concern for its building for his own sake, as he himself says of himself: “Heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool of my feet. What kind of house will you build for me, says the Lord, or what is the place of my rest?” And even this is a small thing, if one considers these words in relation to the greatness of the divine nature, which plainly surpasses all that exists, beyond anything anyone could say or conceive. But it is for the sake of the Israelites themselves that he who cares for human souls makes so much of the building of the temple. For he had ordained that they should assemble in that place and in that temple and render him the worship due to him in accordance with the precepts of the law, and through all these things he wished the people to be held fast in piety, so that from there, fittingly and in due time, the Lord Christ according to the flesh might appear, as was needed for the salvation of all. Therefore he necessarily took care for the construction of the temple, so that the people, through

their assembly in it, might be improved, since, as I said, they were being granted such great and abundant care for the sake of all humankind. For just as God tolerates sacrifices and other such things, though he himself needs none of them at all, on account of our need, so too he concerned himself with the temple, not for his own sake but for the sake of those whom it was fitting to assemble there and render to God the worship due to him on behalf of all people, as I said before. The book also contains a certain announcement of things to come, I mean the events concerning Gog, which one would see better from the text itself. But this is the aim of the book. From here on we must attend to the details.

Verses 1–2. “In the second year under King Darius, in the sixth month, on the first day of the month, the word of the Lord came by the hand of Haggai the prophet, saying.” In the second year of Darius, who reigned over the Persians as the fourth after Cyrus (the first to reign over the Medes and Persians together), when those of the tribe of Judah, and the rest who were eager to go back up with them, had already returned to their own land and had recovered Jerusalem as their dwelling, he says that the blessed prophet Haggai was granted a divine revelation, so that he might address appropriate words to the Jews who had returned, and above all reprove them for neglecting the building of the temple, which those returned from captivity ought above all to have raised with great eagerness. He also notes the month and the day on which the prophet, by divine revelation, delivered his words to the Jews, so as to show in due order how matters went for them while they neglected the building of the temple, and how great a change for the better they experienced when they began to show proper concern for building the temple. What the prophet was commanded by God to say to them he tells next: “Speak to Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, of the tribe of Judah, and to Joshua son of Jozadak, the high priest, saying: Thus says the Lord Almighty: This people says, The time has not come to build the house of the Lord.” For he commands him to say these things, which needed to be taught in reproof of the people's sloth concerning the temple, to Zerubbabel, who, being of the tribe of Judah and descended from the blessed David according to the divine promises, was then ruling the people, and also to Joshua son of Jozadak, who, being descended from Aaron by line of descent according to the Mosaic ordinance, had been entrusted with carrying out the office of the high priesthood. These things were naturally said above all to them as leaders, since it was their duty to rouse the rest to the task. Yet in his words he evidently blames not them but the people, which makes it clear that they had the proper eagerness for the matter but were unable to carry out what they wished, because the people would not cooperate with them in it. That is why he says to them what serves to reprove the people, so that these men might be roused all the more to the work, and the people might receive

the correction they needed, so as to carry out with all eagerness whatever contributed to the building of the temple, and to obey their leaders with great readiness in whatever they commanded them about it, since they gave their commands in accordance with the divine will. Verses 3–5. Turning then to the reproof of the

[?] the time for building has not come? Are you not ashamed to look on while what is the cause of all your salvation lies in such desolation, so that your own houses have been built and, moreover, adorned with very great care, while the site of the temple is still given over to desolation, and none of you has chosen to do anything at all toward building it? “And now thus says the Lord Almighty: Set your hearts on your ways.” Consider, he says, your situation, and examine what you have done in neglecting the divine temple, and what has come of it for you. For it is clear that by “their ways” he means their actions, as he usually does. Verses 6–8. Then he says: “You sowed much and brought in little; you ate, but not to the full; you drank, but not to drunkenness; you clothed yourselves, but were not warmed by your clothes; and he who gathered wages gathered them into a bag with holes.” Consider in what great want and scarcity of necessities you found yourselves because of that sloth: from much seed you gathered little fruit, and you did not have enough food, drink or clothing to satisfy your pressing need, since all necessities were scarce for you. And so, as was to be expected, the rents you collected, by leasing out fields and from other such arrangements, came to nothing; for since the crops were perishing, it was impossible for those who held the leases to pay you the rents. Just as it is impossible to collect money in a purse or a rag or any bundle at all if it has holes, because the money falls through and is completely lost, so too with the loss of the crops your rents were necessarily lost as well. “Thus says the Lord Almighty: Set your hearts on your ways. Go up to the mountain, cut timber, bring it, and build the house, and I will take pleasure in it and be glorified, said the Lord.” Now that you have considered these things, correct what you are now neglecting and take care for the building of the temple: cut timber, and bring in the other materials

needed for the building with great eagerness. And I, for my part, pleased with the building of the temple carried out by you, will do such things for your benefit as will make me known to all as able to bestow the greatest benefits on those willing to obey me with goodwill. Verses 9–11. Then, again reminding them of what they had suffered before because of their sloth, he says: “You looked for much, and it came to little; and it was brought into the house, and I blew it away,” as if to say: I was not allowing the land to give you its fruits, and what seemed to be produced I was destroying. And he goes on to add: “Therefore thus says the Lord Almighty: Because my house lies desolate, while each of you runs to his own house, therefore the heaven will withhold its dew, and the earth will withhold its produce from you; and I will bring a sword upon the land, upon the mountains, upon the grain, upon the wine, upon the oil, upon all that the land brings forth, upon people, upon cattle, and upon all the labors of their hands.” By these words he wants to remind them of what they had suffered while neglecting the temple. When, he says, you looked on while my house lay desolate and were busy building your own houses, then, he says, the rain was held back, and the earth did not give its fruit, and I destroyed all the fruits of the earth as though with a sword, often striking both people and cattle, and, in short, destroying everything you labored for. He added this after urging them to go up, cut timber, bring it, and take care of the building, frightening them with the memory of what had happened so that they would not receive the command sluggishly. So he adds: Verses 12–14. “Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, of the tribe of Judah, and Joshua son of Jozadak, the high priest, and all the remnant of the people heard the voice of the Lord their God and the words of Haggai the prophet, as the Lord their God had sent him to them; and the people feared before the Lord.” This shows that the words spoken to them had not been in vain: all of them, fearing the threat contained in what was said, turned to what they ought to do, so that the prophet, sent by God, said to them, “I am with you, says the Lord.” This was to show that as soon as they changed their ways and became zealous for building the temple, God at once promised to give them his care in all things. For this is what “I am with you, says the Lord” signifies; it means “being with you, caring for you, and supplying all your needs.” “And the Lord stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, of the tribe of Judah, and the spirit of Joshua son of Jozadak, the high priest, and the spirit of the remnant of all the people; and they went in and did work on the house of the Lord Almighty, their God.” For not only did he himself promise his own care,

God, but at the same time he also strengthened the zeal of both the leaders and all the people, so that they set everything else aside and devoted themselves to building the temple and to seeing how the work might be brought to completion. Then, strengthening their zeal still further, God appears again to the prophet and says this:

Verses 1–5. — “Speak now to Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, of the tribe of Judah, and to Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest, and to all the remnant of the people, saying: Who among you saw this house in its former glory? And how do you see it now? Is it not as though it were not there before you? And now be strong, Zerubbabel, says the Lord; and be strong, Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest; and let all the people of the land be strong, says the Lord Almighty; and my Spirit stands in your midst.” For if any of you, he says, knew the ancient glory of this house, and the kind of things I often did for it, or for the people because of the zeal shown in it, you would have realized how great the change is between then and now. For now most of you, who do not know those things but see the present state, look at it as though it did not exist, because of the desolation that holds it. But persevere in your zeal for the building, and carry everything out with fitting diligence until the temple is finished. For then you will perceive my care, and as you fulfil the duties owed to God in the temple, you will obtain [?] from then on. And I will be among you, he says, shown through the events themselves, and you will obtain the grace that comes from me, all but standing over you, managing and governing your affairs. For by “my Spirit” he means the grace that comes from him. Those of the Old Testament did not know that the Holy Spirit has his own hypostasis, recognized as a person in his own right alongside God. (p. 420) For all who lived before the coming of Christ the Lord knew God and creation, and nothing else besides, and divine Scripture taught its own people this in that age. In the invisible creation it recognized nothing unique, but called all the invisible, ministering beings by the common names of angels and powers, which, it taught, serve the divine commands in all things. So they could not know the Holy Spirit in his own hypostasis alongside God. For it was not possible to number what is unique among the ministering beings, nor to rank anything alongside God by speaking of it as a person in its own right, since they knew of nothing of the kind. But Christ the Lord taught us these things, who delivered to his own apostles: “Go and make disciples

of all the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” From this we learn of a person proper to the Father, a person proper to the Son, and a person proper to the Holy Spirit, and we hold that each of these alike belongs to the divine and eternal substance, since there is one discipleship by which they were instructed in the teaching of divine knowledge, and one baptism performed in the name of these. But the [?Old Testament], as I said, did not know the Holy Spirit as having his own person and his own hypostasis, distinct from God. Rather, it called God's grace “Holy Spirit” or “Spirit of God”, or else his oversight, or his care, or his disposition toward something, or anything of that sort. (p. 421) “Where shall I go from your Spirit? And from your presence where shall I flee?” He means that it is impossible to be outside your oversight, since you are present to all. At any rate he goes on to address God, no longer mentioning the Spirit: “If I ascend into heaven, you are there,” meaning: wherever I may be, I stand under your authority, by which, being present to all as you will, you govern my affairs. “Your good Spirit will lead me on level ground,” meaning: you who have always governed my affairs with goodness will by that same goodness bring me back now too. “Do not take your Holy Spirit from me,” meaning: do not take away from me your special and chosen care. So also here he says, “And my Spirit stands in your midst,” meaning: my grace and my disposition toward you will be with you, standing over you and providing you with its benefit. For just as he speaks of God's “soul”, naming in this way not some hypostasis but his disposition toward something (as when he says, “My soul hates your new moons and your sabbaths,” meaning the disposition by which he hated what they did, since they were wicked in their ways), so too he speaks of the Spirit. But let this much be said for the sake of greater precision. Verses 6–10. — In what preceded, God had sufficiently roused the people through the prophet to the work of building and made them more eager. (p. 422) But he saw them reckoning where they might find so much while still impoverished from the captivity, enough to complete the temple properly and to restore to it all its fitting beauty, such as it had before in its buildings, its holy vessels and everything else. So he adds: “Take courage, do not be afraid.” Do not be afraid, he says, about these things and how it can be done. “For thus says the Lord Almighty: Once more I will shake the heaven and the earth and the sea and the dry land; and I will shake all the nations together; and the choice treasures of all the nations will come; and I will fill this house with glory, says the Lord Almighty. For great will be the glory of this house, the latter more than the former, says the Lord Almighty; and in this place I will give peace, says the Lord Almighty,

and peace of soul as a possession for everyone who builds, to raise up this temple.” Do not worry about the scarcity of what you need, he says. For, all but shaking all the nations together, I will let them come against you, many as they are and full of great wealth. He means Gog and his hosts. When they have come, he says, I will then make the greatness of the glory of this house plain through my care. For the silver they have, (p. 423) and the gold, and in short everything they have, is mine, since all things are mine, as the whole of creation is my work. These I will take away and transfer to you. In doing so I wrong no one who holds them, since they held what was not theirs; I am rightly giving what is mine to my own. So the glory then displayed concerning this house through what I accomplish, as I receive your prayers in it and give you the mastery over your enemies, who are so many and of such a kind that they defeat counting by their numbers and are invincible in power and military experience, will appear to all greater than the glory once displayed concerning this house. For the deed is greater than what happened formerly against the Assyrians or certain others, because the present enemies surpass those of old not only in number but also in power and military experience. Having overcome all of them beyond all expectation by my power, you will live in complete peace, remaining untroubled in your souls because you are rid of every enemy. And having gathered as many spoils as possible from the enemies' possessions and acquired them for yourselves, you will readily have, if you wish, the means to furnish and raise up this temple, so that it may have its proper beauty, for the sake of the prayer and worship of those who assemble in it. Verses 11–15. — (p. 424) Through all the foregoing he had sufficiently urged and spurred them on to the work of building, and had also made them hopeful through the promises that they would share in great abundance once they had conquered their enemies, so that they would have everything in plenty both for building the temple and for whatever else they wished. From then on he thought it good to bring them correction in other matters too, in which they were sinning. He speaks as follows: “On the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, in the second year of Darius, the word of the Lord came to Haggai the prophet, saying: Thus says the Lord Almighty: Ask the priests about the law, saying: If a man carries holy meat in the fold of his garment, and the fold of his garment touches bread or stew or wine or oil or any food, will it be made holy? And the priests answered and said, No. And Haggai said: If someone defiled by a dead body touches any of these, will it be defiled? And the priests answered and said, It will be defiled. And Haggai answered and said: So is this people, and so is this nation before me, says the Lord; and so are all the works of their hands; and whoever approaches there will be defiled.”

He wants to rebuke them for handling the priestly vessels and everything else that belongs to the worship of God carelessly and casually, and not with fitting fear. (p. 425) That is why he ordered the prophet to put this question to the priests, since it lay with them to do such things either carelessly or with fitting fear. And he very aptly framed the question from trivial things, in order to make the offence concerning the [?holy] vessels appear all the greater. So he says: if someone puts holy meat, that is, meat consecrated from some sacrifice or offering, into some part of his own garment, and then this fold touches some other wine or oil or any food whatever, will that thing become holy through the touch of the fold of the garment in which the meat lay? And they consistently said that such a thing does not become holy, since the fold of the garment is not able, merely because holy meat lies in it, to impart holiness to another food. Then he asks again: if someone who is defiled for any reason touches such things, does he certainly defile them or not? And they said that he does defile them. Through these questions he meant to say: just as the fold of the garment cannot sanctify what comes near it on account of the holy thing lying in it, whereas a defiled person who touches such things certainly defiles them, so you too must realize, when you handle the priestly vessels, or whatever belongs to God in any way, casually (p. 426) and without fitting reverence, that their holiness does not sanctify you; rather your way of life, being defiled, heaps insult on the holy things, if indeed you touch them improperly [?]. Hence the prophet also gives the answer as though God were saying: Such indeed is what you do whenever you touch any of the holy things that belong to me. So you should know that everyone who approaches me (for by approaching me I mean touching what belongs and is dedicated to me), if he does so casually, carelessly and contemptuously, not only gains nothing from the touch but is even defiled, being further wronged and harmed because he touched such holy things casually. “Because of their early-morning undertakings they will be in pain before their wickedness, and you hated those who reproved in the gates.” “Their undertakings” means what they undertook to do improperly. For on account of the outrageous deeds you attempted, he says, rising early for this purpose and carrying out the outrages with all zeal, you have fallen into the heavy evils that have come upon you; and all the more because you did not accept the reproof of the prophets, (p. 427) but resented them as they stood at the gates in order to offer correction by their words to all alike who went in and out. Verses 16–20. — “And now set it on your hearts, from this day and before, before stone was laid on stone in the temple of the Lord: what were you like? When you threw twenty measures into the bin, it became ten measures of barley; and when one went to the wine vat to draw out fifty measures, they became twenty. I struck you with barrenness and with

blight, and with hail all the works of your hands; and you did not turn to me, says the Lord Almighty. Set now your hearts from this day and onward, from the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, and from the day on which the temple of the Lord was founded. Consider in your hearts whether it will still be noticed on the threshing floor, and whether the vine and the fig tree and the pomegranate and the olive trees still bear no fruit. From this day I will bless.” By comparing again the former times, when they neglected the building of the temple, with the present, since they had begun to be zealous for the work, he wanted to show the difference in what had happened to them: how barren things had been while they were neglectful, and how many good things they had experienced since they began to show great eagerness in attending to the building of the temple. Consider then, he says, the time before this day, (p. 428) when you did not yet care about building the temple, and what state you were in. You said [?] that the sheaves were enough to yield twenty measures of grain, yet scarcely ten came out of them, because the crops had been ruined. Indeed, you gathered fruit from the vine enough for a yield of fifty measures, and scarcely brought in twenty, because those too had been dried up by the air. I brought upon you plagues of barrenness and blight, and I wiped out all your labours with hail; yet even in the face of these things you remained unbending. But that was before, he says. Now consider, besides those things, what has come to you from the day on which you became zealous for building the temple. For you will find that neither the produce of the threshing floor nor that of the trees can be recognized when compared with what it was then. Before, no fruit at all was given you from them; but since you became zealous for my temple, I have filled all you possess with blessing and given you abundant enjoyment of its fruits. Then, having again urged and roused them to the work by recalling the past and comparing it with what came after, since they were still uncertain because of their poverty, he encourages them again and speaks as follows: (p. 429) Verses 21–23. — “And the word of the Lord came a second time to Haggai the prophet on the twenty-fourth day of the month, saying: Speak to Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, of the tribe of Judah, saying: Once more I shake the heaven and the earth and the sea and the dry land; and I overturn the thrones of kings, and I will destroy the power of the king of the nations, and I overturn chariots and riders; and horses and their riders will go down, each by the sword of his brother.” He says the same things as before, for that is what “And the word of the Lord came a second time to Haggai” indicates. And yet in the earlier passages the prophet is seen to have received divine revelation many times and to have spoken to the people in accordance with it. But he says “a second time” because he himself now promises again the things about Gog, so that they would not disbelieve what was said because of its magnitude, but would hold their conviction without doubt, since God had promised the same things not only once

but a second time as well. For he says to him: All but shaking everything together, I will overthrow many kings adorned with royal thrones, wiping out all their power and overturning their chariots along with those who ride in them, so that they fall upon one another, (p. 430) and both the horses and those mounted on them become one another's slaughterers, and great carnage is wrought as they are destroyed by one another. This I will do so that it may be clear from everything that the rout in the war and the victory are not the work of your hand, but that the whole has been accomplished by my power. Verse 24. — “On that day, says the Lord Almighty, I will take you, Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, my servant, says the Lord, and I will make you like a seal; for I have chosen you, says the Lord Almighty.” Then indeed, he says, O Zerubbabel, having counted you worthy to be my own leader of the Israelite people, I will enable you to prevail over all, so that it becomes clear from the deeds themselves that you have been made king securely by my decree and appointed to this dignity by my good pleasure. Everyone will easily understand that you could never have done these things unless you held the kingship by my will and won so great a victory with my help. For since a seal, when it is applied, is thought to provide some security for what is placed inside, this is what he means by “I will make you like a seal”: I will show you to be the security and confirmation of the whole people, since it obtains so much under your leadership, because you have been chosen for this by my decree. So also in the Gospels he says, “For on him God the Father has set his seal,” meaning: he has firmly shown him to be the one who procures the greatest goods for all people. (p. 431) And the blessed Paul says, “For you are the seal of my apostleship,” meaning: you who have believed confirm my apostleship for me. In the same way here too he says, “I will make you like a seal,” meaning: I will show your kingship to be firm, for the security of all your people, since it has been set forth by my good pleasure. And it is reasonable that, while everywhere else he addresses Zerubbabel and Joshua together, here he directed his word to Zerubbabel alone, since the leadership in war was bound to belong above all to the king.
[?] of the Prophet [?Zechariah]. The blessed Zechariah clearly also prophesied at the same time as the prophet Haggai. For in the second year

of Darius, as one can learn from divine Scripture itself, the one says that he began prophesying by divine revelation, and so does the other likewise. So both clearly appear to have prophesied after the return of the Israelite people, who had been brought back from Babylon to Judea. For when Cyrus, the first to reign over the Persians and the Medes together, permitted them to return to their own land, (p. 432) a large multitude went up to Jerusalem and Judea under the leadership of Zerubbabel. They laid the foundations of the temple and set up the altar in it. But the work was being prevented from reaching completion, at times by the malice of those who harassed them, at other times by their own sloth. So the blessed prophet Haggai, by divine revelation, rebuked them for their sloth and convicted them of neglecting the work out of a wicked disposition, since they were zealous about their own houses, not only to build them but to finish them with great elegance, while they neglected the house of God. In this way he roused them all to the work, as the prophet's book itself shows. The blessed Zechariah, likewise by divine revelation, confirms the people's return through his own predictions. He gives assurance that Jerusalem too will again have its proper beauty, with a king in it appointed by divine decree and counted worthy of the [?] there, governing its affairs and fighting in the front line for all in the wars against foreigners, and with the priesthood once more recovering its proper adornment along with its ancient splendour. By these things he meant to persuade those who had already gone up (p. 433) that their dwelling in those places would be secure. For it was likely that even after their return they were still uncertain whether they would remain securely, whether because of the severity of the captivity they had suffered, which they would never have expected to endure, or because their return had been so unexpected. He also meant to teach others who were still in captivity to return to Judea, which above all gave those who had gone up confidence that the return was secure. He is seen to behold many different revelations and explains the meaning of each. He also announces the attack of Gog and his hosts, and their utter destruction to come, and that the Jews, ruled and led in battle by Zerubbabel, will prevail over them unexpectedly and against all human hope. He also mentions the afflictions that would come upon them after that, which happened to them in the times of the Maccabees at the hands of the successors of the Macedonian kingdom. One should not be surprised if through revelation he presents certain things that had already happened as though they were still to come, as when he says that he saw the four horns that had scattered Israel being shattered. For it is quite clear that these things were not yet to happen but had already happened. For if by the four horns he signifies the Assyrian, the Babylonian, the Mede and the Persian, (p. 434) as some would have it

[?] word, it is clear that both the Assyrians and the Babylonians had already paid the penalty by that time. Cyrus overthrew the Medes, and after him Darius was the fourth. From the Persians the Israelites suffered nothing harsh. On the contrary, they were treated well by that kingdom: first Cyrus, its first king, released them from captivity, and after that Darius gave the rest of the Jews leave to go up to their own land. And if someone wants the four horns to signify other powers that ill-treated the Israelites during the captivity, it is clear that those too had come to an end. But the prophet seems to mention such things because divine grace was now showing this to him. Through the divine revelation he himself would have firm faith in what had happened, and he would teach his hearers to be fully persuaded that the punishment of those who had grieved them stands, and that the benefits given to them also stand secure. We have not said this idly. We said it so that in the detailed interpretation, when we see things that have already happened presented as if they were still to come, we may not be surprised or puzzled by this way of speaking. (p. 455) So much for the subject of the book. From here on we must attend to the details, as divine grace may grant.

Verses 1–4. "In the eighth month of the second year of Darius, the word of the Lord came to Zechariah son of Berechiah, son of Iddo, the prophet, saying [?]." Here he has stated the time at which he was granted the divine revelation, and next he adds what he was commanded to say to the people. "The Lord was angry with your fathers with great anger." The prophet made an opening suited to the occasion. The memory of the evils of the captivity was still fresh and vivid for them, since they had only just been freed from it and had been able to return to their own land. So it was fitting that before saying anything else he should remind them of the calamity that had just occurred, so that the memory of what had happened might keep them from having to experience the same things again. "For you know," he says, "how great a punishment I brought on your fathers in my anger, and into what evils I made them pass because of their disobedience. I removed them from their own land and led them captive into a foreign land that they had never seen before." "And you shall say to them, Thus says the Lord Almighty: Return to me, says the Lord of hosts, and I will return to you, says the Lord of hosts. And do not be like your fathers, whom the former prophets reproached, saying, (p. 456) Thus says the Lord Almighty: Turn back now from your evil ways and from your evil practices. But they did not listen, and they did not attend to hear me, says the Lord Almighty." "But now at least, turning away from

the example of your own fathers, look to me. Keep your eyes fixed on what I say and counsel you, so that I in turn may choose to watch over you and take care of your affairs. Guard against imitating your fathers in any way. They received much and frequent counsel and exhortation from the earlier prophets, urging them to turn from their wickedness and so escape the punishment for their evil deeds, yet they would neither attend to those who taught them nor take any account of them." Verses 5–6. "Your fathers, where are they? And the prophets, will they live forever? But receive my words and my statutes, all that I command by my Spirit to my servants the prophets, which overtook your fathers." "And indeed you would do well to reckon this too: neither your fathers nor the prophets are still alive. The death common to our nature overtook both, and did not let either of them extend their life very long. (p. 457) But your fathers departed after receiving the punishment for their disobedience, while the prophets, even after leaving this present life, showed the truth of their words by what happened. Even after they died, what they had said came to fulfilment all the same, since it had been spoken according to my mind. Looking to this, then, you should not treat what I say through the prophets as a matter of no importance. You should accept everything they tell you through spiritual grace, since none of what they say can prove false, and it is not without danger for you to neglect it." At these words the people answered, as was natural, since events had borne ample witness to the truth of what was said, and they gave clear proof of their good disposition. "And they answered," he says, "and said: As the Lord Almighty has determined to do to us according to our ways and according to our practices, so has he done to us." By "has determined" he means "had determined," for he is not speaking of present things but of things that have already happened. "We acknowledge," he says, "that whatever God declared would happen to us, passing sentence in proportion to what we did, we have in fact suffered. So we are thoroughly persuaded (p. 458) that the truth of what God says cannot be disputed, and that it is not without danger for us if we choose to neglect what he says." After this the prophet goes on to recount a revelation that God showed him. From it he himself received a sure assurance of the good things in store for the people, and he confidently announced what he had been shown to those who heard him. He speaks thus. Verses 7–10. "On the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month, which is the month Shebat, in the second year of Darius, the word of the Lord came to Zechariah son of Berechiah, son of Iddo, the prophet, saying." "The word of the Lord came" means "I was granted a divine revelation." So, going on to relate the revelation, he says, "I saw by night." For

neither the word of the Lord nor the Lord would say "I saw by night." Clearly it is the prophet who says it [?]. Having shown by that phrase that a divine revelation had come to him, he recounts in these words what the revelation was. That is why he says, "I saw by night," meaning, "I saw a revelation of this kind." [?] And he describes what it was like: "And behold, a man mounted on a red horse, and he was standing among the shady mountains, and behind him were horses, red and dappled and white. And I said, What are these, Lord? And the angel who spoke in me said to me, I will show you what these are. And the man who stood among the mountains answered (p. 459) and said to me, These are the ones whom the Lord has sent out to go to and fro through the earth. And they answered the angel of the Lord who stood among the mountains and said, We have gone to and fro through all the earth, and behold, all the earth is inhabited and at rest." It is clear that everything shown to the prophet was a sign of certain realities (59). Joseph saw sheaves, and the sun and moon and stars, and each of these pointed to some future reality. Pharaoh saw ears of grain and cows, some sleek and others thin, and here too the things shown signified something else. In the same way the prophet sees these things through divine revelation, and each thing shown him was a sign and indication of some reality. So too blessed Peter saw a sheet let down from heaven, full of all kinds of animals, clean and unclean, and what appeared pointed to certain other things. [?] In the same way blessed Zechariah, recounting the revelation, says first of all that he saw a man mounted on a red horse, standing among the shady mountains. What some people say, (p. 440) that he saw the Son of God here, is full of great error and folly, and not far from impiety either. For it is clear that none of those who lived before the coming of Christ the Master knew the Father and the Son (61). They did not know God the Father as Father of God the Son, nor God the Son as Son of God the Father, being the very same thing that the Father is, since he is from him. For the names "father" and "son", (59) [Scholion:] Foolish boor! Unless they were asleep and seeing unreal dreams from a melancholic disposition, their words were surely about realities. But the interpreter does not consider this, since it is obvious. He considers what kind of reality the word signifies, and which one. (61) Scholion. Most foolish of men, and truly deluded! They did not avoid these names because they did not know the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. They avoided them because the people they were speaking to could not bear to hear such things. For this reason they used other names, equivalent to these and carrying the same meaning. Otherwise, how would we have come to know God in three persons, if not from the prophets?

were used under the Old Testament in this way: God was called father in a general sense, because of his care for the people whom he there considered worthy of his attention, and those who had something more by way of closeness to God were called sons. But God the Father, as I have already said, as Father of God the Son, and God the Son as Son of God the Father, absolutely no one of those times knew. Those who were instructed in true religion before the coming of Christ the Master knew only God and creation. They recognized God as the eternal being and the cause of all things, and creation as, to put it briefly, everything that he brought from non-being into being. Sufficient proof of this comes from the blessed apostles. They spent a long time with the Master during his coming, and they confessed him to be the Christ, having learned this through much teaching. But they did not know him as Son of God in the sense I have described. They called Christ son of God only by way of closeness to God, following the custom of the holy and righteous men of earlier times (61). That is why Philip says to the Lord, "Show us your Father, and it is enough for us." He would not have said this if he had known who the Son is and who the Father is, for then he would surely have known that the divine nature cannot be seen. (p. 441) So the Lord says to him, "Have I been with you so long, and you have not known me, Philip?" This shows that he did not know even the one he thought he knew. That is also why he asks to see the Father, desiring something impossible. So the Lord adds, "Whoever has seen me has seen the Father," showing that in his divinity he is what the Father is, invisible like him, and that the vision of the one is also the vision of the other. And elsewhere the Lord says to them more plainly, "I have spoken these things to you in figures. But the hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures, but will tell you plainly about the Father." This shows that they heard the Father's name as if in a riddle, taking it in a human sense, as a relationship. But they would truly know the Son when they knew him to be God from God, from him by essence, and in essence the same as he is. And if the prophets and those [?]

before them had all known the Father and the Son, and had been taught this from the divine Scriptures, the apostles would have known it before anyone else. But it is clear that they did not know it. They learned it when the grace of the Spirit came upon them after the ascension of Christ the Master into heaven. That is why the Lord says to them, "I still have many things to tell you, but you cannot bear them now. But when that Spirit of truth comes, (p. 442) he will guide you into all the truth." If they already knew the divinity of the Only-begotten, and the Father as God and Father of God, what greater thing was left for them to learn later? So no one before the coming of Christ the Master knew the divinity of the Only-begotten, and none of the prophets speaks of it (62). Another claim is also full of utter folly, or to put it more truly, of derangement: that whenever the Old Testament mentions an angel and the Lord, it means the Son of God. Such people ought at least to be ashamed, since blessed Paul's words distinguish the Son from the angels and show that the gap between them is as great as that between a servant and a master. He says: "Of the angels he says, He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire. But of the Son he says, Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; the scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom." He shows how great the difference is between the Son and the angels, and that these titles cannot be made to apply to the same being. The invisible powers, appointed for service, are fittingly called angels and ministers because of the ministry to which they were assigned. The Son does not accept these titles, but rightly receives this one alone: "Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; (p. 445) the scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom." This is to call him the eternal King and Lord of all, who governs the universe with perfect uprightness. Blessed Paul has shown us so great a difference. How then is it not senseless and mad to dare to combine things that cannot be combined, and to say that the Son can be called both angel and Lord? It is clear that whenever something of this kind occurs in divine Scripture, the angel it mentions is the one appointed to serve in the things shown, since "they are all ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation," as blessed Paul says. And when it names the Lord, it is not calling the angel by that name. It is ascribing the work that is done to God, just as the prophets also often say the things that belong (62) Scholion. This too you think out of ignorance. Isaiah hints at three hypostases through the thrice-holy. In the same way, when he says, "And he is called the angel of great counsel," he says that he is an angel, not according to the essence of angels but according to his [?]. For if he was sent by the Father as from a cause, he is an angel, for he announced

to God, not counting what is said as their own, but tracing its cause back to God. One can see this straight away in the present prophet. Having said, "The word of the Lord came to Zechariah, saying," he added, "The Lord was angry with your fathers with great anger." Yet strictly it would have been more consistent to say, "The word of the Lord came to Zechariah, saying: I was angry with your fathers," so that the word of the Lord that came to the prophet would not seem to be speaking about some other lord who was angry. But it is clear that once the prophet has named the one who gave the revelation, by saying "The word of the Lord came," (p. 444) he goes on to add the words that God himself spoke. He is not speaking his own words, but setting out what God said. In the same way, when he speaks of an angel and then also names the Lord, "angel" refers to the one who ministers, and "Lord" to the one who commanded that those things be done through the angels. Indeed, it is clear that whenever God so wills and angels appear to people in perceptible form, they usually take on human form, which is familiar to those who see them and are taught by them. One could learn this no less from the New Testament. Divine Scripture, narrating the events of the resurrection of Christ the Master, says that an angel was seen who had rolled away the stone. Then, describing what he was like and how he appeared, it says, "His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing white as snow." And after the Lord's ascension into heaven, while the disciples stood gaping at the strangeness of what had happened, it says, "Behold, two men stood by them in white clothing." They were angels, teaching them what they needed to know about what had happened. In the same way, here too he sees an angel in human form, appointed by grace to serve those who are coming to salvation.

Verses 8–10. The vision, then, showed an angel, while the details surrounding him pointed to realities. He was mounted on a horse to show the speed with which the invisible powers must accomplish whatever God commands, (p. 445) and on a red one to show the anger he felt on the people's behalf against the foreigners. He stood in the midst of shady mountains. The mountains made plain the loftiness and firmness of the power of the one ministering, and their shade pointed to the shelter that God was promising to provide for his own people. So the prophet asks, "What are these?" The revelation itself moved him to ask the question, so that the teaching might have a way to proceed. "And the angel who spoke in me answers," he says, "I will show you what these are." He means the very man whom he saw mounted on a red horse. And he says "who spoke

in me" because he did not hear a voice coming from outside, but one impressed on his mind through revelation. In the same way blessed Peter heard, "Rise, Peter, kill and eat." It is clear that no such voice came to him from the heavens, or else knowledge of what was said would have filled the whole world. The voice was impressed on him as if it came to him from heaven. It is clear that the angel he says spoke to him is the one mounted on the red horse. For after he said, "I will show you what these are," the prophet adds, "And the man who stood among the mountains answered and said to me, These are the ones whom the Lord has sent out to go to and fro through the earth." (p. 446) This clearly shows that the man who appeared to him among the shady mountains was the very one speaking in him. He had promised to show him what these things about the horses [?] meant, and he taught him by going on to say: These are the ones whom God regularly sends to go about the whole earth and carry out the appropriate ministry everywhere, as God wills. It is clear, then, that he is speaking of angels, for this is the work of angels. He does not mean the horses. That is why the one interpreting says that these were sent to go to and fro through the earth, meaning not the horses but their riders. These riders, being angels, were bound to appear on horses too, like the one mounted on the red horse. The horses showed the swiftness of their ministry. The red ones [?] showed the anger they felt against the foreigners, and the white ones pointed to the splendor that would come to the Israelites through the angels' ministry. In carrying out this ministry, the angels bring punishments on those who deserve them and bestow gifts on those whom God wishes to reward in this way. Verses 11–12. The proof of what has been said is in what follows. "For they answered," he says, "the angel of the Lord who stood among the mountains, and said, We have gone to and fro through all the earth, and behold, all the earth is inhabited and at rest." One could not say that the horses answered him, for what kind of voice could come from horses? (p. 447) Clearly he means the riders of the horses. Like the one who appeared on a red horse among the shady mountains, they appeared in human form, and so they naturally conversed with him in a way that matched how they appeared. As the prophet heard what was said through revelation, he received their teaching. For it is clear that the whole revelation and everything seen in it, whether question or answer or anything else, was all impressed on his mind [?] in the revelation. In this way the prophet received the teaching through all of it, so that he himself might have firm faith about what was to come and pass on the benefit to others. The one mounted on the horse among the mountains seems to point to the angel set over the nation of the Israelites, in keeping with the saying, "He set the boundaries

[?] …of the nations according to the number of the angels of God." So then, since the rest of the angels, sharing (as is natural) in the concern for the matters at hand, were talking with one another, they also informed him that the whole earth was at that time at rest. He took this as his occasion: the one who had been seen among the shady mountains, being entrusted with the care of the people, and being somewhat troubled that while everything else was at peace, only the affairs of Jerusalem were in turmoil, offers to God a prayer and supplication on behalf of the whole nation. "For," he says, "the angel of the Lord answered and said"; that is, the one standing among the mountains answered what the others had said, that the whole earth was inhabited and at rest: "Lord Almighty, how long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, which you have disregarded these seventy years?" It is as if he were saying: "To all the other nations on earth you have granted secure habitation and the peace in which you appointed them to live; only your Jerusalem, it seems, and the other cities of Judah do not enjoy this common gift. But since their sins, their zeal for impiety and their disobedience have been the cause of this, heal their condition with mercy; or, looking to the number of years they have spent in these calamities, reckon the punishment of the evils that have held them for so long a time as sufficient for what they sinned. Pardon all their sins by your own mercy and give them back their former prosperity, so that Jerusalem may be inhabited in its earlier form and the other cities of Judah may be established once again." Verses 13–17. To this he adds: "And the Lord Almighty answered the angel who spoke in me with good words and words of comfort." By this, too, he showed that this prayer was also the prayer of the one among the shady mountains who spoke in him. He says that God answered him with words full of great goodness, holding the promise of many good things, and able to bring every kind of comfort to those in such great and such grievous straits. At this the angel too took courage and informs the prophet of what had been told him by God, which contained a promise of the greatest good things that God would display toward Jerusalem from then on. He speaks as follows: "And the angel who spoke in me said to me: Cry out, saying, Thus says the Lord Almighty: I have been jealous for Zion and for Jerusalem with a great jealousy, and with great anger I am angry at the nations that join in the attack; for I was angry only a little, but they joined in the attack for evil.
