Therefore thus says the Lord: I will return to Jerusalem in compassion, and my house will be rebuilt in it, says the Lord Almighty, and a measuring line will yet be stretched out over Jerusalem. And the angel who spoke in me said to me: Cry out, saying, Thus says the Lord Almighty: Cities will yet overflow with good things, and the Lord will yet have mercy on Zion and will yet choose Jerusalem." For, he says, having received such an answer from God, the angel was himself delighted at what was

said, and he told me to take courage about everything from then on, so that I too might confidently announce to everyone that God is greatly angry, on behalf of Jerusalem, against those who showed such cruelty toward them: "Out of their own wickedness they brought on them a punishment greater than my anger. Therefore, for all these reasons, I will show great mercy toward Jerusalem, so that my house, once built in it, will provide the customary benefit to those who gather to it, and Jerusalem will be extended further than it is now; and, to put it briefly, all the cities belonging to it will be established in an abundance of many goods. For then I will show great mercy toward it; I have resolved to do every good thing for it and for those who belong to it from now on." It is quite clear that when he says, "I am angry at the nations that join in the attack, for I was angry only a little, but they joined in the attack for evil," he is speaking of the Babylonians who sacked the city and of those who in any way helped them in this, and that by these words he signifies the punishment that would come upon them. For the Babylonians had already paid the penalty: their kingdom had been destroyed and their city completely taken by Cyrus, king of the Persians; and those who had helped them, the Idumeans and all the rest, had been punished. So what we said in the introduction is clear: God recalls many things that had already happened, confirming them by his own promises. The Israelites at that time greatly needed this, since even after their deliverance they were uncertain about their own situation, so much so that, having begun the divine temple, they did not even bring it to completion, whether because of the harassment of their adversaries or because their own slackness was naturally increased by the malice of their enemies. He said, then, that he had learned two things from the revelation: that God would punish those who had wronged the people, and that he would restore Jerusalem once again to its former prosperity. Verses 18–21. To confirm both of these, he next sets out other revelations. Having seen them, he himself held a firm belief in what had been said, and he persuaded all the people to think the same. First he speaks of the punishment of the adversaries, which he had also mentioned first in the preceding revelation: "And I lifted up my eyes and saw four horns. And I said to the angel who spoke in me, What are these, Lord? And he said to me, These are the horns that scattered Judah and Israel and Jerusalem. And the Lord showed me four craftsmen. And I said, What are these coming to do, Lord? And he said, These are the horns that scattered Judah and Israel, and they crushed them, and no one among them lifted up his head; and these have come out to sharpen them into their hands, the four horns, the nations that lift up a horn against the land of the Lord to scatter it." Now those who like to tell fables say that the four horns are the Assyrian, the Babylonian, the Mede and the Persian.

They refuse to pay attention to the fact that divine Scripture often states a number not to be precise about the number but to indicate something else. So they strive to fit names to the number, and are naturally forced into fable-telling and the fabrication of fictions. This has happened to them in many other places as well, and indeed in the prophecy of blessed Micah, who says, "Seven shepherds and eight bites of men will rise up against the Assyrian." They strive to count the shepherds as seven men and the bites as eight men, and for this reason they are forced to say things deserving the greatest ridicule. In the same way, here too they say that the four horns are the ones we mentioned above. They do not consider that the Assyrian and the Babylonian had long since paid the penalty, that the Medes had been overthrown by Cyrus, and that the Persians are found to have done the Jews no wrong at all, but on the contrary released them from captivity. Divine Scripture does not mean particular, specific people by the four horns. Rather, since we say that the inhabited world is divided into four extremities, east and west and north and south, Scripture often mentions these regions to indicate something that happens in many places. So, for example, blessed David says of the Israelites: "Let them say so, those redeemed by the Lord, whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy and gathered out of the lands, from east and west and north and sea." For it is quite clear that God did not gather Israelites scattered to the four ends of the world; he brought back to their own land those who were captives under the Babylonians and Assyrians alone. Scripture says "from east and west and north and sea" in order to say that he gathered those dispersed in many places and brought them back home. In the same way, here too he speaks of four horns to mean those who had come against them from many directions and wished to harm them in every way, whether Assyrians or Babylonians or Idumeans or Moabites or the other neighboring peoples, or anyone else at all. For this reason he also sees four craftsmen, meaning the ministering powers, who brought punishment on them from many directions, each of them punishing those among them according to the divine sentence. He speaks of "sharpening" the horns in the sense of whittling them thin and removing all their bulk, meaning that the power which surrounded those who had attacked them would be destroyed. Having confirmed by this revelation the punishment of those who had wronged the Israelites, the prophet speaks of another revelation shown to him, which indicates the renewal of Jerusalem. He speaks as follows: Verses 1–5. "And I lifted up my eyes and saw, and behold, a man, and in his hand a measuring line. And I said to him, Where are you going? And he said to me, To measure Jerusalem, to see how great its breadth is and how great its

length. And behold, the angel who spoke in me was standing, and another angel was going out to meet him. And he said to him, Run and speak to that young man, saying, Jerusalem will be inhabited abundantly because of the multitude of people and cattle in its midst; and I will be to it, says the Lord, a wall of fire all around, and I will be its glory in its midst." Since builders customarily measure out on the ground with a line the breadths and lengths and outlines of a building, he necessarily sees an angel again, in human form as usual, holding such a line. When the prophet asked him in the revelation where he was going, he said that he was going to measure the building of Jerusalem, what kind of building it should be and how large. Then he speaks of the angel who spoke in him, whom he had seen earlier in human form, seated on a red horse among the shady mountains (for it became clear to us from what came before that he said it was the same angel he had seen among the mountains and who also spoke in him). He says that he now saw this angel standing, as if delighted at what was happening, because the prayer he had offered to God on behalf of Jerusalem and the nation had reached its fulfillment. Not only had the punishment to be brought on those who had wronged them been shown, but the one holding the measuring line had also appeared, a sign that the building of the city would now be under way. Then he says that another angel was sent and spoke to him, telling him to speak to the young man, that is, clearly, the one holding the measuring line. He called him this because the prophet saw him in the revelation in the appearance of a young man, which indicated that he would carry the work in hand through to completion with all his strength. So, he says, the angel who was sent tells the angel who spoke in me to run quickly and tell the young man that Jerusalem will be inhabited in very great abundance, crowded with people and with the cattle that serve them, so that, knowing this, he might extend the breadth and length of the city further, since it would have to be large enough for the multitude of those who were to live in it. "For," he says, "we will give it complete security from me, greater than a wall made of fire would provide, one able to burn up those who attack. And I will be seen in the very deeds, through my care for them, so that they will be spoken well of and praised by all for the greatness of the benefits bestowed on the city." It should also be noted in passing that the angel who was sent says to the angel who spoke in him, that is, to the one mounted on the red horse among the mountains, "Run and speak to that young man." But if, as those who like to tell fables say, the one who appeared among the shady mountains was the Son of God, how could the angel have dared to say to him, "Run and speak to that young man, saying, Jerusalem will be inhabited abundantly"? For an angel

to give orders to the Son of God would have been impossible, and even to think so is the height of impiety. But that an angel should tell an angel what must be done is nothing surprising, since it is the part of servants to tell one another their master's decisions, and much more so of those sent for this purpose by the Lord of all, as was happening here too. Since the angel who spoke in him had offered the prayer for the city, the angel sent by God's will fittingly tells him to run and say what was needed to the young man. It was as if he were bringing him the good news that his prayer had reached its fulfillment and that God had decided on better things for Jerusalem; and he too, as one whose request to God had prevailed, ought gladly to carry out what he had been commanded and, with all speed, make known to the one sent to build the city what God had decided about it. Verses 6–7. Now the prophet, necessarily filled with courage by what had been shown to him, cried out, saying: "Ho, ho, flee from the land of the north, says the Lord; for I will gather you from the four winds of heaven, says the Lord. Escape to Zion, you who dwell with the daughter of Babylon." For he commands the rest of those still in captivity to hurry with great haste to Mount Zion, taking courage from God's promises about Jerusalem, since he had promised to gather them into it from everywhere. Here again "from the four winds" indicates not a particular number but "from everywhere," so that the Jews still living in the land of the Babylonians might take courage and all hasten to Jerusalem. Living there, they would have secure safety from then on, as God guarded them according to his own promises. It is clear that Babylon had been destroyed by then and that the whole rule of the Babylonians had come to an end by the time of King Darius; nevertheless he speaks this way to point to those who ought to go up at that time. For not a few went up in the time of Darius. Still, he tells them to return from Babylon, meaning from the captivity they had endured under the Babylonians. It is obvious that he is announcing what will happen in the form of a command. Verses 8–12. "For thus says the Lord Almighty: After glory he has sent me against the nations that plundered you; for whoever touches you is like one who touches the pupil of his eye. For behold, I am bringing my hand upon them, and they will be plunder for those who served them, and you will know that the Lord Almighty has sent me." "For I tell you these things," he says, "at the command of God who spoke them, who has sent me to make known to you his glory and the greatness of the power he will display against those who wronged you. He is as angry at those who wish to cause you any pain as he would be if someone injured the pupils of his eyes." It is quite clear that he wanted to express the exceptional nature of God's care in human terms. "So heavy a punishment," he says, "will I bring upon your enemies that they will be besieged

and sacked by those whom they previously held as slaves, so that it will become clear from the events themselves that I bring you this good news by the will of God, the Lord of all." Then he also turns his speech to the city, for he has long been accustomed to call Jerusalem the daughter of Zion: "Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Zion; for behold, I am coming, and I will dwell in your midst, says the Lord." That is: "Live in delight from now on, for you will have me in you, revealed through my care." "And many nations will flee to the Lord on that day, and they will be his people, and they will dwell in your midst, and you will know that the Lord Almighty has sent me to you. And the Lord will take Judah as his inheritance, his portion in the holy land, and he will yet choose Jerusalem." "Such care," he says, "will I show toward you that many foreigners too will flee to you and confess as their God me, whom they have come to know through you. Leaving their own places, they will choose to dwell in you because of my care. Then above all you will know that I bring you this good news by the will of God, the Lord of all, who will give back to Judah its ancient portion of the land and make all Jerusalem glorious before everyone." Verse 13. Then, consistently, he adds: "Let all flesh show reverence before the face of the Lord, for he has roused himself from his holy clouds." So it is fitting for everyone alike, both his own people and foreigners, to fear God from now on. From the higher places, where he is accustomed to dwell and which he makes holy by his own dwelling, he has been moved to come to our aid. It befits everyone to fear him: his own people, so that they never again transgress the law, and foreigners, so that they no longer attempt anything against those who belong to him. Having thus confirmed by these revelations what was indicated in the earlier revelation, that God will punish the adversaries and that he will do good to Jerusalem and to all the Jews who belong to it, he turns to other revelations that were necessary for the matter at hand. While they were in captivity they had been deprived of both king and priest, which were the most important things for holding the nation together. The king rendered his proper service in war and in the administration of other affairs; the priest led the prayers and supplications and all the worship due to God. The prophet Hosea foretold this too: "For many days," he says, "the children of Israel will sit without a ruler, without sacrifice, without an altar, without priesthood, without Urim." Through the present revelation God shows the prophet, for the instruction of all the people, that these things too, which were the greatest, foremost and most necessary for holding the community together, and of which they had naturally been deprived during the captivity, would now be given back to them by God, since the city together with the nation was about to recover all its proper order. He speaks, then, as follows:

[?] …a turban and a clean headdress on his head." He necessarily sees the restoration of the priesthood in the person of the priest, since the priesthood does not appear on its own but in those appointed to administer it. So he sees Joshua the great priest (he calls "great" the one who, by succession, performs the ministry that belongs to Aaron) standing before an angel, since angels have been entrusted with oversight of all people. As the Lord says in the Gospels: "Their angels always behold the face of my Father who is in heaven"; and in the Acts of the blessed apostles, speaking of blessed Peter, they say, "It is his angel." So this man too necessarily appears before an angel, that is, before the one entrusted with his care by divine counsel. And the devil also stood there to oppose him, for his work is to work against the good of human beings. He says that the devil then too was doing everything he could to harass him and [?] to hinder him from the ministry appointed to him, which he had not been able to perform during the captivity. He says that God, who chose Jerusalem, rebuked the devil, so that he might know that all diabolical opposition had been brought to an end by God's care. Having chosen Jerusalem, God necessarily gives back to this man too the dignity of the priesthood. As for "Behold, this is like a brand plucked from the fire," it means: "Just as someone might pull out a piece of wood that was about to be consumed by fire all at once and so preserve it, so I too have plucked out this man, who was in the distress of captivity as in a fire and in danger of being almost burned up by it, and have freed him from the evils that surrounded him." Joshua, he says, was clothed in filthy garments. This means the mourning that had enveloped them because of the captivity, in which he lived entirely shut out from the divine ministry, weighed down by slavery. God commands those standing by to remove these garments from him, that is, the ministering powers who serve him.

…serving the divine counsels, they removed from him the garment of captivity and all that mourning, and brought him back to his own city. Then, once this had happened, he says to him: “I have taken away all your iniquities,” showing that the evils of the captivity had been undone, since he had removed the memory of their sins. (p. 465) Next he orders that he put on the full-length robe and that the mitre and the turban be placed on him, as a sign that the authority of the priesthood was from then on entrusted to him. And this happened just as God had commanded. Having said these things to show that the priesthood had been given back to them, and that the priest was once again engaged in his customary ministry, with his own freedom and authority in the matter, the prophet adds (Verses 6–7): “Thus says the Lord Almighty: If you walk in my ways, and if you keep my commands, you too shall judge my house; and if you guard my court, I will also give you those who move about among these who are standing here.” Accordingly, having [?] the authority of the priesthood, he says that these things were spoken so that he might know how he ought to carry out the ministry. “For if,” he says, “you persist in caring for what I have commanded, you will judge everyone with a priest’s authority. And as you provide the proper guard for my court through your own diligence, you will also pass the honour on to successors, who will be in the midst of all the people carrying out the ministry that belongs to them.” Then, showing the restoration of the kingship as well, he speaks as follows: (p. 466) “Hear now, Joshua the great priest, you and your neighbours who sit before you, for they are men who observe portents.” That is: “My word is to you and to all those with you who are entrusted with ruling the people, in teaching, in interpreting the laws, and in the rest of the ministry that concerns the worship of God.” He calls them “observers of portents” because they are able to examine and know the causes of the marvels God performs. What, then, does he say? (Verses 8–9) “For behold, I am bringing my servant Dawn; for the stone that I have set before Joshua: upon the one stone are seven eyes.” “For I,” he says, “am bringing my servant” (meaning Zerubbabel) “and restoring him to the kingship, showing him no less radiant in his authority than the dawn. Him I set like a stone before your eyes, on which you must rely. You are to give him the help that comes from prayer and from the priesthood, and receive from him the zeal he shows in the wars against your enemies, so that you may live in peace and carry out the priesthood as you should. You ought to take courage in this stone, considering that it has seven eyes.” Here too he does not use “seven” as a precise number. He means: “Zerubbabel, whom I have appointed to the kingship, will be able to do these things, since I will give him my great and unspeakable oversight (p. 465) and care, from which some

advantage will come to him. ‘Behold, I am digging a pit, says the Lord Almighty, and I will search out all the iniquity of that land in one day.’ For I will make him so powerful that through his generalship he will rout all the enemies and, as if into a pit, cast them into destruction by my punishment, for the wrongs they chose to do to the land that belongs to me, over which I appointed the king to preside.” Then, showing also the greatness of the help they will enjoy from Zerubbabel’s generalship, he says: “On that day, says the Lord Almighty, each one will call his neighbour under his fig tree.” For while he is their general, the enemies will suffer those things, but those who belong to my people will enjoy their own fruits with great pleasure, so that they will constantly invite one another to feasts. Having shown in these words the restoration of both the kingship and the priesthood, he next sets out a revelation that was shown to him, quite necessarily, after what had been said. He speaks as follows:

(Verses 1–3) “And the angel who spoke in me returned and woke me, as a man is woken from his sleep, and said to me: What do you see?” By the angel who spoke in him he again means the one who appeared in human form on a red horse among the shady mountains; for we learned accurately from the earlier passages that it is this one he everywhere calls “the one who spoke in him.” (p. 466) He says that this angel now woke him, as though he were held in a kind of sleep by contemplating the things already shown. The angel then asked him again what he saw of the things now being shown, so that the prophet would describe the vision and the angel would explain the meaning of what was shown. So he says: “And I said: I have seen, and behold, a lampstand all of gold, and its lamp-bowl on top of it, and seven lamps on it, and two olive trees above it, one on the right of its bowl and one on the left.” The lampstand signifies divine grace, which touches the things on earth and reaches to the things above the earth, since everything is governed by it. Fittingly he saw it all of gold, since it is great and splendid, for gold is the most precious of all earthly materials. The lamp-bowl on top of it signifies the light from divine grace that shines from on high around all who are on earth. He sees seven lamps, showing the completeness and richness of the grace, just as he said above, “Upon the one stone are seven eyes,” to express the greatness of his care. Then there are olive trees on either side of the bowl, one on the right and the other on the left. These signified the kingship and the priesthood, which God granted to be the highest things among human beings: through the one, whatever is useful for ordering the present life is administered, while the other is sufficient to bring human beings to God. (Verses 4–7) (p. 467) Having told the angel that he had seen these things, the prophet adds: “And I asked and said to the angel who spoke in me: What are these, lord? And there answered

the angel who spoke in me, and said to me: Do you not know what these are? And I said: No, lord. And he answered and said to me: This is the word of the Lord to Zerubbabel, saying: Not by great might, nor by strength, but by my Spirit, says the Lord Almighty.” This angel, who the prophet says spoke in him, is the same one who was seen making supplications for Jerusalem, as one entrusted with oversight of all the affairs of Judea, and therefore also offering supplication to God on their behalf. That is why the prophet questions him now [?] and learns each detail. Since everything that was shown signified God’s generosity toward the city and the nation, it was only fitting to learn from him how each of the things shown stood. So he briefly told him the meaning of what was shown: that it signifies the divine grace, which also appointed Zerubbabel to the kingship. Of himself he [can do nothing?], but appointed by the divine [grace?], he has power through it. Then, showing that he himself accomplishes nothing of what pertains to the kingship and the leadership of the people, but that the greatness belongs to the grace of the gift bestowed on him, he says: “Who are you, great mountain, before Zerubbabel, to prevail? And I will bring out the stone of the inheritance, the equality of its grace.” (p. 468) Since he had called Zerubbabel a stone, by “great mountain” he means those who are very powerful in their kingdoms and in the size of their armies and subjects. “For who,” he says, “is so great [?], or so powerful through the number of his subjects and the equipment of his soldiers, as to be able to prevail against Zerubbabel? I have made him successor to the royal inheritance whose promises I made to the forefather of the race, I mean David, and I will fill him wholly with my grace.” This is what he calls “equality of grace,” from which he will necessarily gain the ability to achieve great things against the enemy as general on behalf of his own people. (Verses 8–10) Then, confirming the promises about him: “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: The hands of Zerubbabel laid the foundation of this house, and his hands will complete it; and you will know that the Lord Almighty has sent me to you. For who has despised the long days?” “This very man who laid the foundations of my house will himself bring it to completion, so that it may become clear to all from this that I have come by God’s will to foretell these things to you. Do not, then, disbelieve what is said as though these things were going to happen after a long time. Anyone who thought that my decrees go unfulfilled because of the length of time would be utterly foolish.” This is what he means by “despised the long days.” “For I am able to do everything easily, just as I wish, (p. 469) and to bring with great speed

[?] to completion things that require a long time.” And confirming what had been said: “And they will rejoice and see the tin stone in the hand of Zerubbabel.” “Do not, then, disbelieve what is said,” he says, “since you will see it fulfilled and rejoice as you see Zerubbabel’s power in everything.” This is what he means by the tin stone, indicating the strength he will receive from God. So he also added the reason: “These seven are the eyes of the Lord, which look upon the whole earth.” For the one who oversees, governs and preserves all things richly and in many ways is the very one who made these promises about Zerubbabel and will bring them to completion. Here too “seven” is said of completeness. (Verses 11–14) “And I answered and said to him: What are these two olive trees on the right of the lampstand and on its left? And I asked a second time and said to him: What are the two branches of the olive trees that are in the hands of the two golden spouts, which pour out and bring up the golden oil-funnels? And he said to me: Do you not know what these are? And I said: No, lord. And he said: These are the two sons of fatness, who stand by the Lord of the whole earth.” He asks what the two olive trees mean, one of which was on the right and the other on the left of the lampstand, that is, of the bowl on it, and what the two branches growing out of the olive trees mean. (p. 470) About them he heard: “These are the two sons of fatness, who stand by the Lord of the whole earth.” Since the olive trees were a token of the kingship and the priesthood, which God appointed to rule on earth, he calls Zerubbabel and Joshua the two branches growing out of the olive trees. The one had been brought to the kingship by divine grace, the other appointed to the divine ministry by the grace of the priesthood. That is why he called them sons of fatness, meaning: those sprung from what is greatest and most honoured among human beings, the kingship and the priesthood, and who are all appointed to serve God, the Lord of all. Through all these things, then, the prophet has shown that the affairs of Jerusalem and of the Jewish nation will advance greatly for the better. Those who were hostile to them would be punished, and they themselves would be deemed worthy of God’s great care in everything. Moreover, many others, not easily counted, who were still in that condition at the time, would return from captivity, and both the royal and the priestly dignity would be restored to them through those appointed to this by divine grace. But so that this overflowing announcement of good things would not make them careless, confident in the divine promises but neglecting their duty, he next sees a revelation through which fear was instilled in them, so that they would flee what is worse and pursue what is better. He speaks as follows:
(Verses 1–4) “And I turned and lifted up my eyes, and I looked, and behold, a flying sickle. And he said to me: What do you see? And I said: (p. 471) I see a flying sickle, twenty cu-

bits long and ten cubits wide. And he said to me: This is the curse that goes out over the face of the whole earth; for every thief will be punished by it until death, and every perjurer will be punished by it until death. And I will bring it out, says the Lord Almighty, and it will enter the house of the thief and the house of the one who swears falsely by my name; and it will lodge in the midst of his house and destroy it, its timbers and its stones.” He sees a sickle, which is able to cut off from below whatever it strikes. It is flying, to show that divine punishment comes swiftly on those who deserve it. It has breadth and length so that its size, too, might frighten the hearers. He says that this punishment is set in motion against thieves and perjurers. Yet it is obvious that these are not the only transgressions among human beings; there are many others as well, murder and adultery and the rest, which are not easy even to count. What, then, does he mean? The divine commandments are divided chiefly into these two: our disposition toward God and love for our neighbour. So the Lord, having said, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your mind, and with all your strength; and you shall love your neighbour as yourself,” added, (p. 472) “On these commandments hang the whole law and the prophets.” Wishing, then, to speak briefly of what concerns God and what concerns the neighbour, by perjury, since it is directed against God, he sums up all impieties, I mean offences against God; and by theft, the offences against the neighbour. For since theft is the taking of what does not belong to one, he used theft as a general name for every taking of what belongs to others. In short, he means that this curse is very great and fearful and comes upon everyone, whether he commits impiety against God or wrongs his neighbour in any way. He says that “it will lodge in the midst of his house and destroy it, its timbers and its stones,” meaning that divine punishment will [?] such a person, who sins without repenting, until it wipes him out together with all who belong to him. Having frightened them sufficiently by these words, he shows in what follows that the sin and the punishment for their past deeds have been taken away from them, so that they might know all the better that, having obtained grace for their former sins, they ought to hold more diligently to what pleases God. So he adds: (Verses 5–8) “And the angel who spoke in me went out and said to me: Lift up your eyes and see what this is that is going out. And I said: What is it? And he said: This is the measure that is going out. And he said: This is their iniquity in all the earth. And behold, a talent of lead being lifted up; (p. 473) and behold, a woman was sitting in the middle of the measure. And he said: This is lawlessness. And he threw her into the middle of the measure, and threw the talent of lead into her mouth.” The same

angel he sees again, telling him to look at what seemed to be passing through the present vision. Then the prophet looked and asked, “What is this?” And the angel answered that this was the measure of the punishment the Israelites had to undergo for what they had done. Then he sees a talent of lead, which is heavy by nature and of great bulk in weight, so as to show by it the heaviness of the punishment; and a woman sitting on the measure, whom he said was lawlessness, for the heaviness of the punishment naturally came from lawlessness. Then he threw her into the middle of the measure and placed the talent of lead on her mouth. He showed by this that he had done away with both the sin and the punishment that came from it at once, and had put the whole weight of the evils into her mouth, as if stopping it up and preventing her speech [?]. This was a sign that all her power had been taken away and she was no longer even mistress of her voice, since all such talk had been taken away from those who had formerly reproached them for their sufferings, as people abandoned by God. As blessed David says: “Let the deceitful lips be made mute, which speak lawlessness against the righteous.” He saw these things, then, as proof that the lawless deeds of the Israelites and the punishments for them had been completely taken away. (p. 474) And showing that the punishment had been taken away from them but transferred to their enemies, he adds: (Verses 9–11) “And I lifted up my eyes and looked, and behold, two women going out, and there was wind in their wings; and they had wings like the wings of a hoopoe; and they lifted up the measure between earth and heaven. And I said to the angel who spoke in me: Where are they carrying the measure? And he said to me: To build a house for it in the land of Babylon and to prepare it; and they will set it there on its prepared place.” After those things, then, he sees two women flying with great speed. This is what “wind in their wings” shows: driven by it, as it were, they made their flight swifter. For this reason too he says that their wings were like a hoopoe’s, since that bird’s flight is swift. “These women,” he says, “seized that measure of punishment, raised it on high, and swooping down with great force carried it off.” That is why he said “between earth and heaven,” since for birds flight from a height downward is easier and swifter. “So I asked,” he says, “where they were going and where they were carrying the measure, and I learned from the angel that they were carrying it off to the land of Babylon, to build a house for it themselves and fix its whole dwelling there.” He means that he will carry off all the punishment to Babylon, where it will remain with them and will never again be lifted, in the same way as they [?] your affairs. (p. 475) But to confirm what had been said, he adds again:

(Verses 1–8) “And I turned and lifted up my eyes, and I looked, and behold, four chariots coming out from between two mountains, and the mountains were mountains of bronze. In the first chariot were red horses, and in the second chariot black horses, and in the third chariot white horses, and in the fourth chariot dappled grey horses. And I answered and said to the angel who spoke in me: What are these, lord? And the angel who spoke in me answered and said to me: These are the four winds of heaven, which go out to stand before the Lord of the whole earth. The one with the black horses went out to the land of the north, and the white went out after them, and the red went out to the land of the south, and the dappled and grey went out, and they sought and looked to go about the earth. And he said: Go, and go about the earth. And they went about the earth. And he cried out and called me, and spoke to me, saying: Behold, those who go out to the land of the north have given rest to my wrath on the land.” He speaks of four chariots to signify the powers that are invisibly set over the four regions of the inhabited world and do everything according to the divine will. That is why the angel, when the prophet asked him what these were, said that they were the four winds of heaven that stand before the Lord of the whole earth. For he called the powers in the four regions the four winds of heaven, one for each region; (p. 476) and he says that, being heavenly, they stand before God, that is, they perform a perpetual ministry.(1) He calls them “of heaven” to mean that they are above us, just as when one speaks of “the birds of heaven,” since none of the invisible and ministering powers is above heaven. He also fittingly called them winds, to show that they arrive everywhere with great speed in serving the divine commands. He saw them coming out from between mountains, to show the loftiness and power of their natures; and for this reason he also said that the mountains were of bronze, to show their firmness and vigour in service. The black horses he sent to the north. Their colour signified the dejection into which they were going to plunge all who lived there through the punishment they brought on them. About them the angel says: “Those who go out to the land of the north have given rest to my wrath on the land of the north.” He means that those who went to those places did everything in proportion to my wrath, overwhelming the people with very great punishments, such as were fitting. Behind them came the white horses, who, while the Babylonians were being destroyed and overwhelmed with severe punishments, helped bring about the release of those who were to depart from captivity, showing by their own colour the splendour that would be theirs from then on. (p. 477) And the red…

(1) The manuscript reads ἐπιτελοῦντας.

…went out toward the land of the south, as though breathing anger against those there who had treated the Israelites badly. After them the dappled and the grey horses rushed out, seeking where on earth they should go. This shows that the remaining horses, distinguished by their colors for a varied service, were also concerned to see whether there might be anything else they ought to do, as God thought fit, both to punish the enemies and to benefit the Jewish nation. He says to them, "Go and patrol the earth"; then he adds, "And they patrolled the earth," showing that they were entrusted with bringing their own task to completion, and that once entrusted with it they kept at it. Verses 9–15. "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Take the offerings of the captivity from the rulers, and from the useful men of the land, and from those who have recognized it, from Heldai and from Tobijah and from Jedaiah; and on that day you shall go into the house of Josiah son of Zephaniah, who has come from Babylon. And you shall take silver and gold and make a crown, and set it on the head of Joshua son of Jozadak, the high priest, and say to him: Thus says the Lord Almighty: Behold, a man whose name is Rising; he shall rise up from beneath him, and he shall build the house of the Lord. He shall receive excellence, and shall sit and rule upon his throne; and the priest shall be at his right, and there shall be a counsel of peace between the two of them. And the crown shall be for those who endure, and for the useful men of the land, and for those who have recognized it, and for the favor of the son of Zephaniah, and for a psalm in the house of the Lord. And those who are far from them shall come (p. 478) and build in the house of the Lord; and you shall know that the Lord Almighty has sent me to you. And this shall be, if you will indeed listen to the voice of the Lord your God." Just as the blessed Moses, after coming out of Egypt, took from the people, at God's command, what was needed to build and adorn the tabernacle, so the blessed Zechariah too is ordered to take from those who had come back from the captivity: from the leaders, from those who were in any way suited to this because of their wealth, and indeed from all who had altogether recovered their own possessions. By "the useful men of the land" he means those whose wealth enabled them to contribute something to the need; by "those who have recognized it" he means those who had recovered the land, having received back beyond all hope what they had already lost. So he was to take from all of these, each contributing according to his means, so that the house of God might be built and adorned as was fitting. After naming some who were presumably the best suited to this, he orders him to go into the house of Josiah son of Zephaniah, who had himself also come back from the captivity in Babylon and surpassed the others both in wealth and in eagerness for the work. Taking as much silver and gold as Josiah would provide, he was to make from it a crown that would rest on the priest's head, for the adornment and dignity of the priesthood. (p. 479) Once it was made, he was to set it on the priest's

head and say to him, so that he might take courage about the matters at hand, which were many and very great: "By God's purpose a man has appeared, whose name, taken from the event itself, is Rising." He means Zerubbabel, who through these events would appear illustrious in his royal leadership. "And he shall rise," he says, "from beneath him," meaning: All splendor will come from him to the multitude of the Jews; for he will build the temple, and clothed by divine favor with every excellence, he will remain securely on the royal seat. "From this you will have courage about the matters at hand, for you will be with him in great honor." That is what "He shall be at his right" means, with concord prevailing between the two of you: affairs will become easier for you through his royal authority, and he will gain much divine favor through your priestly ministry. The adornment of the crown placed on him will be the glory not of him alone but of the whole multitude: of those who look to the hope that comes from God, of those who are now contributing what they can toward building the house, and above all of Zephaniah, who has shown such generosity. All this has happened and is happening so that the ministry of the priests may be continual and the hymns of those who assemble may be offered in full to God. (p. 480) "Indeed you will see a great many of those far away flocking together and contributing their own means toward the building of the house, so that the events themselves will make it plain to everyone that I have now come by God's purpose to bring you this good news. And it will indeed come to completion, if you continue eager to obey my ordinances."

Verses 1–5. After this he says that in the fourth year of the reign of Darius some men were sent by certain rulers among peoples foreign to Israel to the priests and prophets at Jerusalem. They were to propitiate God with sacrifices for the sins of which they knew themselves guilty, and to ask and learn whether the temple of God had recovered its proper adornment, so that they might also observe the fasts appropriate to the worship of God, which they had in fact been doing for many years already. When they had done this, and the envoys were present and carrying out the business for which they had been sent, the prophet was ordered by some revelation to speak these things to all the people of the land and to the priests. The envoys who were present also needed to learn them, so that what was said might instruct not only God's own people but also those who had come. What was said was this: "I have no eagerness," he says, "to see you fasting and mourning, for I do not make my worship consist in these things. You were in captivity for seventy years and did not observe a single fast; (p. 481) and yet, without asking anything of the kind from you, when I saw you turn away from wickedness I restored you to your own land. Whether you eat and drink or not, eating is your enjoyment and not eating is your deprivation; it is no concern of mine." And he shows that he is not saying this to them now for the first time:

Verses 6–12. "Are these not the words that the Lord spoke by the hands of the former prophets, when Jerusalem was inhabited and prosperous, along with its cities round about, and the hill country and the lowland were inhabited?" "I said these things to you long ago," he says, "through the prophets, when Jerusalem enjoyed its prosperity, and likewise all the cities under it, since the hill country and the lowland belonging to them were full of inhabitants. Even so, I told you then that I had no regard for your fasting when you fasted without a good intention. What I do have regard for, I taught you through the prophets as the things you most ought to attend to: 'Judge righteous judgment, and each of you show mercy and compassion to his neighbor; do not oppress the widow, the orphan, the stranger, or the poor; and let none of you remember in his heart the wrong his brother has done.' For I counseled you everywhere to take the greatest care for justice, to show compassion toward your neighbors, to refrain from all harm to the poor and those without protection, and to keep clear of wrath and anger against one another, putting out of mind the grievances that arose among you. So, setting fasting aside, I counseled you to do these things." And what happened? "But they refused to pay attention, and senselessly turned their backs, and made their ears heavy so as not to hear, and set their hearts in disobedience so as not to hear my law and the words that the Lord Almighty sent by his Spirit, by the hands of the former prophets." "You were unwilling to take account even of these things, but in your great senselessness you turned away from what was said altogether." (p. 482) That is what "they senselessly turned their backs" means. "You were unwilling to pay attention to what was said, having decided once and for all to disobey my laws, which I explained to you through the former prophets." And what came of this? Verses 13–14. "And great wrath came from the Lord Almighty." "It was for this that you suffered so great a punishment: that I set your fasts aside and counseled you to hold fast to the laws you most ought to keep." [?] "…I will cast them out as in a whirlwind into all the nations that they did not know; and the land shall be made desolate behind them, with no one passing through or returning; and they made a chosen land into a desolation." "For I threatened to wrap all of you, as it were, in a mighty whirlwind and scatter you, and to hand you over to captivity and carry you off to a land you had not known be-

fore. And I declared that your land would be covered with desolation, so that no one would live on it any longer or pass through it, because of its utter desolation. I both threatened these things," he says, "and did them: the land I once chose for your possession I have handed over to desolation." He says "they will cry out" and "it will be made desolate" as though of the future, while describing things that had already happened, changing the tense in his customary way. We have already shown by many examples that this happens frequently in divine Scripture, both in the blessed David and in the other prophets. He has in fact made this plain by saying, "And they made a chosen land into a desolation," for this shows that he is speaking not of something still to come but of something already past and done. What he wanted to say throughout was this: "I rejected your fasting because it was done badly, and I counseled you to do what you ought; and since you paid no attention to this, I brought such a punishment upon you." That is what he said then; and now what?

Verses 1–5. "Thus says the Lord Almighty: I have been jealous for Jerusalem and for Zion with great jealousy, and with great wrath I have been jealous for her." "I have changed my disposition toward her, (p. 484) so that I am very angry with those who wronged her for what she has suffered." And continuing the same thought: "Thus says the Lord: I will return to Zion and dwell in the midst of Jerusalem; and Jerusalem shall be called a true city, and the mountain of the Lord Almighty a holy mountain [?]." "For I will restore my affection for Mount Zion, and I will appear again in Jerusalem through my care for it. I will show it to be a city truly established and set in great prosperity, and I will show the mountain on which the city is built to be holy, as one deemed worthy of my presence." And he adds further to the same: "Thus says the Lord Almighty: Old men and old women shall again sit in the streets of Jerusalem, each with his staff in his hand because of his great age; and the streets of the city shall be filled with boys and girls playing in its streets." "I will keep the city and all its inhabitants so safe from harm," he says, "that they will not suffer untimely deaths from the evils that oppressed them, as they did before. Since the city will be in great prosperity, the lives of its inhabitants will necessarily be prolonged as well, so that, grown weak through the length of their lives, they will need staffs to help them walk. (p. 485) And the city will also be full of boys and girls playing," for this is a sign of a prosperous and populous city and

Verses 6–[?]. Then, since these things seemed somehow impossible given the present circumstances: "Thus says the Lord Almighty: Even if it is impossible in the eyes of the remnant of this people in those days, will it also be impossible in my eyes? says the Lord Almighty." "Even if these things," he says, "seem impossible to you

when you look at how few have now gathered in the city, still it is not impossible for me to bring about so great a change in affairs that the city and everything in it will pass from their present misery into great prosperity." Having established on his own authority that what he has promised is possible, he adds further: "I will also gather to it from many places many other Israelites who are still in captivity, and I will restore them to live in their own land. And I will make myself known to them through my care, so that the events themselves will show that I am truly their God, since I grant them my favor securely and, exercising my justice, punish all who in any way try to harm them." To these promises he joins the following: "Thus says the Lord Almighty: Let your hands be strong, you who hear (p. 486) in these days these words from the mouth of the prophets, from the day the house of the Lord Almighty was founded and the temple was built." "Come then," he says, "heed these promises of mine, which I have often made to you through the prophets, and hasten with great diligence to complete my house, considering how great a change for the better your affairs have undergone ever since you have been occupied with this and with the building of my house." Verse 10. Then he shows the change by comparison with the earlier state of things: "For before those days the wages of men brought no profit, and there were no wages for beasts, and for those going out and those coming in there was no peace from affliction; and I will send all men each against his neighbor." "In former times," he says, "before the building of the temple, you were in great misery. Even when you applied yourselves to working your beasts, you gained nothing from your many labors. Everything was made profitless for you, because you enjoyed no peace, and all of you who went in and out of the city" (that is, those living in the city) "were constantly beset by all kinds of afflictions. What increased your affliction and your lack of peace was that many men from outside were stirred up against you, because I had turned away from you." These words clearly resemble in meaning those of the blessed prophet Haggai, (p. 487) who reproached them for their sloth. He recalled the evils that befell them when they were neglecting the building, and he showed how great a change for the better came to those who chose to devote themselves to building the divine temple. The blessed Zechariah says the same here too: "You were in many miseries," he says, "while you neglected the house. But now that you have changed your minds and show the proper zeal for the house, what has happened?" Verses 11–15. "And now I do not deal with the remnant of this people as in former days, says the Lord Almighty; but I will show peace: the vine shall yield its fruit, the earth shall yield its produce, and the heavens shall give their dew; and I will give the remnant

of my people all these things as an inheritance. And just as you were a curse among the nations, house of Judah and house of Israel, so I will save you, and you shall be a blessing." "What now befalls those who have returned will not be like what happened before. Out of the many who perished, few were left; but I will increase them again and bring them to a multitude, filling them with peace, granting them an abundance of fruits, and, to put it briefly, giving them the enjoyment of all good things. Just as in the past, because of my wrath, you appeared to all as deserving of punishment, (p. 488) so now through my care you will appear blessed in the eyes of all people." And encouraging them still further: "Take courage, and let your hands be strong. For thus says the Lord Almighty: Just as I resolved to do you harm when your fathers provoked me to anger, says the Lord Almighty, and did not relent, so I have now determined and resolved in these days to do good to Jerusalem and to the house of Judah." "Lay aside all fear and all despair; be of good cheer and great courage, and devote yourselves with great zeal to building the temple. Know that just as I formerly decreed punishment against you for the offenses your people committed against me, and carried it out without changing my mind, so now I will certainly carry out the promises I have made concerning Jerusalem and the whole tribe of Judah: that the city will be in prosperity and the people will share in great abundance." Verses 16–17. And he shows what they must do to have confidence that the promises are sure: "Take courage. These are the things you shall do: speak the truth each to his neighbor, and render judgments that make peace in your gates; let none of you devise evil in his heart against his neighbor, and do not love a false oath; for all these things I hate, says the Lord Almighty." (p. 489) "Have confidence, then, in my promises, if you take great care over what I counsel: deal with one another without deceit, and preserve your friendship with one another sincerely; take care to resolve all the quarrels that arise and to come together in a friendship that is fitting and leads to peace, settling your disputes and overlooking the faults that occur; and take every care not to swear falsely. These things are utterly hateful to me. But if you obey my other commands and are willing to carry out zealously what has been enjoined on you, [you will enjoy] good things [?]." Verses 18–19. "And the word of the Lord Almighty came to me, saying: Thus says the Lord Almighty: The fast of the fourth month, the fast of the fifth, the fast of the seventh, and the fast of the tenth shall become for the house of Judah joy and gladness and happy feasts; and you shall rejoice; so love truth and peace." For since earlier, when the foreigners sent by the kings of the nations were present,

[…] he found fault with the fasting, but put in its place what he thought it necessary to do, so as to instruct both his own people and the foreigners who were present at the same time. After the teaching that comes next, he necessarily adds these words, because he wants to show that he does not reject fasting as such, only fasting that is done improperly. If it is done as it should be, he very much welcomes it. So this is what he says: "Formerly, when you fasted for your sins, you mourned your own misfortunes, and it was for those sins that you were surrounded by so many calamities. But now that you have gained your return, it would be fitting for you to keep the fast not with mourning but with pleasure and gladness. Treat fasting as worthy of a festival, since it is enough in itself to bring you close to God. Fasting with pleasure will suit you if you take account of truth and peace." Then he shows how great are the good things for which they ought to keep their fasts with festivity and gladness, and adds: Verses 20–23. "Thus says the Lord Almighty: Yet many peoples shall come, and the inhabitants of many cities. The inhabitants of one city shall come together into one city, saying, 'Let us go and entreat the face of the Lord, and seek the face of the Lord Almighty. I will go too.'" It is nothing surprising, he says, if you do this, since many foreigners as well, who live in different cities, will gather together from each city. This is what "The inhabitants of one city shall come together into one city" means. They will rouse and urge one another to come here, so that they too may keep on entreating God and expecting every good thing from him. So each one will urge the other and say, "I will go too." He means that each, being eager for the thing, will rouse the others to the same eagerness. Then he means that a great many people from many different nations will come to Jerusalem to appease God for their own sins and to seek from him whatever they need. To this he adds: "Thus says the Lord Almighty: In those days ten men from all [the languages of] the nations shall take hold, they shall take hold of the hem of a Jewish man's garment, saying, 'We will go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.'" God will make the return of the remnant so splendid that many people from different nations who had shared in that calamity will see God's care for his people. They will take hold of any one of them at all and use him as their guide for the return to Jerusalem. All of them will be roused to this well enough, because the extraordinary things done for you have given them exact knowledge that God is with you. Here too "ten men" is not meant as a number; it means "many." Next he speaks of those among the nations, some of whom will do this out of fear of God, while others in their arrogance will pay it no heed. That is why he says:

Verses 1–2. "The burden of the word of the Lord in the land of Hadrach, and Damascus is his sacrifice. For the Lord watches over men and all the tribes of Israel, and Hamath within its borders." For the people of Damascus, he says, and those of Hadrach and Hamath, will offer sacrifices to God with great zeal, as to the Master of all things. He watches over human beings as his own works and servants, but gives special care to Israel. "Tyre and Sidon, because they thought themselves very wise: Tyre built herself a stronghold, and heaped up silver like dust and gold like the mud of the streets. Therefore the Lord will take possession of them, and will cast her power down into the sea, and she shall be consumed with fire." The Tyrians and Sidonians, however, [?] showed great pride and disdained my worship. They thought themselves self-sufficient, looked after the security of their walls, and piled up gold and silver like mud. So they will receive a punishment in proportion to their own folly. God will take possession of them and humble them all, handing over all their power to the sea that lies close by, and the city will be the work of fire set by the enemies who attack her. Having said this about Tyre and Sidon, he adds: Verses 5–7. "Ashkelon shall see and be afraid; Gaza too, and she shall be in great anguish; and Ekron, for she has been put to shame for her transgression. The king shall perish from Gaza, and Ashkelon shall not be inhabited, and foreigners shall dwell in Ashdod. I will pull down the arrogance of the Philistines. I will take their blood away from their mouth and their abominations from between their teeth. These too shall be left for our God, and they shall be like a commander of a thousand in Judah, and Ekron like a Jebusite." He means that the heaviest punishment will await the Philistines, because they abandoned the worship of God. He says it in varied ways, listing the cities one by one: Ashkelon will be seized with fear, Gaza will be in anguish, and Ekron will be put to shame among them for the sins for which she also pays the penalty. The king of Gaza will vanish too, Ashkelon will no longer be inhabited, and foreigners will live in Ashdod. He added these things not because one fate will befall Gaza, say, and another Ashkelon [?]. Rather, following his own idiom, he expressed what they share by dividing it up, meaning that all these things will happen to all the Philistines. That is why, after the list, he adds, "I will pull down the arrogance of the Philistines." He means: I will punish them for all their outrageous conduct. I will punish them in proportion to the blood of the Israelites that they shed, and along with them I will pull down all the idols they thought they were worshipping. The punishment brought on them will make many of them too seized with fear at what is happening, and they will take refuge in the worship of God. They will be counted with us and hold the rank of a commander of a thousand, having made themselves part of our portion in this way. Such people from Ekron will also be saved, no less than the Jebusite. Here too, by naming Ekron, he meant those

from the five satrapies who turned to what was right. He shows that those among them who are brought to their senses and turn to what is right will be counted with the people of Israel, and will be saved, snatched from the punishment brought upon them. Verses 8–10. "I will set up a rampart for my house, so that none may pass through or come back, and no oppressor shall come upon them any more, for now I have seen with my eyes." I will raise up strong help for those who belong to me. It will drive all the foreigners far away and will not let them set foot within the borders of my people, so that no one will dare to attack any more or to march against the land that belongs to me. For now I have decided to watch over them and to count them worthy of my providence. By "my house" he means the whole land of Israel, since it belongs to him. Then he makes clearer through whom this will happen and who has been put forward by God for this purpose: "Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; proclaim it, daughter of Jerusalem! Behold, your king is coming to you, righteous and saving. He is meek, mounted on a beast of burden and a young colt. I will utterly destroy the chariots from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem, and the bow of war shall be utterly destroyed, and the multitude, and peace from the nations." Be glad, then, Jerusalem, since God has put forward such a king for you. He has come to you and is able to save his own people through the divine favor that rests on him, and to bring every just punishment on their adversaries. He rides on a lowly animal because he has only just arrived from captivity, but through divine favor he will gain great power. So he will wipe out from Ephraim and from Jerusalem all the chariots of the adversaries, and every horse and every bow of war. He means that he will rout all the enemies, so that none of the adversaries will remain anywhere in the land of Judea. He will also wipe out, he says, a great multitude of the adversaries and leave them without any peace at all, since they are being crushed and destroyed by the [?] from him

It is clear, then, that these things are said here about Zerubbabel. I have been amazed at those who turn to strange interpretations, taking one part as being about Zerubbabel and another about Christ the Lord. This is nothing other than splitting the prophecy between Zerubbabel and Christ the Lord. Such a reading is the height of folly. The true sense of such passages is the one I know I have stated before: the law contained a shadow of everything concerning Christ the Lord. Scripture describes many of the extraordinary things that happened, whether to the people or to those chosen for some task, in rather exaggerated terms when speaking of those very persons, and in the obvious sense the wording does not hold true of them. But such words are found to be true when they are judged in relation to Christ the Lord himself. In everything he put an end to the shadow of the law and brought in his own truth, and so he rightly shows the truth of such sayings as well. Of this kind is what was said to Abraham [?]:

"In you and in your seed all the nations shall be blessed." In the obvious sense this refers to his descendants, but the truth of the saying holds in Christ the Lord, in whom the nations really were blessed. Of the same kind is what was said to blessed David: "His throne is like the sun before me, and like the moon established forever. I will establish his seed forever and ever, and his throne as the days of heaven." In the obvious sense he seems to speak of the successors in whom the kingdom was to continue, but the truth of the matter is shown in Christ the Lord, whose kingdom truly is brighter than any sun and more lasting than any heaven. Of the same kind is the saying "His soul was not abandoned to Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption." Blessed David said this in exaggerated terms about the people of Israel, but it is seen to have come true in actual fact in Christ the Lord. That is why blessed Peter rightly used the saying: "His soul was not abandoned to Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption." One could find many such passages, too many to list now. They were once spoken in exaggerated terms and did not hold exactly true of what was said, but they are found to be so, as has been said, in Christ the Lord. This passage is of the same kind. He was speaking about Zerubbabel, who came from the line of David and led the Jews in keeping with God's purpose. But the matter was seen to find its truth, beyond dispute, in Christ the Lord. In Zerubbabel's case the punishment of the nations was small and the deliverance of his own people modest. That is why he goes on to add, fittingly, "He will utterly destroy the chariots from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem," showing that what Zerubbabel would contribute to them was freedom from wars. But the saying proved true in Christ the Lord, in whom one can truly rejoice with a lawful and everlasting joy. He is truly righteous, since he judges the whole world [?] with this, and he is truly saving, since he brings all people out of destruction into a salvation that is everlasting and secure. Here, then, it was said about Zerubbabel, and the words were measured to fit the one about whom they were written. In the Gospels, however, it has been applied to Christ the Lord, who is seen in every respect to be great and exalted [?] … and righteous and saving, and who makes his benefits lasting, wholly unchangeable and incapable of any change. This, then, is the most consistent and fitting thing both to say and to think. But to say that part of the passage was spoken about Christ, then to move on to Zerubbabel, then from him back to Christ, and then from Christ the Lord back to Zerubbabel again, is nothing other than first making the prophecy incoherent, and then dividing the words of Scripture equally between the servant and the Master. [?] And to argue, as proof that what was said does not apply to Zerubbabel,

that the prophet said "is coming," when Zerubbabel had long since returned from captivity with the rest, is pointless hair-splitting and shows inexperience in the divine Scriptures. Take "He was led like a sheep to the slaughter." It speaks not of something in the future but of something already done, for it does not say "He will be led" but "He was led." By the reasoning of these very wise men, then, not even this would apply to Christ the Lord. They ought to know that Scripture shifts between tenses in varied ways. We have shown this well enough, with many examples, in our commentary on the Psalms and on the prophets. Here, in any case, if one judges by time, the form of the word does not fit the coming of Christ the Lord either. That coming was to happen a long time later, yet he did not say "He will come," which would have suited a future event, but "He is coming," which is normally said of things that are near and happening at once. By this reasoning of theirs, many other things in the prophet will also be found to have been written for no purpose. He also says that Joshua's filthy garments, which signified the captivity, are now being taken off, and that the priestly attire is now being put on him. Yet it is clear that Joshua too had come back with Zerubbabel, freed from captivity and already established in the dignity of the priesthood. That is why the blessed prophet Haggai also clearly addresses Zerubbabel and Joshua together about the need to see to the building of the temple. The prophet also says that the measure of punishment, now taken away together with Israel's sin, was carried off to Babylon. Yet it was Cyrus, king of the Persians, who released the people from captivity and destroyed Babylon, while the prophet clearly says these things under King Darius, who was the fourth after Cyrus. So by the rules of those who lay down such laws, he had no business saying that things which had happened long before were happening now. But clearly the events had already happened, and the prophet sees them through revelation as happening now. In this way all the people would learn, even about events that had already taken place, that nothing had happened by chance, and that every good thing done for them had been accomplished by God's will and decree. So it was not at all unlikely that the prophet, speaking here too of what would come to the people through the rule of Zerubbabel, whom God had purposed and appointed for this, should say, "He is coming, righteous and saving." He shows by this that Zerubbabel is present for these purposes and has been chosen by God for kingship in order to do the things that, in what follows, the prophet says were done for the people through him. Verses 10–12. But let this much be said for the sake of more precise instruction. The prophet, speaking about Zerubbabel and indeed now prophesying

about him, even if as a prophet he too had some vision of the future, adds: "He shall rule over the waters from sea to sea, and from the rivers to the outlets of the earth." Here too he speaks in exaggerated terms, as is customary, meaning that Zerubbabel will overcome many adversaries and hold a great deal of land, which he will hand over to the Jews to live in. The seventy-first psalm of blessed David is of the same kind. In the form of a prayer it points to the prosperity under Solomon, where it says: "His name shall endure before the sun, and before the moon for generation after generation. He shall have dominion from sea to sea, from the rivers to the ends of the inhabited world." Is it not obvious that these things too were said in exaggerated terms? Then he adds: "And you, by the blood of your covenant, have sent your prisoners out of a pit that has no water. You shall dwell in a stronghold, you prisoners of the congregation, and in return for one day of your exile I will repay you double." In these words above all he points to what would happen concerning Gog in the days of Zerubbabel. He says to Zerubbabel that he will kill many and shed the blood of many, and by destroying the adversaries he will secure for himself his kingship over the people, as if by a covenant. He will free everyone from the greatest dangers, in which they were living as if in a pit with no water, meaning in miseries that offered no comfort and no relief. "And you who were once prisoners, the congregation of the Jews, will go on living in great security in your own homes, under the protection of your leader. So, in return for what you suffered while you lived in captivity, the good things now given to you in repayment will be far greater." Verses 13–17. Then, fittingly, he adds: "Therefore I have bent you for myself, Judah, like a bow; I have filled it with Ephraim. I will rouse the children of Zion against the children of the Greeks, and I will wield you like a warrior's sword." He says Judah and Ephraim so as to denote the whole body of the Jews by its chief part. I will make you strong, then, like a bow bent against the enemies. You will charge with great eagerness against all the foreigners who have attacked you and make a great slaughter of them, as great as one would expect from a man who is always plying his sword in battles, wars and killing. And to show where this will come from: "The Lord will appear over them, and his arrow will go forth like lightning. The Lord God Almighty will sound the trumpet and go forth in the storm of his threatening. The Lord Almighty will shield them, and they will devour them and bury them under sling-stones. They will drink their blood like wine, and they will fill the bowls with oil as at an altar." These things will happen, he says, because God, as your general, turns a fearsome eye on those who oppose you and sends swords against them like lightning. And as if with a

trumpet, he will rouse you all to war by his own power and go before you, shaking all the adversaries with his threat. Working alongside you, he will give you so much help that you will remain unharmed while you destroy all the adversaries and bury them under volleys of stones. So eager will you be to destroy them, and so much of their blood will be shed, that you will all but drink it. Then after the victory you will fill bowls with oil and bring them to God as a sacrifice, as a proof of the loving-kindness through which you gained such power. Following on from this, he adds that God will save all his own, guarding them unharmed like sheep. He also gives the reason: "For holy stones are rolling upon his land. For whatever is good is his, and whatever is beautiful is his." There are many among you, he says, who care for virtue. They seem to crawl on the earth along with everyone else and go unnoticed by most people. But for their sake God will not neglect the rest either, since everything good and beautiful is his work. Because he takes the sufferings of the saints and of those who look to virtue as his own, he is ready to do good to others for their sake too. Then, announcing to them the prosperity that will follow the slaughter of the enemies, he adds:

Verses 1–3. "Ask the Lord for rain in its season, early and late. The Lord has made displays of his power, and he will give them winter rain, and to each one grass in the field." Ask him, then, for rains suited to bearing crops. He is accustomed to stir up the air with great terror and to strike awe into everyone on earth by the greatness of what he does, and he is able to give you the rain you need, so that everything necessary for you grows from the earth. By "grass" he means crops in general, as also in "Let the earth bring forth grass of herbage." There too it is clear that he means everything that grows from seed in the earth. Then, to correct them, he again reminds them of what had befallen them before, and adds: "For the soothsayers spoke troubles, and the diviners spoke false visions and false dreams; they comforted in vain. Therefore they withered like sheep and were afflicted, because there was no healing. My anger was kindled against the shepherds, and I will punish the lambs." Formerly, he says, you listened to the diviners, who told you everything with a great deal of falsehood. You neglected my prophets and preferred to believe what those men said. Then, finding your condition incurable and beyond correction, I handed you over to punishment like sheep. I turned one and the same anger against both the rulers and their subjects, and by it I destroyed the one and the other alike. That was when you suffered such things because of them. Verses 4–7. But what now? "The Lord Almighty will visit his flock, the house

…of Judah,” and what follows. To avoid being long-winded, I will not set out the whole wording for now. Instead, by God's grace, I will state the sense and fit it to the prophet's words so that readers can understand them. He says: “I will take care of the house of Judah, whom I made my own flock. In war they will be strong against their adversaries, stronger than a mighty horse that a warrior drives against the enemy. For I foresaw that Zerubbabel must be taken from him, I mean from Judah. So I took him from there and set him over the kingdom, and I made him strong and breathing fury against his adversaries. I did this because I had determined once and for all that the rulers would come from the tribe of Judah, and they ought always to lead the people in war. (p. 505) They will so overpower their adversaries in war that they will trample them like mud on the roads under the feet of passers-by.” In this way, he says, the enemy will lie exposed, suffering harm and unable to devise anything in return. “With confidence they will draw up their ranks against all their adversaries, trusting that divine help is with them. Then those among the enemy who pride themselves on their horses will be put to shame, while these will appear great and strong by my help.” He says “the house of Judah and the house of Joseph” to mean the people, naming the whole by a part. “I will give them a secure dwelling in their own land, since I have loved them and decided not to cast them out of my providence. I will always be with them, and when they ask for my help in their distress, I will hear them. They will prevail in battle over their adversaries.” Here again “those of Ephraim” refers to the people by naming a part. The result is that, having conquered by slaughtering their adversaries, they rejoice in mind more than men filled with wine. Verses 8–12. Their children too will see this and will be glad because of the help that comes to them from God. “So I will give the signal to them all, as if with a trumpet, and gather them and receive them, and free them from every distress. Then they will live securely in their own homes and increase in number as in former times. (p. 505) When they are crowded in their own land because of their own great numbers, they will be scattered among many foreign peoples as well, and they will overpower them and take possession of their land and live in it. All of these, remembering me because of the greatness of what has happened, will not only do no harm but will take every care of them.” This is what is meant by “They will rear their children and return.” It means: they will do these things because they have turned toward me and toward knowledge of me. “Then I will change their lot and bring back those of them who are scattered everywhere, whether in Egypt or in the land of the Assyrians, to their own land. They will live in their own places, and none of them will live outside them any longer. They will pass through a great multitude, hemmed in by the multitude of their adversaries but overpowering them by my power. They will destroy all their strength, [?] and punish those who rage against you like a surging sea, and by their own punishment and

slaughter they will bring so many to nothing.” This is what is meant by “And all the depths will be dried up” [?]. It means: he will dry up those who are so many. “No strength will be left any longer to the Assyrians to do such a thing against them, nor to the Egyptians.” The Egyptians had held them in slavery long ago, and the Assyrians later carried them off as captives. They will be rid of them all.
