In what way? “And I will strengthen them in the Lord their God, (p. 506) and they will boast in his name, says the Lord.” That is: “I will make them strong and unassailable by all their adversaries, so that they take pride both in my name and in my help.” Having said this, he continues:

Verses 1–3. “Open your doors, O Lebanon, and let fire devour your cedars. Let the pine wail, for the cedar has fallen, for the mighty have been utterly ruined. Wail, oaks of Bashan, for the dense forest has been torn down. Hear the cry of the shepherds lamenting, for their greatness has been ruined. Hear the cry of the lions moaning, for the pride of the Jordan has been ruined.” He had said, “I will bring them from everywhere, from Egypt and from the land of the Assyrians,” and that they would never again suffer anything like this. So it follows that he now turns his words to those who were holding them, and says this: “You great ones, who pride yourselves on your size like the cedars of Lebanon and show off your own strength: stop fighting against those who belong to me. Open what is yours as if you were opening doors, and let them all leave you without fear and return to their own land. (p. 507) Do this before my punishment destroys the mighty among you like fire, and the weaker wail when they see the mighty fall.” This is what he means by “Let the pine wail, for the cedar has fallen.” When they see the mighty destroyed, they will naturally despair of themselves. All who pride themselves on any power will wail as they see their own multitude destroyed like a dense forest, while the divine punishment falls on them like fire. “Your leaders, who still dare to resist those who belong to me, will lament when they see all their strength destroyed. Those who trusted in their own strength like lions will also lament, when they see that all who were arrogant against the Jordan have fallen into misery.” Since the river Jordan was part of Judea, the prophet named the river to indicate the land of the Israelites. In short, through all that he foretold, he made known how greatly their condition would improve. Jerusalem would be restored to its former prosperity, with the priesthood and the kingship given back to the nation and the people gathered from everywhere. God would punish their enemies and establish them in a great abundance of good things. He would also give great support to Zerubbabel, who had been chosen for the kingship, and by this they would be strong against their adversaries and would prevail even over the forces of Gog, countless and invincible as they were.

But the Jews did not make good use of the prosperity and peace they had long enjoyed. (p. 508) They changed and ran aground on what was worse, and so everything turned out the opposite for them. Great disorder and confusion seized the nation as the divine laws came to be neglected among them. Some of the lesser people, inclining toward what was worse, naturally fell out with the high priests and leaders of the whole people, who governed it very strictly. Since they could do nothing against these men because of the respect the people had for them, they went to the kings of the Macedonian succession who ruled the regions of Syria. They managed to put their leaders in danger, men who served as priests lawfully and worthily. The high priesthood was transferred to others, against the order of the divine laws, as the kings saw fit. These men all but sold the nation to the kings and wrongly bought the leadership of the people with money. They did a great many evils and threw the whole people into disorder and confusion. The strictness of the laws was completely overthrown, and in its place came disorder and the doing of everything contrary to the divine laws. Because of all this the Jews were beset with countless evils. Then the Maccabees, who could not bear the offence against divine things, (p. 509) and did not think it tolerable to keep quiet while the divine laws were being so transgressed and such great impiety had been brought in and held sway among them, took up war against the kings of the Macedonian succession. Not a few of those who belonged to the nation imitated their resolve and joined in that war. The Macedonians inflicted countless evils on the city and the temple of God, in short, on the whole nation, more than could easily be told. But these things were set right when God, pleased with the resolve of Maccabaeus and those with him, gave them his support. Against all hope they prevailed over the kings, although they were few and were fighting against great power, and so they were able to restore proper order to the nation. The prophet therefore received knowledge of these things too by divine revelation, as was most necessary. He makes known to the people what will happen and hands down knowledge of it in writing to those who come after, in the words about these things that follow. He begins this way: Verses 4–5. “Thus says the Lord Almighty: Shepherd the sheep for slaughter.” Divine Scripture often makes the future known in the form of a command, as in “Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion.” Yet rejoicing is not a matter of command: when pleasant things are present one cannot help rejoicing, and when they are absent one cannot rejoice. But Scripture wanted to make known the joy that would come to them from Zerubbabel's rule, and so it began the statement as a command. (p. 510) A little later we read: “Ask the Lord for rain in season, early and late.” Clearly no one in need would fail to ask if he knew for certain that it would be given,

yet he wanted to say, “God will give you rain abundantly and in its season,” and so he made known what was to come in the form of a command. In the same way here too he foretells, in the form of a command, the evils that would come upon the people. He is saying something like this: “What I do for the people will be as I have already said. The nation will enjoy such great blessings, Jerusalem will have such abundance, and they will overpower their enemies and gather much wealth from them. But they will not use their prosperity as they should. They will look toward what is worse, and they will be under shepherds who lead them like sheep left exposed to slaughter.” Blessed David says something similar about the same people: “We were counted as sheep for slaughter.” He means that they will be thought worthy of no care at all, and will suffer everything as people handed over only to be slaughtered. Then he describes how: “Those who acquired them slaughtered them and did not repent.” The kings who ruled them did not care for them as their own possessions but killed them mercilessly as enemies. This is what “did not repent” shows. “And those who sold them said, ‘Blessed be the Lord, we have become rich.’” Those who sold the nation to the kings and drew revenue from it were so far from being ashamed of such greed (p. 511) that they even thought such wealth deserved thanksgiving. “And their shepherds felt nothing for them.” The oversight of them was entrusted to men who were unwilling to show them any mercy. Verse 6. “Therefore I will no longer spare those who live in the land, says the Lord.” That is: “Because of these things I will abandon them and grant them no providence of mine.” “And behold, I hand the people over, each into the hands of his neighbour and into the hands of his king, and they will cut down the land of Canaan.” “I leave them to suffer incurable harm both from the wicked among their own people and from the kings who make war on them, since by what they do they make themselves deserving of it.” And so nearly all who live in Judea will be killed. This is what “they will cut down the land” means. No help will be given them by God to free them from the domination of their adversaries. “By their own deeds they have exposed themselves to slaughter, and I will lead them to it under the eyes of the Canaanites, as such people would naturally be led.” “I will shepherd the sheep for slaughter” means “I will lead them to slaughter,” not as though he did it himself, but by permitting it. It is also customary for divine Scripture to speak of divine permission as if it were an action. (p. 512) An example is “You turned our paths aside from your way.” God did not turn them aside, but he allowed them to suffer things that were enough to turn them from what was right. And “into the land of Canaan”

means under the eyes of foreigners. It was the heavier blow that those who had known their former prosperity should suddenly see them caught up in such evils. Verses 7–8. “And I will take for myself two staffs; one I called Beauty, and the second I called Cord; and I will shepherd the sheep.” He says: “I gave them offices that served for their governance, the kingship and the priesthood. These above all should have been their adornment and held them together as they ought. Since they have become wicked in character, I will take these away from them, and from now on I will lead them to punishment.” What he said above, “I will shepherd the sheep for slaughter,” he repeats here again when he says, “And I will shepherd the sheep.” “And I will remove the three shepherds in one month.” Here too he does not mean the number three. From Joshua son of Jozadak until those times they had been shepherded by worthy high priests. So he says: “I will bring all those worthy priests to an end at one time, when these people turn to what is worse and choose for themselves the worse and unlawful priesthood instead of the better and lawful one.” As usual, he attributes to God the evils that befell them, so that all the worse things that came upon them would be seen as a form of punishment. Blessed Paul does the same when he says at one point, (p. 513) “God gave them up to a debased mind.” This is not as though God gave them up. Rather, Paul counts as part of the punishment the worse choice of those who lean toward it, since such people are estranged from divine care and so take on an irreversible inclination toward what is worse. So here too he is saying that the oversight of those who once shepherded them well will cease at one time, which is what “in one month” means, and that they will be under wicked men who used this leadership unlawfully. “And my soul will be weighed down against them.” “For this reason above all I conceive the greatest hatred against them, when I see that they have chosen such things in place of such things, thrown away the better and chosen the worse.” Then he shows that he brought this punishment on them justly, because they had become evil by their own wickedness: “For their souls too howled against me.” “I adopted this attitude toward them,” he says, “because they too, like wild beasts, turned their rage against me. What they did to the worthy priests they plainly dared to do against me.” Compare what was said to Samuel: “It is not you they have rejected, but me.” Verses 9–10. “And I said, I will not shepherd you.” “From then on I stopped shepherding them and taking proper care of them as my own sheep.” He showed that in the passage above “I will shepherd” stood for “I will hand them over to punishment.” (p. 514) Here at any rate he has clearly written “I will not shepherd,” meaning shepherding with care, and that they will no longer receive this attention. He then adds:

“What is dying, let it die, and what is failing, let it fail, and let those who are left each eat the flesh of his neighbour.” He says: “I let each receive punishment from his own wickedness, as they destroy one another through quarrels and fights and diligent plotting.” “And I will take my beautiful staff and cast it away, to break my covenant which I made with all the peoples of the earth.” “I will take away the most excellent and best priesthood, which lies somewhere on the ground, cast down by those who threw it down. Because of this I will also turn the attitude of those outside the nation the other way. Foreigners who used to hurry eagerly to my temple, out of reverence for the rites lawfully performed there, will also stop doing so. The confusion and disorder that prevail there will keep them from going up to the temple as they used to.” This then is what he means by “to break my covenant which I made with all the peoples of the earth”: “I will put an end to what used to happen, when even foreigners came.” Again he attributes to himself what results from the wickedness of others, so that, in short, all the worse things appear as signs of wrath. Verses 11–12. “And it will be broken on that day, (p. 515) and the Canaanites, the sheep guarded for me, will know that it is the word of the Lord.” He says: “Then the worship that foreigners offered at the temple will cease, and with it, naturally, the covenant I made with them is dissolved. But those who are truly mine will become known even to foreigners, because they take great care to keep what pleases me. It will also be known that there is a divine decree that hands the wicked over to worse things, while making it so plain that those who seek what is right, few as they are, belong to me [?]. For this reason they are counted worthy of such providence from me that they easily overcome their adversaries, many and powerful as they are.” Next he wants to show the proven character of his own people. He means Maccabaeus and those with him, who chose to wage war on behalf of the nation and the divine laws against the Macedonian kings. So he continues: “And I will say to them: If it seems good to you, give me my wages, or refuse.” He says: “They will be so proven and steadfast toward me that I can confidently say to them: ‘If it pleases you to be under me and to be counted worthy of my oversight, then pay me the wages of your goodwill and obedience. But if it is too hard, while you turn toward me, to suffer all the evils that the enemy now forces you to endure, then openly renounce my oversight.’” (p. 516) This is like what the Lord said to the disciples: “Do you also want to go away?” He did not say this to turn them away from being with him, but by the

…showing them to be more steadfast by his own voice. In the same way he says here too: "I put this before them with confidence, knowing that they will accept suffering harm for my sake, or that they enjoy better things when they receive my oversight." So he adds: "And they weighed out my wages, thirty pieces of silver." Here too he does not mean thirty as a number. He means: "They repaid me with great goodwill of their own, and they went on showing gratitude…"

Verses 13–15. "And the Lord said to me: Put them into the furnace, and see whether it is approved, as I was approved on their behalf. And I took the thirty pieces of silver and threw them into the house of the Lord, into the furnace." He means: "I have put their disposition toward me through the trial of misfortunes, as if through a smelting, to see whether they have proved as true toward me as I toward them. That is, I wanted to see whether their goodwill toward me is as firm as the oversight I firmly give them." So he has thrown them "into the house of the Lord, into the furnace." He fittingly says "into the house," since the whole of their struggle was on its behalf while the enemy was outraging it. He means that they were shown to be approved through the smelting of misfortunes as well. (p. 517) Then, having spoken of the goodwill of his own people, he supplies what was missing from the earlier passage. Since he had said above, "I took my staff, Beauty, and threw it away," he now adds: "And I threw away the second staff, the Measuring-Line, to break the covenant between Judah and Israel." He means: "I took from them both the kingship and the good things that came from it because of their wicked ways." He called the priesthood "Beauty" because it makes people seemly and approved before God. He called the kingship "Measuring-Line" because it measures out and marks off what is fitting for its subjects. Compare the saying, "To you I will give the land of Canaan as the measured portion of your inheritance," which means, "I divided off the land of Canaan, marked it out from all the earth, and gave it to you as an inheritance." Verses 15–16. Then, to show that they will be caught up in these misfortunes for a very long time, he adds: "And the Lord said to me: Take for yourself once more the implements of a shepherd, an inexperienced shepherd. For behold, I will raise up an inexperienced shepherd in the land. He will not look after what is failing, nor seek what is scattered, nor set right what is broken. He will devour the flesh of the choice ones and wrench their ankle-bones." Here again he states what will happen in the form of a command. "For the people's misery," he says, "continues because of those who shepherd them badly, who will handle the priesthood badly." By "a shepherd's implements" he means the works belonging to the office of the priesthood, by which that ministry is customarily performed. "Men will lay hold of the priesthood," (p. 518) he says, "who have no experience of the matter and do not know how to do anything that is required. They do not look after the weak, they make no search for those who stray, and to the injured

they apply no healing at all. Nor do they care for the healthy, that they may keep their own strength. On the contrary, they devour the flesh, and if possible the ankle-bones too, of those who look toward what is better, mistreating them in every way. They harm some of them themselves and others through their associates. Since they themselves incline to the worse, they are hostile to those who love what is right." Upon this he fittingly adds, with great indignation, showing how very great God's anger is at what was happening: "O you who shepherd vain things and have abandoned the sheep! A sword on his arm and on his right eye! His arm shall wither away completely, and his right eye shall be utterly blinded." "These things will not go unpunished," he says, "for you who have used your shepherding for evil and handed God's people over to slaughter. You will pay the penalty in your arms and your eyes: the arms will wither entirely and the eyes will be blinded." He means that through divine punishment they will be stripped of all their strength, and of the authority that made them appear to oversee others. To this he adds:

Verses 1–3. "The burden of the word of the Lord concerning Israel, says the Lord, who stretches out the heaven, lays the foundations of the earth, and forms the spirit of man within him." He means: (p. 519) "I say these things as they were shown to me by revelation from God. He is the maker of all that exists, and he also made man, giving him a soul and a rational will." He means that God permitted these things to happen as he willed. As Lord of all, he also permits human beings, whenever he wishes, to do what seems good to them. What then does he say? "Behold, I make Jerusalem like a shaken doorway to all the peoples round about, and in Judea there shall be a siege against Jerusalem." "Because of the wickedness of its inhabitants," he says, "I have handed Jerusalem over to the greatest weakness. Anyone who wishes may attack it and shake it as they please." This is how the war from the kings of Macedonia came to be stirred up against them. "And it shall be in that day that I will make Jerusalem a stone trampled by all the nations. Everyone who tramples it will mock it utterly, and all the nations of the earth will be gathered against it." From then on foreigners will tread upon it, and all who tread upon it will be free to do whatever they please to it, since many will be gathered against it. That is the reason. Then, having described the misfortunes as happening by God's permission, he goes on to describe the change for the better that they will have when God wills it. Verses 4–5. "In that day, says the Lord Almighty, I will strike every horse with bewilderment and its rider with madness. But upon the house of Judah I will open my eyes, and I will strike all the horses of the peoples with blindness. And all the commanders of thousands of Judah will say in their hearts: We shall find for ourselves the inhabitants of Jerusalem in the Lord Almighty, their God." (p. 520) "For I [?] will not let their experience of misfortunes be drawn out to the end. I will give help to all of them at once,

and through those who look to my help" (he means the Maccabees) "I will strike down all the cavalry of the enemy. Even their riders will fall into utter madness at the greatness of their calamities. This is what I will do to the enemy. But to those of the tribe of Judah, from which the Maccabees who led the war also came, I will give my watchful care and protection. I will cast a kind of blindness over all the enemy's cavalry and so make it powerless against those who belong to me." Then the leaders of Judah will at last perceive that God has given them freedom to go up again to Jerusalem with confidence and to live in it with their former prosperity. They will attend to everything the inhabitants of that place ought to attend to if they mean to please God. Next he adds: Verses 6–8. "In that day I will make the commanders of Judah like a firebrand among stubble. They will devour all the peoples round about, on the right and on the left. Jerusalem will once again dwell by itself in Jerusalem. (p. 521) And the Lord will save the tents of Judah as at the beginning, so that the boasting of the house of David and the pride of the inhabitants of Jerusalem may not be exalted over Judah." "Then," he says, "I will make the leaders of the tribe of Judah so strong against the enemy that they will consume them all with blows and slaughter, like a fire that has fallen on wood or stubble. So great a slaughter of the enemy will they make on this side and that and on every side. From then on Jerusalem will be left to live in peace, suffering no harassment from the enemy. For I will keep safe all those of the tribe of Judah and those who belong to them, and bring them back to their former prosperity. Then those descended from David and all the Jews who live in Jerusalem will stop priding themselves on their own good fortune. The events themselves will make them see that formerly they prospered because I willed it, not because they could secure anything for themselves by their own power. When they were cast out of my care because of their own wickedness, they were exposed as utterly weak and unable to help themselves." And he tells how this will happen: "And it shall be in that day that the Lord will shield the inhabitants of Jerusalem. In that day the weakest among them will be like David, and the house of David like the house of God, like an angel of the Lord before him." "For then they will all perceive that with my help they have such power against the enemy that, though they were weak a little before, (p. 522) they will be known to have power against their foes as great as David was seen to have in his own time by divine aid. The house of David will again be envied and admired." For those who came from it and from his tribe and led the people were seen to be so strong against the foreigners that everyone fled to them for refuge as to a house of God, which gives much help to those who take refuge in it, or as to an angel sent to strike the enemy. In the same way, once, when the Assyrians

had come against Jerusalem, everyone fled for refuge to the house of God, and from there it came about that the angel came upon the enemy and destroyed so great a multitude of them. And how will this come about?

Verses 9–10. "And it shall be in that day that I will seek to destroy all the nations that come against Jerusalem. And I will pour out on the house of David and on the inhabitants of Jerusalem a spirit of grace and compassion." "For then I will wipe out all who have attacked Jerusalem. But on the house of David" (by which he means those from it who lead the people) "and on all who belong to Jerusalem I will show great grace and kindness, providing every kind of care for them." And what will come of this? "And they will look to me, whom they pierced, and they will mourn for him as one mourns for a beloved son, and grieve for him as one grieves for a firstborn." "Then those who formerly chose the opposite of what pleases me, (p. 523) and showed such daring against me, will perceive their own folly and lawlessness. In their repentance they will make great lamentation, such as one makes in grief at the death of a firstborn." Then he says that many in Jerusalem will repent and share in this lamentation. Formerly they chose the opposite of what was right, but when they saw the nation's change for the better, they were naturally bound to repent of their own transgressions. He goes on to list the tribes one by one, showing that each will mourn by itself. In short, he means that repentance will seize all who had chosen the worse. Formerly the nation had inclined greatly toward the worse, and later there was a great change for the better through the leadership of the Maccabees, who obtained divine aid. The enemy was destroyed by them, good order was restored to the city and to God's temple, and the divine laws and the care of the priesthood once more received the zeal they deserved. So the change necessarily brought them to repent of the impieties and transgressions on which they had formerly run aground. Having described the lamentation and the repentance, he speaks of the change for the better, which above all gave rise to such great repentance in everyone.

Verses 1–7. "For in that day," he says, "every place will be opened to the house of David." He means that all will readily receive them as leaders, (p. 524) running to them with every eagerness, since by divine aid they had shown themselves pious and strong against the enemy. Then he shows how, through the rule of the Maccabees, religion too will be restored to what it ought to be. They saw to it that everything worse was abolished and what pleases God prevailed: "And it shall be in that day, says the Lord of hosts, that I will destroy the names of the idols from the land, and they will no longer be remembered. And I will remove the false prophets and the unclean spirit from the land." "For then, through their oversight, all the worship of idols will be taken away,

and all the deceit of the false prophets will be brought to an end, and no one will dare to practise anything of the kind." To show how complete the victory of the good will be, he says that if anyone at that time dares to come forward and pretend to foretell the future, moved by a foreign spirit, he will no longer receive pardon or mercy for this daring and transgression from anyone, not even from those who begot him. They will all but bind him with their own hands [?] and hand him over to punishment because he dares to use false and deluded prophecy. So all who attempt such things at that time will be covered with shame, and the misfortunes that come upon them will turn them to repentance and mourning. (p. 525) This is what he means by "they will put on a garment of hair." Compare the words of blessed David, "You tore off my sackcloth and girded me with gladness," meaning, "You took away my mourning and filled me with gladness." "Such people," he says, "will turn to repentance and put on the garb of mourning. They will disown their own deceit, saying that they know nothing and will have nothing to do with such things. From now on they will busy themselves with working the land, the trade they learned from their parents from their very first day." And if anyone asks them, as they still bear the fresh wounds from those who beat them, where they got these, they will declare plainly, denying nothing, that they received the lashes in their own house for attempting what was not fitting. They received them from those to whom they seemed dearest of all, as sons to their parents. Yet the parents did not spare them when they sinned, since they set their concern for piety above natural affection. Verse 7. The prophet has spoken of the change of affairs for the better: how through the leadership of the Maccabees the enemy was destroyed and the nation came into great good order, so that all impiety and lawlessness was removed from them and everything that accorded with the divine laws prevailed. Then, as if by the same revelation he had received through the working of the Holy Spirit, he was inspired and saw exactly what would happen: what the affairs of the Jews would become and from what state, what correction their affairs would receive through the leadership of the Maccabees, and into what disorder they had fallen (p. 526) through the wickedness of those who received the priesthood and the leadership of the people from the kings, contrary to what was fitting and to the divine laws, and filled everything with the greatest confusion. Filled with the greatest indignation at the wickedness of those who had caused so great an evil, he says: "Sword, awake against the shepherd and against the man who is his fellow citizen, says the Lord Almighty." Here again he announces the future in the form of a command. Turning his speech, as it were, to the sword itself, he says: "Rise up, O sword, against those who have used their leadership so badly, and

against all members of the nation who were eager to share in their wickedness. Strike the shepherd, and let the sheep be scattered. With your blow bring death on those who have used their leadership of the people so badly, and as you strike them, scatter in punishment the whole company of those who acted with them." Having said this in the form of a command to announce what would happen, he adds what follows, using a form of speech that fits what is being announced: "And I will turn my hand against the little shepherds." "For if there are any under the leaders who wish to share in their wicked leadership, and who are themselves eager to lead the way into evil by virtue of whatever rank they seem to have been entrusted with, I will punish them as well." Such men are the ones he calls "little shepherds." Verses 8–9. Then he shows that the punishment is just: "And it shall be in that day, in all the land, says the Lord, that two parts of it will be destroyed and perish, (p. 527) but the third will be left in it. And I will bring the third through fire, and refine them as silver is refined, and test them as gold is tested. He will call on my name, and I will hear him. I will say, 'This is my people,' and he will say, 'The Lord is my God.'" "The facts themselves show," he says, "that such people will suffer a just punishment. They turned the nation so far toward the worse that two parts of the people inclined to evil and were handed over to punishment." By "two parts" he means the majority. "Yet even so, not a few lovers of what is right will be left, even though they are fewer than the others." This is what he means by "the third." "They were tested, as if through fire, by the greatness of the misfortunes brought upon them, and they gave greater proof of their virtue. They endured a great many misfortunes, yet never fell away from their goodwill toward me. They looked to my help and obtained it. For I made them my own and promised them my care, and they placed everything in me, entrusting everything to my lordship and protection." So again, having spoken of the triumph of evil brought about by the wickedness of those who led badly, and of the punishment that this brought upon them, he sets beside it the care he steadfastly showed to those who remained devoted to him.

Verses 1–4. "Behold, a day of the Lord is coming, and the spoil taken from you will be divided in your midst. And I will gather all the nations against Jerusalem for battle. The city will be taken, the houses plundered and the women defiled. Half of the city will go out into captivity, but the rest of my people will not be cut off from the city." (p. 528) "For a time will come," he says, "when a great many foreigners will march against Jerusalem and strip everything within it. The city will be taken by the enemy, everything in the houses will be plundered, and those who have broken into the city will behave with such drunken violence that neither

…to keep from outraging the bodies of the women, and to take a great many of the city captive. Yet even when these things happen in this way because of the wickedness of others, those who enjoyed my goodwill were kept unharmed in the city by my care. Then, in what follows, he speaks of the divine help through which everything was changed for the better for them under the leadership of the Maccabees. God, he says, will go before his own people as in a battle line, according to the custom of war, leading them as their general and drawing up his ranks against their enemies. And standing, he says, on the Mount of Olives opposite Jerusalem, he will shake the mountain and set in motion everything before the city and the city itself, so that the mountain will seem to be split in various directions by the terror of the shaking, and the events of that time will seem like what happened in the earthquake that, as it turned out, was brought about by divine wrath in the reign of Uzziah. He says all this hyperbolically, as is his custom, (p. 529) meaning that through the greatness of the help he gives his own people and his anger against their enemies, everything will seem, as it were, to be shaken. He used the comparison with Uzziah because Uzziah too, though he had nothing to do with the priesthood, tried to lay hold of it; and for this reason God displayed his anger through the greatness of the earthquake. In the same way now, he says, because of those who with impious intent have thrust aside the order of the law and have laid hands on the priesthood improperly, God will display his anger in full, shaking everything, for the punishment of the enemies and the salvation of his own. To this he adds: Verses 5–7. “And the Lord my God will come, and all the holy ones with him.” From the very greatness of the events, he says, God will appear as though he had come from somewhere far off to help us, bringing his whole army with him. He means the invisible powers; for he calls these “the holy ones,” since they are accustomed to serve him in everything he decides concerning human affairs. “And on that day there will be no light, but cold and frost there will be for one day.” He does not mean literally no light, and cold and frost, but speaks as he usually does when he says, “The sun will be darkened,” and “The sun will set for them,” and similar things, because people in calamities have no perception of light but seem then to be in some kind of darkness. So here too he says: people will seem, because of the greatness of what is happening, not even to see light; and as though shaken by cold and frost they will remain trembling and quaking, gnashing their teeth at the greatness of the evils that will come from the divine appearing. (p. 530) It is like what the Lord says: “There will be the gnashing of teeth.” “And that day is known to the Lord.” That is, such things will happen according to God's will, since it pleases him that these things should then come about in this way. It is like the saying, “The Lord knew those who are his,” meaning, he made them his own and considered them pleasing to himself. In the same way he calls the day known

to the Lord, as being pleasing to him, because such things happen on it according to his will, for the punishment of the enemies and the salvation of his own. Hence he adds: “And it will be neither day nor night, and toward evening there will be light.” For while the evils prevail, so great a darkness will be poured over everyone that there will be no difference between night and day, so completely will darkness take hold of everything; but after these things (this is what he means by “toward evening”) light will follow, that is, the divine help, since he does all those things to punish the enemies so that he may win his own people for himself. Accordingly he adds: Verses 8–11. “And on that day living water will go out from Jerusalem.” That is: then a pure and lawful priesthood will be carried out in Jerusalem, and a leadership pleasing to God, and teaching in accordance with the divine laws, which will benefit not only those of the nation at that time but also those who come after. By “the first sea” he means the people of that time, and by “the last” those who come after them. To this he has added, “In summer and in spring it will be so.” (p. 551) That is, at every season, through the divine care, the better things will prevail. And so, he says, over all the earth there will be a King, recognized and confessed to be the only God, the Maker and Lord of the universe; for through the very things he does he displays his care and his authority. And indeed all those on the earth (meaning those of the nation) will remain from then on freed from every error, calling on his name alone as God. Then he speaks of various places, wishing to say through them all that in every part belonging to our land God will continue to be known and worshiped, all error and impiety having been driven out from among us. With this knowledge, he says, all who belong to our nation will from then on dwell securely in Jerusalem, and there will no longer be anyone in the nation who delights in impiety or is estranged from God. This is what he means by “And there will be no more anathema.” For as blessed Paul says, “If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be anathema.” This, then, he says, will no longer exist, since there is no longer anyone estranged from God. Jerusalem will remain inhabited by all with great security, which it will have from the divine care because of its devotion to what is better. With these words he has brought to a close the prophecy about the Maccabees: what would happen at that time, the wrongs they themselves were going to commit, what their enemies would do to them, (p. 552) and also how great a care God would show them, giving his own support to those who stood for what is good. From here he takes up again what he had said before the announcement concerning the Maccabees, where, after speaking of the good things that would come to the nation through Zerubbabel, he added the destruction of Gog and his followers. Here again he takes up the announcement of these things, since they were going to happen soon, so that for events that were going to happen

much later in time, I mean the Maccabean events, what happened recently concerning Gog might serve as a pledge, and so that the prophet might bring his prophecy to a close with a more favorable announcement. He says, then: Verses 12–19. “And this will be the downfall with which the Lord will strike all the peoples who have campaigned against Jerusalem.” For they will prevail, he says, by the divine power over that nation, the greatest and most invincible, so that their flesh will melt away while they are still standing and they will not even be allowed to advance to battle, because God forestalls their attack through the punishment he brings upon them. Their power of sight will also be taken from them by the greatness of the evils that overtake them, and they will remain speechless in their bewilderment at what has happened. In short, he says, such a sudden frenzy will seize them by divine wrath that each one, turning his hand against his neighbor, will not even know it but will think he is attacking strangers, so that for the most part they become each other's work, and more of them fall struck by their own people than by the Jews. (p. 555) But while they are caught up in such evils, he says, Judah too will draw up for battle in Jerusalem; that is, it will go out confidently to war against them under the command of Zerubbabel, who by divine decision had been appointed their king from the tribe of Judah. And they will so overpower their enemies that they will take from them all their possessions, gold and silver and clothing and whatever good thing they might have with them, and increase their own wealth with all of it. This is what he meant by, “And he will gather the strength of all the peoples round about,” calling “their strength” the possessions from which they derived their power. Hence, to make this clear, he added, “gold and silver and clothing in very great abundance.” To these he adds that there will be great destruction of horses and mules and camels and donkeys and all the beasts belonging to them, as many as they had gathered and brought with them, thinking them somehow useful for the war. Such and so great, he says, will be their death and destruction. But those of them who survive, recognizing the power of God from what they have suffered, will make it a law among themselves to go up continually to Jerusalem to render to God the worship due to him, and also to celebrate the Feast of Tabernacles, since that season, being summer, is convenient for those who come from far away. And on many of those who out of contempt fail to do this I will bring punishment, condemning them to lack of rain and the resulting failure of crops, (p. [?]) so that they may realize that they are neglecting the honor due to the Lord of all. Whether it is the Egyptians, or anyone else at any time who adopts this attitude, they will pay the same penalty. What he means is that many foreigners, astonished at the greatness of what has happened, will stream to Jerusalem from many places, rendering to God the worship due to him, so that they even expect punishment if they do not do so. To these he adds: Verse 20. “On that day what is on the horse's bridle will be holy to the Lord Almighty; and the cauldrons in the house of the Lord will be like bowls before the altar.” He means that many things will be dedicated to God by the Israelites from the spoils that they

will take from their enemies, many and beyond counting, just as blessed David did after killing Goliath, when he dedicated the sword to God. He says the same here too: that they will then offer to God the horses' bridles that they took from the slain; for by the bridle, as by a part, he wished to mean the rest of the weapons and spoils that they were going to dedicate, each offering from the spoils whatever seemed good to him according to his own intention. Hence he adds that a great many cauldrons will also be brought, which the enemy had brought with them, thinking them useful for boiling meat, and which, because of their number, will be set out in the divine house like bowls. By the bridle he meant what is dedicated from the weapons, (p. 555) and by the cauldrons what is dedicated from the possessions, just as divine Scripture usually indicates most things by a part when it considers a detailed itemization superfluous. For here too it would have been superfluous to list spears and swords and breastplates, and cauldrons and the things in human use, such as plates, cups, or anything of that kind; but by the part, as I have already said and pointed out many times, he made clear that he meant the whole. Showing the use of the dedicated cauldrons, he adds: Verse 21. “And every cauldron in Jerusalem and in Judah will be holy to the Lord Almighty; and all who sacrifice will come and take from them and boil in them.” The cauldrons that have been brought, he says, will be holy, since they are henceforth dedicated to God; and as a result there will be abundance for those who bring sacrifices, since they will have something in which to boil the sacrifices and so do what is fitting. For does not divine Scripture say something like this in First Kingdoms, when it relates the lawlessness of the sons of Eli: that the priest's servant would come when the meat was being boiled, with a three-pronged fork in his hand, and thrust it into the cauldron, or the pot, or the kettle, and all that the fork brought up the priest took for himself? This, then, is what he meant: that from then on there will be an abundance of cauldrons for those who gather in Jerusalem for the service of God, in which they can meet their needs for the sacrifices. To these he adds: “And there will no longer be a Canaanite in the house of the Lord Almighty (p. 556) on that day.” Since the Canaanites were notorious for their way of life, both for impiety and for depravity of character, he means that from then on all the people of Israel will cease to incline toward impiety or any depravity of character, having been taught by events themselves how great a good is the pursuit of piety and virtue. So too blessed Hosea says: “Canaan, in his hand is a balance of injustice; he has loved to oppress. And Ephraim said, Yet I have become rich, I have found relief for myself.” By the name of Canaan he called the Israelites who did what they ought not, as having imitated their way of life

COMMENTARY ON MALACHI THE PROPHET. The blessed prophets Haggai and Zechariah prophesied by divine inspiration after the people's return from Babylon. Blessed Haggai spoke about the building of the temple and also announced the destruction of Gog and his followers. Blessed Zechariah says these things too, adding also what happened long afterward in the time of the Maccabees; and he sets out many different revelations, through which he showed the varied nature of God's kindness toward them and provided teaching fully able to lead them to a life of piety and diligence. (p. 557) But the Jews, though they had been granted divine providence and the return from Babylon, and had obtained a great many good things, and indeed had come to great prosperity, did not use their ease as they should: the priests on the one hand, and the whole people on the other, did wrong, so that they did not even perform the sacrifices prescribed by the law in the proper way. Necessarily, then, this present prophet, put forward for this purpose by divine inspiration, reproves the wrongs of both the priests and the people (what these were one can learn better from the writings themselves), and he also announces some things that are to come. The prophet's name in the Greek language is Angelos (“Messenger”), and in Hebrew Malachi, since it is customary among the Hebrews to call [?]; hence by translation into the Greek language he has been called Angelos instead of Malachi. He speaks as follows:

Verses 1–2. “The burden of the word of the Lord concerning Israel by the hand of his messenger.” That is, by divine inspiration the Messenger was entrusted with the work of prophecy to reprove Israel, since by this common name he intended to signify both the priests and the people; for all were commonly called Israelites. Then, after this customary heading of the prophetic books, the prophet begins his own words thus: “Lay it to your hearts.” Very well put, since they had neglected until now what they ought to have done. He now bids them consider carefully what is right, (p. 558) to take stock of what they were doing, and to examine how far they had departed from what was fitting, so that they might bring some correction to their own wrongs. Then, after the exhortation and admonition by which he was making them more attentive to their duty, he adds: “I have loved you, says the Lord.” He does well to speak of his love first of all to these ungrateful people, as though they were to be judged above all by this standard, being reproved for the baseness

of their own ways. “And you said, In what have you loved us?” Yet it was clear to everyone how many good things he had been the cause of for them, whether from those that existed earlier, or those that came often afterward, and indeed those that had happened recently. But it is the custom of divine Scripture to speak of a statement in place of an action, and to indicate by a statement the disposition of those who do something. For example: “They said, Who will see them?” instead of, they behaved as though no one were watching what was happening; for they did not actually say this. And: “For he said in his heart, I shall not be moved from generation to generation, without harm.” For they behaved, he means, as though they would never suffer any harm. One could cite many such examples, which it is not the moment to collect now. So here too he says, “And you said, In what have you loved us?” meaning: though you were loved by me and often well treated, you behaved with a wicked and ungrateful mind, as though you had neither been loved by me nor ever received any good thing. (p. 559) Then he states the facts from which they could see how great were the good things they had received compared with others. Verses 3–5. “Was not Esau Jacob's brother? says the Lord; yet I loved Jacob, but Esau I hated; and I made his borders a desolation and his inheritance dwellings of the wilderness. Because if Idumea says, It has been overthrown, but let us return and rebuild its desolate places, thus says the Lord Almighty: They will build, and I will overthrow; and they will be called borders of lawlessness, and a people against whom the Lord has set himself in array forever. And your eyes will see, and you will say, The Lord has been magnified beyond the borders of Israel.” The Idumeans had recently been punished and had experienced a great many evils for what they had done to the Israelites at the time when the Assyrians first, and afterward the Babylonians, came against them. These things had been foretold by blessed David in the Psalms, for he says: “Remember, O Lord, the sons of Edom on the day of Jerusalem, who said, Empty it, empty it, down to its foundations! O wretched daughter of Babylon!” In this he showed that the Babylonians would pay the penalty for the evils they had inflicted on them, and that the Idumeans too would be punished for having joined with them in the evils against the Israelites. Blessed Obadiah the prophet also foretold this afterward. But since those things had now come to pass, and the memory of the punishment that had come upon the Idumeans from God was fresh in everyone's mind, (p. 540) he fittingly shows his love for these people by comparing them with those, beginning from the forefathers of both these and the Idumeans; for Jacob was the forefather of these, and Esau of those. He says, then: Both were brothers; and though the law of nature made everything common to them, I loved

your forefather, but I hated theirs, Esau. And indeed I have continued until now to give proof of my love for you and my hatred for them. For I have laid waste their whole land for your sake, exacting from them the penalty for what they dared to do against you; and I have turned all their possessions into a desolation, which I brought upon them so great and so severe that even if they should ever change their minds and wish to set their affairs right and rebuild their desolate cities and lands, they could not do it at all. For I have decreed desolation against them, and it is in no way possible for their state to be restored; since even if they attempt to build, I will overthrow it again, so that they are given the name “Border of Lawlessness,” as having been laid waste because of their lawlessness. But for you I have resolved to do every good thing, so that you yourselves, having become spectators of the good things given to you, may recognize the power of God, who has made your circumstances shine with so many good things. Verse 6. (p. 541) Then, intensifying the charge: “A son honors his father, and a servant will fear his master. And if I am a father, where is my honor? And if I am Lord, where is my fear? says the Lord Almighty.” It is proper to sons, he says, to do such things as bring credit and dignity to their fathers, and to servants to carry out their masters' orders with great fear. I, he says, am your Lord, since I brought you from nonexistence into being; and out of surpassing kindness and goodness I made you my own and accepted you to be called my sons, and I have granted you the freedom to call me your Father. But I see you showing gratitude in neither respect: you have not been eager to honor me as a father by the nobility of your conduct, nor do you fear me as Master and pay heed to my commands. Having thus made the reproof common to all, he distinguishes both the persons and the deeds, and addressing the priests he says: “You, the priests, who despise my name.” You, he says, who have been entrusted with the divine service and ought to be guides to the rest toward better things, do such things that you make me appear worthless to those who see what you do. “And you said, In what have we despised your name?” Here too he says “you said” in the same way, meaning: through great heedlessness you have no awareness even of so great a wrong, but you behave as though you were doing nothing improper, even though you are doing so great an evil. Verse 7. Then he states what was being done: “Bringing to the altar polluted loaves.” For you do not set out the loaves with care according to the teaching of the law or the ordinances of Moses, (p. 542) but taking common loaves made any which way, contrary to what was prescribed, you place them on the table. By “polluted” he means leavened, which was plainly contrary to the law, which commanded that the loaves brought to the altar be unleavened and in no way leavened. [?]

[?] For every sacrifice, it says, that you offer to the Lord you shall not make leavened. Since this was so clearly prescribed, offering the loaves leavened went against it, and so he rightly accuses them of plainly doing the opposite of what the law commands. “And you said, ‘How have we polluted them?’” Even while you do this, he says, you will not stop to consider how wrong it is. For here again “and you said” refers to their state of mind. He means: you behave as though you were doing nothing, and you commit so great an offense out of insensibility and inattention. “By saying, ‘The table of the Lord is contemptible, and you have despised what is set upon it.’” Here again he uses “by saying” in this way, pointing to their state of mind in place of an act. What he means is this: your doing these things shows that you have nothing else in mind and no other attitude than that my table deserves no care at all, and so, necessarily, that nothing set upon it is worth any regard. (p. 545) This is shown by the careless way you set out the loaves, without caring whether it is done according to the ordinance of the law. He mentioned the loaves first, as the first sin, because the loaves set out on the table ought to have received the greatest care, since in a way they were offered on behalf of the whole people. For God commanded that they be six in number, with two tribes represented in each, so that the twelve tribes would be counted in the six. It was on their behalf that he commanded the loaves to be set out. Verses 8, 9. — Next he adds another offense of theirs as well: “For if you bring a blind animal for sacrifice, it is no evil; and if you bring a lame or sick one, it is no evil.” He says: you think you are not sinning when you offer such things to God in sacrifice. And to show how wrong this is: “Bring it, then, to your governor; will he accept it, will he show you favor? says the Lord Almighty.” If you cannot see for yourself how wrong this is, try bringing it to the one who has been entrusted with ruling over you. See whether he will accept it, and whether out of respect for you he will put up with the insult. Will he not rather do the opposite? Feeling insulted by you rather than honored, he will insult you in return and send you away with your gift, such as it is. Having shown both of their wrongs, the one concerning the loaves and the one concerning the victims, he adds: “And now appease the face of your God and entreat him, (p. 5M [?]) that he may have mercy on you.” But now, at least from here on, correct your former sins. Stop doing such things, and ask God for pardon for what is past as well. And fittingly he frightens them: “These things have happened at your hands.” For you have experienced these evils at close hand. Not long ago you fell into them through neglect of your duty, and remembering them should above all lead you to take every care for what is good. “Shall I show you favor? says the Lord Almighty.” From this you ought to know that I will not show you regard now either when you sin, unless you bring some correction through repentance to the offenses you have committed.

Verses 10–12. — “For among you too the doors will be shut, and you shall not kindle my altar for nothing.” For it is not hard for me even now to bar you from my temple and once again stop you from serving at my altar, since you do such things. In fact I have already done this. I gave the temple over to fire, because I saw you committing incurable offenses in it, and I handed you over to captivity, where you were unable to do anything that belongs to the priestly ministry. “I take no pleasure in you, says the Lord Almighty, and I will not accept a sacrifice from your hands.” For know well that as long as you do such things, I turn away from what you do and do not accept your sacrifices. So you will not even carry off the benefit (p. 545) in hope of which you make the offering of the sacrifices. “For from the rising of the sun to its setting my name has been glorified among the nations, and in every place incense is offered to my name, and a pure sacrifice; for my name is great among the nations, says the Lord Almighty.” Everywhere on earth, he says, all people, wherever they live, pursue my name. Each of them is eager to worship God and to honor his name as Master and Lord, and that is what I truly am. So even if in their error they give my name to those it does not belong to, still it is my name that all of them honor, and in my name they perform their sacrifices, since they consider the Divine the greatest of all and above all. But you are clearly insulting what all others regard as so great and venerable. You treat my table as common and no better than any other. You think what is set upon it deserves no care, and you offer me such things. So you plainly insult my name and are shown to hold in no regard the Divine, which all people consider so great and awesome and venerable, and rightly above all things. Verses 13, 14. — “And you said, ‘These things come from hardship’; and I snorted at them, says the Lord Almighty.” So you pride yourselves, he says, on offering things that come from your own toil and sweat and hardship. (p. 546) But I have cast them away, seeing how much contempt you show in your offering. “And you bring in what was taken by robbery, and the lame, and the sickly, and you offer them in sacrifice. Shall I accept them from your hands? says the Lord Almighty.” And since you bring such things in your sacrifices, I rejected them all the more as worthless and offered from a worthless intention. Then he also lays down a law: “And cursed is the one who was able, and had a male in his flock, and his vow was upon it, and yet sacrifices a blemished animal to the Lord; for I am a great king, says the Lord Almighty, and my name is renowned among the nations.” Everyone, he says, who has vowed a sacrifice, and then, though well off and able to bring from his own flocks a male and sound [?] animal

of the kind that is fitting to offer to God, does not bring it, but sacrifices to God something worthless and blemished, deserves the utmost punishment. For to God, who reigns over all and is known among all people alike for the greatness of his nature, this man, though well supplied with what is needed, brings offerings that are not of that kind.

Verses 1, 2. — “And now this commandment is for you, O priests. If you do not listen, and if you do not take it to heart to give glory to my name, says the Lord Almighty, I will send the curse upon you, and I will curse your blessing; I will curse it, and I will scatter your blessing, and it shall not be among you, because you do not take it to heart.” (p. 547) See, this is my verdict on you who are appointed to the priestly ministry. If not even now you are willing to pay careful attention to what I say, and by caring for the ministry to give God the glory that is fitting and due, I will bring the greatest punishment upon you. I will turn this honor which you now enjoy into dishonor and the experience of evils, and I will take away all your priestly honor, so that none of you will any longer inherit this dignity. It is clear that by “curse” he means punishment and the experience of evils, and by “blessing” the enjoyment of good things. That is why he gives the priesthood this name, since it is a cause of many good things both to those who hold it and to those on whose behalf it is exercised. Verses 3, 4. — Then, to show his indignation even more: “Behold, I set apart the shoulder for you, and I will scatter the maw upon your faces, and I will take you together.” It was commanded in the law that the shoulder be set apart from the sacrifices for God as a special portion. No longer, he says, will I accept even this from you. I need nothing; I ordained it this way for your benefit. But you show neglect toward me in so many things, and yet you think you honor me by setting apart the shoulder for me. So I turn it back to you, as proof of my indignation. I will let you enjoy this too, together with the dung of the animals, since it is fitting that this be brought to you at your feasts, (p. 548) which you defile by the wickedness of your deeds. And I will bring upon all of you together the punishment for what you have done. For this is what “I will take you together” means. “And you shall know that I, the Lord, have sent this commandment to you, that my covenant might be with the Levites, says the Lord Almighty.” Then, from the dishonor and punishment that will come upon you, you will clearly perceive my authority and my power. You will see that I, wishing to do you good, raised you from the beginning to the priestly dignity, and made with you terms like these: that while enjoying the honor I gave you, you would do everything for the benefit of those on whose behalf you exercise the priesthood. But you took no account of any of these things.

Instead you disdained the honor given to you and handed my ministry over to such great neglect. Verses 5–7. — Then, since the priesthood began with Aaron, who was the first to be appointed high priest by divine choice, he adds: “My covenant of life and peace was with him; and I gave him fear, so that he feared me and stood in awe before my name. The law of truth was in his mouth, and no wrong was found on his lips. He walked with me in peace and uprightness, and turned many away from wrongdoing. For the lips of a priest will guard knowledge, and people will seek the law from his mouth, (p. 549) for he is the messenger of the Lord Almighty.” He says: him I chose first and made terms with him. I promised him the enjoyment of long life and peace, and I commanded him to keep the fear of me in his mind and to remember me with great awe. And his conduct in turn was worthy of the honor I gave him. He made it a law for himself to live in truth and to turn away from all falsehood. He never uttered anything unjust, nor anything that harmed those under the priesthood. In return for these things, as I had promised, he lived in peace, never at odds with me in anything and never doing anything contrary to me. That is the meaning of “he walked with me in peace and uprightness.” He also brought many back from worse to better. In short, he did what is most fitting for a priest: he taught the knowledge of the truth, led all those under him back to the divine law, and taught them how they might always be occupied with it. For this is the work of a priest: to hold the rank of an angel, as it were, set over the rest of humankind and leading all back to virtue, which is the very work the angels do for us. These were the terms I made with Aaron, (p. 550) and he acted in keeping with my laws. But you who have succeeded to his priesthood are very far removed from these things. How, and in what way? Verses 8–10. — “But you have turned aside from the way, and you have caused many to stumble in the law; you have corrupted the covenant of Levi, says the Lord Almighty.” For you turned away from zeal for these things, and so made the rest careless about the law as well. And so, in short, by your own wickedness you corrupted all the terms I made with him, which I wanted to remain in force for his successors too. “And I have made you despised and cast off among all the nations, because you did not keep my ways but showed partiality in the law.” He rightly corrects them by reminding them of what had happened shortly before. For finding you doing such things, he says, I handed you over to captivity. I made you count for nothing and put you wholly outside the priestly honor, because you would not take any account of my commands, and you helped the rest to neglect the laws, though it was your duty to correct them. For this is what

“you showed partiality in the law” means. It is as if to say: you would not reprove those who sin against what the law decrees. “Did not one God create you? Is there not one Father of all of you? Why then has each of you forsaken his brother, profaning the covenant of your fathers?” And yet, he says, both you and he (he means Aaron) (p. 551) came from the one God and were judged worthy of the same care and honor. For I spoke to you too, in common with him: “I said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High.” This is especially fitting for those who have taken up the priestly office and from it lead the people. Where, then, did you acquire such corruption in your ways? He set right those of his own time and zealously brought them back to what was required. But you overlook those under the priesthood, who are your own brothers, when they sin in this way and all but trample on the strictness of my laws. So what

happened? Verses 11, 12. — “Judah has been forsaken, and an abomination has been committed in Israel and in Jerusalem; for Judah has profaned the holy things of the Lord, which he loved, and has pursued foreign gods.” So then, since the people too did what they should not, and you priests took no thought for correcting them, you were abandoned by my providence and went off into captivity. This happened because you neglected the service of God, which above all you ought to have pursued with great zeal, and turned aside to the service of idols. In this way he extends the discourse from the priests to everyone, since it was through the priests' wickedness that the rest also became like this. Then, for the correction of all alike, he adds [?]: “The Lord will utterly destroy the man who does these things, until he is brought low, from the tents of Jacob and from among those who offer sacrifice to the Lord Almighty.” (p. 552) But if you do not turn away from these things, he says, utter destruction will overtake all of you. The rest will be brought to the lowest humiliation, and so will you who pretend to act as priests and to offer sacrifices on behalf of others, since neither you nor they can gain anything from the offering of the sacrifices. From here he moves on to another of their transgressions. For when they had returned from captivity and shared in the prosperity God had granted them, they turned to a licentious life and divorced their former wives, casting their eyes on other women however they could. They shamelessly cast off the wives who had lived with them for a long time and had even shared with them the evils of the captivity and the hardships there, and out of licentiousness they turned to other women. Then, since the wives received no help from anyone in their ill-treatment, and no one rebuked what was happening, the women, unable to bear the outrage and dishonor, could only run to God with many tears and much lamenting, asking to receive God's providence, since they had no one else to help them. It is about these things that he speaks as follows:

Verse 13. — “And these things, which I hated, you did: you covered the altar of the Lord with tears, with weeping and groaning from troubles. Is it still worth regarding your sacrifice, or receiving anything acceptable from your hands?” “You covered the altar of the Lord with tears, (p. 555) with weeping and groaning.” He is not speaking to those who were lamenting but to those who caused it. He would not blame the women for running to God and lamenting the evils that had befallen them, since such great necessity and abuse forced them to do so. Clearly he rightly reproaches those who did the wrong and caused such lamenting and tears. So “you covered” means “you caused it to be covered.” You did this, he says, which I forbade above all things and which plainly deserved great hatred. To this he fittingly added: “Is it still worth regarding your sacrifice, or receiving anything acceptable from your hands?” For how, he says, is it even possible for me to accept a sacrifice or anything else you bring, when your wives have come before me with such weeping and such lamentations over the many injustices and outrages they suffer from you? It is not fitting for me to overlook them. So even if I were to overlook your offenses against me, I will certainly not overlook the wrongs done to your wives. This is like what the Lord says in the Gospels: “If you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go; first be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.” [?] For just as there he says the offering is useless unless amends are first made to the one who was wronged, so here too he says that it is not possible for me to accept anything you offer while the women have been so wronged by you [?]

Verses 14, 15. — “And you said, ‘Why?’” Here again he uses “you said” in the same way, meaning: you commit so great an evil as though you were doing nothing at all, so careless is your attitude in so great a transgression. Then, to show how wrong this is, he adds: “Because the Lord bore witness between you and the wife of your youth, whom you have forsaken, though she is your companion and the wife of your covenant. And no other made her, and the remnant of your spirit.” For I, he says, from the beginning, from the first creation, ordained that a man should leave father and mother and cleave to his own wife, so that the two would be one flesh. But you have so neglected my laws that you send away for no reason at all the woman who was joined to you in marriage from your youth and became your life's companion, and you drive her out of her own home. Yet with her you have such covenants through the laws of marriage, that you should be one

flesh and consider what belongs to each of you as common to both. Then you left the woman who was joined to you on such terms and went after another out of licentiousness. You did not even consider that marriage was established for the continuation of the race, (p. 55? [?]) so that the race, which is being destroyed by death, may be preserved through the begetting of children. Marriage, then, was devised by God as a means of continuing the line. This is what “the remnant of your spirit” means, that is: since you are going to lay down the life of this present world, as in “His spirit will go forth and he will return to his dust,” God has left you descendants as a memorial and a remnant of your own being, so that you might not seem to perish entirely. So, looking to the purpose of marriage, you ought to have feared to do this, and not to offend against the laws that God laid down about it from the beginning. You should have kept those laws intact by remaining with your first wives, whom you married in this way and on these terms, instead of sending away your first wives out of licentiousness and moving on to others. And most admirably he added: “And you said, ‘What else does God seek but offspring?’” Since they thought they could beget children just as well from the women they had unlawfully joined themselves to, he says: you do not respect the laws God laid down about marriage as divine laws. Rather, as if you were like irrational beasts, given over only to mating and breeding and made by God for this purpose, you send away your former wives and go to others, thinking it makes no difference whether you beget children from the one or from the other. You ought to know that indifference about one's line befits irrational animals, (p. 556) but those who share in reason should both enter into marriage in accordance with the divine laws and cherish the offspring that come from it. For here too “you said” does not mean that they spoke aloud, since they could not have actually said this, that God seeks nothing else but offspring. He uses it to describe the wicked disposition of their minds, and to show that they did everything in this way, not as rational human beings who ought to live by divine laws, but as if, like irrational beasts, they were given over only to mating and breeding. Then he also lays down a law: “And guard yourselves in your spirit, and do not forsake the wife of your youth.” Therefore, from now on take every care to [?] with your wives in the fitting disposition [?]. [?] iii, 7; Wis. xii, 1 [?].

…or to fall into daily quarrels with her, in case the long passage of time should bring about something even worse, and perhaps even arm him to murder his wife. This is how the Lord too, in the Gospels, answered the Pharisees when they asked, “Why then did Moses give a certificate of divorce?” He replied, “Because of your hardness of heart Moses allowed this, but from the beginning it was not so. For he who made them from the beginning made them male and female, and said, ‘For this reason a man will leave his father and his mother and be joined to his wife, and the two will become one flesh.’” What he means is this: the best course, according to the original law, was for husband and wife to remain together with each other as is fitting. But [?] seeing that your tempers are uncontrollable, he commanded that if the causes arising among you seemed to provoke some anger, you should rather put away your wife than be led by hatred into plotting murder. Then, since it was possible for a man whose wife gave him no cause to invent for himself an unjust hatred out of his inclination toward another woman, he says, “Ungodliness will uncover your thoughts, says the Lord Almighty.” For if, when matters are not so, you invent a cause and send away the wives joined to you from the beginning, God is the examiner of your ungodliness. To this he fittingly added, “And take heed in your spirit, and do not forsake the covenant.” That is, he says, keep the law of marriage with your whole mind and with a fitting disposition and due goodwill, and keep inviolate the covenants with those with whom you first entered into the partnership of marriage.

Verse 17. Having concluded what concerns wives with these words, he speaks of another offence of theirs as well, which is not merely a fault but ungodliness. For many people are unwilling to see their own sins, and will not even accept suffering anything for them; on the contrary, they are indignant when they meet with painful experiences, and that often while suffering less than they deserve. Yet on account of others they readily find fault with God, as though those others sin a great deal but are not punished. This was then happening among some of the Israelites, and the prophet, censuring it, speaks as follows: “You who provoke God with your words. And you said, ‘In what have we provoked him?’ In your saying, ‘Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord, and he himself is well pleased with them; and where is the God of justice?’” That is: I will not pass over that ungodliness of yours either, by which you rouse God to indignation against yourselves without perceiving it. For in “And you said, ‘In what have we provoked him?’” he is here too blaming their disposition, since they had no perception even that they were committing ungodliness in such matters. And showing what the ungodliness was, he says: You say that God seems to be pleased with those who do evil, and that this is clear from the fact that people pay no penalty for such offences; and yet, if God had any regard for justice, he would fittingly have subjected them to the ultimate punishment. What then?

Verse 1. “Behold, I will send out my angel, and he will survey the way before my face; and suddenly the Lord whom you seek will come to his temple, and the angel of the covenant whom you desire.” Since then you say such things, and seek from me concern for justice by way of punishment, I will send an angel to serve what I decide. For this is what “He will survey the way before my face” means: that is, he will be eager, like a forerunner, to carry out what I decide; and I too will be present in him all at once, showing myself by my deeds in the temple. For indeed in all that happens by God's decree, the service is understood to belong to the angels, but it is God who works in them through what he commands to be done. So too he speaks of the food of manna as belonging to angels, inasmuch as they ministered it—“For man ate the bread of angels”—but as belonging to God, inasmuch as he commanded it to be given: “For he commanded the clouds above, and opened the doors of heaven, and rained down manna upon them to eat.” He says “he will come” in his customary way, as though God shows himself to be the cause of what is accomplished in the things done through the angel's ministry. Such too is blessed David's saying, “He bowed the heavens and came down, and thick darkness was under his feet,” meaning: when he came to our help, we perceived it from his deeds. Hence, having said, “The Lord whom you sought will come to his temple,” he added, “and the angel of the covenant whom you desire,” showing that God will display his own presence in the things done through the angel's ministry. So I will come, he says, I whom you seek as the avenger of offences; and the angel will also be present who ministered the covenants I have often made with you. Seeking him, you will find him punishing your transgression of your covenants with me. These things the prophet said in keeping with what he had said before. But it is not surprising that this saying was applied to the coming of blessed John the Baptist, since the events then proved the saying true: blessed John came as forerunner and servant of what had been decreed, and together with him the Lord Christ, to whom he bore witness, appeared present, in whom the [?] of all people was to be accomplished

[?] seems to be ignorant of the difference between what is written here and what was accomplished at the coming of the Lord Christ. Even though he, like a judge, separated the wicked from the better among the Jews, bringing those who believed in him to a better state and handing over the unbelieving to punishment, it is nevertheless obvious that the aim of his coming was the common good of all, which blessed John made plain when he said, “Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world.” And what follows shows the aim of the words still more clearly. For he adds:
